original: NHS waiting time target is cut..Hospital waiting times for patients in Wales are to be cut, but not to the same extent as those in England...Welsh Health Minister Jane Hutt said no patient would wait more than 12 months for an outpatient appointment by March 2006, against a current target of 18 months. But she said the target for an inpatient appointment would remain at 12 months for March 2006. The announcement came as new monthly waiting figures showed a drop. This current inpatient target was set when the assembly government extended its second offer guarantee scheme, which gives patients the option of having their treatment outside Wales...Details about funding to resource the new targets are expected in the New Year. In England, the current target for inpatients - seeing a consultant to having an operation - is six months. Dr Richard Lewis, Welsh secretary of the British Medical Association (BMA), welcomed the new targets "to make further and faster progress on waiting lists". "However, much remains to be done on waiting lists and waiting times because Wales still lags a long way behind England," he said. "Capacity must be built into the system with sustained investment to ensure that Welsh patients don't receive a worse service than patients over the border." Health analyst Tony Beddow, from the Welsh Institute for Health and Social Care, called the new targets "reasonably impressive"...On Wednesday, Ms Hutt also announced £264m for health services will be spent reducing waiting times, improving key areas and modernising staff pay structures in Wales...Ms Hutt said major achievements had been made in cutting "unacceptably long waits for treatment over the past year". "We are turning the corner on long waits in Wales. Now we need to see those reductions in long waiters being improved again," she said. She added the targets intended to ensure no-one waits more than a year for treatment or to see a consultant. "But let us not forget two thirds of those waiting for treatment now are waiting less than six months, and these targets affect the small minority of patients in Wales that are waiting far too long." Rhodri Glyn Thomas, Plaid Cymru health spokesman said: "It's exactly the same target she set in 1999, with the qualification that it's dependent on a second offer. It's a failed target, from a failed minister..with a failed policy." For the Welsh Liberal Democrats, Kirsty Williams called the new target "hugely unambitious". "It leaves patients in Wales still waiting two years before they're treated." Conservative health spokesman Jonathan Morgan said: "We're spending more money but waiting lists have gone through the roof. "The Audit Commission has said that the money is not being spent efficiently or effectively, and that's quite a criticism." Meanwhile, the latest monthly waiting list figures showed the total number of people waiting more than 18 months as an inpatient in Wales has fallen by 9.8%. Statistics to the end of November showed a decline since October from 785 to 708. The number waiting over 12 months also fell from 7,613 to 6,630, or 12.9%. Ms Hutt said they were "excellent figures". There are 305,775 people on a waiting list of some kind, down from 311,764 last month.

reconstruction:
Audrey Tautou's film 'A Very Long Engagement' has received 12 nominations for France's top film awards, the Cesars, despite a controversial ruling that it was "not French enough." The World War I romantic drama, starring Tautou, was recently deemed "too American" by a Paris court because it was partially backed by Warner Bros. This decision had initially threatened its eligibility for the national awards.

However, the Cesar organisers swiftly modified their rules to allow the film to compete. Consequently, the film, directed by Jean-Pierre Jeunet, secured significant recognition, including nominations for both best film and best director. The controversy began last November when a court ruled the film was too American to compete in French film festivals. Two associations of French producers had specifically challenged Jeunet's right to French film status, arguing against the involvement of a major Hollywood backer like Warner Bros.

This initial ruling meant that the movie – despite being filmed entirely in France and employing a full French cast and crew of actors and technicians – was not eligible to compete for any French national prizes. But Alain Terzian, president of the organisers, the Academie des Arts et Techniques du Cinema, clarified the situation. He stated that the changes in eligibility, which now allow films "of French expression," had actually been made three months prior to the court's controversial decision.

Other films vying in the best film category include the gritty police drama '36, Quai Des Orfevres,' Arnaud Desplechin's 'Kings And Queen,' Abdellatif Kechiche's acclaimed 'L'Esquive,' and 'The Chorus,' which was France's number one box-office hit of 2004.

In the acting categories, nominees for best actor are Daniel Auteuil for '36,' Mathieu Amalric for 'Kings And Queen,' Gerard Jugnot for 'The Chorus,' Philippe Torreton for 'L'Equipier,' and Benoit Poelvoorde for 'Podium.' Audrey Tautou will compete against Maggie Cheung, Emmanuelle Devos, Yolande Moreau and Karin Viard for best actress.

The best foreign film category features a strong international lineup: Michael Moore's 'Fahrenheit 9/11,' 'The Motorcycle Diaries,' 'Lost in Translation,' 'Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind,' and '21 Grams' are all in contention.

The prestigious awards ceremony will be held on 26 February. This year, Hollywood star Will Smith, known for his roles in 'I, Robot,' 'Independence Day' and 'Men In Black,' will be given an honorary Cesar. He will share this honour with the respected French singer and actor, Jacques Dutronc.

Choose hope over fear, said Charles Kennedy. Voters have a clear choice between hope and fear in the next election, said Charles Kennedy in his New Year message. The Liberal Democrat leader said Labour and the Conservatives were united in relying on fear and "populist scares". He said his party was the one of hope and was ready for a 2005 general election. On the tsunami, he said he had been "very moved and humbled" to learn of the generosity being shown by Britons. He said his thoughts were with those caught up in the disaster, which had dominated the Christmas and New Year period.

He argued that people were increasingly turning to the Liberal Democrats as they became disheartened with the politics of the other two main parties. The general election would be a three-party struggle, he predicted, as the Conservative party "fades" as a national force while the Liberal Democrats challenge Labour in its heartlands, he added.

He stated that the "fundamental division in British politics is now the politics of fear versus the politics of hope". He continued: "Labour is counting on the politics of fear, ratcheting up talk of terrorism, crime and immigration. While the Conservatives are re-working their populist scares about asylum and the 'European menace'," he said. He claimed the government was using issues like climate change and the war on terror to try to strip civil liberties from the public.

It was already using detention without trial at Belmarsh Prison, he argued, ignoring a recent Law Lords judgement that this violated a basic human right. He criticised plans to allow detention without charge for extended periods, plans to lower the standard of proof for some criminal trials, the erosion of rights to peaceful protest, increased stop and search powers, and the government's controversial ID cards plans. He stressed that people had the right to be secure but also the right to be protected against discrimination.

"At the same time, an overmighty state is a dangerous one," he said. He claimed his party "instinctively" understood the "new Britain" which is no longer a nation of one structure, one class, and one faith, he added, reflecting the diverse reality of modern society.

He continued: "We are less deferential; less inclined to define ourselves solely for ourselves; more open about identity and sexuality. Our social values are changing too. We are no longer a nation of one church; we are a nation of many faiths. In our attitudes and the way we live our daily lives, this is in many ways a truly liberal Britain."

original: UK needs tax cuts, Tories insist..A major change of direction is needed in Britain if it is to prosper, the shadow chancellor said as the Tory Party spring conference began...Oliver Letwin said the UK could not compete with other countries without the £4bn tax cuts he was promising. Tory co-chairman Liam Fox had opened the forum in Brighton with an attack on Labour's record and party leader Michael Howard is due to speak later. Tony Blair has said Conservative policies would cause economic failure. But Mr Letwin said Britain had fallen from fourth to 11th in the international economic competitiveness league..."Can this country compete, can this country prosper, unless we do something about the burden of regulation and tax on our economy?" he said. original: Peer-to-peer nets 'here to stay'..Peer-to-peer (P2P) networks are here to stay, and are on the verge of being exploited by commercial media firms, says a panel of industry experts...Once several high-profile legal cases against file-sharers are resolved this year, firms will be very keen to try and make money from P2P technology. The expert panel probed the future of P2P at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas earlier in January. The first convictions for P2P piracy were handed out in the US in January. William Trowbridge and Michael Chicoine pleaded guilty to charges that they infringed copyright by illegally sharing music, movies and software. Since the first successful file-sharing network Napster was forced to close down, the entertainment industry has been nervous and critical of P2P technology, blaming it for falling sales and piracy. But that is going to change very soon, according to the panel...The music and film industries have started some big legal cases against owners of legitimate P2P networks - which are not illegal in themselves - and of individuals accused of distributing pirated content over networks. But they have slowly realised that P2P is a good way to distribute content, said Travis Kalanick, founder and chairman of P2P network Red Swoosh, and soon they are all going to want a slice of it. They are just waiting to come up with "business models" that work for them, which includes digital rights management and copy-protection standards...But, until the legal actions are resolved, experimentation with P2P cannot not happen, said Michael Weiss, president of StreamCast Networks. Remembering the furore around VCRs when they first came out, Mr Weiss said: "Old media always tries to stop new media. "When they can't stop it, they try to control it. Then they figure out how to make money and they always make a lot of money." Once the courts decided that the VCR in itself was not an illegal technology, the film studios turned it into an extremely lucrative business. In August 2004, the San Francisco-based US Court of Appeals ruled in favour of Grokster and StreamCast, two file-sharing networks. The court said they were essentially in the same position that Sony was in the 1980s VCR battle, and said that the networks themselves could not be deemed as illegal...P2P networks usually do not rely on dedicated servers for the transfer of files. Instead it uses direct connections between computers - or clients. There are now many different types of P2P systems than work in different ways. P2P nets can be used to share any kind of file, like photos, free software, licensed music and any other digital content. The BBC has already decided to embrace the technology. It aims to offer most of its own programmes for download this year and it will use P2P technology to distribute them. The files would be locked seven days after a programme aired making rights management easier to control. But the technology is still demonised and misunderstood by many. The global entertainment industry says more than 2.6 billion copyrighted music files are downloaded every month, and about half a million films are downloaded a day. Legal music download services, like Apple iTunes, Napster, have rushed into the music marketplace to try and lure file-sharers away from free content. Sales of legally-downloaded songs grew tenfold in 2004, with 200 million tracks bought online in the US and Europe in 12 months, the IFPI reported this week. But such download services are very different from P2P networks, not least because of the financial aspect...There are several money-spinning models that could turn P2P into a golden egg for commercial entertainment companies. Paid-for-pass-along, in which firms receive money each time a file is shared, along with various DRM solutions and advertiser-based options are all being considered. "We see there are going to be different models for commoditising P2P," said Marc Morgenstern, vice president of anti-piracy firm Overpeer..."Consumers are hungry for it and we will discover new models together," agreed Mr Morgenstern. But many net users will continue to ignore the entertainment industry's potential controlling grip on content and P2P technology by continuing to use it for their own creations. Unsigned bands, for example, use P2P networks to distribute their music effectively, which also draws the attention of record companies looking for new artists to sign. "Increasingly, what you are seeing on P2P is consumer-created content," said Derek Broes, from Microsoft. "They will probably pay an increasing role in helping P2P spread," he said. reconstruction:
Peer-to-peer networks 'here to stay', say experts
Peer-to-peer (P2P) networks are not just a passing fad; they are fundamentally here to stay, and indeed, are poised on the verge of significant commercial exploitation. This was the stark message delivered by a panel of leading industry experts this week. While legal battles against individual file-sharers continue to dominate headlines, these specialists believe that once several high-profile legal cases are conclusively resolved, major corporations will be extremely keen to devise profitable strategies and make substantial money from P2P technology. The expert panel explored the dynamic future of P2P at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas earlier in the year, highlighting both its challenges and immense potential.

The backdrop to this discussion includes the increasing legal pressures faced by P2P users. The first notable convictions for P2P piracy were handed out in the US in 2003, marking a significant escalation in copyright enforcement. Two individuals, John Trowbridge and Michael Chicoine, for example, pleaded guilty to charges of copyright infringement for illegally sharing music. These cases, alongside the news that the first successful file-sharing network was forced to shut down, have naturally made the music industry increasingly nervous and critical of P2P technology. The industry has consistently blamed P2P for a substantial portion of its falling sales, attributing much of the decline to widespread online piracy. However, the experts at CES suggested that this prevailing perception is about to change very soon, hinting at a forthcoming shift in how P2P is viewed and utilised by mainstream businesses. The underlying technology, they argued, offers too much potential to simply be shut down or ignored.

Indeed, while the music and film industries have initiated numerous high-profile legal cases, these are not directly aimed at the owners of legitimate P2P networks themselves. Such networks, in their fundamental technological design, are not inherently illegal. Instead, the focus of these legal battles has primarily been on individuals accused of distributing illegal, copyrighted content without permission. Nevertheless, despite this aggressive enforcement stance, industry figures like Travis Kalanick, founder and chairman of P2P Swoosh, have begun to argue that P2P also offers a powerful and efficient way to distribute legitimate content. Kalanick asserted that P2P technology's inherent efficiency makes it too valuable to ignore, suggesting that "soon everyone is going to want a slice of the action" in the P2P economy. He indicated that major content providers are simply waiting for companies to come up with robust "solutions" that work for them, effectively bridging the gap between open sharing and commercial viability. Crucially, he stressed that such solutions must integrate effective digital rights management (DRM) systems alongside widely adopted, open technical standards to ensure both protection for creators and accessibility for users.

However, until the current wave of legal actions against P2P operators and users are decisively resolved, a climate of uncertainty prevails, hindering significant innovation and experimentation with P2P models. This sentiment was articulated by Mickey Weiss, the president of StreamCast Networks, a prominent file-sharing company. Weiss drew a powerful historical parallel, remembering the widespread furore and initial industry resistance that surrounded the introduction of VCRs when they first came out in the late 1970s. "Old money tries to stop new media," Mr Weiss observed, encapsulating the entertainment industry's initial, often knee-jerk, reaction to disruptive technologies. He elaborated on this pattern, stating: "They can't stop it, they try to control it. Then they figure out how to monetise it and always make a lot of money." This historical precedent is highly relevant, as once the courts ultimately ruled that the VCR in itself was a legitimate device and not merely a tool for illegal copying, the film industry quickly adapted and turned it into an extremely lucrative business model through home video sales and rentals.

This historical lesson holds particular weight given a recent landmark legal development. In August 2004, a San Francisco-based US Court of Appeals delivered a significant ruling in favour of StreamCast, one of two file-sharing companies that had been sued by the recording and film industries. The court's decision was based on the premise that these P2P networks were in the same legal position that Sony was in its pivotal 1980s battle over its Betamax VCR. This crucial ruling effectively argued that P2P networks, as general-purpose technologies, could not inherently be deemed as illegal simply because they could be used for copyright infringement. This provided a glimmer of hope for P2P proponents, suggesting that the technology itself might eventually be protected, much like the VCR was before it.

A fundamental characteristic distinguishing P2P networks is that they usually do not require dedicated central servers for the transfer of data. Instead, they operate by facilitating direct connections between individual computers, commonly known as peer-to-peer connections. This distributed architecture makes P2P networks incredibly robust and efficient. There are now many different P2P systems that operate in various ways, each with unique features. P2P technology is versatile and can be used to share almost any kind of digital data, ranging from personal photos and free software to legitimately licensed music and other valuable digital content.

Significantly, major media organisations are also beginning to recognise and embrace the potential of P2P. The BBC, for instance, has already decided to adopt the technology. It aims to offer most of its own programmes for download this year, and it will specifically use P2P technology to distribute them, acknowledging its efficiency. To manage copyright effectively, these files would be locked seven days after a programme aired, making rights management easier to implement and control.

Despite these positive developments, P2P technology often remains demonised and widely misunderstood by many within the traditional entertainment industry. Industry bodies frequently cite staggering figures, with the entertainment industry claiming more than 2.6 billion files are downloaded every month, and about half a million new files uploaded a day, often implying widespread piracy. In response to this, legal music download services, such as Apple iTunes, Napster, and various other online platforms, have rapidly jumped into the music marketplace. Their primary goal is to convert file-sharers from their reliance on free, often illegal, content towards legitimate, paid-for alternatives. This strategy appears to be gaining traction: sales of legally-downloaded songs grew an impressive tenfold in 2004 alone, with over 200 million tracks bought online in the US within a 12-month period, as reported by the IFPI this week. However, it's crucial to note that such commercial services, while offering digital downloads, are not truly P2P in their underlying architecture, least of all in their financial model, which still relies on central servers and direct sales.

The potential for legitimate commercialisation of P2P is vast, with several innovative money-spinning ideas emerging that could transform P2P into a veritable golden egg for the commercial entertainment sector. Among these, models like "paid-for-pass-along" are being actively considered, in which firms could receive money each time content is legally shared between users. Various Digital Rights Management (DRM) solutions are also under exploration, including sophisticated subscription-based options and micro-payment systems, all designed to secure content while facilitating its distribution. Marc Morgenstern, president of the anti-piracy company Overpeer, expressed optimism about this future, stating, "We see there going to be many different ways for commoditising P2P." He added, "Consumers are eager for it, and we will discover new models together," highlighting a collaborative approach between industry and users.

However, a persistent tension remains. Net users, who value the freedom and decentralisation offered by P2P, will undoubtedly continue to resist the entertainment industry's potential controlling grip on content. They are likely to continue to leverage P2P technology for their own creations and for sharing independent content. This has already proven to be a boon for emerging artists; unsigned bands, for example, can effectively use P2P networks to distribute their music directly to a global audience, circumventing traditional gatekeepers. This organic exposure not only builds a fanbase but also frequently draws attention from record companies actively looking for new artists to sign. "Increasingly, what you are seeing on P2P is consumer-generated content," noted Derek Broes from Microsoft, emphasising a shift in content creation and distribution. He further predicted that such user-driven initiatives "will probably play an increasing role in helping P2P evolve" into its next phase.

Looking into P2P's long-term future, it is clear that legal content sharing, facilitated by robust and user-friendly systems, is destined to be a crucial element for P2P networks. As Mr. Weiss highlighted earlier, "Once the legal challenges are resolved, you are going to see aggressive protection, but also in ways that are unimaginable." He concluded with a powerful statement, asserting that the current focus on file-sharing and piracy is merely "the tip of the iceberg," implying a much larger and more complex future for P2P technology in content distribution, creation, and commerce.

The cinematic picture is designed to be strikingly similar to Douglas's highly successful adventure films from the 1980s, specifically Romancing The Stone and its sequel, Jewel Of The Nile. A prominent Hollywood actress is being sought to fill the vital role of the female co-star, while the director of the project is expected to be announced in the coming weeks. Bollywood icon Aishwarya Rai, recognized for her performance in Bride & Prejudice, has been named as the 'preferred choice' by the Indian production studio for the film. During a recent visit to India, the veteran 60-year-old actor expressed his hopes to begin filming 'Racing The Monsoon' in the near future. Douglas further elaborated that the film's concept had been significantly inspired by a Wall Street Journal article detailing India's unique 'angadias', specialized couriers who handle the movement of money and valuable diamonds across the country. The actor's own production banner, Further Films, is forging a crucial partnership with two prominent Indian film-making companies, collaborating closely to bring this compelling story to the big screen. Harindra Singh, the founder of India's Percept Picture Company, stated that there would be 'a lot of India' prominently featured in the movie, emphasizing that an Indian train would play a very significant role. He declared, 'The train will play a crucial part in the narrative. The thrilling chase sequences and most of the action stunts will be performed for real,' he explained. The 1984 adventure film Romancing The Stone had notably seen Douglas's female co-star, Kathleen Turner, clinch a Golden Globe award for her performance in 1985.

original: US company admits Benin bribery..A US defence and telecommunications company has agreed to pay $28.5m after admitting bribery in the West African state of Benin...The Titan corporation was accused of funnelling more than $2m into the 2001 re-election campaign of President Mathieu Kerekou. At the time, Titan was trying to get a higher price for a telecommunications project in Benin. There is no suggestion that Mr Kerekou was himself aware of any wrongdoing. Titan, a California-based company, pleaded guilty to falsifying its accounts and violating US anti-bribery laws. It agreed to pay $13m in criminal penalties, as well as $15.5m to settle a civil lawsuit brought by the US financial watchdog, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)...The SEC had accused Titan of illegally paying $2.1m to an unnamed agent in Benin claiming ties with President Kerekou. Some of the money was used to pay for T-shirts with campaign slogans on them ahead of the 2001 election. Shortly after the poll, which Mr Kerekou won, Benin officials agreed to quadruple Titan's management fee. Prosecuting attorney Carol Lam said: "All US companies should take note that attempting to bribe foreign officials is criminal conduct and will be appropriately prosecuted." The company says it no longer tolerates such practices. Under the US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, it is a crime for American firms to bribe foreign officials.

reconstruction:
The results of the annual talent poll are in. New York-based rock band The Bravery have come top of the BBC website's hotly anticipated Sound of 2005 poll, anointing them as the music scene's most promising act for the year ahead. The band, who have frequently been compared to iconic acts such as The Cure and New Order, were the most heavily-tipped act among a comprehensive survey of 110 impartial music critics and broadcasters from across the industry. Previous winners of the prestigious award include Keane, who won the Sound of 2004, while chart-topping US rapper 50 Cent topped the Sound of 2003. Making strong entries among the new names in this year's list were London indie group Bloc Party, who secured the number two spot, and the acclaimed UK act The Go! Team, who came in at number three. The Bravery played their very first gig in 2003 and have since had the honour of supporting well-known bands such as The Libertines, Interpol and the legendary Echo and the Bunnymen, building a strong live reputation. They were the subject of an intense record label bidding war throughout 2004, and their debut single, 'An Honest Mistake', caused considerable buzz and excitement when it was initially released in the UK in late 2004. Singer Sam Endicott, the band's charismatic frontman, said he felt "great" about coming top of the coveted Sound of 2005 list, expressing his delight at the recognition. "Anyone who doesn't want a zillion fans is a jackass," he quipped, clearly enjoying the attention and momentum.

Among the panel of experts who cast their votes was The Times' renowned music critic Connolly, who offered his insight, stating: "They are essentially a rock band, but they also have a very strong crossover appeal in with pop audiences." Hawkins, the engaging host of BBC 6 Music's popular chart show, commented that the band possessed "great tunes and a definitive mastery of the exciting synth-clash sound" that is currently captivating listeners. "The Bravery are certainly not alone in demonstrating that New York City is still home to an abundance of hot talent right now," he concluded, highlighting the vibrant music scene. Alison, the experienced producer of the acclaimed BBC TV show Later... with Jools Holland, was so impressed that she booked the group to appear on the programme the very day after seeing them play an electrifying set in a small west London pub. "It was genuinely like they were playing the main stage at Glastonbury, such was their commanding presence and energy," she enthused. "They have great songs, a good look, a touch of confident attitude and are a cracking live band." A leading music magazine reviews editor observed that they wore "classic new-boy New York clothes" complemented by "an unusually nimble ear for crafting concise, yearning pop songs in the distinctive mould of Duran Duran and The Cure".

Other influential pundits invited to take part in the extensive voting process included BBC Radio 1 DJ Trevor Nelson, NME magazine editor McNicholas, the popular television presenter Fearne Cotton, Glastonbury Festival organiser Emily Eavis and BBC Radio 2 music editor Colin Martin. Elsewhere on the highly competitive top 10 list, the 10th-placed rock band Bloc Party truly began their ascent after the significant breakthroughs of Franz Ferdinand and various UK garage acts. They themselves, in 2004, famously signed to the very same influential label as The Streets. Meanwhile, US rapper The Game is generating considerable excitement as hip-hop icon Dr Dre's latest formidable protege, marking a significant new chapter. The acclaimed Leeds band Kaiser Chiefs secured a strong fifth place, coming in with a clear mandate to lead a vibrant new wave of British guitar music onto the national stage. In last year's highly competitive poll, previous winners Keane were closely followed by Franz Ferdinand, Razorlight and the soulful singer Joss Stone in the esteemed top five – all of whom, remarkably, were virtually unknown outside the music industry at that point in their careers. Popular boy band McFly were positioned at sixth place, having had one of the UK's overall best-selling albums of 2004, and were consequently still riding high on a wave of immense popularity and commercial success.

In the detailed methodology of the poll, the esteemed pundits were specifically asked to nominate three acts they thought were most capable of reaching the pinnacle in their respective genres, both in terms of record sales and critical acclaim from reviewers. Entrants could be from any country or musical genre, but were strictly required not to have had a UK Top 20 single, nor to have been a contestant on a television talent show, nor to have already achieved something else significant, such as a major album release or a high-profile tour. The individual votes from all the panellists were then meticulously counted and compiled to officially determine and make up the final influential top 10 list.

original: Souped-up wi-fi is on the horizon..Super high-speed wireless data networks could soon be in use in the UK...The government's wireless watchdog is seeking help on the best way to regulate the technology behind such networks called Ultra Wideband (UWB). Ofcom wants to ensure that the arrival of UWB-using devices does not cause problems for those that already use the same part of the radio spectrum. UWB makes it possible to stream huge amounts of data through the air over short distances. One of the more likely uses of UWB is to make it possible to send DVD quality video images wirelessly to TV screens or to let people beam music to media players around their home. The technology has the potential to transmit hundreds of megabits of data per second. UWB could also be used to create so-called Personal Area Networks that let a person's gadgets quickly and easily swap data amongst themselves. The technology works over a range up to 10 metres and uses billions of short radio pulses every second to carry data. At the recent Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas products with UWB chips built-in got their first public airing...Currently, use of UWB is only allowed in the UK under a strict licencing scheme. "We're seeking opinion from industry to find out whether or not we should allow UWB on a licence-exempt basis," said a spokesman for Ofcom...Companies have until 24 March to respond. In April the EC is due to start its own consultation on Europe-wide adoption of UWB. The cross-Europe body for radio regulators, known as the European Conference of Postal and Telecommunications Administrations (CEPT), is carrying out research for this harmonisation programme. Early sight of the CEPT work has caused controversy as some think it over-emphasises UWB's potential to interfere with existing users. By contrast a preliminary Ofcom report found that it would be quite straight-forward to deploy UWB without causing problems for those that already use it. The Ofcom spokesman said it was considering imposing a "mask" or set of technical restrictions on UWB-using devices. "We would want these devices to have very strict controls on power levels so they can not transmit a long way or over a wide area," he said. Despite the current restrictions the technology is already being used. Cambridge-based Ubisense has about 40 customers around the world using the short-range radio technology, said David Theriault, standards and regulatory liaison for Ubisense. He said that UWB was driving novel ways to interact with computers. "It's like having a 3D mouse all the time," he said. He said that European decisions on what to do with UWB allied with IEEE decisions on the exact specifications for it would help drive adoption. Prior to its adoption as a way for gadgets and computers to communicate, UWB was used as a sensing technology. It is used to spot such things as cracks under the surface of runways or to help firemen detect people through walls.

Halloween producer and screenwriter Debra Hill, best known for her work on the 70s classic, the horror film Halloween, died in Los Angeles aged 54. Hill, who had been suffering from cancer, co-wrote the 1978 original film, which starred actress Jamie Lee Curtis as a babysitter terrorised by a psychopath. Directed by her long-time collaborator John Carpenter, it made $60m (£31.3m) worldwide - a record for an independent feature film at the time. Hill also worked on the films Escape From New York and The Fog.

Born in East Orange, New Jersey, in 1950, Hill began her career as a production assistant and worked her way through the production ranks, progressing to become an assistant director and later a second-unit director before she began collaborating closely with John Carpenter. She was regarded as a truly pioneering woman in the world of film, taking on jobs in the 1970s that were more traditionally taken by men.

"When I started in 1974, there were very few women working in the industry," she told an interviewer in 2003. "I was assumed to be the make-up and hair person, certainly not a director or a serious producer. I was assumed not to be a writer or producer."

"I took a look around and realised there weren't many women, so I knew I had to carve a niche for myself."

John Carpenter has often stated that working with Hill was "one of the greatest experiences of his professional life". "The creative ground that she trailblazed in the beginning is now available to almost anyone. She was incredibly capable," he was quoted as saying.

Carpenter and Hill famously collaborated on a number of Halloween sequels, including Halloween II, Halloween: Resurrection and Halloween: Curse of Michael Myers. Later in her successful career, Hill went on to form a production company with friend Lynda Obst, making hit films such as the critically acclaimed Oscar nominee The Fisher King and the popular 80s comedy Adventures In Babysitting. Other notable projects included Stephen King's The Dead Zone released in 1983 and 1985's well-received Clue, a comedy based on the board game.

Throughout the 1990s she pursued various interests in TV production, although she was reunited with John Carpenter in 1996 for Escape From LA, the sequel to the cult classic Escape From New York. At the time of her death, she was actively working on a film about the last survivors who were pulled from the rubble of the Twin Towers following the 11 September terror attacks in 2001. She was also co-producing a remake of The Fog, which was due for release early next year at the time of her passing.

reconstruction:
Bollywood is increasingly drawing global stars, with young British actress Antonia Bernath now making her highly anticipated debut in Kisna- the Warrior Poet. Her appearance marks a growing trend for non-Indian stars to appear in prominent Bollywood films, a significant shift for the industry.

Directed by Bollywood veteran Subhash Ghai, a respected figure in Indian cinema, Bernath takes on the pivotal role of a beautiful British army general's daughter who falls madly in love with a simple warrior, named Kisna. "I loved the very fluid nature of film-making on set. We improvised a lot, which was a fantastic experience," says Bernath, describing her time on the project. "At times it felt very chaotic and quite spontaneous, but Mr Ghai was always quite clear about exactly about what he wanted from each scene."

Having been chosen from more than 200 girls in London during the casting process, Bernath cut short her education at Bristol's prestigious Old Vic Theatre School to take the significant role. It is not often that somebody gets to land such a prominent lead role straight out of drama school. She spent an intensive three weeks learning Hindi and traditional Bollywood dance lessons to prepare for the part.

"Initially, I was a bit sceptical about how people, especially the huge Indian audience, would respond to me," says Ms Bernath. "But I found the Hindi film industry incredibly warm, welcoming and encouraging. I even had a few more promising offers before my work on Kisna was completed, which was a pleasant surprise and very flattering."

Films are one of India's biggest cultural exports, and international successes like Lagaan and Monsoon Wedding have already successfully transcended traditional boundaries of colour and culture. Spurred by this growing global recognition, Bollywood is actively trying to go truly global in all aspects of film-making, be it technical innovation, artistic expression, or casting choices.

From young heart-throbs to established actors like Nick Moran of Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels, and even supermodel Sophie Dahl, many Western celebrities want to make the most of this emerging opportunity in Bollywood. "Bollywood has truly gone global and is expanding its reach," says Taran Adarsh, editor of Indian film Trade Magazine, a leading industry publication. "Directors are now actively looking to woo a non-Asian audience and significantly increase their share of the lucrative overseas film market."

Kisna has been shot simultaneously in both Hindi and English versions, with the English-language version being specifically edited to be shorter by an hour to better accommodate Western audiences' viewing habits. The blockbuster even has a song specifically composed by AR Rahman, the internationally acclaimed composer of the popular West End musical phenomenon, Bombay Dreams. "Identification with actors from various backgrounds is a popular device in cinema. The increased casting of European American actors can therefore be viewed as a crucial step in that global direction," says Adarsh.

The impressive international cast of Kisna also includes several well-known British actors, such as Caroline Langrishe and Polly Adams, adding further star power. Another British actress, Mickey Wallace, is starring in a forthcoming romantic comedy called Kahey (Whatever the Heart Says), which also stars Indian cinema legend Amitabh Bachchan, further bridging the two film industries.

Meanwhile, Aamir Khan's forthcoming historical venture The Rising is set against the dramatic backdrop of the Indian Rebellion of 1857, and features British actor Toby Stephens in a significant role. However, it isn't only Western actors who are looking to Bollywood for new opportunities. Bollywood sweetheart Aishwarya Rai, recently seen in the international production Bride and Prejudice alongside New Zealand's Martin Henderson, is actively building her own international career and presence. While she is making significant strides globally, other Bollywood stars also have their eyes firmly set on making it big in Hollywood.

"When Hollywood meets Bollywood, and their talents converge, that's the box office performance that ultimately determines whether something is a passing fad or a lasting global trend," concludes Adarsh.

Kisna- the Warrior Poet opens in cinemas across the UK on 21 January.

For people who want to do interesting things with their music, photos and home movies then a Mac Mini is an ideal first computer or companion to a main computer. "It's a good little machine with a reasonable amount of power and just perfect for the average computer user who wants to leave the tyranny of Window and viruses," said Mark Sparrow, technical and reviews editor at Mac Format magazine. He added: "In essence, it's a laptop in a biscuit tin, minus the screen and the keyboard. "The software bundle that comes with the mini makes your average budget PC look a bit sick." The relatively low price of the machine has also encouraged the more technically-savvy to experiment with their Macs. One user has already created a "dock" to enable him to plug in and out his Mac Mini in his car...The small size of the machine makes it a practical solution for in-car entertainment - playing movies and music - as well as navigation. original: Pernod takeover talk lifts Domecq..Shares in UK drinks and food firm Allied Domecq have risen on speculation that it could be the target of a takeover by France's Pernod Ricard...Reports in the Wall Street Journal and the Financial Times suggested that the French spirits firm is considering a bid, but has yet to contact its target. Allied Domecq shares in London rose 4% by 1200 GMT, while Pernod shares in Paris slipped 1.2%. Pernod said it was seeking acquisitions but refused to comment on specifics...Pernod's last major purchase was a third of US giant Seagram in 2000, the move which propelled it into the global top three of drinks firms. The other two-thirds of Seagram was bought by market leader Diageo. In terms of market value, Pernod - at 7.5bn euros ($9.7bn) - is about 9% smaller than Allied Domecq, which has a capitalisation of £5.7bn ($10.7bn; 8.2bn euros). Last year Pernod tried to buy Glenmorangie, one of Scotland's premier whisky firms, but lost out to luxury goods firm LVMH. Pernod is home to brands including Chivas Regal Scotch whisky, Havana Club rum and Jacob's Creek wine. Allied Domecq's big names include Malibu rum, Courvoisier brandy, Stolichnaya vodka and Ballantine's whisky - as well as snack food chains such as Dunkin' Donuts and Baskin-Robbins ice cream. The WSJ said that the two were ripe for consolidation, having each dealt with problematic parts of their portfolio. Pernod has reduced the debt it took on to fund the Seagram purchase to just 1.8bn euros, while Allied has improved the performance of its fast-food chains.

original: Disaster claims 'less than $10bn'..Insurers have sought to calm fears that they face huge losses after an earthquake and giant waves killed at least 38,000 people in southern Asia...Munich Re and Swiss Re, the world's two biggest reinsurers, have said exposure will be less than for other disasters. Rebuilding costs are likely to be cheaper than in developed countries, and many of those affected will not have insurance, analysts said. Swiss Re has said total claims are likely to be less than $10bn (£5.17bn). Swiss Re believes that the cost would be substantial but that it is unlikely to be in double-digit billions, the Financial Times reported. Munich Re, the world's largest reinsurance company, said that its exposure is less than 100m euros (£70m; $136m)...At least 10 countries have been affected, with Sri Lanka, Indonesia, India and Thailand among the worst hit. The region's resorts and Western tourists are expected to be among the main claimants...Lloyds of London told the Financial Times it expected its exposure to be limited to "holiday resorts, personal accident, travel insurance and marine risks". A spokeswoman for Hanover Re, Europe's fifth-largest reinsurance firm, estimated tsunami-related damage claims would be in the low double-digit millions of euros. The company has paid out about 300 million euros (£281m; $400m) to cover damage caused recently by four major hurricanes in the US...But insurers have not had long to assess the economic impact of the damage and reports of more casualties and destruction are still coming through..."So many things are unclear, it is just too early to tell," said Serge Troeber, deputy head of Swiss Re's natural disasters department. "You need very complicated processes to estimate damages. Unlike the hurricanes, you can't just run a model." He anticipated that his own company's total claims would be less then those from the hurricanes, which the company put at $640m. reconstruction:
Reinsurers, facing potential claims of 'less than $10bn' according to early estimates, have sought to calm fears among investors that they face huge losses after an earthquake and tsunami killed at least 38,000 people in southern Asia and East Africa. Munich Re and Swiss Re, the world's two biggest reinsurers, have said that their exposure to the disaster will likely be less than initially feared, especially when compared to major catastrophes in more insured regions. They also noted that rebuilding efforts, particularly in the poorer, less developed countries of the region, will prove significantly more challenging and costly than in wealthier nations, analysts said.

Swiss Re has said total claims for the disaster are expected to be less than $10bn (£5.17bn). Swiss Re believes that the total insured cost will be substantial but that it is unlikely to be in the double-digit billions, the Financial Times reported. Munich Re, the world's largest reinsurance company, confirmed that its own direct losses were expected to be around $100m (£70m; $136m), a figure that has remained relatively stable in its preliminary assessments.

At least 10 countries have been affected by the disaster, with Sri Lanka, Indonesia, and India among the worst hit. The region's popular resorts and the substantial number of Western tourists present at the time of the disaster are expected to be among the primary drivers of insurance claims, covering travel, health, and personal accident policies.

Lloyd's of London, the venerable insurance market, told the Times it expected its exposure to be primarily linked to "holiday, personal accident, life insurance and marine risks" rather than large property damage claims in the affected areas. A spokeswoman for Hanover Re, Germany's third-largest reinsurance company, estimated its tsunami-related damage claims in the low single-digit millions of euros, a figure considered manageable for the firm. The company, which recently paid out about 300 million euros (£281m; $400m) for damage caused by four devastating hurricanes in the US, highlighted the contrast in insured losses between highly developed and less developed regions.

But insurers have not had to fully assess the full economic impact of the damage, and reports of more casualties and widespread destruction are still coming through, making a definitive assessment extremely challenging. "Many things are unclear, it is just too early to tell," said Balz Grollimund, deputy head of Swiss Re's natural disasters department. "You have very complicated processes to estimate damages in these regions. Unlike the highly insured areas affected by the recent US hurricanes, you can't just model the losses based on property values and standard policies here," he explained.

He anticipated his own company's losses for the tsunami disaster would be considerably less than those incurred from the string of US hurricanes earlier in the year, which the company put at $640m. Allianz, a major German insurer, said it did not yet know what its overall exposure would be, but that tidal waves were unlikely to have a "material" or "significant" impact on its global business, given its limited presence in the affected areas. Zurich Financial Services, another major insurer, could not yet accurately assess the final cost of the disaster to its operations, citing ongoing uncertainty.

The overall financial impact on US insurance companies, however, is not expected to be heavy, said industry analysts. Most US insurers have relatively little direct exposure in Asia and do, in any event, typically pass a lot of the catastrophic risk to larger global reinsurance companies or special catastrophe funds, limiting their direct liability. Insured damage could therefore amount to just a fraction of the "billions of dollars worth of economic damage" in countries such as Sri Lanka, India, Thailand, Indonesia, the Maldives, and Malaysia, said one Equity insurance analyst, highlighting the vast difference between economic and insured losses in developing nations.

"US insurers have virtually no exposure to this type of event in that region. It's far more likely the European-based reinsurance companies might have some, but even then, it's not expected to be a catastrophic hit," said Paul Newsome, an insurance analyst at AG Edwards & Sons. Indeed, many of the affected countries, such as Indonesia, Sri Lanka or the Maldives, do not usually buy comprehensive insurance for these kinds of natural disasters, particularly at a national infrastructure level, said a London-based insurance broker with extensive experience in the region.

Preliminary estimates from the United Nations of humanitarian aid needed for the worst-hit countries like Sri Lanka, India, Indonesia, and Thailand currently stand at about $5bn (£2.6bn), a sum similar to the emergency cash offered after Hurricane Mitch. Hurricane Mitch killed about 10,000 people and caused an estimated $10bn in damage across Central America in 1998. However, the human impact of the recent tsunamis on the individuals involved is truly incalculable.

"We cannot calculate the cost of these poor and nameless villages and fishing communities that have just been wiped out. Hundreds of thousands of lives have been shattered and countless people have died," said Jan Egeland, Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator at the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).

Tourists cutting short their holidays in affected areas may also suffer a financial impact too. The Association of British Insurers (ABI) warned that standard travel insurance policies do not normally cover cancellations or cutting short a holiday due to acts of God or natural disasters, unless specifically stated. While it said that loss of possessions will generally be covered under typical policies, the Association stressed the crucial importance of checking the exact wording of travel insurance policies, especially regarding clauses on natural catastrophes and unforeseen events, to understand the extent of coverage.

A crucial decision regarding the future of super-casinos in Scotland is set to be made by the Scottish Parliament. The UK government has put forward plans for a series of Las Vegas-style resorts across the UK, with one of these high-profile complexes likely to be earmarked for Scotland. Despite the broader Westminster legislation, Scottish ministers will still retain the ultimate power to decide whether a super-casino should be allowed to operate within Scotland. However, opposition parties have expressed significant doubts, suggesting that this promised autonomy will not be fully realised in practice.

A public consultation focusing on this contentious issue is due to conclude on Wednesday, with its findings expected to inform the subsequent parliamentary debate. The Scottish Executive has indicated its belief that the overarching gambling legislation should primarily be managed by Westminster. This new, comprehensive law is designed to regulate internet gambling for the very first time, and a key objective is to prevent children and other vulnerable individuals from becoming involved in gambling activities.

In Glasgow, potential locations for a super-casino have been widely discussed, with sites such as Ibrox and the Scottish Exhibition and Conference Centre (SECC) frequently cited as possibilities.

The legislation currently progressing through Westminster aims to permit casino complexes that offer more than just traditional gaming. They are expected to provide extensive facilities for high-stakes gambling, alongside substantial live entertainment venues and a vast array of fruit machines offering significant cash prizes.

However, the Scottish Conservative party has strongly criticised the current approach. They argue that the fundamental decision on super-casinos should be definitively made in Scotland, asserting that the Scottish Executive is shirking its responsibility by not fully embracing this devolved power.

India calls for fair trade rules ahead of the G7 meeting of leading industrialised nations, insisting no country is to be cowed by newcomer economic powers. Speaking in London on Friday, ahead of the meeting, India's finance minister, P. Chidambaram, criticised the restrictive trade practices of the G7 nations. He objected to significant subsidies on agriculture that make it difficult for developing nations like India to effectively compete. He also called for reform of the United Nations, the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

P. Chidambaram, India's finance minister, argued that these organisations need to take into account the changing world economic order, and India and China's integration into the global economy. He said the fundamental issue is not simply protectionism but "the terms of engagement." Mr Chidambaram is attending the G7 meeting as part of the G20 group of developing and industrialised nations, which represents two-thirds of the world's population.

At a conference on global enterprise hosted by UK Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown on Friday, he said that he was in favour of flexible exchange rates because they help countries cope with external shocks. "A flexible exchange rate is one channel for absorbing both positive and negative economic shocks," he told the conference. India, along with China, Brazil, South Africa and Russia, has been invited to the G7 meeting taking place in London on Friday and Saturday.

China is expected to face renewed pressure to revalue its fixed exchange rate, which G7 nations, in particular the US, have blamed for a surge in cheap Chinese exports. "Many countries have tried to use fixed exchange rate policies. I do not wish to make any judgements," said Mr Chidambaram. Separately, the IMF warned that India's budget deficit was too large and would hamper the country's economic growth, which it forecast at around 6.5% for the year to March 2005. In the previous fiscal year to March 2004, the Indian economy grew by 8.5%.

American Serena Williams also won, edging Russian Elena Dementieva 7-6 7-5 for her second victory of the event. The event is split into two groups of four with the top two from each advancing to the semi-finals...Mauresmo's win was her ninth in a row as she tries to overtake Lindsay Davenport for the number one spot. Mauresmo spent five weeks at number one after the US Open before injury ushered Davenport back in front. "Since then, I feel very confident on court and my game is there. I want to get the ranking back, but it's very different than before I was number one. "It was an obsession, but now I take it in a relaxed way." Mauresmo completed her first match in the season-ending championship in 54 minutes as Russia's Zvonareva struggled to return her serve and failed to achieve a single break point..."She got mad a little bit and I played some great tennis," said Mauresmo, who was runner-up to Kim Clijsters in last year's final. Zvonareva has lost both her games so far, having crashed 6-2 6-4 Kuznetsova in the Staples Centre on Wednesday. "Sometimes not everything works," she said. "It was lots of pressure. Maybe that is why I couldn't do 100%. But I was fighting." Sharapova, who lost 6-2 6-2 to Kuznetsova in Beijing in September, said: "In Beijing, she was coming off such a big winning streak [14 matches] and she was unstoppable. reconstruction:
Have hackers recruited your PC? More than a million computers on the internet have been hijacked to launch attacks and pump out spam and viruses. The security researchers who have spent more than a year monitoring 100 remotely-controlled machines made this discovery. The largest of these so-called zombie networks identified by the team was made up of 50,000 hijacked home computers. Data was gathered from machines that appeared innocent but which hackers had compromised.

The findings were detailed in a report on 'zombie' or 'bot-nets' of hijacked computers, published by the Honeynet Project - a consortium of security experts that operates networks of computers designed to act as "honey pots" to lure hackers and gather information about their methods of work. While 'bot-nets' have been known about for some time, accurate estimates of how widespread they are have been hard to come by until now.

To gather its information, the German Honeynet Project created software tools to log what happened to the machines on their network. Taking control of the machines proved worryingly easy. The longest time a machine survived being found by an automatic attack tool was only a few minutes. The shortest was just seconds.

The research found that, once compromised, machines tend to report to specific channels on IRC (Internet Relay Chat) servers and wait for instructions. Many of the vulnerabilities, especially in the Windows operating system, were exploited by 'bot controllers' to find and take over target machines. Particularly coveted were home PCs sitting on broadband connections that are never switched off.

The networks under surveillance – the 'bot-nets' – which can involve from a few hundred to tens of thousands of machines, are used for a variety of illicit purposes. Many are used as relay points, to route unwanted spam to others or as launch platforms for viruses. However, the research team found that many are put to very different uses. For instance, the team saw 'bot-nets' used to launch 226 distributed-denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks on 99 separate targets.

DDoS attacks bombard websites with data in an attempt to overwhelm the target. Using a 'bot-net' of machines spread across different networks and geographical locations makes such attacks extremely hard to defend against. In one instance, a DDoS attack was used by a firm to knock a rival offline. Other 'bot-nets' were used to abuse the Google Adsense program, falsely generating rewards for adverts from the search engine. Some networks were used to abuse or manipulate online polls and games. Criminals also seem to be starting to use 'bot-nets' for mass identity theft, sending out phishing emails that look like those of legitimate banks, so that confidential information can be gathered, and to 'peep' into network traffic to intercept sensitive data.

"Leveraging the immense power of these bots, it is viable to take down almost any website or network instantly," said the researchers. "Even in the hands of the unskilled, 'bot-nets' are a dangerous and powerful weapon."

original: Beijingers fume over parking fees..Choking traffic jams in Beijing are prompting officials to look at reorganising car parking charges...Car ownership has risen fast in recent years, and there are now two and a half million cars on the city's roads. The trouble is that the high status of car ownership is matched by expensive fees at indoor car parks, making motorists reluctant to use them. Instead roads are being clogged by drivers circling in search of a cheaper outdoor option. "The price differences between indoor and outdoor lots are unreasonable," said Wang Yan, an official from the Beijing Municipal Commission for Development and Reform quoted in the state-run China Daily newspaper. Mr Wang, who is in charge of collecting car parking fees, said his team would be looking at adjusting parking prices to close the gap. Indoor parking bays can cost up to 250% more than outdoor ones...Sports fans who drive to matches may also find themselves the target of the commission's road rage. It wants them to use public transport, and is considering jacking up the prices of car parks near sports grounds. Mr Wang said his review team may scrap the relatively cheap hourly fee near such places and impose a higher flat rate during matches. Indoor parking may be costly, but it is not always secure. Mr Wang's team are also going to look into complaints from residents about poor service received in exchange for compulsory monthly fees of up to 400 yuan ($48; £26). The Beijing authorities decided two years ago that visiting foreign dignitaries' motorcades should not longer get motorcycle outriders as they blocked the traffic. Unclogging Beijing's increasingly impassable streets is a major concern for the Chinese authorities, who are building dozens of new roads to create a showcase modern city ahead of the 2008 Olympic Games.

The government was told that using anti-terror legislation brought in after 11 September to hold the men indefinitely without charge broke human rights laws...Mr Clarke told The Times: "I think we should be prosecuting much more energetically our ability to deport the individuals concerned to the countries from which they come." Deals to allow the UK authorities to deport foreign terror suspects to their home countries or countries of origin without risk of being tortured or sentenced to death are being sought. Home Secretary Charles Clarke told the Times he hoped that agreement with several countries could be swiftly reached in the wake of a recent court ruling. This follows a House of Lords judgement that the indefinite detention of 12 men at Belmarsh prison, London, and Woodhill, Milton Keynes, was found to be unlawful under human rights law. The 12 men affected by the ruling are from various countries including Algeria, Morocco, Egypt and Tunisia. The Law Lords told the government that using anti-terror legislation brought after the September 11 attacks in the US to hold the men without charge broke human rights principles. Mr Clarke told The Times: "I think we should be more energetically pursuing our ability to deport the individuals concerned to the countries from which they come." He said this was a route that was being actively developed in collaboration with Foreign Secretary Jack Straw, a strategy which he called "a very positive one" for dealing with the issue. Mr Clarke said that he was seeking "memorandums of understanding" between overseas governments and the UK authorities to ensure suspects would not be subjected to inhuman treatment, torture or the death penalty on their return. However, he added: "I do not think the entire solution' for this government is to be found solely in deportations, but they will certainly help." "There are other strands that we have to pursue in our wider counter-terrorism strategy." But the Liberal Democrat's shadow home secretary, Mark Oaten, accused Mr Clarke of avoiding the fundamental issue of how to deal with the detainees. "The issue being dodged at this stage is to deal with the principle, to deal with how we effectively tackle this problem in the future," he told BBC News. "And I want him to grasp the wider issues and find the necessary legal means at how we can actually secure convictions in this country by allowing, for example, intercept communications and telephone tapping to be admissible as evidence," Oaten said. It has earmarked 100 trillion won ($96bn) for the first six months of 2005, which amounts to 60% of its annual budget. It aims to create 400,000 jobs and will focus on boosting demand, as well as providing citizens with money to spend. Millions of South Koreans are defaulting on their credit card bills, and the country's biggest card companies have been hovering on the verge of bankruptcy for months. As part of its spending, the government will ask financial firms to "roll over mortgage payments due in the first half of 2005". It also pledged to look at ways of helping families on low incomes. The government voiced concern about the effect of redundancies in the workforce. "Given the spillover and ripple effect in the construction sector, a sharp downturn in the construction industry could have other adverse effects," the ministry said. As a result, South Korea will give private companies also the chance to build schools, hospitals, and other buildings. It also aims to look at the real estate tax system. Other plans on the table include promoting new industries such as bio-technology and nano-technology, as well as offering increased support to small and medium sized businesses. "We will focus on job creation and economic recovery, given that unfavourable domestic and global conditions are likely to affect the Korean economy in 2005," the ministry added.

reconstruction:
Disney settles disclosure charges. Disney has settled charges from US federal securities regulators that it failed to disclose that family members of its directors were employed by the company in breach of regulatory requirements. The entertainment giant was censured and fined by the Securities and Exchange Commission, but furthermore agreed to refrain from further violations. Disney failed to tell shareholders that between 1999 and 2001 it employed three adult children of then current directors on its payroll. The firm neither admitted nor denied wrongdoing in the settlement document, as is common practice in such agreements.

The three Disney directors identified in the central focus of the SEC's investigation - Reveta Bowers, Stanley Gold and Raymond Watson - have all since left the company, with Ms Bowers and Mr Watson both retiring, and Stanley Gold quitting in 2003, prior to the conclusion of the investigation. Their children were paid between $60,000 (£30,800) and $150,000 per year, the SEC statement detailed, being employed in various capacities across different divisions of the entertainment conglomerate.

The SEC also found that Disney did not disclose that a 50% Disney-owned joint venture company, Lifetime, employed the wife of current director John Bryson, who earned $1m a year. She remains with the company in a senior position.

The investigation also highlighted that Disney failed to disclose payments amounting to a substantial sum to Air Shamrock, an airline wholly owned by fellow Disney board member Roy Disney. Finally, Disney did not reveal that it had provided more than $200,000 in total for office, secretarial support services, a leased car and driver to former director Thomas Murphy, who served on the board for many years.

"Shareholders have a significant interest in full information regarding the business relationships between the company and its board of directors, as these can present potential conflicts of interest," said SEC enforcement director Linda Thomsen. "Failure to comply with the SEC's rules in this area materially impairs shareholders' ability to evaluate the independence and overall performance of directors, thereby impacting their investment decisions."

Along with the owner's picture, name and personal details, the new Seafarers' Identity Document incorporates a barcode representing unique features of its holder's fingerprints. The cards are due to be issued in February next year, in line with the revised UN Convention on Seafarers' Identity Documents of June 2003. Tests currently under way in the Caribbean are designed to ensure that new cards and their machine readers, produced by different companies in different countries, are working to interoperable standards. Results of the current tests, which involve seafarers from a wide range of occupations and nationalities, will be published by the International Labour Organisation (ILO) by the end of November. She said French, Jordanian and Nigerian nationals would be the first seafarers to get the new ID cards since their countries have already ratified the convention. It aims to combat international terrorism whilst guaranteeing the welfare the one million seafarers estimated to be at sea. The convention highlights the importance of access to shore facilities and shore leave as vital elements to a sailor's wellbeing and, therefore, it says, to safer shipping and cleaner oceans. "By increasing security on the seas as well as border control and protection, the cards will hopefully reduce the number of piracy problems around the world," said Ms Musselman. reconstruction:
A luxury cruise liner, sailing the warm waters of the Gulf of Mexico, is the unlikely setting for pioneering tests of technology designed to enhance global security and combat serious crime at sea. As holidaymakers enjoy balmy breezes, their ship's crew is participating in trials of enhanced versions of the new world's internationally issued biometric cards, the digital equivalent of a passport. These documents aim to provide a more secure and verifiable form of identification for maritime professionals.

As well as the owner's picture, name and other vital personal details, the new Seafarers' Identity Document (SID) will incorporate a high-tech barcode and other unique features, including digitally stored data of its holder's fingerprints. This multi-layered approach to identification is intended to significantly increase security. The new SIDs are due to be issued in the coming year, in line with an important UN resolution adopted in June 2003. This global initiative seeks to address growing concerns over identity fraud and maritime security.

The extensive tests currently under way in the Caribbean are crucial to ensure that new cards and associated machine readers, produced by different companies and in various countries, are working to interoperable standards. Such compatibility is paramount for global adoption and effectiveness. The comprehensive findings of the current tests, which involve seafarers from a wide spectrum of nations and backgrounds, will be published by the International Labour Organisation (ILO) towards the end of this year. These findings will inform the final specifications for the global rollout.

Crystal Cruises, which operates the luxury vessel Crystal Harmony, is exploring the use of biometrics technology for its own operations but has not yet made a final decision or committed to the technology for widespread implementation. Authenti-corp, the US consultancy specialising in secure identity solutions, has been working closely with the ILO to develop its technical specifications for the cards. Their expertise is vital in ensuring the system's robustness.

"'If you're responsible for a nation's ID system in a country, you want to be sure that when the seafarer lands in a port, say, in my country, you can accurately verify their identity with whatever equipment we have installed," Authenti-corp's CEO, Musselman, told BBC's Go Digital programme. "Interoperability across different national systems is key to the success of this initiative," she added.

She said French, Jordanian and Nigerian nationals would be among the initial groups of seafarers to get new ID cards since their countries were among the first to have ratified the convention. This phased rollout will allow for further testing and refinement. The convention aims to combat international terrorism and organised crime at sea, primarily by guaranteeing the fundamental rights and secure identity of the one million seafarers estimated to be at sea. This protection extends to their professional and personal lives.

The convention also strongly emphasises the importance of access to port facilities and shore leave as vital elements for a sailor's wellbeing and, it is believed that by improving conditions through it, this will contribute to safer and cleaner oceans. Ensuring humane conditions for seafarers is a core principle.

"By increasing the overall level of security, as well as improving border controls and protection, these cards will hopefully reduce the growing instances of piracy around the world," said Musselman. "This is a critical step towards securing global trade routes." Ultimately, it will empower seafarers to travel and work more efficiently and securely in various ports, and will allow people responsible for managing their borders to quickly and confidently ascertain that the people presenting themselves are, in fact, bona fide seafarers.

He added **the** government is in **negotiations with** Aguas Argentinas about what role it might **take** in **the** event that a State contribution is agreed. **However**, the Argentine newspaper Clarin **reported that Suez indicated it would** not accept any change to its legal structure and, in practice, State participation on its **management** board. Planning Minister **De Vido did not rule out** the possibility **of** cancelling Aguas' water **concession contract**. He added he **did no**t like to do 'futurology'.

But last week, Argentine Economy Minister, Roberto Lavagna, told French media in Paris that the government was considering allowing **a tariff increase of** 16% in tariffs and a **commitment of government funding for** Aguas Argentinas infrastructure investments. Speaking in Buenos Aires, Mr De Vido **reiterated his opposition to a significant** tariff **hike** and insisted that annual investment in **water infrastructure was** at the **centre** of the discussions. He added **that in the coming** weeks the future of Aguas Argentinas would be **defined**.

**France's Suez owns** 40% of Aguas Argentinas (39.9%), while Spain's **Agbar**, **a company from** Barcelona, is its biggest shareholder **with** 25.01%. During the last financial crisis in Argentina, **the** firm sued the state **claiming** that converting its **service charges** from dollars **to** pesos, and then during devaluation, had affected **the** company and made **it extremely difficult** for it to meet its contractual **commitments**.

reconstruction:
France coach Bernard Laporte has tinkered with his team, making four personnel changes to the starting line-up for Saturday's pivotal Six Nations Championship clash with Wales. He has opted to hand a start to Yannick Nyanga in the back row instead of Grand Slam winner Imanol Harinordoquy, who consequently drops to the bench but is back in the squad. Other changes see youngster Julien Laharrague earning his first full international cap at full-back, Aurelien Rougerie making a welcome return after injury on the wing, and Yannick Jauzion coming in at centre. Laporte has resisted widespread pressure to restore Frederic Michalak to the fly-half berth. Dependable veteran Yann Delaigue keeps the number 10 jersey, despite the continuing clamours for the attacking flair of Michalak. The 26-year-old Laharrague gets his chance at full-back despite regularly playing on the wing for his club Brive. "We are launching him into the great bath," commented team manager Jo Maso. "This is a great opportunity for him, above all, to prove himself." "There are still 25 matches left before the World Cup, so we are keen to see as many players as possible perform. The competition for places is very high and the selection is open."

Yannick Jauzion, France's player of the year 2004, would have missed the first two matches of the Championship had South African-born Jean-Marie Liebeneberg been fit. The Stade Toulousain star wins his 23rd cap and is reunited with Damien Traille, with whom he forged an effective midfield partnership during the 2004 season. "The return of Jauzion is a huge plus for us," stated coach Laporte. "We are truly counting on him at international level to provide leadership."

**Team:**
Julien Laharrague (Brive), Aurelien Rougerie (Clermont Auvergne), Yannick Jauzion (Stade Toulousain), Damien Traille (Biarritz Olympique), Christophe Dominici (Stade Francais Paris), Yann Delaigue (Castres Olympique), Dimitri Yachvili (Biarritz Olympique), Julien Bonnaire (Bourgoin), Yannick Nyanga (Beziers), Serge Betsen (Biarritz Olympique), Jerome Thion (Biarritz Olympique), Fabien Pelous (Stade Toulousain, captain), Nicolas Mas (Perpignan), Sebastien Bruno (Sale Sharks), Sylvain Marconnet (Stade Francais Paris).

**Replacements:**
William Servat (Stade Toulousain), Olivier Milloud (Bourgoin), Jean-Baptiste Lamboley (Stade Toulousain), Imanol Harinordoquy (Biarritz Olympique), Pierre Mignoni (Clermont Auvergne), Frederic Michalak (Stade Toulousain), Jean-Philippe Grandclaude (Perpignan).

The lawsuit seeks to represent anyone in the US who has purchased an HP inkjet printer since February 2001. HP, the world's biggest printer firm, declined to comment on the lawsuit. HP ink cartridges use a chip technology to sense when they are low on ink and advise the user to make a change...But the suit claims the chips also shut down the cartridges at a predetermined date regardless of whether they are empty. "The smart chip is dually engineered to prematurely register ink depletion and to render a cartridge unusable through the use of a built-in expiration date that is not revealed to the consumer," the suit said. The lawsuit is asking for restitution, damages and other compensation. The cost of printer cartridges has been a contentious issue in Europe for the last 18 months. The price of inkjet printers has come down to as little as £34 but it could cost up to £1,700 in running costs over an 18-month period due to cartridge, a study by Computeractive Magazine revealed last year. The inkjet printer market has been the subject of an investigation by the UK's Office of Fair Trading (OFT), which concluded in a 2002 report that retailers and manufacturers needed to make pricing more transparent for consumers.
