original: New delay hits EU software laws..A fresh delay has hit controversial new European Union rules which govern computer-based inventions...The draft law was not adopted by EU ministers as planned at a Brussels meeting on Monday during which it was supposed to have been discussed. The fresh delay came after Polish officials had raised concerns about the law for the second time in two months. Critics say the law would favour large companies over small ones and could impact open-source software innovation. "There was at one point the intention to put the item on today's agenda. But in the end we could not put it on," an EU spokesman told the Reuters agency. He added that no date had been chosen for more discussion of the law...In December, Poland requested more time to consider the issue because it was concerned that the law could lead to the patenting of pure computer software. Its ministers want to see the phrasing of the text of the Directive on the Patentability of Computer-Implemented Inventions changed so that it excludes software patenting. Poland is a large EU member, so its backing for the legislation is vital. The EU says the law would bring Europe more in line with how such laws work in the US, but this has caused some angry debate amongst critics and supporters. A fresh delay hit new European rules which govern computer-based inventions, a proposal that was not adopted by ministers as originally planned at a Brussels meeting Monday during which it had been supposed to have been discussed. The decision not to proceed came after Polish officials had raised concerns about the law for the second time in the last two months. Critics say the law would favour large multinational corporations over smaller, independent ones and ultimately stifle genuine software innovation. "There was one point where we were trying very hard to put the item on today's agenda. But in the end we could not put it on," a spokesman for the EU presidency told Reuters. He added that no date had been set as yet for more discussion of the proposed law. In November, for instance, Poland requested more time and clarity to fully understand and address the issue because it concerned that the current draft could open the door to the patenting of computer programs and business methods. Its ministers want to see the text of the Directive on the Patentability of Computer-Implemented Inventions changed to explicitly state that it excludes software patenting. Poland is a large EU member state, and a significant player in its technology sector, so for the country's economy the outcome of this debate is vital. The European Commission, which drafted the proposal, says the legislation would bring Europe more in line with how laws work currently in the US, but the proposal has caused significant debate and strong division amongst critics and even some supporters. In the US, the patenting of certain types of business methods is widely permitted. For example, in the US, Amazon.com holds a patent for its "one-click" online ordering system. Critics say a similar model implemented in Europe would hurt software developers who do not possess the extensive legal expertise and financial might of larger companies. But supporters say current law does not adequately protect the innovative products and solutions for which they have spent years and significant investment developing.

The country produced 14.27 million tonnes of crops in 2004, which was 24% higher than in 2003 and 21% more than the average of the past five years, a report has indicated. In 2003, production totalled 11.49 million tonnes, the report from the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) said. Good rains, increased use of fertilizers and improved seeds contributed significantly to the rise in production. Nevertheless, 2.2 million Ethiopians will still need emergency assistance this year, according to the same report. The report calculated that the country would require food aid for 2005 to the tune of 387,500 tonnes. On top of that, 89,000 tonnes of fortified blended food and vegetable oil are required for "supplementary food distributions for a survival programme targeting children under five and expectant and nursing women" to be implemented. However, in the eastern and southern pastoralist areas, a drought has killed crops and drained wells. Last year, a total of 965,000 tonnes of assistance was provided to help some 11 million Ethiopians. The Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) strongly recommends that the food aid is bought locally. "The purchase of cereals for aid assistance is recommended as far as possible, so as to assist domestic markets and local farmers," said Henri Josserand, chief of FAO's Global Information System. Agriculture is the main economic activity in Ethiopia, representing 45% of its gross domestic product. About 80% of the country's population depend directly or indirectly on it for their livelihoods.

reconstruction: Israel seal trade deal. In a sign of a thaw in relations between Egypt and Israel, the two countries have signed a trade deal with the US, allowing Egyptian goods made in partnership with Israeli firms free access to American markets. The agreement, signed in Cairo, will establish what are called "qualifying industrial zones" in Egypt. Products from these zones enjoy duty free access to the US, provided that 35% of components are the product of Israeli-Egyptian cooperation. The US describes this as the most important economic agreement between Egypt and Israel in two decades. The establishing of these zones has stalled for years. There is deep sensitivity in Egypt to any co-operation with Israel as long as the broader peace process with the Palestinians remains unresolved. But in recent weeks an unusual rapprochement has crept into relations between the two countries. Both sides exchanged prisoners earlier this month, with Egypt handing back an Israeli citizen who has served eight years in prison after being convicted for espionage. President Hosni Mubarak has described Israeli Prime Minister Sharon as the best hope for moving towards peace. The Egyptian government now believes Sharon is moving towards the political centre and away from the positions of right wing groups. It also believes the US, by facilitating this deal, is doing more to engage seriously in the quest for a peaceful settlement. But there are also pressing economic reasons for Egypt's entry into the trade arrangement. It faces a huge challenge to its key textile export sector, as existing preferential trade agreements are about to expire after new regulations come into force at the beginning of the year.

The filmmaker, who directed Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban, will now produce mainstream as well as smaller-scale, international-language films. The 2001 rites-of-passage drama -- about two boys who embark on a spontaneous road trip with an older woman -- brought Cuaron international attention and significant box office glory. Nokia phone owners are being warned to watch out for malicious wallpaper. Those downloading the software will find the icons on their 7610 swapped for images of skulls. The malicious program also locks many of the 7610's functions, making it hard to use and harder to repair. The program is the latest in a series of viruses produced for mobile phones.

The file, nicknamed Skulls, is thought to have surfaced on shareware sites where users can pick up free add-ons, like wallpaper and ringtones, for their phones. Symbian was unsure if Skulls was a virus or a programming flaw. After being discovered, the file is thought to have been removed from the sites where users were unwittingly downloading it.

The program is masquerading as software offering new background images and themes for the screen of the 7610 phone. The Skulls program is labelled as a file called: 7610. extended. theme. manager. Once installed, the program replaces all icons on the main screen with skulls and renders working applications, like contacts, calendar, and notebook, into non-functional versions, making the phone almost useless. The only thing the phone can do is make and take calls.

Symbian, however, played down the malicious program's significance, stating users would only fall victim if they went through specific installation steps, often involving ignoring security warnings. Symbian said that the spread of the Skulls program is likely to be limited as the program cannot jump from one phone to another by itself.

However, a Finnish security lab said it had reports of 7610 users being caught out by it. The lab has advised those caught to contact them to remove the program and get their phones working again. The Skulls program is thought to have been written by someone under the alias Tee-222. Mobile phones produced by Sony, Motorola, BenQ, and Fujitsu are unaffected by the Skulls program.

**O'Driscoll and Gregan lead Rugby Aid stars**

Brian O'Driscoll will lead the Northern Hemisphere team in the Rugby Aid match at Twickenham. O'Driscoll heads a star-studded cast for the contest to raise funds for the tsunami appeal. The South will be led by George Gregan, one of four Wallabies, four Springboks and four All Blacks including captain Tana Umaga. Schalk Burger is fit after injury to take his place in the starting XV. He joins fellow Springboks John Smit, Visagie and Victor Matfield in the South African pack, with Jaque Fourie among the centres.

For the North side there have been the withdrawals of the Scottish duo Gordon Bulloch and Chris Cusiter, plus France's Fabien Pelous. But Leicester's England centre Ollie Smith has been added to the squad, giving him a late opportunity to impress Lions coach Sir Clive Woodward, who is in charge of the North side. "I think it's fantastic for Ollie," Martin Wells told BBC Radio. "He was going to have the week off but I hope Clive gets the chance to see the form that he and England have been seeing all year." The North side will also feature Lions candidates such as the Scottish pair Gregor Townsend and Chris Paterson, Wales scrum-half Dwayne Peel and Ireland lock Paul O'Connell.

"I'm looking forward to working with such outstanding players," Woodward said. "Both teams are fielding strong sides and I hope that fans will come out and get behind us to raise as much money as possible for deserving causes." Despite the withdrawal of Wales wing Rhys Williams, who is injured in the Celtic League, other members of their Six Nations squad - Ceri Sweeney, John Yapp and Jonathan Thomas - will also play. "Not only is it for a great cause but it gives these players an opportunity to play with and against some of the best players in the world," said WRU chief executive Steve Lewis.

Fans can watch the teams train for free at Twickenham on 4 March. Woodward will put his North team through their paces at 1030 GMT, with the South side, coached by former Wallabies coach Eddie Jones, due at the stadium at 1330 GMT.

**North Squad**
*   **Backs:** Chris Paterson (Scotland), Ben Cohen (England), Brian O'Driscoll (Ireland, capt), Damien Traille (France), Ollie Smith (England), Ceri Sweeney (Wales), Denis Hickie (Ireland), Matt Burke (Australia)
*   **Forwards:** Andrea Lo Cicero (Italy), Pieter de Villiers (France), John Yapp (Wales), Raphael Ibanez (France), Paul O'Connell (Ireland), Marco Bortolami (Italy), Jonathan Thomas (Wales), Simon Taylor (Scotland), Lawrence Dallaglio (England), Sergio Parisse (Italy)
*   Others to be added...

**South Squad**
*   **Backs:** Chris Latham (Australia); Brian Lima (Samoa), Jaque Fourie (South Africa), Tana Umaga (New Zealand), Sitiveni Sivivatu (Fiji); Andrew Mehrtens (New Zealand), George Gregan (Australia, capt)
*   **Forwards:** Carl Hayman (New Zealand), John Smit (South Africa), Chris Jack (New Zealand), Ali Williams (New Zealand), Victor Matfield (South Africa), Schalk Burger (South Africa), Phil Waugh (Australia), Toutai Kefu (Australia)
*   **Reserves:** Elvis Taukafa (Tonga), Eusebio Guinazu (Argentina), Semo Sititi (Samoa), Henry Tuilagi (Samoa), Moses Rauluni (Fiji), Thinus Delport (South Africa), Nicky Little (Fiji)

Films on war triumph at Sundance. A documentary looking at US foreign policy over the past 50 years has picked up one of the awards at the 2005 Sundance Film Festival in Utah, in the US.

Why We Fight scooped the grand jury prize for documentaries at the world's leading independent film festival. British director Sean McAllister's The Liberace of Baghdad - a portrait of a wedding singer in war-torn Iraq - also picked a special jury prize in the world documentary category. Both Why We Fight and The Liberace of Baghdad were made for the BBC. Why We Fight is due to be screened on BBC Four in March.

The festival was founded by actor Robert Redford in 1981. This year's event - which ended on Sunday after an 11-day run - has been dominated by themes of war and politics. In the new world cinema drama, the Angolan film The Hero triumphed to the grand jury prize. The film - an Angolan/French/Portuguese production - tells the story of a veteran of the country's civil war who returns to face a new battle for survival.

Other films competing in the new cinema documentary category also focused on conflict and oppression. Finnish film Three Rooms looks at the war in Chechnya and Shake Hands With Devil: The Journey of Romeo tells the story of a UN mission to Rwanda during the 1994 genocide. But it was the Dutch film A Perfect Candidate - a study of extended family ties in Indonesia - which took the special jury prize. Meanwhile, the British production titled The Wall, which looks at Israel's controversial security barrier separating it from the Palestinians, took the other world jury prize for documentaries.

In the US drama category, Me and You and Everyone We Know was named winner of the grand jury prize. It tells the story of a forbidden tug-of-love between a shoe salesman, his Russian employer and his teenage sons.

In its 24-year history, the Sundance Film Festival has launched successes such as Reservoir Dogs, Blair Witch Project and The Full Monty. Recent editions of the festival provided a platform for films like Open Water, Napoleon Dynamite, Garden State and Super-Size Me.

The festival is held in the mountain resort of Park City, Utah, east of Lake City, which sees its population rise from 7,500 to 45,000 during the festival.

They will also talk to Fisheries Minister Ross Finnie and scientists. MPs are deciding whether to recommend a new system of "community quotas" to conserve fish stocks. The scheme is a variation on the local management committees already being established by the European Union...Details are contained in a Royal Commission report for the UK Government, along with the more controversial idea of closing some mixed fishing grounds completely. They will also speak to Mr Finnie, representatives of the Royal Society and the Sea Fish Industry Authority. Committee chairman Austin Mitchell said some way has to be found of harvesting mixed fisheries without wasting stocks.

original: Hi-tech posters guide commuters..Interactive posters are helping Londoners get around the city during the festive season...When interrogated with a mobile phone, the posters pass on a number that people can call to get information about the safest route home. Sited at busy underground stations, the posters are fitted with an infra-red port that can beam information directly to a handset. The posters are part of Transport for London's Safe Travel at Night campaign...The campaign is intended to help Londoners, especially women, avoid trouble on the way home. In particular it aims to cut the number of sexual assaults by drivers of unlicensed minicabs. Nigel Marson, head of group marketing at Transport for London (TfL), said the posters were useful because they work outside the mobile phone networks. "They can work in previously inaccessible areas such as underground stations which is obviously a huge advantage in a campaign of this sort," he said...The posters will automatically beam information to any phone equipped with an IR port that is held close to the glowing red icon on the poster. "We started with infra-red because there are a huge number IR phones out there," said Rachel Harker, spokeswoman for Hypertag which makes the technology fitted to the posters. "It's a well established technology." Hypertag is also now making a poster that uses short-range Bluetooth radio technology to swap data. Although the hypertags in the posters only pass on a phone number, Ms Harker said they can pass on almost any form of data including images, ring tones and video clips. She said that there are no figures for how many people are using the posters but a previous campaign run for a cosmetics firm racked up 12,500 interactions. "Before we ran a campaign there was a big question mark of: 'If we build it will they come?'" she said. "Now we know that, yes, they will." The TfL campaign using the posters will run until Boxing Day.

Sited strategically at busy underground stations across the capital, the posters are fitted with an infra-red transmitter that beams relevant information directly to any compatible mobile handset. In particular it aims to significantly cut the number of sexual assaults perpetrated by drivers of unlicensed minicabs operating illegally during peak night-time hours. Nigel, head of the safe travel group at Transport for London, explained that the posters were particularly useful because they function entirely outside the conventional mobile phone networks. "The system can work in previously inaccessible areas such as deep underground stations, which is obviously a huge and clear benefit in a campaign of this sort where connectivity is key," he added. The intelligent posters beam information to any mobile phone equipped with an IR port that is held close to a prominent red icon clearly marked on the device itself. "We started primarily with infra-red technology as a huge number of existing handsets with IR capability are currently out there in public hands," said Rachel Harker, spokeswoman for Hypertag, the innovative company which makes the technology and infrastructure for these groundbreaking posters. "It's an already well-established and reliable technology." Hypertag is also now making a new generation of poster that uses short-range Bluetooth to swap digital data and content with a wider range of modern phones. Although Hypertag initially developed the posters to be primarily used on mobile phones, Ms Harker noted that they can actually pass on almost any form of rich digital content, including important text messages, useful still images, and even informative video clips. She acknowledged that there are no precise, definitive figures yet for exactly how many people are currently using them, but highlighted that a previous successful trial campaign for a security firm racked up an impressive 12,500 successful interactions in a short period. "Before we even launched this particular campaign, there was a big question mark, a real sense of uncertainty, surrounding the central idea of: 'will we get the public's engagement, will they actually use it and find it helpful?'" "Now, thankfully, we know for sure, yes, they will." The entire campaign and the specially designed posters will continue to run across London until Boxing Day.

Tony Blair and Gordon Brown criticised by MPs. MPs have criticised Tony Blair and Gordon Brown amid renewed reports of a rift between the two. A public display of what are normally private feuding among senior members could damage Labour's election hopes. The Prime Minister insisted nothing would derail Labour's campaign, despite a new book saying he has upset many by going back on his pledge to step aside. Mr Blair will again be in the eye of the storm at the party's poster launch. In what is hoped will be perceived as a show of unity, Mr Blair is due to turn up alongside Alan Milburn - the party's election supremo - and John Prescott, the Deputy Prime Minister, for the event in London on Tuesday. Relations between Mr Brown and Mr Milburn are reported to be strained ever since Mr Blair brought him back into the Cabinet to run Labour's election campaign, a role successfully carried by Mr Brown in 1997 and 2001.

Mr Blair told the parliamentary Party on Monday: "You know here, in Cabinet and government, we're going to get on with the job of leading the Labour Party forward with a unified position and winning the third term that people need."

The prime minister and his chancellor were seconds apart from each other for a meeting of the Cabinet and were reported to be on as good terms as it gets. New speculation about the state of their relationship was sparked by claims in Gordon Brown's Britain, by Telegraph journalist Robert Peston, which suggested Mr Blair had gone back on a pledge to make way for Mr Brown. Labour MP Paul Flynn said Mr Blair and Mr Brown had received a "scorching" from the party's backbenchers, adding: "This is a Labour Party like no other."

Backbencher Stephen Pound said MPs had threatened to expose those fuelling the reports if Mr Blair and Mr Brown did not stop what he called the "poisonous briefing". Lord Hattersley, a former MP, challenged Mr Brown to deny reports that he had told a fellow minister he did not believe Mr Blair's assurances. Mr Prescott said MPs were entitled to complain about a lack of discipline after reading recent press reports.

"They told us clearly, it was the troops telling their leaders: get into line," he told BBC Radio 4's Today on Tuesday. Mr Prescott admitted there were disagreements. But he said Mr Blair and he could work successfully together and had delivered a strong economy and better public services.

The new book claims Mr Prescott hosted a dinner in 2003 where the prime minister told Mr Brown he would not stand at the next election because he had lost trust over the Iraq war. Mr Blair had changed his mind in June 2004, amid growing concern from Cabinet colleagues and suspicion that the chancellor was manoeuvring him, according to Peston. Mr Prescott said there was a dinner but denied the discussions were as reported. "As a former waiter of 10 years, I have a good ability to recall what was said," he added.

Mr Blair has denied he has done deals over the leadership, while Mr Brown has said he will not let "anything distract" from helping a unified election campaign. The Conservatives say the two men are behaving like squabbling children, and the Liberal Democrats claim personal ambition is putting their own interests before the national good.

original: Beastie Boys win sampling battle..US rappers Beastie Boys have won their long-running battle over the use of a sample in their song Pass the Mic...The punk-rappers used three notes of music from flautist James Newton's Choir in their track from 1992. Although the group had paid a licence fee for the sample, Mr Newton said his copyright had been infringed. But the US Court of Appeal upheld its original decision that the group did not have to pay an additional fee to license the underlying composition. The Beastie Boys - Michael Diamond, Adam Horowitz, and Adam Yauch - are considered to be one of early pioneers of sampling music...Sampling, now a standard practice among musicians, involves taking a segment of one track and using it in a different song. A three-judge panel of the court held in 2003 that the band had abided by copyright protections by paying a licence fee for a sample of Mr Newton's recording. That finding upheld a lower-court dismissal of the case in favour of the Beastie Boys. "We hold that Beastie Boys' use of a brief segment of that composition, consisting of three notes separated by a half-step over a background C note, is not sufficient to sustain a claim for infringement of Newton's copyright," Chief Judge Mary Schroeder wrote in her opinion. Mr Newton is a critically acclaimed jazz and classical flutist, composer, performer, and university professor. Mr Newton and the Beastie Boys were not available for comment.

The sale has destroyed Yukos, once the owner of Yuganskneftegas, said founder Mikhail Khodorkovsky. "Yuganskneftegas has been sold in the best traditions of the 90s. "They screwed up the financing," said Ronald Smith, an analyst at Renaissance Capital in Moscow. "And Gazprom doesn't have this sort of money lying around."..Gazprom has denied that it is behind the purchase. original: Tories attack burglar 'U-turns'..Tory leader Michael Howard has accused Tony Blair of performing U-turns over rules on using force against burglars...The government has ruled out amending the present law, which allows "reasonable force" in self defence. Mr Howard branded the decision unacceptable, saying: "It is not householders who should be frightened, it's the burglars." Home Secretary Charles Clarke said ministers had kept to their pledge to review the law...Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir John Stevens last month backed a Tory attempt to change the law so only householders using "grossly disproportionate" force could be prosecuted. The pressure prompted the prime minister to say the police and Crown Prosecution Service would be consulted as part of a review of the law. He told MPs: "If we get the right response from those people, we will, of course, support a change in the law." Instead, the government has decided no change is needed but there will be a publicity campaign so people are clear they are entitled to defend themselves. On Thursday, Mr Howard told BBC Radio 4's Today programme Mr Blair had initially refused the law change, then had come round to the idea and was now backtracking again. He said: "We've had three policy positions in three months and two U-turns. "It's not surprising Gordon Brown told him: 'There's nothing you could say to me now that I could ever believe.'"..Mr Howard said the "grossly disproportionate" test matched the hurdle ministers had introduced for civil cases where burglars where claimed compensation from householders. The issue entered the public spotlight when Norfolk farmer Tony Martin was jailed for shooting dead a 16-year-old burglar in 1999 as he ran away from the farm. But the home secretary said Mr Howard was wrong to say the law was biased in favour of burglars. The barrister who had represented Mr Martin had said the rules were "weighted overwhelmingly" in favour of the householder, said Mr Clarke. He said: "The problem is there has not been enough understanding of it - that was the point Sir John Stevens was making and the prime minister was making." The new guidance would help ensure clarity on the issue, added Mr Clarke. The director of public prosecutions, Ken Macdonald, says only 11 householders or occupiers of business premises have been prosecuted in the last 15 years. Those cases included a warehouse manager who had waited for a burglar, tied him up, beat him and set him alight, he said. Tory MP Patrick Mercer's private member's bill to change the law received a first reading in Parliament on Wednesday and goes to a full debate next month.

original: Howard rebuts asylum criticisms..Tory leader Michael Howard has gone on the offensive in response to people questioning how a son of immigrants can propose asylum quotas...Mr Howard, whose parents fled the Nazi threat to come to the UK, says the claim would mean no-one from an immigrant family could become premier. His comments come in a BBC documentary called 'No More Mr Nasty'. TV presenter Anne Robinson said as home secretary he gave the impression he would "like to kick your cat". Ms Robinson, a friend of the Tory leader, also revealed that as a Cambridge student Mr Howard was "much loved by women and he was a courteous and kind and rather dashing lover" - although she denied having personal experience. "I wasn't at Cambridge - and it's not personal experience - but I know people who were."..Documentary maker Michael Cockerell was given behind-the-scenes access to Mr Howard for his film portrait. The Tory leader was asked about to respond to people who said that if there had there been a quota on immigration and asylum in the 1930s, his parents might not have been allowed into the country...He replies: "What is the inference of that? "That if you reach the view that you need to control immigration in the interests of the country you're not allowed to put a view forward if you happen to be descended from immigrants? "That seems to me an absolutely extraordinary proposition? It would certainly mean no one from immigrant parents could be prime minister."..Ms Robinson, who presents The Weakest Link tells Cockerell that she despaired at his hardline image when he was home secretary in John Major's government. "I used to have to sit on my hands because he'd get on television and give a passable impression of someone who'd like to kick your cat or would put your baby in prison if he cried. I mean it was very, very Draconian." The film shows Mr Howard laughing at Rory Bremner's impression of him as Dracula, which he calls "good fun", apart from the serious falsehood of a comment suggesting he wants fewer black people in the UK. The film shows the private side of the Tory leader watching television at home or playing table tennis with his wife, ex-model Sandra. Asked if she enjoys a game of ping pong she confesses: "Yeah, it would be more enjoyable if I could win occasionally too, but otherwise it's quite fun."..Former Downing Street communications chief Alastair Campbell, now working on Labour's election campaign, says a "touchy-feely" image does not fit Mr Howard. He says Tony Blair was not worried by his opponents' early performance in their Commons clashes because Mr Howard lacked a "big strategy", including on issues like Iraq. The Tory leader brands such criticisms as "absolutely rubbish", arguing that he has been consistent on his support for the war but critical of Mr Blair's failure to tell the truth on intelligence. Former Tory chancellor Ken Clarke says Mr Howard has a bigger problem changing perceptions of the Tory party than his personal image. Mr Clarke says the party is improving and it is "conceivable" it could win the next election. But he adds: "It has got to change itself a bit and broaden its appeal."..- Michael Howard: No More Mr Nasty is being shown on BBC2 on Saturday 12 February at 2005 GMT.

original: UK bank seals South Korean deal..UK-based bank Standard Chartered said it would spend $3.3bn (£1.8bn) to buy one of South Korea's main retail banks...Standard Chartered said acquiring Korea First Bank (KFB) fulfilled a strategic objective of building a bigger presence in Asia's third largest economy. Its shares fell nearly 3% in London as the bank raised funds for the deal by selling new stocks worth £1bn ($1.8bn), equal to 10% of its share capital. Standard Chartered expects about 16% of future group revenue to come from KFB...The South Korean bank will also make up 22% of the group's total assets. The move, a year after Citigroup beat Standard Chartered to buy Koram bank, would be the South Korean financial sector's biggest foreign takeover. This time around, Standard Chartered is thought to have beaten HSBC to the deal. KFB is South Korea's seventh largest bank, with 3 million retail customers, 6% of the country's banking market and an extensive branch network...The country's banking market is three times the size of Hong Kong's with annual revenues of $44bn. Standard Chartered has its headquarters in London but does two thirds of its business in Asia, and much of the rest in Africa. "We're comfortable with the price paid...the key here has been speed and decisiveness in making sure that we won," said Standard Chartered chief executive Mervyn Davies at a London press conference. Standard Chartered said KFB was a "well-managed, conservatively run bank with a highly skilled workforce" and represented a "significant acquisition in a growth market". In London, Standard Chartered's sale of 118 million new shares to institutional investors pushed its share price down, and contributing to the FTSE 100's 0.3% decline. Standard Chartered's shares were 28 pence lower at 925p by midday. Some analysts also queried whether Standard Chartered had overpaid for KFB. The deal, which requires regulatory approval, is expected to be completed by April 2005 and to be earnings accretive in 2006, Standard Chartered said...Rival banking giant HSBC, which is based in London and Hong Kong, was also in the running. Standard Chartered is believed to have gained the initiative by putting together a bid during the Christmas break. "They were able to move so quickly it caught HSBC by surprise," the Financial Times newspaper quoted an insider in the talks as saying. HSBC will now have to wait for the next South Korean bank in line to be sold off - thought likely to be Korea Exchange Bank, also currently in the hands of a US group. Standard Chartered said it was buying 100% of KFB, an agreement that would bring an end to the bank's complex dual ownership. The South Korean government owns 51.4% of KFB, while the remaining shareholding, and operational control, are in the hands of US private equity group Newbridge Capital. Newbridge bought its stake during the government's nationalisation of several banks in the wake of the 1997 Asia-wide currency crisis which crippled South Korea's financial institutions...South Korea's economy is expected to grow by 4.5% this year. Although often thought of an export-driven economy, South Korea's service sector has overtaken manufacturing in the last decade or so. Services now make up roughly 40% of the economy, and consumer spending and retail banking have become increasingly important. In the aftermath of the Asian financial crisis, the government encouraged the growth of consumer credit. Bad loan problems followed; LG Card, the country's biggest credit card provider, has been struggling to avoid bankruptcy for months, for instance. But analysts believe South Korea's financial services industry is still in its infancy, offering plenty of scope for new products. Standard Chartered sees "the opportunity to create value by the introduction of more sophisticated banking products". Since 1999, KFB has been restructured from a wholesale bank into a retail bank focused on mortgage lending, which makes up 45% of its loans.

reconstruction: **Standard Chartered seals major South Korean deal.** UK-based bank Standard Chartered said it would spend $3.3bn (£1.8bn) to buy one of South Korea's main retail banks. Chartered said acquiring First Bank (KFB) fulfilled a strategic ambition to establish a bigger presence in Asia's largest market. Its shares fell sharply by nearly 3% in London as the bank announced plans to raise funds for the deal by selling new equity worth £1bn ($1.8bn), equivalent to 10% of its existing share capital. Standard Chartered expects about 16% of its future revenue to come from KFB alone. The South Korean bank will make up 22% of the group's total pre-tax profit. The acquisition, a year after Citigroup beat Chartered to buy another Korean bank, would be the South Korean financial sector's biggest foreign acquisition to date. With little other competition around, Standard Chartered is thought to have moved swiftly to secure the deal. KFB is South Korea's seventh largest bank, boasting 3 million retail customers and approximately 6% of the country's extensive branch network. The South Korean banking market is three times the size of Hong Kong's, with annual revenues reaching $44bn. Standard Chartered has its headquarters in London but does two-thirds of its business in Asia, with much of the remainder in Africa. "We're comfortable with the price paid... the key here has been speed and making sure we won," said Standard Chartered chief executive Mervyn Davies at a London press conference held on Monday. Standard Chartered described KFB as a "well-managed, conservatively run bank with a highly skilled workforce" and said it represented a "significant acquisition in a highly attractive growth market". Later in London trading, Standard Chartered's placement of 118 million new shares to institutional investors further pushed its shares down, contributing significantly to the FTSE 100's 0.3% decline for the day. Standard Chartered's shares were trading 28 pence lower at 925p by midday. Some market analysts immediately questioned whether Standard Chartered had overpaid for KFB. The deal, which requires customary regulatory approval, is expected to be formally completed by April 2005 and to become earnings accretive from 2006, Standard Chartered confirmed. Rival banking giant HSBC, which has dual headquarters in London and Hong Kong, was also understood to be in the running. Standard Chartered is believed to have gained the upper hand and taken the initiative by making a surprise move during the recent Christmas break. "They managed to move so quickly and decisively that it caught HSBC completely by surprise," the Financial Times newspaper quoted an unnamed source close to the talks as saying. HSBC will now presumably have to wait for the next South Korean bank in line to be put up for sale - likely to be Korea Exchange Bank, currently in the ownership of a US private equity group. Standard Chartered said its 100% acquisition of KFB would, importantly, put an end to the bank's complex ownership structure. The South Korean government currently owns 51.4%, while the management rights and day-to-day operational control are in the hands of US private equity firm Newbridge Capital. Newbridge bought its stake during the South Korean government's nationalisation of several distressed banks in the wake of the devastating 1997-98 Asian currency crisis that crippled many of South Korea's financial institutions. South Korea's economy is widely expected to grow by 4.5% this year. Although often primarily thought of as an export-driven economy, South Korea's burgeoning service sector has expanded significantly over the last decade or so. Services now make up roughly 40% of the overall economy, and consumer retail banking is becoming increasingly important. In the immediate aftermath of the Asian crisis, the government actively encouraged the growth of consumer credit. This, however, led to some significant problems; LG Card, the country's biggest credit card company, has been struggling to avoid outright bankruptcy for several months, for instance. However, many analysts believe South Korea's consumer credit market is still relatively in its infancy, offering plenty of scope for new and innovative products. Standard Chartered sees "the enormous opportunity to create the next generation of more sophisticated banking products and services". Since 1999, KFB has successfully been restructured from a largely wholesale bank into a retail-focused bank, with a particular emphasis on mortgage lending, which now makes up 45% of its total loans.

reconstruction: Godzilla gets Hollywood Walk of Fame star. Movie monster Godzilla has received a star on Hollywood's Walk of Fame, honouring his 50th anniversary and the launch of his 28th film, *Godzilla: Final Wars*. An actor dressed as the giant creature breathed smoke over fans on Hollywood Boulevard as Godzilla received the 2,271st star on Hollywood's iconic Walk of Fame. "He should be here for this historical and momentous star, a true honour for a global icon," said *Godzilla: Final Wars* producer Shogo Tomiyama. "But, he cannot physically be here," he added, with a chuckle. Hollywood's honorary mayor, Johnny Grant, presided over the ceremony, declaring: "I do hereby proclaim this Day in Hollywood 'Godzilla Day'." He then joked to the assembled crowd: "He's big, he's wild, and I'm getting the hell out of here!" The premiere of *Godzilla: Final Wars* at Grauman's Chinese Theatre followed the star ceremony on Hollywood Boulevard. The creature, portrayed by a suit actor, was joined by co-stars from the film, including pop star and actor Masahiro Matsuoka. Director Ryuhei Kitamura, however, hinted that this might not truly be *Final Wars*, as it has been billed by the studio. "That's what the producers say. But that's a lie," he declared with a mischievous grin. "[Godzilla's] been working tirelessly for the last 50 years. So, I think Godzilla definitely deserves a long vacation." And producer Tomiyama added a hopeful note: "So long as Godzilla can continue to fascinate people across the world, I believe he will certainly be resurrected by new generations of enthusiastic filmmakers in the future, ensuring his legacy lives on." Godzilla first appeared in Japan in 1954 as a terrifying giant lizard woken from its slumber by atomic tests, a metaphor for the horrors of nuclear warfare.

The prime minister's official spokesman said the Cabinet was still used to achieve a consensus on important issues. But he added: "You cannot, in a modern government, take every decision in Cabinet. It's just not possible."..Lord Butler said the government had too much freedom to "bring in bad Bills" and "to do whatever it likes" and it relied too much on the advice of political appointees. The former cabinet secretary said in an interview with The Spectator magazine: "I would be critical of the present government in that there is too much emphasis on selling, there is too much central control and there is too little of what I would describe as reasoned deliberation which brings in all the arguments." Mr Howard described Lord Butler's intervention as "very important". "This is from someone who was an insider at the very heart of the Blair government. "It is certainly the most damaging testimony I can ever remember from someone in such an eminent position."..Lord Butler's report earlier this year into Iraq intelligence said the government's September 2002 weapons dossier did not make clear intelligence about claims that Saddam Hussein had stockpiles of chemical and biological weapons was "very thin". The reason for this is that it would have weakened ministers' case for war, Lord Butler said in his Spectator interview, which was conducted by the magazine's editor, Conservative MP Boris Johnson. He said: "When civil servants give material to ministers, they say these are the conclusions we've drawn, but we've got to tell you the evidence we've got is pretty thin. "Similarly, if you are giving something to the United Nations and the country you should warn them."..Asked why he thought the warnings were not there Lord Butler said: "One has got to remember what the purpose of the dossier was. The purpose of the dossier was to persuade the British why the government thought Iraq was a very serious threat."..When asked whether he thought the country was well-governed on the whole, he replied: "Well. I think we are a country where we suffer very badly from Parliament not having sufficient control over the executive, and that is a very grave flaw. "We should be breaking away from the party whip. The executive is much too free to bring in a huge number of extremely bad Bills, a huge amount of regulation and to do whatever it likes - and whatever it likes is what will get the best headlines tomorrow. "All that is part of what is bad government in this country." Lord Butler's assessment was backed by his predecessor as Cabinet Secretary, Lord Armstrong. Lord Armstrong told BBC Two's Newsnight: "I agree ... there doesn't appear to be the sort of informed collective political judgement brought to bear on decision-making that those affected by decisions are entitled to expect." Liberal Democrat deputy leader Menzies Campbell said he thought Lord Butler's comments were "well justified" and Mr Blair's style of leadership was "corrosive of the whole system of government". But Labour former minister Jack Cunningham accused Lord Butler of basing his comments on the first eight months of the incoming Labour administration, when he was cabinet secretary. Mr Cunningham told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "Taken together, Robin Butler's comments are partial, inaccurate and cannot be taken as anything other than politically biased against the Labour government."

Butler launches attack on Blair. Former civil chief Lord Butler has criticised the way Tony's government operates, it is operating with an over-reliance on informal advice and too little collective decision-making. He also attacked the way the war was 'sold' to the public, with important warnings on the quality of the intelligence left out. Tory leader Michael Howard said Butler had 'most damning testimony' he could have given. Downing Street said Blair should not change his style.

Lord Butler said Mr Blair bypassed the Cabinet and relied instead on informal groups of advisers to help him make decisions. The prime minister's official spokesman said the Cabinet was still used to achieve a consensus on important issues. But he added: 'You cannot, in every instance, involve every minister in every decision. It's just not possible.'

Butler said government had too much freedom to 'bring bad Bills' and 'to do what it likes' and relied too much on the advice of political advisers. A former cabinet secretary said in an interview with The Spectator magazine: 'I would be critical of the government in that there is too much emphasis on selling, there is too much central control and there is what I would describe as deliberation which is lacking in all respects.' Mr Howard described Lord Butler's intervention as 'very important'. 'This is someone who was an insider at the very heart of the government.' 'It is the most damaging testimony I ever remember from such an eminent position.'

Lord Butler's report last year on Iraq intelligence said the government's September 2002 weapons dossier did make clear that the intelligence on Saddam Hussein's chemical and biological weapons was 'thin'. And for this it must have weakened Britain's case for war, Lord Butler said in the Spectator interview, which was conducted by the magazine's editor, Conservative MP Boris Johnson. He added: 'When civil servants give material to ministers, they say these are the conclusions we've drawn, but we've got to tell you the evidence we've got is pretty weak.' He continued, 'But, if giving something to the United Nations and the country, we should warn.'

Asked why he thought the warnings were not more prominent, Lord Butler said: 'One has got to look at what the purpose of the dossier was. The purpose was to persuade the public why the government thought Saddam was a very serious threat.'

When asked whether he thought the country was well-governed on the whole, he replied: 'Well. I think we are a country where we have very little Parliament exercising proper control over the executive, which is very serious.' 'We seem to be breaking the party system. The executive is too free to bring a number of bad Bills, introduce excessive regulation and to do whatever it pleases - and whatever it will get the best headlines tomorrow.' 'All is symptomatic of what is a bad government for this country.' Butler's assessment was backed by his predecessor as Cabinet Secretary, Lord Armstrong. Lord Armstrong told BBC Two's Newsnight: 'I agree... there doesn't appear to be the sort of informed collective judgement brought to bear on decision-making that those affected by decisions are entitled to expect.'

Liberal Democrat leader Menzies Campbell said he thought Lord Butler's criticisms were 'well justified' and Mr Blair's style of leadership was 'of fundamental damage to our system of government'. But former minister Jack Cunningham accused Lord Butler of making partisan comments on the first eight years of the incoming Labour administration, when he was cabinet secretary. Mr Cunningham told Radio 4's Today programme: 'Taken together, Robin Butler's comments are unwise, inaccurate and cannot be seen as anything other than biased against the government.'

original: Goldsmith denies war advice claim..The attorney general has denied his statement to Parliament about the legality of the Iraq war was drafted by Downing Street officials...Lord Goldsmith said Lord Falconer and Baroness Morgan played no part in drafting the answer. He added the answer represented his view that the war was legal, but was not a summary of his advice to the PM. The government has resisted calls to publish the full advice, saying such papers are always kept confidential...In a statement, Lord Goldsmith said: "I was fully involved throughout the drafting process and personally finalised, and of course approved, the answer." He said the answer had been prepared in his office with the involvement of Solicitor General Harriet Harman, two of his own officials, three Foreign Office officials, a QC, Christopher Greenwood and the then Lord Chancellor, Lord Irvine of Lairg..."No other minister or official was involved in any way." He suggested the claim that Lord Falconer and Lady Morgan had drafted the answer were the result of a mis-transcription of his evidence to the Butler Inquiry into pre-war intelligence. "As I have always made clear, I set out in the answer my own genuinely held, independent view that military action was lawful under the existing (UN) Security Council resolutions," he said. "The answer did not purport to be a summary of my confidential legal advice to government." Former foreign secretary Robin Cook said Lord Goldsmith's admission that his parliamentary answer was not a summary of his legal opinion suggested Parliament may have been misled. "The attorney general may never have presented his answer as a summary, but others certainly did," he said. "What is clear from his statement today is that he does not believe that it was a full, accurate summary of his formal opinion."..Earlier, Tony Blair dismissed questions about the attorney general's advice, and said his Parliamentary statement had been a "fair summary" of his opinion. "That's what he (Lord Goldsmith) said and that's what I say. He has dealt with this time and time and time again," Mr Blair told his monthly news conference in Downing Street. He refused to answer further questions on the issue...On the question of whether such papers have always been kept confidential, Tory MP Michael Mates, who is a member of the Commons intelligence and security committee and was part of the Butler inquiry, told the BBC: "That, as a general rule, is right, but it's not an absolute rule." He said there had been other occasions when advice had been published, most recently regarding Prince Charles's marriage plans. The government could not pick and choose when to use the convention, he said. Mr Mates added: "This may be one of those special occasions... when it would be in the public interest to see the advice which the attorney general gave to the prime minister."..The claims about Lord Falconer and Baroness Morgan's involvement were made in a book published this week by Philippe Sands QC, a member of Cherie Blair's Matrix Chambers. He also says Lord Goldsmith warned Tony Blair on 7 March 2003 that the Iraq war could be illegal without a second UN resolution sanctioning military action...A short statement about Lord Goldsmith's position presented in a written parliamentary answer on 17 March 2003 - just before a crucial Commons vote on the military action - did not suggest this. Former minister Clare Short, who resigned from the government over the Iraq war, said the ministerial answer was the same statement that was earlier shown to the cabinet as it discussed military action. She said the full advice should have been attached, according to the ministerial code, and demanded a Lords inquiry into the matter. The Conservatives and Liberal Democrats say they still want the publication of the full legal advice given by the Attorney General. Lib Dem foreign affairs spokesman Sir Menzies Campbell said Lord Goldsmith's statement still did not clear up the outstanding issues. "If his original advice of 7 March accepted that military action might be illegal, how was it that he resolved any such doubts by the time the Parliamentary answer was published on 17 March?" he said. "Only the fullest disclosure will now do."

reconstruction:
Lord Goldsmith has clarified how the attorney general prepared his statement to Parliament on the legality of the Iraq war by stating that he and Baroness Morgan played a part in drafting the document. He said the answer set out his view that the war was legal, but he added it was not a summary of his confidential advice to the PM. The government has resisted calls to publish the advice, saying such documents are always kept confidential.

In a statement, Lord Goldsmith said: "I was fully involved throughout the drafting process and personally finalised, and of course approved, the answer." He said the answer had been prepared in his office with the help of Solicitor General Harriet Harman, some of his own officials, three Foreign Office officials, Diana Greenwood and Lord Chancellor, Lord Falconer of Lairg. "No other minister or official was involved in any way." He denied that Lord Falconer and Baroness Morgan had claimed his answer was the only piece of legal evidence to the Butler inquiry into pre-war intelligence.

"As I have always made clear, I set out in that answer my own sincerely held, independent view that military action was lawful under existing (UN) Security Council resolutions," he said. "That answer did not purport to be a summary of my confidential advice to government."

Robin Cook said Lord Goldsmith's admission that his parliamentary answer was not a summary of his confidential advice meant Parliament may have been misled. "The attorney general may never have presented his answer as a full summary, but he certainly did present his legal view," Mr Cook said. "What is clear from his statement today is that he does not believe it was a full, comprehensive summary of his advice."

Earlier, Tony Blair, questioned about the attorney general's advice, had said the Parliamentary statement was a "summary" of his opinion. "That's what he (Lord Goldsmith) said and that's what I say. He has dealt with this time and time and time again," Mr Blair told his monthly news conference in Downing Street. Mr Blair refused to answer further questions on the issue.

On the question of why such papers have been kept confidential, Tory MP Michael Mates, a member of the Commons intelligence and security committee and who was part of the Butler inquiry, told the BBC: "That, as a general rule, is the standard practice, but it's not an absolute rule." He said there had been other occasions when legal advice had been published, such as Prince Charles's marriage plans. The government could choose when to depart from the convention, he added. Mr Mates said: "This may be one of those special occasions... when it would be in the public interest to see the advice which the attorney general gave the prime minister."

Claims about Lord Goldsmith's and Baroness Morgan's involvement were made in a book published this week by Philippe Sands, a member of Cherie Blair's Matrix Chambers. He also says Lord Goldsmith warned Tony Blair on 7 March 2003 that the Iraq war could be illegal without a UN resolution sanctioning military action. A statement about Lord Goldsmith's position presented in a written parliamentary answer on 17 March 2003 - a crucial Commons debate on the military action - did not suggest this.

Clare Short, who resigned from the government over the war, said the answer was the same statement that had been referred to earlier in Cabinet as it discussed military action. She said the advice should have been published, according to ministerial convention, and demanded a Lords inquiry into the matter. The Conservatives and Liberal Democrats still want the full disclosure of the advice given by the Attorney General. Liberal Democrat foreign affairs spokesman Sir Menzies Campbell said Lord Goldsmith's statement was still not clear.

"If his initial assessment of 7 March might be illegal, how was he able to have resolved any such doubts by the time his Parliamentary statement was published on 17 March?" he asked. "Only the fullest transparency will now do."

This is because of possible malfunctions with the braking systems. The affected vehicles in the product recall are from the 2004 and 2005 model years, GM said. Those vehicles with potential faults are the Chevrolet Avalanche, Express, Kodiak, Silverade and Suburban; the GMC Savana, Sierra and Yukon...The NHTSA said a pressure accumulator in the braking system could crack during normal driving and fragments could injure people if the hood was open. This could allow hydraulic fluid to leak, which could make it harder to brake or steer and could cause a crash, it warned. reconstruction:
**Manchester United navigate tricky Exeter test, avoid FA Cup upset**

Manchester United narrowly avoided a major FA Cup upset, edging past League Two side Exeter City in a tense and dramatic third round replay at St James Park. Despite a spirited display from the Grecians, Cristiano Ronaldo scored the opening goal for the visitors, slipping the ball with typical Portuguese flair between Paul Jones' legs after just nine minutes. However, a resilient Exeter wasted host chances to make the scoreline safe as their goalkeeper, Paul Jones, pulled off some great saves, keeping the tie alive until Wayne Rooney put the result beyond doubt on 87 minutes with a clinical low finish.

The Grecians had chances of their own to level the score, with striker Sean Devine twice volleying wide and forcing United's American goalkeeper Tim Howard to make a crucial save. United boss Sir Alex Ferguson was taking few chances after the frustrating 0-0 draw at Old Trafford in the original game, and consequently named a strong starting line-up, including seasoned campaigners like Paul Scholes and Ryan Giggs as key players in his attacking midfield.

Exeter began brightly with a lively pace and enthusiasm, with midfielder Andrew Roscoe and Steve Flack seeing early shots go just wide of the target, much to the delight of the packed home crowd. However, it did not take United long to assert their authority and their superior quality began to tell, with the hosts soon found themselves a goal down. Paul Scholes orchestrated a superb move, delivering a lovely pass in to Ronaldo on the left-hand side of the penalty area - and the nimble Portuguese winger coolly slotted the ball between the spread legs of Jones to open the scoring and settle United's early nerves.

United had several opportunities to finish the tie as a contest, pushing for a second goal, but a powerful shot from Ronaldo blazed over before Jones saved from Scholes from point-blank range. The visitors' pressure was unrelenting and Paul Scholes had another goal-bound shot blocked while Wayne Rooney slammed over the bar again from a good scoring position. Despite United's dominance, in first-half stoppage time Exeter had their best spell of the match and a genuine goal-scoring opportunity as Alex Jeannin swung in a dangerous cross from the left wing, which Sean Devine managed to bravely flick towards goalwards, but the ball flew wide of Tim Howard's goal, sending a ripple of anxiety through the United bench.

The home side came out after the interval in determined fashion and started the second half strongly, with Howard having to show safe hands to confidently collect two searching crosses into the United box, as Exeter pressed for an equaliser. Rooney looked like he might finally seal the result with a powerful shot from the edge of the area, but the heavy in the St James Park mud slowed the ball considerably, allowing Jones to raced back to gather it on his goalline, preventing a certain goal. Moments later Louis Saha had a golden chance to make a telling difference, but he only managed to head Paul Scholes' brilliant cross wide of Jones' goal after being six yards out, a costly miss from close range.

After Rooney had completely mishit a free-kick 20 yards out, Exeter midfielder Andy Taylor then showed him how it should be, his superb shot from distance forcing a stop from a diving Howard. The home fans were clamouring for an equaliser and they did believe they had found the ball into the net only for Devine's well-taken effort to be ruled out for an obvious offside decision, much to the frustration of the Exeter faithful. However, United finally put the game to bed when the persistent Wayne Rooney rounded Jones with three minutes to go and slotted the ball into an empty net to secure a home tie with Middlesbrough in the fourth round.

The group's survey of export orders picked up in the last three months of 2004 to their highest levels in five years. The rise in sterling's exchange rate being cited as a major concern. However, the BCC found the whole economy still faced "major risks" and warned that growth was set to slow. It forecasted economic growth would slow from more than 3% in 2004 to a rate below 2.5% in 2005 and 2006.

Manufacturers' domestic sales growth fell back in the quarter, the survey of 5,196 firms found. Employment in manufacturing fell and was at its lowest for over a year.

"Despite some positive news for the export sector, there are worrying signs for manufacturing," the BCC said. "These results reinforce our concerns over the economy's ability to sustain strong growth."

The outlook for the service sector was also "modest" despite a slowdown in exports and orders in the quarter, the BCC added.

The BCC reported that during the quarter both the manufacturing and service sectors saw activity fall, although overall levels failed to reach those seen at the start of 2004. The reduced threat of interest rate increases had led to improved confidence, it said. The Bank of England raised interest rates five times between November 2003 and August last year. But rates have been kept on hold since then amid signs of falling consumer confidence and slowdown in output.

"Pressure on costs, the increase in regulations, the threat of higher taxes remain serious," director general David Frost said. "While consumer spending is set to decelerate significantly over the next 12-18 months, it is unlikely that investment and exports will grow sufficiently strongly to pick up the slack."

Microsoft gets into the blogging game. The software giant is set to plunge into the world of blogging. It is launching a test service to allow people to publish their own personal blogs, online, called Spaces. Microsoft is somewhat behind established rivals like Google and AOL, which already offer services that make it easy for people to set up their own web logs and online journals. Blogs, short for web logs, have become a popular way for people to write about their lives and express opinions on a wide array of subjects.

Spaces is free to anyone with a Hotmail or MSN Messenger account. Users will be able to choose from a selection of layouts for the page, upload images and share photo albums, and other media files. The service will be supported by banner ads displayed prominently on each blog page. "This is a tool for people to express themselves creatively and freely," said MSN's general manager, Blake.

This is Microsoft's first significant move into blogging, which has taken off as a major web phenomenon in the last few years, attracting millions of daily users. Companies like Google already offer free services through its Blogger site, for example, and AOL provides its members with online journals.

Accurate figures for the number of blogs in existence are hard to come by due to the rapid pace of creation and deletion. According to blog analysis firm Technorati, the so-called blogosphere has doubled in the last five and a half months and grown five-fold in the past 18 months. Technorati estimates that the number of blogs in existence has reached 4.8 million worldwide, though some speculate that less than a quarter are still regularly active or maintained.

Prime Minister's critics were vociferous, asking: So who, if anyone, truly is playing politics with the security of the nation? Michael Howard has absolutely no doubt it is the Prime Minister, who is, "ramming" through Parliament controversial anti-terror measures without adequate time for proper debate or scrutiny. That's not necessarily so, the Tories believe the Prime Minister is playing the fear card so he can look tough in the run up to the general election. And they believe Tony Blair is using the issue to accuse them of being soft on terrorism. Why on earth wouldn't the Prime Minister simply take up the Tories' offer to extend the powers temporarily and allow for a full and proper debate of the laws, he wondered aloud? The Prime Minister is giving every clear indication it is the Tories who are playing fast and loose with this issue by attempting to score cheap political points in parliament. Is the opposition against the proposed laws "in principle", in which case delaying a final decision for further debate would indeed be a more democratic and sensible approach? What this whole affair is truly about, believes Mr Blair, is simply the Tories spotting an opportunity to embarrass, undermine, maybe even defeat the government. That is far more important to them than the actual content of the legislation itself.

Liberal Democrat leader Charles Kennedy was also accused by some of playing politics with the very serious issue at hand. He preferred that, as with other similar contentious matters like identity cards, the government's immediate instinct was authoritarian and overly controlling. As is his usual style nowadays, the Prime Minister was rough with him, as he very often is with Howard - adopting an exasperated tone, suggesting he believes the Lib Dems have, once again, just completely missed the point. Apart from all that, it was more or less business as usual. The very first backbench question to the Prime Minister from Derby's Bob Laxton asked him, rather pointedly, if he would carry on the excellent work and commitment of pouring more resources into schools. Later, Labour MP Sion Simon went so far as to claim openly the Tories were a shower and declared vociferously that we should have a snap general election now. The almost unbearable tension over the election date was palpable. But this was certainly not the appropriate place to make such a momentous announcement that day, he stammered. But can anyone be in any doubt that the actual announcement is only a matter of days away - an announcement expected during the week beginning 4 April for a snap election on 5 May is where the big money is currently being placed across the board. And perhaps this simple undeniable fact means everyone is seen playing politics with just about everything at this particular juncture in time.

reconstruction:
UK games industry veteran and computer games maker Peter Molyneux has been honoured in the New Year list. The head of Surrey's Lionhead Studios was granted the OBE for services to the computer games industry. Mr Molyneux has been behind some of the most successful and genre-defining games of the last 15 years, including Populous, Theme Park, Dungeon Keeper and the innovative Black & White. He is widely credited with pioneering and popularising the so-called god-game genre.

Speaking to the BBC website, Mr Molyneux said the honour was a complete surprise. "It's truly come out of the blue," he said, "I never would have guessed in a million years that I'd have that kind of honour bestowed upon me." He said he was surprised as much by the timing as by the recognition itself, noting that not long ago, many people thought computer gaming was a passing fad. "They used to dismiss it like a craze that everyone thought would just go away," he said. "However," he added, "the gaming world now stands proudly alongside the movie industry as a major force for cultural impact."

"Britain plays a crucial and pioneering part in it," he said, referring to the UK's significant contribution. "Indeed, it's one of the founding nations that has helped to make the industry what it is today." Mr Molyneux has been pivotal in the computer games industry for almost 20 years. His career really took off at Bullfrog Studios, which he co-founded, and which in 1987 produced Populous, widely regarded as one of the first and most influential of the God-games. The title famously gave players control over the lives of a small population of people, who would build their own settlements and worship the player as a deity. Molyneux said that his deep involvement with the industry started as far back as a time when, in the very early days, game making was widely considered more a hobby than a serious career.

"I honestly thought everyone would treat Populous as something quite weird," he recalled, "but to my surprise and delight, it became a huge and unexpected success." He eventually left Bullfrog in 1997 to set up a new venture, Lionhead Studios, which quickly went on to produce the highly ambitious and widely acclaimed fantasy game Black & White. One of the eagerly anticipated next titles to emerge from Lionhead puts players directly in charge of a bustling movie studio, challenging and tasking them with producing a hit film. The renowned games maker says he still has one pressing problem to solve. "Being an absolute, unrepentant geek," he chuckled, "I've got absolutely no idea what I'm going to wear when I go and pick up this tremendous honour," he said.

reconstruction:
Tories quango blitz plans. Plans to abolish 162 quangos have been unveiled by the Conservatives as part of their radical proposals for how government can be run more efficiently. The abolition of these "quasi-autonomous non-governmental organisations", Tories say, would save more than £4.3bn. This sweeping reform aims to tackle what the party describes as an overgrown and unaccountable state.

Among the key targets are strategic health authorities, responsible for overseeing NHS services, and the new Office for Fair Access (OFFA), the access regulator for universities. Shadow frontbencher John Redwood said that Britain urgently needed a slimmer and lower cost state to be competitive in the global economy, arguing that excessive bureaucracy was stifling economic growth and burdening taxpayers.

The plans would abolish regional assemblies and other regional bodies, as well as various boards tackling development and housing across the country. Their powers would be reallocated, either devolved to local councils to enhance democratic accountability, or transferred to national government departments for greater strategic coherence. The Conservatives argue that this shift will bring decision-making closer to the people and eliminate redundant layers of administration.

Specifically on health, they say health authorities are not needed, arguing it is better that local people, rather than remote officials, have direct control over hospitals and surgeries. This, they suggest, would lead to more responsive and patient-focused healthcare services, cutting through red tape and empowering communities.

Announcing the bold proposals, Mr Redwood launched a strong attack on the government, stating: "Mr Gordon Brown has forgotten the hardworking interests of taxpayers, and broken the pledges he made on public spending. Far from improving public services, taxpayers' money has led only to more bureaucrats, more regulation and ever-increasing taxes." He criticised the Labour government for presiding over a period of public sector expansion that, in his view, had delivered poor value for money and failed to deliver genuine improvements.

His leader, David Cameron, reinforced the message, arguing a fundamental change in direction was required to get a firm grip on spending. "This is the Britain of the forgotten, burdened by a bureaucratic state," he said. He painted a picture of ordinary citizens struggling under the weight of government, adding: "Meanwhile, people are working harder. They've seen their pensions knocked for six by a volatile economy. They're being squeezed by taxes. The forgotten are paying the price of bureaucratic Britain, and it's a price we can no longer afford." Mr Cameron’s comments underscored the party's focus on fiscal responsibility and reducing the tax burden on families.

The government has, for its part, announced plans to cut 100,000 civil servants as part of its own efficiency drive. But Chief Secretary to the Treasury, Paul Boateng, sharply criticised the Conservative plans, dismissing them as unworkable and irresponsible. "The Conservatives are committed to cutting public spending by an estimated £35 billion," Mr Boateng warned. "Cuts on this massive scale cannot possibly be found from 'bureaucracy' alone but would inevitably require severe cuts to front-line services such as schools, hospitals and police. Their figures simply do not add up, and their proposals would devastate vital public services." He accused the Tories of making false promises to the electorate.

The Liberal Democrats said they would also cut the number of Whitehall departments in a bid to make sure funding directly reaches front-line services. While sharing concerns about inefficiency, their approach emphasized streamlining central government rather than wholesale abolition of arm's-length bodies.

Tories say health authorities are not needed and it is better that local people, rather than officials, run hospitals and surgeries. Announcing the plans, Mr Redwood said: "Mr Blair has forgotten the plight of taxpayers, and broken the pledges he made." Far from improving public services, taxpayers' money has led only to more bureaucrats, more regulation and higher taxes." His leader, Mr Duncan Smith, argued a change in direction was needed to get a grip on spending. "This is the Britain of the forgotten bureaucratic," he said. "All over the country, people are working harder. They've seen their pensions knocked for six. They're being squeezed by taxes. The forgotten are paying the price of bureaucratic Britain." The government has announced plans to cut 100,000 civil servants as part of its efficiency drive. But Chief Secretary to the Treasury Paul Boateng criticised the plans. "The Conservatives are committed to cutting public spending by a further £35 billion,". "Cuts on this scale cannot be found from' bureaucracy' but would require cuts to front-line services such as schools, hospitals and police." The Liberal Democrats said they would cut the number of Whitehall departments to make sure money reaches frontline services.

reconstruction:
For the first time ever, the number of surfers using Microsoft's Internet Explorer (IE) has dropped to below 90%, say web analysts.

Net traffic monitor, OneStat.com, reported that open-source web browser Firefox 1.0, released on 9 November 2004, appears to be drawing away IE. While IE's market share has fallen by almost 5% to 88.9%, rival browsers - primarily Firefox - have grown by around 5%.

Firefox is made by the California-based Mozilla Foundation which was set up by browser maker Netscape in 1998. Although there have been some other versions of Firefox, version 1.0 was the first complete and official public release.

"It seems that many users are now switching from Microsoft's Internet Explorer to the increasingly popular new Firefox," said Niels Brinkman, the co-founder of the Amsterdam-based web analytics firm, OneStat. Collectively, other browsers - including Firefox 1.0 - have captured 7.4% of the market, the figures suggest.

The Mozilla Foundation said that more than five million copies of its free software had been downloaded globally since its official release. Supporters of the open-source software in the US managed to raise $250,000 (£133,000) to advertise the release of Firefox 1.0 with a full-page advertisement in The New York Times, according to the Mozilla Foundation. There was a record million downloads on its first day of release.

The figures echo a recent report from US-based net analyst firm WebSideStory which suggested IE had 92.9% of users in October and a higher figure of 95.5% in January. Microsoft has dominated the browser market for some time after taking the crown from Netscape, and its market share has always stayed at around the 95% mark.

Firefox is proving attractive to many users because it is open-source. That means people are free to adapt the software's core code to incorporate other innovative features, like new add-ons or to significantly customise the program. Fewer security holes have also been identified so far in Firefox than in IE.

Adam Randle, Microsoft Windows product manager, in his response to the figures, said: "We certainly respect that customers choose alternative browsers and that is about more than a handful of features."

"Microsoft continues to make significant investments in IE, including the recent release of Service Pack 2 with advanced security, and continues to encourage a vibrant community and selection of third-party add-ons for Internet Explorer."

The Mozilla Foundation wants 10% of the market by the end of 2005. Other competitors, like Opera and Apple's Safari, are also challenging IE's long-held dominance on the market. Opera is expected to release its latest version, 7.60, by the end of the year.

OneStat.com compiled the statistical data for this report from net users in 100 countries.
