reconstruction:
Watchdog probes reports of e-mail deletions. The Information Commissioner, Richard Thomas, is urgently asking for details of orders telling staff to delete e-mails more than three months old. Mr Thomas has strongly condemned the "totally unacceptable" deletion of official e-mails to prevent their release under freedom laws before the Act comes into force on January 1. Government records should only be deleted if they served "no purpose", Mr Thomas said.

The Tories and the Lib Dems have questioned the wisdom of the new rules. Tory leader Michael Howard has written to Tony Blair demanding new rules on official e-mail retention. On Monday, Lib Dem constitutional affairs spokesman Lord Beith warned that the deletion of emails by government departments could harm the ability of key public inquiries like the Hutton Inquiry. The timing of the new rules just before the Freedom of Information Act comes into force was "too perfectly timed to have been coincidence", Mr Beith said.

But a Cabinet Office spokesman said the policy was in line with the new laws or to prevent "the destruction of important records". Mr Beith urged the Information Commissioner to look at the government's "e-mail regime" to ensure it could fully support the freedom of information regime.

Mr Thomas said: "The new Act makes it very clear that it is an offence to destroy records in order to prevent their disclosure, and doing so could lead to a criminal prosecution."

Recent guidance was also issued on the retention of official e-mails in a code of practice from the Information Commissioner. E-mails are subject to the freedom of information laws, no matter how sensitive or trivial the content of the e-mail, said Mr Thomas.

"If in doubt retain, that has been the long-standing principle of the civil service and other public authorities. That is, unless you've got no further legitimate administrative use or legal requirement for the particular record that it may represent, then it may be considered for deletion."

But any deliberate action taken with the intent to prevent the possibility of later disclosure is to be totally condemned.

The Freedom of Information Act, which comes into force in England, Wales and Northern Ireland from January 1 next year, will mark a significant change in public access to official documents. Similar measures are being brought in at the same time in Scotland. The legislation gives the public a right of access to information held by about 100,000 public bodies, subject to various exemptions. Its implementation will be monitored by the Information Commissioner and his office.

reconstruction: The extensive art portfolio of fashion designer Gianni Versace is up for sale. The collection is expected to fetch up to £9m ($17m) when it is auctioned in New York and London later this year. Among the pictures for sale are works by Roy Lichtenstein, Andy Warhol and Henri Matisse. The collection was formerly housed at Versace's lavish, eight-storey New York townhouse. The 51-year-old designer was shot dead at his home in 1997 by serial killer Andrew Cunanan, who later killed himself. The auction, at Sotheby's, will feature some 45 contemporary, modern and 19th Century paintings. One of the key highlights of the sale is Roy Lichtenstein's iconic 'Blue Nude' which has been given an estimate of £1.8m ($3.4m). Tobias Meyer, Sotheby's worldwide head of contemporary art, said: "The collection perfectly reflects Mr Versace's wide-ranging taste and impeccable eye, and many of the pieces were commissioned directly by the designer himself. Outstanding later examples from champions of the Pop Art movement, such as Roy Lichtenstein, are juxtaposed with masterpieces from the most influential artists of the 1980s, including Jean-Michel Basquiat and the striking works of Julian Schnabel, as well as Cindy Sherman." Sullivan has spent two days being vigorously cross-examined by lawyers for former WorldCom chief executive Bernard Ebbers. Attorney Reid Weingarten sought aggressively to portray Sullivan as a pathological liar and on Thursday he quizzed him extensively about his decision to commit massive fraud to meet analysts' profit estimates. Prosecutors allege that the company's senior executives responded to this crisis by orchestrating a massive accounting fraud over a crucial two-year period. WorldCom finally emerged from bankruptcy protection in 2004, and is now operating under the name MCI. original: Jackson film 'absolute disaster'..A PR expert has told the Michael Jackson child abuse trial that the TV documentary at the heart of the case was an "absolute disaster"...Ann Kite told the court in the Californian town of Santa Maria she was hired to "crisis manage" the fallout after the programme had aired in 2003. Jurors saw the film, in which the pop star held hands with the alleged victim, on Tuesday. Mr Jackson denies 10 charges of child abuse and false imprisonment. If convicted, he could face up to 21 years in prison...Ms Kite suggested Jackson's associates had been intent on launching a smear campaign against the accuser's family after the airing of Martin Bashir's film Living with Michael Jackson. She told the court that in the aftermath of the broadcast, a Jackson lawyer had told her the boy's mother would be made to look like a "crack whore". Jackson's defence questioned Ms Kite's credibility, pointing that she worked for the singer's team for less than a week before being fired, and had never met or spoken to the star...Ms Kite said she received a phone call on 13 February 2003 from a Jackson associate, Marc Schaffel, who said the boy and his family had left the Neverland ranch where they had been staying...Ms Kite told the court she had later asked Jackson's lawyer, David LeGrand, what had happened. "I said, `Don't make me believe that these people were hunted down like dogs and brought back to the ranch'," she said. Ms Kite began to work for Mr Jackson in February 2003, after the controversial film was televised in the US and Europe. The documentary sparked a media storm and the subsequent investigation into Mr Jackson's relationship with the boy. In the film, the singer said he did not see anything wrong with sharing a bed with a child...Questioned by the prosecution, Ms Kite said her plan had been to move media coverage of the star away from a focus on his human frailties to concentrate more on his musical genius. Ms Kite said that an additional problem was the release of documents relating to a previous allegation of child abuse against Mr Jackson. The Smoking Gun website publication was "beyond disaster", Ms Kite said. Correspondents say the reference is important because it was unclear whether the prosecution would be able to bring up the previous case in front of the jury...The judge is studying whether the prosecution's first witness, reporter Martin Bashir, is in contempt of court. The defence protested after Mr Bashir, who interviewed Jackson for the TV documentary, refused to answer nearly all their questions, citing a California "shield" law intended to allow journalists to protect their sources. In the prosecution's opening statement on Monday, Tom Sneddon told the court that Mr Jackson had shown the boy porn and plied him with wine, in order to molest him. original: Macy's owner buys rival for $11bn..US retail giant Federated Department Stores is to buy rival May Department Stores for $11bn (£5.7bn)...The deal will bring together famous stores like Macy's, Bloomingdale's and Marshall Field's, creating the largest department store chain in the US. The combined firm will operate about 1,000 stores across the US, with combined annual sales of $30bn. The two companies, facing competition from the likes of Wal-Mart, tried to merge two years ago but talks failed. Sources familiar with the deal said that negotiations between the two companies sped up after May's chairman and chief executive Gene Kahn resigned in January. As part of the deal, Federated - owner of Macy's and Bloomingdale's - will assume $6bn of May's debt, bringing the deal's total value to $17bn. Directors at both companies have approved the deal and it is expected to conclude by the third quarter of this year...May has struggled to compete against larger department store groups such as Federated and other retailers such as Wal-Mart. Federated expects the merger to boost earnings from 2007 but the deal will cost it $1bn in one-off charges..."We have taken the first step toward combining two of the best department store companies in America, creating a new retail company with truly national scope and presence," said Terry Lundgren, Federated's chairman. Some analysts see the merger as a rescue deal for May. "Without this deal May would have been, to put it bluntly, washed up," said Kurt Barnard, president of Barnard's Retail Consulting Group. Federated has annual sales of $15.6bn, while May's yearly sales are $14.4bn.

original: Wi-fi web reaches farmers in Peru..A network of community computer centres, linked by wireless technology, is providing a helping hand for poor farmers in Peru...The pilot scheme in the Huaral Valley, 80 kilometres north of the capital Lima, aims to offer the 6,000-strong community up-to-date information on agricultural market prices and trends. The Agricultural Information Project for Farmers of the Chancay-Huaral Valley also provides vital links between local organisations in charge of water irrigation, enabling them to coordinate their actions. More than 13,000 rural inhabitants, as well as 18,000 students in the region, will also benefit from the telecoms infrastructure...The 14 telecentres uses only free open source software and affordable computer equipment. The network has been three years in the making and was officially inaugurated in September...The non-government organisation, Cepes (Peruvian Centre for Social Studies) led the $200,000 project, also backed by local institutions, the Education and Agriculture ministries, and European development organisations. "The plan includes training on computers and internet skills for both operators and users of the system," said Carlos Saldarriaga, technical coordinator at Cepes. Farmers are also taking extra lessons on how to apply the new information to make the most of their plots of land. The Board of Irrigation Users which runs the computer centres, aims to make the network self-sustainable within three years, through the cash generated by using the telecentres as internet cafes...One of the key elements of the project is the Agricultural Information System, with its flagship huaral.org website. There, farmers can find the prices for local produce, as well as information on topics ranging from plague prevention to the latest farming techniques. The system also helps the inhabitants of the Chancay-Huaral Valley to organise their vital irrigation systems. "Water is the main element that unites them all. It is a precious element in Peru's coastal areas, because it is so scarce, and therefore it is necessary to have proper irrigation systems to make the most of it," Mr Saldarriaga told the BBC News website. The information network also allows farmers to look beyond their own region, and share experiences with other colleagues from the rest of Peru and even around the world...Cepes says the involvement of the farmers has been key in the project's success. "Throughout the last three years, the people have provided a vital thrust to the project; they feel it belongs to them," said Mr Saldarriaga. The community training sessions, attended by an equal number of men and women, have been the perfect showcase for their enthusiasm. "We have had an excellent response, mainly from young people. But we have also had a great feedback when we trained 40 or 50-year old women, who were seeing a computer for the first time in their lives." So far, the Huaral programme promoters say the experience has been very positive, and are already planning on spreading the model among other farmers' organisations in Peru. reconstruction:
Wi-fi web reaches remote and underserved communities in Peru. A network of community computer centres, linked by wireless technology, is providing a helping hand for farmers in the agricultural heartland of the Huaral Valley. The pilot project, located in the Huaral Valley, approximately 80 kilometres north of the capital, Lima, aims to offer the 6,000-strong farming community access to up-to-date agricultural market prices. The Agricultural Information Project for Farmers of Chancay-Huaral Valley also provides crucial links between local organisations involved in the management of water irrigation, enabling them to effectively coordinate actions. More than 13,000 rural inhabitants, as well as 18,000 students in the region, also stand to benefit significantly from this new digital infrastructure. The 14 telecentres operate using only free open source software systems and cost-effective computer equipment. The network has been under development for several years in the making and was finally launched through the efforts of... The non-government organisation, Cepes (Centre for Social Studies) led a significant funding effort amounting to $200,000, also backed by local institutions, including the Ministries of Education and Agriculture, and the European Union, which provided additional support.

"The comprehensive plan includes training programmes focusing on computers and the effective use of the internet for both operators and users of the system," said Carlos Saldarriaga, the project's coordinator. Farmers are actively taking extra lessons on how to implement new methods to make the best possible use of their limited plots of land. Furthermore, a dedicated Board of Users which oversees and manages each individual computer terminal, aims to make the network self-sustainable within a relatively short timeframe, utilizing the cash generated by using the community centres as cafes or public internet access points for a small fee. One of the absolutely key elements of this entire project is the innovative Agricultural Information System, with its dedicated .org website. Through this online portal, farmers can readily access the latest prices for local produce, as well as essential information on a wide range of topics from effective plague prevention to the most advanced farming techniques. The system also empowers inhabitants of the Chancay-Huaral Valley region to organise their vital irrigation schedules more efficiently.

"Water is absolutely essential for life for all. It is a precious element in these particularly dry and often arid areas, because it is so scarce, and it is therefore necessary to put in place and maintain proper irrigation systems to the benefit of all the local communities," Saldarriaga told the BBC News website. The network also allows farmers to look beyond their own confined valley, and share experiences with other fellow farmers located in various other parts of Peru and indeed around the world. Cepes has been keen to emphasise that the active involvement of the local farmers themselves has been key in the overall project's success.

"Throughout the last several years, the local people have provided a significant thrust to the project; they strongly feel it belongs to them," said Mr Saldarriaga. The community training sessions, attended by an equal number of local men and local women, have been the perfect medium and opportunity to foster their active participation and ownership.

"We have received very encouraging and positive feedback, mainly from young people. And we have had a particularly heartwarming feedback when 40 or 50-year old individuals, were for the first time in their lives able to experience using a computer." So far, the Huaral project coordinators say experience has been very positive, and they are already planning on replicating and expanding the model among other remote communities across the entirety of Peru.

"This is a truly pioneering project, and we have been very keen to explore its potential in other geographical regions and similar contexts," underlined Mr Saldarriaga. The Cepes coordinator recalls a remarkable incident that happened in Cuyo, a 50-family community that previously had no electricity, during the construction of a telecentre site. It was necessary to build a micro-hydraulic dam in order to generate 2kW worth of electrical power for the computers, the communications equipment and cabin lights.

"It was already dark when the technicians realised they didn't have any light to test the generator, so they turned to the local store to buy light bulbs," recalls Carlos Saldarriaga. "The answer was 'we don't sell any', so they had to wait until the next day to do the testing." Now, with the wireless network, Cuyo as well as other remote communities is no longer living in digital isolation.

original: Brown to outline presidency goals..Next year will be "make or break" for development in poorer countries Gordon Brown will say as he sets out UK goals for its EU and G8 presidencies...The chancellor is due to outline a series of key targets the government will be judged on in 2005. They will include doubling aid from donor countries and eliminating debt owed by the poorest nations. Mr Brown also wants other G8 nations to match his target for overseas aid - spending 0.7% of national income...He also wants the richer countries to do more to help the development of vaccines for Aids and malaria. The chancellor is travelling to America next week as part of his persuasion drive over the issue. He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "We need more resources allied to progress on trade and progress on debt relief if we are going to make an impact on the problems of ill health, of illiteracy, of poverty, particularly in Africa but right through the developing countries."..His proposals were effectively a new "Marshall Plan" for the world, including an international finance facility, which would issue bonds in an attempt to double global aid cash to $100bn a year. Agreement in the Doha development talks could also give developing nations the trading ability they needed, he argued. The European Union's Common Agricultural Policy had caused aggravated trade problems, he said, but there was now an agreement to end export subsidies...Mr Brown said much had been achieved on issues such as debt relief in the last seven years. But with 30,000 children were dying unnecessarily every day more was needed, including 100% debt relief multilaterally. "That is why next year is a test," he said. "If after five years of making promises the world is not prepared to honour them, then people will be justified in saying they promised but they did not produce results." The Catholic aid agency Cafod will host Mr Brown's speech on Wednesday...Cafod wants Britain to use its influence to pressure countries like the US to make firm commitments to tackle global poverty. Mr Brown said America too needed to take more action but defended President George Bush for guaranteeing resources to countries which introduced reforms to tackle corruption. Oxfam's Paying the Price report this week said 45 million children will die needlessly before 2015 and aid budgets are half their 1960 levels. The charity's director, Barbara Stocking, said: "2005 offers the chance for an historic breakthrough, but unless world leaders act now the year will end in shameful failure." The report said the G8 of top industrialised nations had agreed in 1970 to spend 0.7% of their incomes on aid...But 34 years later none of the organisations members had reached this target and many had not yet set a timetable. Mr Blair, who has described Africa as a "scar" on the world's conscience, has already said tackling world poverty would be one his G8 priorities along with climate change and the Aids epidemic. But Band Aid founder Bob Geldof in July said he was sick of hearing "guff" about scars on the world. It was pathetic that Britain was the 4th richest country in the world but only the 11th most generous aid donor, he added. Conservative shadow international development secretary Alan Duncan accused Mr Brown of missing his target on providing anti-retroviral drug treatment to three million Africans by 2005. Instead, only 500,000 people would benefit, he said. "There's no point in him demanding praise and adulation for setting a whole new raft of targets when he has so woefully failed to meet the ones he already has," added Mr Duncan.

Global blogger action day. The global web blog community is being called into action in support of two imprisoned Iranian bloggers, Mojtaba Saminejad and Arash Sigarchi. The one-month- old Committee to Protect Bloggers' is asking blogs to dedicate their sites on 22 February to the "Mojtaba Arash Day". Sigarchi and Saminejad are both in prison in Iran, held without clear charges for online writings. Blogs are digital platforms which express thoughts and opinions to a global audience. Iranian authorities have been cracking down on prominent online voices for some time. This is widely seen as an attempt to stifle dissent. "I hope this day will focus attention on these detained people," Curt Hopkins, director of the Committee, told the BBC News website. He highlighted escalating censorship and risks faced by online journalists.

The actions which it says bloggers can take include writing to local Iranian embassies to demand their release. The Committee has dubbed Tuesday "Free Mojtaba Arash Day" as part of its first campaign to galvanise global support. It is calling on the blogsphere- the name for the worldwide community of bloggers- to do what it can to help raise awareness of the plight of Mojtaba and Arash as well as other "net-dissidents" facing similar persecution. "If you have a blog, the least you could do is put up a post or link on that blog 'Free Mojtaba and Arash'," said Mr Hopkins. He noted the powerful collective impact. "That way you could see that phrase 7. 1 million times. That alone would shed some light on their struggle and pressure authorities." He added, "If you don' have one, find a blog to link to that- it takes 30 seconds." This aims to create a significant virtual protest.

Technorati, a search engine focused on blogs, tracks six million blogs and says more than 12, 000 are created daily. A blog is created every 5. 8 seconds, according to a US think-tank, Perseus Development, illustrating the rapid growth of the blogosphere.

The Committee to Protect Bloggers was started by blogger Hopkins and counts fired blogger Ellen Simonetti as a member. She since started the International Bloggers' Bill of Rights, a petition to protect bloggers at work from unfair dismissal or censorship. Although not the only website to address free speech rights issues by any means, the Committee aims to be a central hub organisation, information and support for bloggers in particular and their right to freedom of speech globally. It seeks to provide assistance and a network for bloggers facing threats.

The Committee, although only recently formed, hopes to be a focal point for action on similar cases of online censorship in the future, and will operate as a non-profit organisation. "Blogging is this weird no man' s land. People think of it as being one thing or another depending on their definition of it," said Mr Hopkins. "Some see bloggers as citizen journalists, others as simply online publishers." "Some think of bloggers kind of like journalists, and some like me view it as a platform." But they do a lot of important work, often at personal risk, and are out there in the cold, without institutional backing.

It addresses free speech rights issues in countries which have a track record of suppression of independent voices. The information in the media is often of concern to bloggers. The rights of bloggers and what they have to say on their blogs is a thorny issue and has much potential for controversy. High-profile cases where employees have been sacked for what they have posted on personal websites, and blogs, have highlighted the precarious situation that the blogosphere currently faces. These incidents underscore the need for clear guidelines and legal protections.

"It's a big messy situation," explained Mr Hopkins. He added: "It is just such a new way of doing business, so there will be clampdowns from authorities and employers." But the issues ultimately get tested is through courts which, said Mr Hopkins, "are a vital part of the whole conversation about free speech." "If haven' t already protected bloggers in your company, you will have to address them tomorrow- you don' have a social media policy now you had better start looking for one. Mr Hopkins said the blogosphere- is doubling every five months- was powerful because it doesn't take so much time or specialised expertise to create a blog."

"Everyone does- mums, radicals, conservatives," he said. Many companies offer easy- to- use software to create a blog and distribute it to a global audience. "Accessibility is the essential element. What I call 'templating software' gives every single person on Earth the chance to have a blog." You' don't even need to host your own.

The 71-year-old served in Northern Ireland from 1981 to 1987 during the premiership of Margaret Thatcher. As a Northern Ireland minister he dealt with education and later security where he rode out the mass IRA escape from the Maze in 1983...In education, he encountered criticism over school closures and the future of the Catholic training colleges. He also merged the New University of Ulster and the Ulster Polytechnic to create the University of Ulster. Sir Nicholas was replaced as the member for Kensington and Chelsea by the flamboyant Alan Clark, after being deselected by his constituency in December 1996. His deselection followed a series of scandals including being found slumped in the street by police during the Tory Party conference in Bournemouth and taken back to his hotel...Sir Nicholas claimed strong painkillers he was taking for a back problem had reacted badly with a small amount of alcohol. Former Northern Ireland minister Sir Nicholas Scott has died aged 71 in a London hospice. The Conservative MP for Kensington and Chelsea had been diagnosed with Alzheimer's.

The 71-year-old served in Northern Ireland from 1981 to 1987 at the Northern Ireland Office. While in Northern Ireland he dealt with education and later security, managing the fallout from the mass escape from the Maze Prison in 1983.

In education, he encountered criticism over school closures and the future of Catholic teacher training. He also oversaw the merger of the New University of Ulster and Ulster Polytechnic to create Ulster University.

Sir Nicholas was a strong defender of Anglo-Irish relations and was held in high esteem by the Dublin government and officials. However, he experienced strong opposition from some within his own party, of whom he famously called "Sons of Discord".

After leaving Northern Ireland in a reshuffle, he became a UK minister. Sir Nicholas was replaced as the member for Chelsea by Alan Clark, after being deselected by his constituency in December 1996. His deselection followed a series of incidents, including being found in the street by police at the Tory conference in Bournemouth and taken to his hotel.

Nicholas said painkillers he was taking for a back problem had reacted badly with a small amount of alcohol. After his sacking, he said bitterly that despite the support of Cabinet and Tory grandees, Eurosceptics in his party were "absolutely determined to get rid of me".

His career included a very public disagreement with his daughter Victoria over rights for the disabled. Sir Nicholas was accused of misleading Parliament when he denied his department had used wrecking tactics to kill the Disability Bill in 1994. Victoria, a lobbyist for disabled rights, condemned her father's actions and joined calls for him to resign. He joined the backbenches months later.

In the 20 years since that day, mobiles have become an integral part of life and now 90% of Britons own a handset. They have become so popular that many use their handset as their main phone, rather than use a landline.

The first call over a portable phone was made in 1973 in New York, but it took 10 years for the commercial mobile network to be launched. The UK was not far behind the rest of the world in setting up networks in 1985 that let people make calls while they walked. The first call went from St Katherine's dock to Vodafone's headquarters in Newbury, which at the time was above a curry house. For the first nine days of 1985, Vodafone was the only firm with a mobile network in the UK. Then, on 10 January, Cellnet (now O2) launched its service.

Mike Dolan, a Vodafone spokesman, said that when phones first launched they were the size of a briefcase, cost £2,000 and had a battery life of no more than 20 minutes. "Despite this, they were hugely popular in the mid-80s," he said. "They became a must-have gadget and a status symbol among young business folk." This was because they used analogue signals to communicate, which made it easy to eavesdrop. He said it took Vodafone four years to sign up its first million customers, but Cellnet took just 18 months. "It's very easy to forget that in 1983 when we put the bid document in, we were a total of just two people," he said. "Cellnet was forecasting half that." Vodafone now has 14m customers in the UK alone.

Vodafone and Cellnet were the only mobile operators in the UK until 1993, when One2One (now T-Mobile) launched. Orange UK launched in 1994. Both these new entrants operated digital mobile networks and now all operators use this technology, which superseded the analogue spectrum the old networks had. Called Global System for Mobiles (GSM), this is now used by every mobile phone on the planet and helps more than 1.2 billion people make calls.

Mr Caudwell said the advent of digital technology also enabled them to introduce all those things, such as text messaging and roaming, that made mobile phones so popular.

Savvy shoppers are also using the net to find the hot presents that are all but sold out in High Street stores...Almost half of the UK population now shop online according to figures collected by the Interactive Media in Retail Group which represents web retailers. original: Voters 'don't trust politicians'..Eight out of 10 voters do not trust politicians to tell the truth, a new poll conducted for the BBC suggests...And 87% of the 1,000 adults quizzed by ICM for BBC News 24 said politicians did not deliver what they promised. The poll comes after Foreign Secretary Jack Straw predicted trust would be "the key choice" at the next election. Both the Tories and the Lib Dems are keen to emphasise a perceived lack of trust in Tony Blair, following his claims over Iraqi weapons...But according to the BBC poll, 61% said the issue of trust made no difference to whether or not they would vote at the next election, widely expected on 5 May. The poll also looked at what lay behind the lack of trust in politicians. Some 87% said politicians did not keep the promises they made before elections, while 92% said they never gave "a straight answer". Just under three-quarters of respondents (73%) said politicians had shown themselves to be dishonest too often...Mr Straw told activists in Blackburn on Thursday that voters would have to decide at the next election which party "best deserves" their "future trust". "That in the end is the key choice at the next election."..He acknowledged that the public had lost faith in Labour, but suggested it could persuade people to "reinvest their trust with us" if the party could overcome Tory attempts to spread cynicism in politics. The Conservatives are keen to highlight the trust issue. During his response to Gordon Brown's Budget statement on Tuesday, Michael Howard compared the chancellor's figures to the prime minister's claims about Iraq's weapons of mass destruction...The Lib Dems are also keen to highlight the trust issue, with Charles Kennedy has claiming voters had a "fundamental lack of trust in the prime minister". And the Green Party unveiled a billboard opposite the Palace of Westminster accusing the government of lying over the Iraq war...Former education secretary Estelle Morris told BBC News 24 that there was a "real problem of trust" between the public and the politicians. She said she did not feel her own colleagues could be trusted, but suggested the "three-cornered relationship" between the press, politicians and the public had a hand in the issue. The public was often turned off by sitting on the sidelines in "the battle of words" between the politician and the journalist, she added. Lib Dem foreign affairs spokesman Menzies Campbell said the Iraq war had hit trust in politicians hard. reconstruction:
At a glance: Tory health plans unveiled. The UK's Conservatives have unveiled plans to introduce health checks for immigrants if they are coming to the UK to live and work in Britain from outside the EU.
Here's a guide to the plan:
For those who wish to live and work in Britain from outside the EU, if they plan to stay six months or more and are from a country with lots of TB, they would have a chest x-ray before travelling to the UK.
All people from outside the European Union who intend to come for a year or more will have to undergo a full medical examination.
Tests would be carried out for Tuberculosis, Hepatitis B and HIV. A positive test for TB would automatically mean visa applications being turned down for entry.
All other conditions would be dealt with on a case by case basis by medical professionals.
People would have to prove they are of an acceptable standard, are not a danger to public health, or impose undue costs or demands on the NHS. They would, if appropriate, have to be able to undertake the work or study for which they applied to come here in the United Kingdom.
Those coming to Britain for six months would not be medically tested unless they intended work in health, childcare or teaching. Children and pregnant women wanting to live in permanently would need to have a chest x-ray for TB. Under 16s would not face tests for hepatitis and HIV as part of these checks.
The Tories say people fleeing persecution will not be denied entry in Britain because of poor health. Instead, they undergo health checks to ensure they receive medical treatment and do not spread disease to the wider population.
Their government figures show that the incidence of TB in England has increased by 25% in the last 10 years and two-thirds of these cases were born overseas. They also believe there should be stricter controls on who comes to Britain to ensure that public health is not put at risk. They would limit access to the NHS for those not entitled to it as a general principle.
Applicants must undergo checks in their home country. However, asylum seekers will be tested in the UK once their refugee status is established and approved.
The Home Office already routinely checks people for TB before they come into the UK for six months or more from high-risk countries. Recent medical checks were carried out on 175,000 passengers at Heathrow and 10,000 at Gatwick. From these tests, about 100 infectious cases of TB were found in the last year.
The Tories say 47 other countries have similar requirements of this kind. The party has looked at the way the system works in Australia, Canada and New Zealand to inform their proposals.
The Tory proposals are "quite closely modelled" on the New Zealand system of medical screening.
Labour claims this is more than a "desperate attempt to catch up with Labour's five-year plan" for asylum, which was announced last week. This plan says health checks for TB will be targeted on people from high-risk areas before they are given clearance. Those diagnosed with the disease would then have to seek treatment at home before being allowed into the UK. The Liberal Democrats have said they "are in danger of pandering to prejudice rather than challenging it with effective solutions".

original: Camera phones are 'must-haves'..Four times more mobiles with cameras in them will be sold in Europe by the end of 2004 than last year, says a report from analysts Gartner...Globally, the number sold will reach 159 million, an increase of 104%. The report predicts that nearly 70% of all mobile phones sold will have a built-in camera by 2008. Improving imaging technology in mobiles is making them an increasingly "must-have" buy. In Europe, cameras on mobiles can take 1.3 megapixel images. But in Japan and Asia Pacific, where camera phone technology is much more advanced, mobiles have already been released which can take 3.2 megapixel images. Japan still dominates mobile phone technology, and the uptake there is huge. By 2008, according to Gartner, 95% of all mobiles sold there will have cameras on them...Camera phones had some teething problems when they were first launched as people struggled with poor quality images and uses for them, as well as the complexity and expense of sending them via MMS (Multimedia Messaging Services). This has changed in the last 18 months. Handset makers have concentrated on trying to make phones easier to use. Realising that people like to use their camera phones in different ways, they have introduced more design features, like rotating screens and viewfinders, removable memory cards and easier controls to send picture messages...Mobile companies have introduced more ways for people to share photos with other people. These have included giving people easier ways to publish them on websites, or mobile blogs - moblogs. But the report suggests that until image quality increases more, people will not be interested in printing out pictures at kiosks. Image sensor technology inside cameras phones is improving. The Gartner report suggests that by mid-2005, it is likely that the image resolution of most camera phones will be more than two megapixels. Consumer digital cameras images range from two to four megapixels in quality, and up to six megapixels on a high-end camera. But a lot of work is being done to make camera phones more like digital cameras. Some handsets already feature limited zoom capability, and manufacturers are looking into technological improvements that will let people take more photos in poorly-lit conditions, like nightclubs. Other developments include wide-angle modes, basic editing features, and better sensors and processors for recording film clips...Images from camera phones have even made it into the art world. An exhibition next month in aid of the charity Mencap, will feature snaps taken from the camera phones of top artists...The exhibition, Fonetography, will feature images taken by photographers David Bailey, Rankin and Nan Goldin, and artists Sir Peter Blake, Tracey Emin and Jack Vettriano. But some uses for them have worried many organisations. Intel, Samsung, the UK's Foreign Office and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratories in the US, have decided to ban camera phones from their buildings for fear of sensitive information being snapped and leaked. Many schools, fitness centres and local councils have also banned them over fears about privacy and misuse. Italy's information commissioner has also voiced concern and has issued guidelines on where and how the phones can be used. But camera phone fears have not dampened the manufacturers' profits. According to recent figures, Sony Ericsson's profits tripled in the third-quarter because of new camera phones. Over 60% of mobiles sold during the three months through to September featured integrated cameras, it said.

Camera phones' must-haves' set to grow. Four in ten phones with cameras in them will be sold in Europe by the end of 2004, more than previously thought, says a report from Gartner. Globally, the number will reach 159 million, an increase of 104%. The report predicts 70% of all phones will have a built-in camera by 2008.

Improving camera technology in mobiles is making them an increasingly desirable feature. In Europe, mobiles can currently take 1.3 megapixel images. But in Japan and Asia, where camera technology is much more advanced, mobiles have already been released which take 3.2 megapixel images. Japan still dominates the technology, and the demand is huge. By 2008, according to Gartner, 95% of all phones sold there will have cameras in them.

Camera phones faced some teething problems when they were first launched, such as with poor quality images and limited uses for them, as well as the complexity and expense of sending them via MMS (Multimedia Messaging Service). This has changed over the past 18 months. Handset makers have focused on trying to make phones easier to use. Realising people use their camera phones in different ways, they have introduced innovative design elements, better viewfinders, removable memory cards and easier controls to send messages.

They have introduced more ways for users to share photos. This has included giving people easier ways to upload them to websites, or mobile blogs - moblogs. But the report suggests that until the image quality significantly improves, people will not be interested in printing them out. Sensor technology in camera phones is constantly improving. The report notes that by mid-2005, it is likely that the image resolution of most camera phones will reach two megapixels.

Dedicated digital cameras currently range from two to four megapixels on average, and up to six megapixels on a high-end camera. But a lot of work is being done to make camera phones more like dedicated digital cameras. Some handsets already feature optical zoom capability, and manufacturers are looking into technological innovations that will let users take more photos in poorly-lit conditions, like nightclubs. Other planned features include wide-angle modes, editing features, and improved sensors and processors for capturing video.

Images taken from camera phones have even made it into the art world. An exhibition next month to aid the charity Mencap, will show snaps taken from the camera phones of top artists. 'Fonetography', will feature images by photographers Bailey, Rankin and Lord Snowdon, Sir Peter Blake, Tracey Emin and Jack Vettriano.

Intel, Samsung, the UK's Ministry of Defence and Lawrence Livermore Laboratories in the US, decided to ban them from their buildings for fear sensitive information being snapped and transmitted. Many schools, fitness centres and local authorities have also banned them over fears about privacy and misuse. Italy's information commissioner has voiced concerns and issued guidelines on where and how they can be used.

However, camera phone fears have not hindered manufacturers' profits. According to recent figures, Sony Ericsson's profits surged in the third-quarter because of camera phones. Over 60% of mobiles sold during the period featured cameras, it said.

reconstruction: Liberia's economy starts to grow. The Liberian economy began to show clear signs of recovery in 2004, but more focused efforts are needed to ensure long-term sustainable growth, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has said. An IMF mission to the country made these comments in a report published 10 days after high-level talks on the ongoing transition. The IMF said that, according to preliminary data provided by Liberian authorities, the country's economy rose 2% in 2004, after a steep 31% decline in 2003. Liberia is actively recovering from a 14-year civil war that finally came to an end in 2003. The power-sharing National Transitional Government of Liberia will remain in place until general elections on 11 October, which will be the first truly democratic polls and the first since the conflict. The IMF said Liberia's economy gained momentum last year thanks to "strong recovery in rubber production, domestic manufacturing and vital local construction, including essential post-conflict reconstruction projects". The Fund, however, remains notably concerned about what it sees as a persistent lack of transparency in government actions. In particular, it pointed to the lingering mystery surrounding the sale of iron ore stockpiles and the alleged disappearance of significant import and export revenues. These matters are now being actively investigated by the Liberian authorities, and the IMF has called for findings to be made public without delay. It also said it was crucial that the Central Bank, the national bank, be effectively managed on a sound and transparent basis, built to allow Liberia's large external debt to be comprehensively addressed. "The IMF team stands ready to assist the (Liberian) authorities in all the areas mentioned," said the report. "It also agreed with (Liberian) authorities that the sensitive period until the inauguration of a new government will pose exceptional challenges to fiscal management, and expresses its willingness to continue to assist."

Foxx's portrayal of soul-singer Ray Charles in Ray had already earned him a prestigious award. Swank triumphed for her role as a female boxer in Million Dollar Baby. The bill, first proposed in 1993, was passed under the leadership of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. The previous law, dating from 1945, gave priority first to workers, second to tax revenue and finally to unsecured creditors. The new legislation changes this, giving priority to secured creditors and workers. The new regulations will limit claims to 150 times the minimum salary, which is equivalent to $94. The law makes it more attractive for companies to declare bankruptcy. When a firm is declared bankrupt it will gain protection from creditors for 180 days while a recovery plan is worked out. The reforms were opposed in the past by leftist parties, including Mr Lula's Worker Party. They considered that they infringed on workers' rights. It became a key argument in favour of the reforms, that the country's bank lending margins were among the highest in the world and were damaging the economy. reconstruction:
Women 'must not hide'. Hiding women in the home, hidden behind veils, is a backward view, President Pervez Musharraf of Pakistan has said during his visit to Britain. He was speaking to the BBC's Newsnight programme a few hours before visiting the Pakistani community in Manchester.

He cited his own wife as an example. "My wife is travelling around with me. She is very religious but she is moderate," General Musharraf said. His comments come after Pakistan's High Commissioner to Britain, Dr Maleeha Lodhi, controversially said Pakistanis should integrate more into British society.

Dr Maleeha Lodhi had previously stated that people could not expect others to listen to their grievances if they remained separate and did not engage with wider British society. General Musharraf echoed some of these sentiments, telling the BBC: "I abhor people that say women should be confined to their homes and should not move out - absolutely." He stressed the importance of education and modern values for progress in Pakistan and within Pakistani communities abroad, urging them to embrace enlightenment while retaining their cultural identity.

The president was also asked if he thought the war on terror had made the world less safe. "Yes, I do," he replied. "I would add that we are not addressing the core issues, so therefore we can never address terrorism in totality," he explained. He elaborated: "We are addressing the immediate context but we are not fighting its strategic long-term context, which is where the real problem lies."

He blamed international inaction on key geopolitical issues as a major contributing factor. "It is the political disputes and we ignore them, and the issue of illiteracy and poverty. This combined forms the root of extremism and terrorism," he asserted, calling for a more holistic approach to tackling the global threat.

On Monday, President Musharraf met Prime Minister Tony Blair at 10 Downing Street, on his first official visit to London since the September 11th attacks. The leaders held extensive discussions on bilateral relations, regional security, and the ongoing fight against terrorism. He is due to visit the Pakistani community in Manchester on Tuesday, where he will likely reiterate his call for moderation and integration, and meet with business leaders.

Meanwhile, The Sun newspaper said Tuesday it had been handed a sensitive dossier outlining the details of Osama bin Laden's alleged plot against Britain. The paper said the document, reportedly of al-Qaeda origin, had been found in London by a member of the public. It said the dossier contained details of his movements and also confidential radio channels, and call codes for his terror network, raising serious security concerns.

Speaking in London on Monday, General Musharraf insisted that al-Qaeda was "on the run" in Pakistan, following extensive operations by Pakistani security forces along the Afghan border. However, he added that more was needed to fully eradicate the threat, stating what was "outstanding to do" was to tackle "the core of what causes, what creates an extremist environment which then leads on to terrorism." He clarified that "that is the resolution of political disputes" and the eradication of injustice and deprivation globally.

Following their discussions, Mr Blair said the two leaders had talked about a range of issues, including Afghanistan, the wider war on terror, the situation in the Middle East and the ongoing dispute over Kashmir. "We agreed that in Afghanistan there is some cause for optimism about the progress that has been made there, particularly in establishing a democratic government and rebuilding the country," said Mr Blair.

"In respect of Iraq, we agreed that whatever the issues of the past, the important thing now is to see through the strategy and ensure Iraq is capable of becoming a stable and democratic state, free from tyranny and external interference," he concluded. The leaders reaffirmed their commitment to working together on these critical global challenges.

original: Yahoo celebrates a decade online..Yahoo, one of the net's most iconic companies, is celebrating its 10th anniversary this week...The web portal has undergone remarkable change since it was set up by Stanford University students David Filo and Jerry Yang in a campus trailer. The students wanted a way of keeping track of their web-based interests. The categories lists they devised soon became popular to hundreds of people and the two saw business potential in their idea...Originally dubbed "Jerry's Guide to the World Wide Web" the firm adopted the moniker Yahoo because the founders liked the dictionary definition of a yahoo as a rude, unsophisticated, uncouth person. The term was popularised by the 18th Century satirist Jonathan Swift in his classic novel, Gulliver's Travels. "We were certainly not sophisticated or civilised," Mr Yang told reporters ahead of the anniversary, which will be officially recognised on 2 March...They did have business brains however, and in April 1995 persuaded venture capitalists Sequoia Capital, which also invested in Apple Computer and Cisco Systems, to fund Yahoo to the tune of $2m (£1.04m). A second round of funding followed in the autumn and the company floated in April 1996 with less than 50 employees. Now the firm employs 7,600 workers and insists its dot com culture of "work hard, play hard" still remains. It is one of just a handful of survivors of the dot-com crash although it now faces intense rivalry from firms such as Google, MSN and AOL. Jerry Yang, who remains the firm's "Chief Yahoo", is proud of what the company has achieved. "In just one decade, the internet has changed the way consumers do just about everything - and it's been a remarkable and wonderful experience," he said. Through it all, we wanted to build products that satisfied our users wants and needs, but it's even more than that - it's to help every one of us to discover, get more done, share and interact."

The portal has undergone significant evolution and expansion since it was set up by Stanford University students Filo and Jerry Yang from a trailer. Hitachi said the 1.3m (4.2ft) Emiew was the world's fastest-moving robot yet. Two wheel-based Emiews, Pal and Chum, were introduced to reporters at a press conference in Japan. They will be guests at Expo later this year. Sony and Honda have both built sophisticated robots to show off in public.

Explaining why Hitachi's Emiew used wheels instead of legs, Toshihiko Horiuchi, from Hitachi's Mechanical Engineering Research Laboratory, said: "We aimed to create a robot that could live and co-exist with people. We want the robots to be useful to people... If the robots moved slower than people, they would be frustrated."

With sensors on the head, chest, and near the ground, Chum demonstrated how they react. "I want them to walk about like Shinjuku and other shopping districts in the city without bumping into people," Pal told reporters. Hitachi said Pal and Chum, which have a height of about 100cm, could be "ready" for practical office and domestic use in as little as five to six years.

Robotics researchers have long challenged themselves to develop robots that mimic the gait of a human. At a recent AAAS (American Association for the Advancement of Science) annual meeting in Washington, researchers showed off bipedal designs. A three-person research group use the same principles to achieve human-like gait.

Sony and Honda have both used robots, which are not commercially available, as a show-off of computing power and engineering. Honda's Asimo was first unveiled several years ago. Asimo, Honda's robot, and Sony's Qrio have tried to trump each other with what the robots can do at technology events. Asimo has visited the UK, Germany, the Czech Republic, and Ireland as a world ambassador. Sony's Qrio, meanwhile, was dancing world records and, until last year, the two were the dominant players. But Emiew was unveiled. It is capable of 3km/h, which its makers claim is almost as fast as a human's walking pace. Last year, Toyota also stepped into the ring and unveiled a trumpet-playing humanoid.

By 2007, it was predicted there will be almost 2.5 million "entertainment and household" robots in homes, compared to 137,000 currently, according to the UN. By the end of that year, 4.1 million robots will be doing jobs in industry, said a report by the UN Economic Commission for Europe and Robotics. Hitachi is one of the companies with a home cleaning robot on the market.

reconstruction: Mobile gaming takes off in a big move, becoming one of the fastest-growing leisure activities among the tech-savvy population in India, a recent report indicates. The mobile gaming market is set to generate $26m (£13.8m) by the end of 2004, according to market analysts In-Stat/MDR. In 2003, mobile phone users grew by 1.4 million to reach 44.9 million, for the first time surpassing the total number of landlines, said the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India. Market watchers say cheap rates and a huge potential market is driving the growth. India has a significant population of under-25s, and many young people in urban areas are fast acquiring must-have gadgets and services. India's overall mobile market is projected to bring in $336m (£178m) by 2009, the same report stated. The market for mobile gaming is expected to explode in the next few years. Industry analysts predict that as many as 220 million people will be playing games on their mobile phones by 2009, generating billions of dollars for mobile companies. Value-added services other than just voice calls are increasingly being offered by mobile operators in India, as a result of the huge rise in subscribers, which has grown both significantly and rapidly. "The collaboration between this sector's publishers, developers, aggregators, and providers, is also stimulating innovative business models," said Clint Wheelock, In-Stat/MDR's wireless research director. "Mobile gaming is fun; it also represents a key element of a complete entertainment experience, and a highly lucrative market opportunity for all industry players." Currently, India has six big telecom operators and four mobile content providers who actively offer games to their subscribers, the report added. According to In-Stat/MDR, the country is tipped to become one of the most promising and dynamic markets in the next wave of global mobile growth. In January 2003, there were only 10 million subscribers in India. Many residents choose mobile phones in rural areas in order to bypass the poorer telecoms infrastructure. Despite this rapid growth, the penetration rate is still much lower than that of other developed nations. Less than 20% of India's entire population own a mobile phone, compared with well over 50% in many European countries. This trend echoes the rapid uptake of mobiles in many other developing economies around the world, which continues to accelerate as people use them to leapfrog slower and more expensive state-run fixed-line telephone services.

Lifestyle choices and priorities, better hardware alone is not going to help mobile phone companies sell more handsets, new research suggests. Instead, phone companies are keen to get more out of their customers, focusing on how technology integrates into daily life, not just for technology's own sake. Consumers are far more interested in how handsets fit in with their lifestyles than they are in screen size, onboard memory or the technology inside, an in-depth study by company Ericsson found. "Historically there has been too much focus on using technology for technology's sake," said Dr Michael Bjorn, senior advisor on mobile media at Ericsson's consumer research lab. "We have to stop saying that technology will change lives," he added. "We try to speak to consumers in their own language and help them see how technology fits with what they are doing," the study's report stated. In its study, Ericsson interviewed 14,000 mobile phone owners about the ways they use their devices. "People's habits remain the same," Bjorn explained. "They just move the activity to the mobile phone as it's a much more convenient way to do it."

One good example of this is journal writing among younger people, he said. While personal diaries have always been a popular form of self-expression, a mobile phone-- especially with a camera-- helps keep it in a digital and shareable form. Youngsters' text messages also express their desire for connection and contact with friends and lets them do it in a slightly different way. Dr Bjorn said that although consumers don't always immediately embrace every new feature or use their phone to its full technological potential from day one, the sheer variety of the technologies they make possible does gradually drive new habits and lifestyles. Ericsson's research has shown that consumers divide into different "tribes" that fall into distinct categories based on their attitudes towards technology adoption. Dr Bjorn said groups dubbed "pioneers" and "materialists" were most interested in trying new things and were behind the initial surge in the use of new mobile phone features. "For instance," he said, "older people are using SMS much more than they did years ago." It was younger users, children of ageing mobile owners, who often encouraged other people to try new features and helped them see how they could integrate these innovations into their own daily lives.

Another key factor influencing the speed of change in mobile phone use was the simple ease with which new features were initially bought by early adopters, the pioneers and materialists. Initially, when about 25% of people have handsets with advanced camera functions on them, such as integrated cameras, consumers are still worrying that if they send a picture, the recipient at the other end will actually be able to see it. Once this significant psychological and social barrier is passed, the use of new innovations tends to take off rapidly. Dr Bjorn stated that early reports on camera phone usage in Japan seemed to imply that the innovation was going to be a complete flop. However, he said, now 45% of the Ericsson customers questioned use their mobile phone at least once a month. This is up from 29% in 2003. Similarly, across Europe, the percentage of people taking photos with camera phones is starting to rise significantly. In 2003, only 4% of the people who owned a phonecam used it to snap a picture at least once a month. Now, just a few years later, the figure is 14%. Similar positive trends are seen in many other European nations. Dr Bjorn explained that people used camera phones in a very different way compared to how they use traditional film and standalone digital cameras. "The usage patterns for standalone digital cameras are almost replacing usage for analogue cameras," he said. "They tend to be used primarily on significant events such as weddings, holidays and birthdays." By contrast, he said, camera phones were being used much more spontaneously to capture a casual moment and woven seamlessly into everyday life.

reconstruction: O' Sullivan keeps his powder dry... an old sporting adage that suggests holding back, keeping your true strength hidden until the opportune moment. For a team gunning for ultimate glory, which is precisely what Ireland's rugby squad is aiming for, this strategic approach seems to be exactly what coach Eddie O' Sullivan appears to have meticulously done quite extensively during the run-up to this season's much-anticipated Six Nations Championship. He had, in fact, decreed after the disappointing 2003 Rugby World Cup that there should be a fundamental shift towards decent conditioning throughout the year, especially during the crucial pre-season. That vision became a tangible reality at the end of last summer, commencing with a rigorous and focused 10-week period dedicated to physical preparation at the very start of the current season. It may well have annoyed our esteemed Scottish, and in particular our vocal Welsh, rugby cousins who huffed and puffed vociferously at the perceived disrespect apparently shown to the then-struggling Celtic League schedule. We will, of course, diplomatically say nothing of Mike Ruddock's controversial 'poaching' of eight key players from the Gwent Dragons squad that faced Leinster on Sunday. However, in defence of O' Sullivan, he is certainly well within his absolute rights to prioritise national interests, particularly when one is talking about the national side and the immense pride that universally goes along with representing one's country. The Irish Rugby Football Union (IRFU) have unequivocally thrown their substantial weight behind O' Sullivan's long-term vision, and it must be said that in the main, this support manifests through the provision of secure central contracts for key players. Keith, for instance, who is just returning from a serious broken leg, can testify that everyone else 'is', in their own words, remarkably fresh and metaphorically at the oche, fully prepared to embark upon this season's demanding campaign... But I sincerely doubt O' Sullivan is going to lose any sleep about handling his critics or worrying about external perceptions. He is simply not that kind of person to be swayed by such distractions. However, he can certainly look at the visibly fatigued and unfortunately injury-hit England, as well as the equally overtaxed France squads who have, regrettably, been consistently overworked, then quite rightly pat himself on the back for his judicious planning and astute foresight. But there remains the paramount question of successfully turning and effectively transferring that accumulated freshness and physical conditioning into consistently positive results when the referee finally signals the eagerly anticipated start of the championship. Already, in numerous media reports and expert analyses, Ireland are being emphatically earmarked as hot favourites to sweep the board and claim all available silverware this season. A first Grand Slam since the legendary Jackie Mullen famously led the team to a clean sweep of victories way back in 1948. With their arch-rivals England visiting Lansdowne for what will be the very last time before the historic old darling is sadly and irrevocably demolished to make way for the new stadium, Ireland looks perfectly placed to achieve something truly special. But in the dark days of yore, when the very life was seemingly squeezed out of them, often under a burden that proved too great to bear, Ireland have historically crumpled under the pressure. Take, for example, the magnificent Triple Crown-winning side of 1985, spearheaded by the inspirational Ciaran Doyle. They were widely expected to decisively up the ante for a Grand Slam, only to be cruelly denied a second in Ireland's rugby history. What, then, tragically happened in 1986? You see, the undeniable truth is that in any highly competitive sporting arena, to truly succeed at the highest level, you simply have to go out there and prove a definitive point to the world, to your rivals, and most importantly, to yourselves. It is, quite frankly, the fundamental nature of the beast. But O' Sullivan's meticulously prepared side are very capable of making this salient point emphatically and demonstrating their genuine potential. For the first time in an astonishing 19 years, they demonstrably can live up to their burgeoning success and take a truly significant further step up the international rugby ladder. O' Sullivan has consistently kept faith with his core group of players, and they have emphatically repaid him in spades with their dedication and performance... and by all indications, there is much, much more to come. He has some wily old dogs strategically placed within his squad, experienced veterans who will come to this season's championship with a completely different box of tricks, honed over many seasons, and a renewed verve to finally secure victory. They absolutely can succeed, but for now, we must just whisper it, lest we tempt fate!

reconstruction:
Yukos sues four firms for $20bn.
Russian oil firm Yukos has sued four companies for their involvement in last year's seizure and subsequent sale of key oil production unit Yuganskneftegas. Yukos is seeking more than $20bn (£11bn) in damages after its main production unit was forcibly sold in December to cover an allegedly inflated bill for back taxes. The companies named in the suit are gas giant Gazprom, its oil unit Gazpromneft, investment company Baikal, and state oil firm Rosneft. Yukos submitted the suit in a Houston bankruptcy court, where it filed for Chapter 11 protection. As for its wider battle in Russia, Yukos has asked the court to force the Russian government to agree to take its tax dispute to an international arbitrator. It also has a plan to reorganize its remaining assets as part of its Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings.

The clash between Yukos and the Kremlin came to a head last year when Yukos was presented with a demand of more than $27bn in back taxes and unpaid fines. To help settle the bill, Russia then moved to sell off Yuganskneftegas.

Yukos has declared the sale illegal and has turned to courts worldwide in an effort to regain the production business. It also vowed to use all legal avenues at its disposal to go after any firm that attempted to buy or acquire its assets. The unit was eventually sold this month for $28.3bn. While many have questioned whether a US court has any jurisdiction over Russian companies, Moscow officials have dismissed Yukos' wrangling as nothing but meaningless legal posturing. In Houston, bankruptcy Judge Arthur J. Clark is scheduled to start a two-day hearing on 16 February to hear arguments on whether a US bankruptcy court is the proper forum for the dispute.

A threat of action from its bankruptcy filing in Houston did have a significant impact on last month's auction, however. Concerned that they would be caught up in a court battle, Gazprom and Gazpromneft withdrew from the initial auction, and Yuganskneftegas was sold to little-known investment firm Baikal Finance Group. Just a few days later, Baikal resold control of the company to state-oil group Rosneft for $9.3bn. Rosneft, meanwhile, has agreed to merge with Gazprom, effectively bringing a large chunk of Russia's very profitable oil business under state control.

Yukos maintains that the rights of its shareholders have been ignored and that it is has punished for the ambitions of its former chief, Mikhail Khodorkovsky. Mr Khodorkovsky, once Russia's richest man, is in prison, having been charged with fraud and tax and evasion.

reconstruction:
Web radio takes Spanish rap global. If you were to spin the radio dial in the United States, you would undoubtedly encounter plenty of Spanish-language music. But what you will not readily discover is Spanish-language hip-hop.

Hip-hop and rap are, in fact, quite popular and well-established in the Spanish-speaking world, yet they have historically faced considerable trouble marketing their work abroad. Now, however, a pioneering company is successfully bringing rap and hip-hop music directly to computer screens and speakers everywhere.

Los Caballeros de Plan G, for instance, are currently one of Mexico's hottest hip-hop acts. They enjoy a strong and dedicated fan base within their hometown of Monterrey. Nevertheless, most hip-hop fans, particularly those residing across the Spanish-speaking world, are unlikely to hear the group's tracks featured on conventional radio broadcasts.

"You can't really count on the mainstream radio for hip-hop in Spanish... it's just not readily available," explains Manuel Millan, a native of San Diego, California. "It's genuinely hard to integrate the hip-hop scene into mainstream media. These groups usually possess a very distinct sound, and their work is not widely known around the country or, indeed, around the rest of the world."

Millan and his friends therefore set out to change this paradigm. Their objective was to make groups like Los Caballeros de Plan G readily accessible to a global audience. Given that mainstream radio stations were generally unreceptive to this kind of music, and starting their own dedicated station was economically unfeasible, Millan and his associates instead launched a comprehensive website: latinohiphopradio.com. Its very name, they believe, says it all: it is a web-radio platform, exclusively playing the hottest Spanish rap and hip-hop tracks.

The website, which is navigable in both English and Spanish, has been meticulously designed to be exceptionally user-friendly. All the listener has to do is simply click a button to start playback. There are no conventional DJs. It is merely a stream of music delivered over the internet for free.

Suddenly, with the advent of latinohiphopradio.com, Los Caballeros de Plan G are producing what can truly be described as "export quality" music. This innovative web platform might indeed be just the right medium for Spanish language hip-hop right now. The genre itself is, as Millan terms it, in its "infant stages" of development. Yet, the production values are improving rapidly, and artists such as Argentina's Yoda are actively pushing to make the quality better and better. Yoda is currently considered one of the hottest artists featured on latinohiphopradio.com.

"He's widely considered the godfather of Argentina's Latin hip-hop scene," Millan remarks. "He genuinely hasn't had that much exposure as far as anywhere else in the world, but he's definitively the one to watch out for as he is poised to become the next big thing in the Spanish-speaking world – a true pioneer of the sound."

Currently, the acclaimed Chilean group Makisa is also prominently featured in latinohiphopradio.com's top 10, as is the accomplished Cuban artist Papo Record. "Each country's got its unique cultural flavor, and these artists diligently try to infuse that essence into their own original music," Millan explains.

Latinohiphopradio.com has successfully been up and running for a couple of months now. The site actively attracts a broad array of listeners from across the entire Spanish-speaking world. Right now, Mexico leads the way in listenership, impressively accounting for 50% of all listeners. However, web audiences in Spain are also enthusiastically tuning in, with 25% of the website's total traffic originating from there.

This phenomenon is not entirely surprising, as Spain is widely recognized to be a cultural leader in Spanish-language music and broader artistic expression. Millan suggests that Spain is actually just behind the United States and France in terms of rap and hip-hop consumption and influence.

This situation might, however, be gradually changing, as more and more American artists are finding larger and more receptive audiences there. Nevertheless, one prominent Spaniard is still firmly entrenched in the radio's prestigious top 10. His name is Tote King, and Millan firmly believes that he is unquestionably the Spanish hip-hop leader. In his powerful track "Uno Contra 20," or "Against 20," Tote King makes it crystal clear that he is indeed well aware of that fact. "It's basically bragging that he's one of the best emcees in Spain right now," Millan confirms. "And it's very much true. He is the real deal, his rap is exceptionally powerful, and it's profoundly authentic."

Latinohiphopradio.com is hoping to significantly expand its operations in the coming months and years. Eventually, their ambition is to encompass the entire scope and diverse world of Spanish hip-hop and rap. Clark Boyd reporting on technology for The World, a BBC World Service and WGBH-Boston co-production.

It was one of the last dates he did in London."..: The album Exodus came out in 1977 and that provided five hits and confirmed his global superstar status. "By 1979 he was the biggest touring attraction in the world. I remember going to see dates in Milan and Turin and they were enormous concerts."..: Bob was one of the most mesmeric people I've ever had the privilege to work with. "He must have had an iron will to succeed. Bob was a very driven individual. You realised from the start there was a manifest destiny within him that he believed in. He didn't suffer fools gladly. At the risk of stating the obvious, he was an extraordinary song writer and his stage act was perhaps the greatest I've ever seen. I saw him many times."..: "I recall in 1978 he came to the UK for Top of the Pops and a Daily Mirror journalist did a half-hour interview. It was interrupted to do a rehearsal. He came back into the dressing room to resume the interview but saw a World Cup match on TV..."He sat down in front of the TV and after 10 minutes it was obvious he wasn't going to move. That was the end of it. The Mirror had a very truncated interview. "The last time I saw him was in London in 1980. I arranged for him to play four days of football indoors in Fulham. "Bob was a good player. We are talking about Jamaican-style football. He was an attacking midfield player. His team assembled wherever his gigs were. We played in Brazil against some World Cup-winning players."..: It was always a struggle for him to connect with Black America. Reggae did not correspond with disco in the 70s. If you went to Africa he would be recognised everywhere, in places John Lennon or Elvis wouldn't be. "No disrespect to the other artists but a case can be made for him as the greatest, the best and the most influential artist in popular music."..: Well 1981 was to be the year he toured Africa with Stevie Wonder. He had only performed in Zimbabwe and Guinea before. "Of course the 1981 tour never happened, but the whole of Africa would have embraced him. We can't speculate but he was at the height of his powers and just 36 years old. I had no sense his career was going to go downhill."..: "Bob was endlessly optimistic about the way Africa would turn out. He realised that nothing was perfect but he had total belief in the power of mankind. "I'm sure if he were alive today he would believe Africa would firstly become politically free and secondly be able to defeat the Aids epidemic."..: "The final tune of his final album was Redemption Song - one of the most incredible classics of all time."
