reconstruction:
Unforgettable memories of Marley... To mark the 60th anniversary of the birth of reggae superstar Bob Marley, Patrice Partridge - Marley's former head of press at Island Records - remembers the man behind the legend... Patrice Partridge worked closely with Marley from 1977 until the Jamaican musician's untimely death in 1981...: "I joined Island Records in 1977 and the first time I saw him perform live was at the Rainbow Theatre in London. It was one of the last dates he did in the city."

The album Exodus came out in 1977 and that provided and confirmed his monumental international appeal. By 1979 he was the hottest touring attraction in Europe. I remember going to see him play dates in Milan and they were absolutely incredible, completely sold out.

Bob was one of the most remarkable people I've ever had the privilege to work with. He must have had an iron will and incredible determination to succeed. Bob was a very driven man, with an unwavering vision. You knew from the very start that there was a manifest destiny within him; he was destined for global greatness. He didn't suffer fools gladly. And at the risk of stating the obvious, his songwriting was extraordinary, and his stage presence was perhaps the greatest I've ever seen. I saw him perform countless times.

I recall in 1978 he was in the UK for a performance on Top of the Pops and a Daily Mirror reporter was scheduled to do a half-hour interview. Bob was supposed to do a soundcheck rehearsal. He came back into the dressing room to resume the interview but the World Cup was on TV... He sat down in front of the TV and within 10 minutes it was obvious he wasn't going to move. That was the end of it. The Mirror reporter had to unhappily truncate the interview.

The last time I saw him was in London in 1980. We had arranged to play a couple of days of football indoors at the Fulham training grounds. Bob was a very good player. We are talking about true Jamaican-style football, very skilful and passionate. He was an attacking midfield player, always leading the charge. His team was assembled wherever his gigs were taking place. We even played in matches against some World Cup-winning players.

It was a significant struggle for him to connect with Black America initially. Reggae music did not correspond to the prevailing sound of disco in the 70s, which dominated the airwaves. But Bob, by the 1990s, became one of the truly great icons in Black America and indeed across the entire Third World. By 1991, ten years after his passing, he was selling more records than at any time in his life. Black America finally saw him as their own hero for the very first time.

In global terms, his music has never been surpassed. If you went to Africa, Bob Marley's image and music would be recognised everywhere, in places where even John Lennon or Michael Jackson might not be. No disrespect to those incredible artists, but it can be truly said for him, that he was simply the best and most universally recognised artist in music.

In 1981 he was scheduled to have toured Africa with Stevie Wonder. He had only performed in Zimbabwe and Guinea before, so this would have been huge. If that monumental 1981 tour had happened, the whole of Africa would have embraced him completely. We can't speculate on what might have been, but he tragically died at the height of his powers at only 36 years old. He had absolutely no sense that his career was going to go downhill; in fact, it was just soaring.

Bob was endlessly optimistic about the way the world would turn and evolve. He realised that change was a gradual process, but he had total belief in the power of music and its message to bring about that profound social and political change. I'm sure if he were alive today he would have seen Africa become truly politically free and be able to help address the Aids epidemic with his powerful voice and influence.

The iconic title track of his final album was Redemption Song - one of the most incredible classics of all time, a true testament to his enduring legacy.

original: EU-US seeking deal on air dispute..The EU and US have agreed to begin talks on ending subsidies given to aircraft makers, EU Trade Commissioner Peter Mandelson has announced...Both sides hope to reach a negotiated deal over state aid received by European aircraft maker Airbus and its US rival Boeing, Mr Mandelson said. Airbus and Boeing accuse each other of benefiting from illegal subsidies. Mr Mandelson said the EU and US hoped to avoid having to resolve the dispute at the World Trade Organisation (WTO)..."With this agreement the EU and US have confirmed their willingness to resolve the dispute which has arisen between them," Mr Mandelson said. "I hope our negotiations in the next three months will lead to an agreement ending subsidies to development and production of large civil aircraft." Last year, the US terminated an agreement with the EU, reached in 1992, which limits the subsidies countries can hand over to civil aircraft makers. The US filed a complaint against Brussels with the WTO over state aid to Airbus, prompting a retaliatory EU complaint over US support for Boeing. However, both sides agreed to suspend their requests for WTO arbitration at the beginning of December, to allow bilateral talks to continue. EADS and BAE Systems, the European defence and aerospace firms which own Airbus, welcomed Mr Mandelson's announcement. "It has always been preferable that any differences between the US and Europe on this matter be overcome through constructive discussion rather than through legal recourse," the companies said in a joint statement...Separately, the world's largest package delivery company, UPS, said it had placed an order for 10 Airbus A380 superjumbo freight-carrying jets, with an option to buy 10 more of the triple-decker aircraft. The US company said it needed to expand its air freight capacity following strong international growth, and would begin receiving deliveries of the A380s from 2009. However, UPS said it was cutting a previous order for smaller Airbus A300s from 90 planes to 53. So far, Airbus has delivered 40 A300s to UPS. Airbus overtook Boeing as the world's largest manufacturer of commercial airliners in 2003.

reconstruction:
Lib Dems' 'bold' election policy. Charles Kennedy has told voters the Liberal Democrats will offer them an "honest choice" at the next general election.

Unlike the other big parties battling over who will impose the lowest taxes, Mr Kennedy, going into the looming election, has pledged to increase them.

It is a policy that clearly differentiates the Lib Dems and ensures there is a stark contrast with the other two main parties. His party's previous pledge to increase taxes by a penny on the pound to spend on public services was already adopted by the government, he has pointed out.

Now he is promising to levy a "modest" increase of the same amount on incomes over £100,000 a year to allow the party to finance a series of key policy commitments.

These commitments are: to scrap student tuition fees, provide free long-term personal care for the elderly, and replace the council tax with a local income tax. That last policy will also see about 3% of the most well-off paying more, while others, the vast majority of households, will pay less overall.

Labour and the Conservatives have predictably attacked his policies as being both unworkable and not properly costed or justified.

Inevitably, both insist there is no need to raise taxes to fund improvements in vital public services.

The Tories claim they can improve services AND cut taxes through £35bn in savings, while Labour has offered £22bn in savings but has yet to map out precise tax proposals, although it is thought they will propose little in the way of direct tax increases.

In the argument between the Lib Dems and the other parties over taxation and spending, there are clear echoes of the arguments that raged between Labour and the Conservatives in the 1980s and early 1990s.

But, unlike that old Tory-Labour debate, Mr Kennedy believes voters are ready to accept "modest" tax increases on the well-off in order to fund significant improvements in public services.

That is a view partly endorsed by recent polls suggesting people would rather have more spent on public services, even if it means paying a little more tax.

There is a clear ideological shift to the Lib Dem approach, and with Mr Kennedy stressing that politicians "foment artificial arguments" about tax cuts, he is directly challenging the consensus built by Labour and Michael Howard's proposals for further tax reductions.

Once again, with the two big parties singing similar songs on tax, Mr Kennedy is stressing the different, more liberal approach championed by his party.

Mr Kennedy was also in buoyant mood over his party's election chances, declaring they were not to be "bit players" in this general election contest.

He repeated his pledge not to do a post-election deal or coalition with either Labour or the Conservatives after the election results are known.

Mr Kennedy went on to say that a Labour government returning with only a small majority would amount to a "massive vote of no confidence" in Tony Blair's government and its policies.

The confident Lib Dem leader believes he may well find himself in a key, pivotal position in a vastly different House of Commons after the next general election. It is a dream the third party has cherished many times before, but one they feel is now within reach.

original: Digital UK driven by net and TV..The UK's adoption of digital TV and broadband has helped make it the fourth most digitally-savvy nation in Europe, according a report by Jupiter Research...But the UK still lags in terms of broadband speeds compared to others. The most digitally sophisticated Europeans, in terms of use of digital goods such as mobiles, TV, net and cameras, are the Scandinavians. About 14 million households in the UK, 60%, have digital TV, according to the communications regulator Ofcom. The least digital of the European nations was Greece, in 17th position, according to the Digital Life Index...Scandinavian countries Sweden, Denmark and Norway came out top in the report, but there were some differences in technology trends. original: US state acts to stop 'spammers'..US state Texas has filed a lawsuit against two men believed to be among the world's top five spammers...It is seeking millions of dollars in damages in a civil lawsuit filed earlier this week. The Texas attorney general said it started the legal action as messages sent by the alleged spammers broke three laws governing e-mail marketing. The company named in the lawsuit denied any wrongdoing and said it complied with all relevant laws...The Texas lawsuit was filed against Ryan Samuel Pitylak, a University ofTexas student, and Mark Stephen Trotter of California. Both are thought to be the top executives in three companies - PayPerAction LLC., Leadplex LLC. and Leadplex Inc - that are suspected of sending out many millions of unwanted e-mail messages. "Illegal spam must be stopped," said Greg Abbott, Texas attorney general announcing the legal action. "Spam is one of the most aggravating and pervasive problems facing consumers today." The attorney general alleges that messages sent by Mr Pitylak and Mr Trotter's companies broke the 2003 Controlling the Assault of Non-Solicited Pornography and Marketing Act (Can-Spam) as well as the Texas Electronic Mail and Solicitation Act and Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act. All three acts confer cash penalties for each violation of their terms. If the men are found guilty and all penalties are applied, the two men could face a damages bill running into millions. Mr Abbott said the messages sent by the pair broke laws by using misleading subject lines, not identifying themselves as adverts and offering services for which they had no licence to do so in Texas. Lawyers for the alleged spammers said the lawsuit was groundless and the two men would defend themselves strongly against the accusations. "Leadplex and PayPerAction are legitimate internet marketing companies that are in complete compliance with the federal Can-Spam Act," said Lin Hughes, speaking on behalf of Mr Pitylak and Mr Trotter. In a similar move the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has won a court order that stops an international group of spammers sending sexually explicit e-mail. The FTC took the action because the messages being sent violated several parts of the CAN-Spam Act. In particular, the pornographic messages did not identify themselves as being sexually explicit, had deceptive subject headings, did not have working opt-out mechanisms, failed to mention they were adverts and did not give the sender's real world address. The court order stops the spammers sending e-mail and freezes assets prior to a hearing on a permanent injunction.

It is seeking millions of dollars in damages in a civil lawsuit filed this week. The attorney general started legal action as messages sent by the spammers broke laws governing e-mail. A company named in the lawsuit denied any wrongdoing, saying it complied with all relevant rules and regulations.

The lawsuit was filed against Ryan Pitylak, a University of Texas student, and Mark Stephen Trotter of California. Both are thought to be executives in three companies - PayPerAction LLC, Leadplex LLC and Leadplex - that are believed to be responsible for sending out many millions of unwanted e-mail messages.

"'Spam must be stopped,' said Greg Abbott, the attorney general who filed the legal action. 'Spam is one of the most pervasive problems facing consumers today.'"

The attorney general alleges that messages sent by Mr Pitylak and Mr Trotter's companies broke the 2003 federal Controlling the Assault of Non-Solicited Pornography and Marketing Act (Can-Spam), as well as the Texas Electronic Mail Solicitation Act and the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act. All three acts confer cash penalties for violation of their terms. If they are found guilty and maximum penalties are applied, the two men could face fines running into millions of dollars.

Mr Abbott said the messages sent by the pair had misleading subject lines, failed to identify themselves as adverts and offered products for which they had no licence to sell in Texas.

A spokesman for the spammers said the lawsuit was groundless and the men would defend themselves strongly against the allegations.

'Leadplex and PayPerAction are legitimate internet marketing companies and are completely compliant with the federal Can-Spam Act,' said Lin Hughes, speaking on behalf of Mr Pitylak and Mr Trotter.

This move follows an announcement by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) that it has won a court order against an international group of spammers sending sexually explicit e-mail. The FTC took the action because the messages being sent violated several provisions of the CAN-Spam Act. The order stops the spammers from sending more e-mail and freezes their assets pending a hearing for a permanent injunction.

However Frankenheimer pulled out in 2002, a month before he died...Skarsgard then replaced Neeson in the role of Father Merrin, made famous by Max Von Sydow in the 1973 film. Principal footage was shot in Morocco and Rome at a reported cost of $32m. However, in August 2003 it emerged that producers Morgan Creek were shelving Schrader's version of the film, having complained it was not scary enough. original: Fears raised over ballet future..Fewer children in the UK are following in the dainty footsteps of dancers like Darcey Bussell, and carving out potential careers as ballet dancers...New research from the Royal Academy of Dance (RAD) has found fewer children over the age of 10 are attending ballet classes and taking exams in the discipline. The organisation blames the growing popularity of computer games and other changes in lifestyle. And there are fears that if the trend is not reversed, there could be fewer British ballet stars in the future. The RAD found that the number of youngsters taking their ballet exams drops by almost 70% after the age of 10 or 11. Dance teacher Eve Trew, who has taught ballet for over 48 years, told BBC News she had seen a "vast" change over the years. She blamed modern lifestyles for the fall in ballet attendance. "I think the children of many years ago did not have as many hobbies," she said. "The trouble now is that they are wide open to computers, Gameboys and everything else children have got. "As a result, there is less time being spent on ballet lessons."..Hazel Gilbert, 23, an information manager from Newcastle, gave up ballet at the age of 10 and is typical of the problem. "It's not a very cool thing to do when you go to 'big' school and I think you have to be very focused on ballet to want to carry on doing it," she said. "I used to love it, but after a certain age it becomes much more disciplined and I didn't want that. "I started getting into other things, like swimming and kickboxing, and ballet just wasn't something I wanted to do any more." Ms Trew, who runs a dance school in Gateshead, admitted it would be "very difficult" to reverse the trend and said many young ballet dancers were no longer willing to make the sacrifices to succeed. "You have to be very dedicated and you have to be very disciplined. "It is a career that you have got to really want to do because it is such hard work. "Children these days have not got the time to spend perfecting it... that is very sad."..Currently, only two out of 16 principal dancers at the Royal Ballet - Darcey Bussell and Jonathan Cope - are British, compared to 16 of the 21 principals in 1985. But a spokesman for the English National Ballet told BBC News that although only two out of their 12 principal dancers were British, around a quarter of the company's dancers were from the UK. He said competition at open auditions in London was "fierce" between talented dancers from all over the world. The RAD have launched a new competition to try and reverse the decline in British ballet. Dame Antoinette Sibley, president of the RAD, launched the Fonteyn Nureyev Young Dancers competition earlier this week...Aimed at children aged 10 to 13, it is hoped the contest will help keep British ballet evolving. A spokeswoman for the RAD said: "It is our responsibility to re-ignite the passion and nurture young dancers for the long-term future of ballet. "We need to provide them with a framework and a goal to work towards, with constant support and coaching in an environment where they can work with their peers and possibly leading artists and choreographers. "Perhaps more importantly provide them with the opportunity to experience 'performance' themselves. "What better way to reignite a passion for ballet than to let them experience the thrill of performance?"

Fewer children in the UK are following in the footsteps of dancers like Darcey Bussell, and research from the Royal Academy of Dance (RAD) has found that fewer children over the age of 10 are attending ballet classes and taking exams in the discipline. The organization blames the growing popularity of games and other hobbies. And there are fears that if the trend is not reversed, there could be fewer British ballet stars in the future. The number of youngsters taking their ballet exams drops almost 70% after the age of 10 or 11. Dance teacher Eve, who has taught for 48 years, told BBC News she had seen a "vast" change over the years. She blamed modern lifestyles for the fall in attendance. "I think the children many years ago did not have as many hobbies," she said. "The trouble now is that they are wide open to computers, Gameboys, and everything else." As a result, there is less time spent on ballet lessons. Hazel Gilbert, 23, an information manager from Newcastle, gave up ballet at the age of 10 and is aware of the problem. "It's not a cool thing to do when you go to 'big' school, and I think you have to be very focused on ballet to want to carry on doing it," she said. "I used to enjoy it, but after a certain age, it became more disciplined, and I didn't want that. I started getting into other things, like swimming and kickboxing, so ballet just wasn't something I wanted to do anymore." Ms. Trew, who runs a dance school, said it would be challenging and said many young ballet dancers were no longer willing to make sacrifices to succeed. "You have to want it, and you have to be very disciplined. It is a career that you have got to want because it is such hard work. Children these days have not got the time to spend on it, and that is very sad." Currently, only two of 16 principal dancers at Birmingham Royal Ballet—Darcey Bussell and Jonathan Cope—are British, compared to 16 out of 21 principals in 1985. But a spokesman for the English National Ballet told BBC News that although only two out of 12 principal dancers were British, a majority of the 'corps de ballet' were from the UK. He said competition was open and "fierce" between talented dancers all over the world. The RAD has launched new initiatives to try and reverse the decline in British ballet. Dame Antoinette Sibley, president of RAD, launched the Dancers competition earlier this week. Aimed at children aged 10 to 13, it is hoped the competition will help ballet keep evolving. A spokesman for the RAD said: "It is our intention to re-engage the passion and nurture young talent for the long-term future of ballet. We need to provide them with a framework and something to work towards, with constant coaching and an environment where they can work with their peers and possibly professional artists and choreographers. Perhaps more importantly, provide them with the opportunity to 'perform' themselves." What better way to ignite a passion than to let them experience the thrill of performance?

access to its network. BT has pre-empted a possible break-up of the company by offering to cut wholesale prices and give its network rivals better access. The move comes after regulator Ofcom said in November that the offer "lacked equality of phone lines". At the time, Ofcom warned BT of the possibility of fines or splitting into separate companies. Ofcom is carrying out a strategic review aimed at promoting greater competition in the UK telecom sector. BT's rivals have frequently accused it of misusing its status as the former telecoms monopoly and controller of access to many customers to favour its retail arm. This submission was delivered to the watchdog ahead of the deadline for the second phase of consultation.

"Central to the plans by BT to offer lower wholesale prices, faster broadband services and transparent, non-discriminatory access to BT's local network," the former monopoly said in a statement. "The United Kingdom has the potential to create the exciting and innovative telecoms market in the world," BT chief executive Ben Verwaayen said. "BT has a vital role to play, and today we are putting forward a set of far-reaching proposals towards a new regulatory framework," he said. BT wants lighter regulation in exchange for the changes, as well as removal of the break-up threat.

The plan includes setting up a new Access Services division - with separate boards which would include independent members - to guarantee equal access for rivals to the "local loop", the cables that run between exchanges and households. The company unveiled plans to cut the wholesale prices of its most popular broadband product by 8% from April in areas of high customer demand. It added that it plans to invest £10bn over the next five years to create a "21st Century network". To meet the growing demand for greater bandwidth, BT would begin trials in April with a view to launching super-speed services nationally from the summer.

Telecom analysts Ovum welcomed the move, saying BT had "given a lot of ground". "The big question now is how the industry, particularly BT's rivals, react to these proposals and how far they go. Now real negotiation begins," director of telecoms research Tony Lavender said. Internet service provider (ISP) Plus.net also responded, saying "we will back this plan entirely if BT sticks to them". "BT has been fair and will introduce a level playing field. The crucial scenario is how their business plans impact us as a provider," Plus.net chief executive Lee said. Chris Panayis, managing director of ISP Freedom2surf said that it would make the situation clearer for his business. "I think it's the first productive dialogue we've had from BT," he said.

However, other rivals backed the price cuts but said regulation was still needed to ensure fair competition. "This is a step in the right direction, but as long as BT alone can change the dynamics of the whole market at will, the process of opening up UK's local network to investment remains fragile," an ISP spokesman said. "Ofcom needs regulation of BT's wholesale broadband service [IPStream] to provide rules for local loop unbundling if consumers are to see benefits of increased competition and infrastructure investment." More than 100 firms, consumer groups and interested parties are expected to respond to the regulator during this consultation. Ofcom is expected to spend the next few weeks examining the proposals before making a decision within the next few months.

original: Stars pay tribute to actor Davis..Hollywood stars including Spike Lee, Burt Reynolds and Oscar nominee Alan Alda have paid tribute to actor Ossie Davis at a funeral in New York...Veteran star Ossie Davis, a well-known civil rights activist, died in Miami at the age of 87 on 4 February 2005. Friends and family, including actress Ruby Dee his wife of 56 years, gathered at the Riverside Church on Saturday. Also present at the service was former US president Bill Clinton and singer Harry Belafonte, who gave the eulogy. "He would have been a very good president of the United States," said Mr Clinton. "Like most of you here, he gave more to me than I gave to him."..The 87-year-old was found dead last weekend in his hotel room in Florida, where he was making a film. Police said that he appeared to have died of natural causes. Davis made his acting debut in 1950 in No Way Out starring Sidney Poiter. He frequently collaborated with director Spike Lee, starring in seven Lee films including Jungle Fever, Do The Right Thing and Malcolm X. Attallah Shabazz, the daughter of activist Malcolm X, recalled the famous eulogy delivered by Davis at her father's funeral. "Harlem has come to bid farewell to one of its finest hopes," she said, quoting the man she knew as Uncle Ossie. "Ditto." "Ossie was my hero, and he still is," said Aviator star Alan Alda, a family friend for over forty years. "Ossie was a thing of beauty.".."I want so badly someday to have his dignity - a little of it anyway," added Burt Reynolds, Davis's co-star in the 90s TV comedy Evening Shade. Before the midday funeral, scores of Harlem residents formed a queue outside the church to pay their respects to Davis. "It is hard to fathom that we will no longer be able to call on his wisdom, his humour, his loyalty and his moral strength to guide us in the choices that are yet to be made and the battles that are yet to be fought," said Belafonte, himself an ardent civil rights activist who had been friends with Davis for over 60 years. "But how fortunate we were to have him as long as we did."

Consumers drive French economy. France's economic growth accelerated in the last three months of 2004, significantly boosted by strong consumer spending, a new report shows. Gross domestic product (GDP) rose 0.8% in the final quarter, compared with the preceding three-month period, the official data revealed. That expansion translated into an impressive annual growth rate of 2.3%, its fastest rate in two years. Consumer spending surged by 1.2% in the fourth quarter, and there also was a significant rebound in business investment which provided the extra shove.

However, economists warned that France was facing serious challenges if it was to keep expanding at its current robust pace. "France has what appears to be robust economic growth," said Marc Toutai, an economist with Natexis Populaires. "But, if we check the figures in detail, there's a fundamental problem."

"Household consumption is still very strong. But French households have spent perhaps too much to consume. The economy can't sustain this high rate without a significant improvement in the job market. There's too much of a gap between growth and employment."

Unemployment levels are currently stuck at about 10%, and it is difficult to bring them down despite government attempts at reform. Another worry is that the economic situation in Germany, which is one of France's two most important trading partners, is currently struggling with stagnation.

Despite the underlying concerns, analysts pointed out France was outperforming the majority of its European Union partners and that its economy was performing much better than in previous years. As well as remarkably strong domestic demand, exports of goods and services climbed by 1.3% in the fourth quarter - the biggest increase in foreign sales for a decade.

"It's economic picture seems to be increasingly positive and broad-based," said Eric Claquin, an analyst at CCF. "In the beginning of 2004, growth was mainly driven by consumer spending. Here it gets significant support from both business investment and exports, though household consumption is still a major contributor." But most economists expect economic growth to fall to 2.0 percent in 2005.

Winn-Dixie files for bankruptcy. US group Winn-Dixie has filed for bankruptcy protection to tackle fierce competition in a market dominated by Wal-Mart. Winn-Dixie, once one of the most profitable of US grocers, said its Chapter 11 filing would allow it to successfully restructure its operations. Its 920 stores across the South-East US will remain open, though analysts said the company was likely to off-load a significant number of sites. The Jacksonville, Florida-based firm disclosed total debts of some $1.87bn (£980m). In its petition, Winn-Dixie listed its biggest creditors as foods giant Kraft Foods, which it owes $15.1m, and other major suppliers.

Industry observers say Winn-Dixie failed to keep up with changing consumers' demands and had also been hampered by a portfolio of ageing stores in need of significant investment and refurbishment. A 10-month restructuring plan last year was deemed a failure, and following a larger-than-expected loss earlier this month, Winn-Dixie's slide into Chapter 11 bankruptcy became inevitable.

Winn-Dixie's new chief Peter Lynch said the company would use the Chapter 11 breathing space to "take the necessary action to turn itself around." "This involves achieving significant cost reductions, improving the customer service in all its stores, and generating a sense of excitement in the stores," he said.

Yet, Evan, a senior analyst at Gimme Credit, said Mr Lynch's task "would not be easy at all, as the bankruptcy filing would undoubtedly put off customers." "The real issue is what's going to happen over the next one or two quarters now that they are in bankruptcy and customers see this in the newspapers," he added.

Mendes shot from 50 yards and United goalkeeper Roy Carroll spilled the ball into his own net before hooking it clear. Jol added: "We are not talking about the ball being a couple of centimetres or an inch or two over the line, it was a metre inside the goal. I didn't think we played particularly well but I am pleased- even now- with a point, although we should have had three." Mendes believe the 'goal' should have been given after seeing a replay. He said:" My first reaction was to turn to celebrate." It was a goal, well over the line- I've seen one so far over the line and it was not given in my career."' It's really, really frustrating. What can you do but laugh about it? It's nice to score and to celebrate in my own stadium even though it didn't count." It's not every game you score from the halfway line." Manchester United Sir Alex Ferguson agreed with Tottenham and said the incident highlighted the need for video technology." I think it hammers home the point a lot of people are asking for that's that technology should play a part in the game," Ferguson told MUTV." What I was against originally was the time factor with video replays." But I read an article the other day that suggested that if a referee can't make up his mind after 30 seconds of watching a video then the game should carry on..." Thirty seconds is the amount of time it takes to organise a free- kick or take a corner or goal- kick. So it wouldn't be a massive amount of time." I think you have to start off using it for goal- line decisions. I think that would be the opening into something new." When the whole world apart from the referee can see there should have been a goal at Old Trafford, it reinforces what I feel- there should be video evidence," Wenger said."' It's a perfect example where the referee could have asked to see a replay and would have seen in 10 seconds that it was a goal."

Camera phones are 'must-haves'. A new report says that four times more mobiles with cameras will be sold in Europe by the end of 2004 than in the previous year, says a report from analysts Gartner. In total, the number sold will reach 159 million units, an impressive increase of 104%. The same report predicts that nearly 70% of all mobile phones will have a built-in camera by 2008.

Imaging technology in these devices is making an "irresistible purchase" buy. In Europe, the cameras on mobiles can take 1.3 megapixel images. However, in Japan and Asia Pacific, camera phone technology is much more advanced and sophisticated; mobiles have already been released which can capture 3.2 megapixel images. Japan is at the forefront of this technology, and the uptake there is huge. By 2008, according to Gartner, 95% of all mobiles sold there will have cameras.

Camera phones initially had some problems when they were launched as people struggled with poor quality images and finding practical uses for them, as well as the expense of transmitting them via MMS (Messaging Service). This has changed in the last 18 months significantly. Handset makers have concentrated on trying to make phones easier to use. Recognising that people like to personalise their camera phones in various ways, they have incorporated advanced design features, like rotating screens and keypads, removable memory and easier methods to send messages.

Mobile companies have introduced numerous ways for people to share photos with other people. This includes giving people ways to publish them on websites, blogs and online photo galleries. But the Gartner report suggests that more consumers will be interested in printing pictures at retail kiosks.

The sensor technology inside phones is rapidly improving. The Gartner report states that by mid-2005, it is likely the image resolution of most camera phones will be more than two megapixels. Consumer digital cameras typically range from four, and up to six megapixels on a high-end camera. But a lot of work is being done to make camera phones more like digital cameras. Some handsets already feature limited optical zoom, and manufacturers are looking into technological improvements that people can use to capture better quality photos even in challenging environments like dimly lit nightclubs. Other developments include wide-angle modes, flash features, better sensors and processors for recording film.

Images from camera phones even made it into the art world. An exhibition next month for the charity Mencap, will feature snaps from the camera phones of top artists. This exhibition, Fonetography, will display images taken by photographers David, Rankin and Nan Goldin, alongside artists Blake, Emin and Vettriano.

But some of the potential implications for them have worried many. Intel, Samsung, the UK's Foreign Office and the Livermore National Laboratories in the US, have decided to ban camera phones from their buildings for fear of sensitive information being compromised and leaked. Gyms, leisure centres, and local councils also banned their use over fears about privacy infringement and misuse. Italy's information commissioner has also taken action and has issued guidelines on privacy protection and how phones can be used.

Camera phone fears have not dampened the manufacturers' profits. According to recent industry figures, Ericsson's profitability tripled the past quarter because of new camera phones. Over 60% of mobiles sold during the three months through to September featured cameras, the report indicated.

reconstruction:
A Nirvana box set has finally gone on sale, featuring 68 unreleased tracks, after years of protracted legal wrangles. The comprehensive collection, titled *With the Lights Out*, was originally intended to be released in 2001, to mark the 10th anniversary of their seminal album *Nevermind*.

However, its release was significantly delayed due to a dispute. It was Courtney Love, the widow of Nirvana frontman Kurt Cobain, who did not want the track *You Know You're Right* to be included on the compilation. The heated legal dispute between surviving band members Krist Novoselic and Dave Grohl, and Courtney Love, was eventually settled in 2002, paving the way for the box set's eventual release.

Work on the box set had actually begun as early as 1998, but the ensuing legal battles continually put the project on hold. The core of the legal wrangling centred on a specific recording of the previously unreleased track *You Know You're Right*, which was widely regarded by fans and critics alike as one of the most important and sought-after unreleased songs of Nirvana.

The new four-disc box set, released on Tuesday, features three CDs of rare studio recordings, demos, and live tracks, alongside a DVD showcasing previously unreleased performance footage. The DVD notably includes the first known performance of *Smells Like Teen Spirit*, the iconic track that catapulted Nirvana onto the international stage in 1991 and defined a generation.

"It's not always pretty, or always in tune. This is not Nirvana Unplugged. It's unedited," said Charles Cross, author of the acclaimed Nirvana biography *Heavier Than Heaven*, describing the raw nature of the material. The band's explosive and influential development ended tragically when their principal songwriter and frontman, Kurt Cobain, died by suicide in April 1994, bringing a premature end to one of rock's most significant acts.

reconstruction:
Manchester United strolled to a comfortable victory and progressed into the FA Cup quarter-finals with a dominant display. Wayne Rooney made a winning, if controversial, return to Merseyside as United eased into the next round of the competition at Goodison Park.

The former Everton striker received a predictably hostile reception from the Goodison faithful, but in each half Quinton Fortune and Cristiano Ronaldo found the net with well-taken goals, silencing the jeers and ensuring United's passage. Fortune opened the scoring after 23 minutes with a header, before Ronaldo scored after Nigel Martyn parried Paul Scholes' powerful free-kick into his path. Bent missed Everton's best chance of the first half when his close-range effort was brilliantly saved by United goalkeeper Roy Carroll. The match was later disrupted when Everton substitute goalkeeper Richard Wright was struck by a missile thrown from the crowd.

Rooney's emotional return was always expected to be a potential flashpoint, and he was involved in an angry verbal exchange with a section of the home support even before kick-off, underlining the intensity of the occasion. Indeed, his every touch was greeted with a deafening chorus of boos from the crowd that once idolised the 19-year-old striker, a testament to the raw emotion surrounding his departure from the club.

Everton started brightly, showing attacking intent in the opening exchanges and putting United under early pressure. Fortune needed to be particularly alert to scramble away a goal-bound header from Bent, preventing the hosts from taking an early and deserved lead. But that proved to be the catalyst for United to assert their authority, completing the first half with a supreme passing display on a Goodison Park pitch that was cutting up and making fluid football inherently difficult, yet United adapted well.

Fortune gave United a crucial lead after 23 minutes, rising high above the Everton defence to meet Cristiano Ronaldo's perfectly weighted cross from eight yards. The Portuguese youngster had been allowed far too much time and space down the right flank by a passive Gary Naysmith, allowing him to pick out his unmarked team-mate with ease.

United dominated possession for large spells without creating too many clear-cut chances, and they ultimately paid the price for their profligacy in front of goal just two minutes before the half-time whistle. Mikel Arteta played a superb through-ball into the penalty area, creating a golden opportunity for Bent. However, held back subtly by Heinze, he hesitated for a crucial moment, allowing Roy Carroll to rush out decisively and smother the danger before a shot could be taken.

United almost doubled their advantage just three minutes after the restart, after 48 minutes, when Ronaldo's fierce low drive from 25 yards took a deflection off Tony Hibbert, forcing Nigel Martyn to dive full-stretch and produce a brilliant save to keep Everton in the game. And Martyn's big rescue act arrived three minutes later as Everton's Kevin Campbell went clean through on goal after a defensive mix-up. But once again the veteran keeper was in inspired form, bravely denying Campbell with another crucial one-on-one save.

But there was ultimately nothing Martyn could do when United finally doubled their lead after 57 minutes, firmly establishing their control over the tie and putting the result beyond doubt. Paul Scholes' subsequent free-kick took a significant deflection off the defensive wall, wrong-footing Martyn who could only parry the ball out helplessly for Cristiano Ronaldo, who had the simplest of tasks to tap home from close range and seal his brace.

Everton's problems were further compounded when striker James McFadden limped off with an injury, necessitating an early substitution and further depleting their already stretched attacking options for the remainder of the match. And there may be further trouble ahead for Everton and the FA after their substitute goalkeeper Richard Wright required treatment on the pitch after he was struck on the head by a missile thrown from behind the goal, an unfortunate and ugly incident that marred the closing stages of the match and will surely be investigated.

Rooney's persistent search for a goal on his emotional return to Everton was ultimately halted by the impressive Martyn in injury-time when he outpaced defender David Weir to get clear, but was once again denied by the England international keeper who saved well low down.

- Manchester United coach Alex Ferguson praised his side's professionalism: "It was a fantastic performance by us, especially considering the atmosphere. In general, I think Everton have missed a couple of key, experienced players and some young players are having to come in to fill their shoes, which is tough."
Of Cristiano Ronaldo, Ferguson added: "Ronaldo is a phenomenon, a truly special talent. He's persistent and never gives up, always looking for the ball. I don't know how many fouls he had on him today but he keeps getting up and wants the ball. He's truly a fabulous player, a credit to the game, and he responded perfectly to the crowd."

original: Speech takes on search engines..A Scottish firm is looking to attract web surfers with a search engine that reads out results...Called Speegle, it has the look and feel of a normal search engine, with the added feature of being able to read out the results. Scottish speech technology firm CEC Systems launched the site in November. But experts have questioned whether talking search engines are of any real benefit to people with visual impairments...The Edinburgh-based firm CEC has married speech technology with ever-popular internet search. The ability to search is becoming increasingly crucial to surfers baffled by the huge amount of information available on the web...According to search engine Ask Jeeves, around 80% of surfers visit search engines as their first port of call on the net. People visiting Speegle can select one of three voices to read the results of a query or summarise news stories from sources such as the BBC and Reuters. "It is still a bit robotic and can make a few mistakes but we are never going to have completely natural sounding voices and it is not bad," said Speegle founder Gordon Renton. "The system is ideal for people with blurred vision or for those that just want to search for something in the background while they do something else. "We are not saying that it will be suitable for totally blind people, although the Royal National Institute of the Blind (RNIB) is looking at the technology," he added. But Julie Howell, digital policy manager at the RNIB, expressed doubts over whether Speegle and similar sites added anything to blind people's experience of the web. "There are a whole lot of options like this springing up on the web and one has to think carefully about what the market is going to be," she said. "Blind people have specialised screen readers available to them which will do the job these technologies do in a more sophisticated way," she added...The site uses a technology dubbed PanaVox, which takes web text and converts it into synthesised speech. In the past speech technology has only been compatible with broadband because of the huge files it downloads but CEC says its compression technology means it will also work on slower dial-up connections. Visitors to Speegle may notice that the look and feel of the site bears more than a passing resemblance to the better known, if silent, search engine Google. Google has no connection with Speegle and the use of bright colours is simply to make the site more visible for those with visual impairments, said Mr Renton. "It is not a rip-off. We are doing something that Google does not do and is not planning to do and there is truth in the saying that imitation is the sincerest form of flattery," he said. Speegle is proving popular with those learning English in countries such as Japan and China. "The site is bombarded by people just listening to the words. The repetition could be useful although they may all end up talking like robots," said Mr Renton.

reconstruction:
Speech takes search to the web. A new search engine, Speegle, is looking to attract web surfers with an engine that reads results aloud. Called Speegle, it has the look and feel of a normal search engine, but with the added feature of being able to read out results. Scottish speech technology firm CEC Systems launched the site last November. But some critics have questioned whether talking search engines are of any real use to people with visual impairments.

The Edinburgh-based CEC Systems has married speech technology with the ever-popular web search, aiming to make search less daunting for surfers baffled by the huge amount of information on the internet. According to search engine Ask Jeeves, around 80% of surfers visit search engines as their first call on the net. Users can select one of three voices to read the results of their query and summarise news from sources such as the BBC and The Press Association.

"It is still a robotic voice, it can make a few mistakes and is never going to have a completely natural sounding voice, but it's not bad," said Graeme Renton, chief executive of Speegle. "The system is ideal for people with blurred vision or for those that just want to search for something in the background while they do something else. It will not be for totally blind people, although the Royal National Institute of the Blind (RNIB) is looking at the technology," he added.

Julie Howell, digital policy manager at RNIB, expressed doubts over whether similar sites added anything meaningful to blind people's experience of the web. "There are a whole lot of options like this springing up all over the web and one has to think about what the market is going to be," she said. "Blind people have specialised screen readers available to them which do exactly what these sites do, but in a more sophisticated way," she added.

Speegle uses a technology called PanaVox, which takes text and converts it into synthesised speech. In the past speech technology has often only been compatible with broadband because of the large files it uses, but thanks to advanced file compression it also works on slower dial-up connections. Visitors to Speegle may notice that its look bears a passing resemblance to the better known, silent, Google. "Google has no connection with Speegle and the choice of colours is simply to make the site more accessible to people with visual impairments," said Mr Renton.

"It is not a rip-off. We are doing something that Google does not do and is not planning to do and there is truth in the saying that imitation is the sincerest form of flattery," he added. Speegle is proving popular with those learning English in countries such as Japan and China. "The learner is bombarded by just too many words. But repetition could be useful although they may all end up sounding like talking robots," said Mr Renton.

original: Profits slide at India's Dr Reddy..Profits at Indian drugmaker Dr Reddy's fell 93% as research costs rose and sales flagged...The firm said its profits were 40m rupees ($915,000; £486,000) for the three months to December on sales which fell 8% to 4.7bn rupees. Dr Reddy's has built its reputation on producing generic versions of big-name pharmaceutical products. But competition has intensified and the firm and the company is short on new product launches. The most recent was the annoucement in December 2000 that it had won exclusive marketing rights for a generic version of the famous anti-depressant Prozac from its maker, Eli Lilly. It also lost a key court case in March 2004, banning it from selling a version of Pfizer's popular hypertension drug Norvasc in the US. Research and development of new drugs is continuing apace, with R&D spending rising 37% to 705m rupees - a key cause of the decrease in profits alongside the fall in sales. Patents on a number of well-known products are due to run out in the near future, representing an opportunity for Dr Reddy, whose shares are listed in New York, and other Indian generics manufacturers...Sales in Dr Reddy's generics business fell 8.6% to 966m rupees. Another staple of the the firm's business, the sale of ingredients for drugs, also performed poorly. Sales were down more than 25% from the previous year to 1.4bn rupees in the face of strong competition both at home, and in the US and Europe. reconstruction: Japanese stocks have started the new year brightly, climbing to their highest levels since December 13, 2004, amidst growing optimism that the country's economic recovery will continue to strengthen throughout 2005. This positive sentiment marks a significant shift. The benchmark Nikkei 225 index of leading shares rose sharply, adding a substantial 7.6% in early trading to close at 11,488.76 points. This strong performance reflects renewed investor confidence. Forecasters are now more bullish about the market's prospects. "In 2005 it could well rise toward 13,000," commented Naoki Murata, a strategist at Morgan Stanley. Such a climb would indicate a sustained recovery. However, this palpable optimism in the financial markets stands in sharp contrast to the persistent pessimism and cautious outlook that continues to pervade the broader Japanese business community. The disconnect highlights ongoing challenges. Indeed, earlier this month, the Bank of Japan's closely watched quarterly Tankan survey of Japanese manufacturers revealed a significant setback. It indicated that business confidence had fallen for the first time since the final quarter of 2003, raising concerns about the recovery's robustness. A combination of factors, including sluggish domestic economic growth, a worrying trend of rising raw material prices, and a stronger yen making Japanese exports less competitive on international markets, were widely blamed for this unexpected fall in confidence among executives. Despite these headwinds and the cautious mood, many traders remain confident. They anticipate that the continued strength of the global economy will significantly benefit Japan, a nation uncomfortably close to sliding back into recession in recent months. Furthermore, they suggest that decisive structural reforms within Japan's economy and a definitive end to the corporate sector's lingering "bad debt" problems and other fundamental issues should ultimately help to secure a more sustainable and robust economic recovery for the nation, they say.

It features a stellar line-up of contemporary artists including Coldplay's Chris Martin, Dido, Robbie Williams, and the Sugababes, all lending their voices to a crucial cause.

The original 1984 rendition of 'Do They Know It's Christmas?', orchestrated by Bob Geldof and Midge Ure, also hit number one, selling an astonishing 750,000 copies in its debut week and ultimately achieving 3.5 million total sales globally. It is a traditional first-person-viewed game that lets you control just one character, in the midst of a battlefield where cohorts shout orders at you. On a contrasting note, Medal of Honor: Pacific Assault does all it can to make you feel part of a tight-knit squad and plum into the middle of all-out action. Its arenas are the war's Pacific battles, including Guadalcanal and Pearl Harbour. You play as one character throughout, a raw rather green US soldier.

Both games rely on a carefully stage-managed structure that keeps things ticking. When this works, it is a brilliant device to make you feel part of a story. When it does not, it's tedious. A moment from an early scene in Pacific Assault, you come under attack at the dockyard in Hawaii. You are first catapulted into a gunboat attacking the shore of Oahu, made to save a sinking rescue crewman, before seizing the anti-aircraft guns. It's one of the finest set-pieces ever seen in a game. But shuffling the player along a studiously-determined path, forcibly witnessing a series of pre-set moments of action, is a perilous business which can make the whole affair feel more stilted than organic. Unlike games like Half Life 2 that disguise its linearity by various means of misdirection. This pair of games do ultimately accomplish, however, being successful with imparting a hands-on atmospheric experience.

Call of Duty comes with a bombastic and engaging presentation. Finest Hour has a more sombre tone, framing everything in moody music, archival footage and lots of voice-over. Being able to play different roles is an interesting ploy that adds new layers to this type of endeavour, even if it sacrifices the narrative. The game's drawback could be said to be its format; they differ, but wartime shooters often do seem to work on PC. The control is a big reason why, along with the sharper graphics a high-end computer can deliver and the apparent notion that PC is allowed to get away with a bit more subtlety. Call of Duty on PC was more detailed, gameplay-wise, and this new adaptation feels a little rough and ready. The PS2 controller is tricky, and not helped by flaky collision-detection. You can be right next to an enemy with zero question as to your aim, yet bullets will just refuse to hit. Checkpoints are so few and far between that when you get shot, which happens often, you are harshly thrown far back, and will find yourself covering tracts of scorched earth again and again. The game is meant to be a challenge, and it is, and players like it that way. It provides as dynamic a battlefield as you will find, and even though it is not as refined as its PC parent, its sense of being in the thick of action is thoroughly impressive.

Both of these games feature military AI who are disturbingly poor shots and prone to standing in the open. reconstruction:
Brown shrugs off worries about the state of the economy as he delivers his Pre-Budget Report to the House of Commons. Gordon Brown is planning to freeze petrol duty increases, and will fund a £1bn package to avoid big council tax increases and to boost spending on childcare and maternity leave, it was announced today. In his annual Pre-Budget Report, the Treasury's forecasts for economic growth were slightly increased but insisted that the government's fiscal targets would be met in the medium term. He hailed the longest period of growth in UK "industrial history" and denied he was "gloating", despite the favourable economic outlook he presented. But Oliver Letwin, for the Tories, launched a strong attack on the government's spending policies and rising national debt, dubbing Mr Brown "Sir Wastealot", and accusing him of recklessness. The shadow chancellor said Mr Brown's "golden rule" had "dross hands" and he was simply borrowing to spend, not invest, predicted over the coming five years, totalling £170bn in public borrowing. Mr Letwin told MPs: "The tide is out on the 'credibility of this government'. He is spending, borrowing and taxing much too much because he is not getting the taxpayer's money's worth from public services."

Vincent Cable, for the Liberal Democrats, accused Mr Brown of presiding over an economy built on complacency and ignoring looming risks, particularly from the global economic environment. He said: "Last week the minister offered the politics of fear; this week the chancellor has offered the economics of complacency." There are serious challenges ahead from the weakening dollar, rapid changes in the UK market and rising personal debt. But they have not been confronted effectively by the government, he argued. Brown rejected the Liberal Democrat's call to open the Treasury's books to the National Audit Office, insisting that decisions on taxation and public spending should remain the remit of elected ministers, rather than being delegated to external bodies. Some critics claimed that his public finances are wishful thinking, while others questioned the accuracy of his forecasts. BBC Economics editor Evan Davis said the figures were largely credible but also a considerable gamble given the uncertainties ahead. Mr Brown's insistence he was "not gloating" was seen as a pointed rebuttal to a recent intervention from new European Commissioner Peter Mandelson, who had previously warned against economic triumphalism. In his speech, he set out a 10-year strategy for transforming childcare for families if Labour wins the next general election, describing it as a cornerstone of the party's future domestic agenda.

It includes a £285m cash injection to extend paid maternity leave from six to nine months, with the option for some of the leave to be transferable from the mother to the father, providing greater flexibility for working parents. He also committed to increasing free education for three and four-year-olds to 15 hours a week from April 2007, a move welcomed by early years campaigners. And funds would be provided to keep schools open from 0800 to 1800GMT to provide after-school care for children while their parents work, aiming to ease the burden on families. Taken together, the measures create a "welfare system that is truly family-friendly for the first time in history", Mr Brown declared, emphasising the long-term vision of his proposals. He announced a cash hand-out for pensioners and vulnerable groups, payments of £50 for the over-70s as an extra element of the winter fuel allowance, a popular measure designed to help with living costs. In a move ministers say should keep tax rises below 5% next year, the chancellor confirmed he was providing an extra £1bn for local councils, to help them maintain front-line services. The money is expected to be sourced from government efficiency savings in departments such as health, he added, without providing specific details of where cuts would be made.

Mr Brown reiterated that he was set to meet all his fiscal rules - to borrow only to invest and keep national debt "low and prudent" - both in this economic cycle and the next, a key pledge of his chancellorship. Borrowing figures for 2003/04 are £35bn - £2.5bn lower than the £37.5bn in March's budget, as already indicated by the Treasury for this financial year, providing some positive news for the Chancellor. Borrowing is tipped to fall to £31bn by 2005/06 - but still £2bn more than Mr Brown predicted in his March budget statement, indicating a slight increase in projected future borrowing. Economic growth would stand at 1.75% this year and rise to 2% in years to follow, Mr Brown confirmed, reaffirming the government's optimistic outlook for the economy. He pledged an additional £105m for national security and anti-terrorism measures, highlighting the government's commitment to public safety. Business groups have generally welcomed the government's efforts to improve competitiveness and to invest in skills and innovation, recognising the importance of these areas for economic growth. But there remain worries about the costs of more flexible working arrangements for employers, with some warning of the administrative burden on small and medium-sized enterprises. Simon Walker, from the Federation of Small Businesses, said: "The proposals on paid maternity leave and childcare have clearly been made with a general election in mind, with little thought to the practical impact on small businesses, which often struggle to absorb additional costs or staff absences."

original: India's Reliance family feud heats up..The ongoing public spat between the two heirs of India's biggest conglomerate, Reliance Group, has spilled over to the board meeting of a leading company within the group...Anil Ambani, vice-chairman of India Petrochemicals Limited (IPCL), stayed away from a gathering of senior managers on Thursday. His resignation was not accepted by his brother, who is also the boss of IPCL. The IPCL board met in Mumbai to discuss the company's results for the October-to-December quarter...It is understood that the board also considered Anil's resignation and asked him to reconsider his decision. original: Court mulls file-sharing future..Judges at the US Supreme Court have been hearing evidence for and against file-sharing networks...The court will decide whether producers of file-sharing software can ultimately be held responsible for copyright infringement. They questioned if opening the way for the entertainment industry to sue file-sharers could deter innovation. They also said that file-trading firms had some responsibility for inducing people to piracy...The lawsuit, brought by 28 of the world's largest entertainment firms, has raged for several years. Legal experts agree that if the Supreme Court finds in favour of the music and movie industry they would be able to sue file-trading firms into bankruptcy. But if the judge rules that Grokster and Morpheus - the file-sharers at the centre of the case - are merely providers of technology that can have legitimate as well as illegitimate uses, then the music and movie industry would be forced to abandon its pursuit of file-sharing providers. Instead, they would have to pursue individuals who use peer-to-peer networks to get their hands on free music and movies. The hi-tech and entertainment industries have been divided on the issue. Intel filed a document with the Supreme Court earlier this month in defence of Grokster and others, despite misgivings about some aspects of the file-sharing community. It summed up the attitude of many tech firms in its submission which states that its products "are essentially tools, that like any other tools, capable of being used by consumers and businesses for unlawful purposes"...Asking firms to second-guess the uses that its technologies would be put to, and to build in ways of preventing illegitimate use, would stifle innovation, it said. The Electronic Frontier Foundation, a civil rights watchdog, is also defending StreamCast Networks, the company behind the Morpheus file-sharing software. The case raises a question of critical importance at the border between copyright and innovation, it said. It cites, as do many, the landmark ruling in 1984 which found that Sony should not be held responsible for the fact that its Betamax video recorder could be used for piracy. Defenders remain optimistic that the judges will rule in favour of the peer-to-peer networks, upholding the precedent set by the Sony Betamax case. A small band of supporters were outside the court as the lawyers entered, wearing "Save Betamax" t-shirts. "The Betamax principles stand as the Magna Carta for the technology industry and are responsible for the explosion in innovation that has occurred in the US over the past 20 years," said Gary Shapiro, chief executive of the Consumer Electronics Association. Supreme Court Justice Stephen Breyer said that inventions from printing to Apple's iPod could be used to illegally duplicate copyrighted materials but had, on balance, been beneficial to society. He said that while file-trading software can be used to illegally trade movies and music, conceptually the technology had "some really excellent uses"...Based on Tuesday's hearing it seems unlikely that the Betamax ruling will be overturned but file-sharing firms might still be held responsible for encouraging or inducing piracy. Grokster's lawyer argued that the company should be judged by its current behaviour rather than what it did when it first set up. But this argument was dismissed as "ridiculous" by Justice David Souter. CEA boss Mr Shapiro thinks the case is the most important that the Supreme Court will hear this year. "It's about preserving America's proud history of technological innovation and protecting the ability of consumers to access and utilise technology," he said. The case has already been heard by two lower courts and both found in favour of the peer-to-peer networks. They ruled that despite being used to distribute millions of illegal songs, file-sharing could also be used to cheaply distribute software, government documents and promotional copies of music.

The lawsuit, brought by 28 of the world's largest entertainment companies, has raged for several years. Legal experts widely agree that if the Supreme Court finds in favour of the music and movie industry, they would be empowered to sue file-trading firms into bankruptcy. But if the justices rule against them – and determine that the file-sharers at the centre of the dispute are merely providers of technology that can have legitimate as well as illegitimate uses – the music and movie industry would be forced to abandon their broad legal fight against file-sharing. Instead, they would have to pursue individual users peer-to-peer to get their hands on free music and movies.

The hi-tech and entertainment industries have been on the offensive. Intel, a major technology company, filed a document with the Supreme Court earlier this month in defence of Grokster and others, despite some aspects of the file-sharing community that it might disagree with. It told the court in its submission that its "products are essentially tools, that like any other, are capable of being used by consumers and businesses for both legal and legitimate purposes". Asking firms to second-guess the myriad uses their technologies would be put to, and to build in ways of preventing illegitimate uses, would severely stifle innovation, it said.

The Electronic Frontier Foundation, a prominent civil rights group, also backs StreamCast Networks, the company behind the Morpheus file-sharing software. The case raises questions of fundamental importance at the border between copyright protection and technological innovation, it said. It cites, as many others do, the landmark ruling in 1984 that Sony should not be held responsible for the fact that its Betamax video recorder could be used for piracy, establishing a crucial precedent for new technologies.

Lawyers for Grokster and other peer-to-peer firms remain optimistic that the judges will rule in favour of their position, upholding the precedent set by Betamax. A small band of supporters were outside the court as the justices entered, wearing "Betamax" T-shirts and carrying signs. "The Betamax principles stand as a Magna Carta for the technology industry and are responsible for the explosion in innovation that occurred in the world over the last 20 years," said Gary Shapiro, chief executive of the Consumer Electronics Association. Justice Stephen Breyer said that inventions from photocopiers to Apple's iPod, which could be used to copy copyrighted material, had, on balance, been extremely beneficial to society. He noted that while file-trading software can be used to trade pirated movies and music, the technology also had "some really great uses" for legal purposes.

Based on Tuesday's hearing, it is widely considered unlikely that the Betamax ruling will be directly overturned, but file-sharing firms might still be held responsible for encouraging or inducing copyright infringement. Grokster's lawyer argued strongly that the firm should be judged by its current behaviour rather than what it did when it first started up its service. But this argument was dismissed as "ridiculous" by David Nimmer, a prominent lawyer representing the entertainment industry. The CEA boss thinks the case is the most significant that the Supreme Court will hear this year, with far-reaching implications for the tech sector.

"It's about preserving America's history of technological innovation and protecting the ability of consumers to access technology," he said. The case has already been heard by two lower courts, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals and the Central District of California, and both found in favour of the peer-to-peer networks. They ruled that despite being used to distribute millions of illegal songs, file-sharing could also be used to cheaply distribute independent films, government documents, and promotional copies of music.

The Mid-Bedfordshire MP had denied a claim that he was paid for guiding visitors around the Palace of Westminster. Conservative leader Michael Howard has now accepted the MP's resignation, it has been announced...Mr Sayeed was suspended from Parliament for two weeks last month after the Commons standards and privileges committee said his conduct had fallen "well below the standards expected". The Conservative Party had already been withdrawn the whip for a month. But his constituency association voted against a move to deselect him, with Mr Sayeed winning 173 of the 299 votes. After the vote, Mr Sayeed said only a fifth of association members had voted against him and he intended to get on with winning the election. But the vote prompted constituency association president Sir Stanley Odell to resign in protest. The Standards and Privileges Committee inquiry was launched after the Sunday Times alleged English Manner Limited charged clients for access to Westminster through Mr Sayeed. Mr Sayeed had denied the claims, saying the suspension was "unjust and wrong" but he made an "unreserved" apology to MPs in the Commons chamber. He insisted that the committee's report had contained a "few errors of fact". Mr Sayeed has been MP for Mid-Bedfordshire since 1997. He represented Bristol East from 1983 to 1992.

Mid-Bedfordshire MP Mohammed Sayeed is standing down at the next general election on the grounds of ill-health. This decision comes after a period of significant controversy for the long-serving Conservative politician. His announcement follows Mr Sayeed's survival of a recent attempt to be deselected as a candidate in his constituency, amidst serious allegations that he had profited from the private use of his status as a Member of Parliament.

The MP had consistently denied a claim that he charged substantial fees to clients for guiding them around the Palace of Westminster, utilising his parliamentary access for personal gain.
Conservative Party leader Michael Howard has now formally accepted Mr Sayeed's decision not to seek re-election, a party spokesman has announced. This brings an end to months of public speculation surrounding the MP's future.

Mr Sayeed was previously suspended from the House of Commons for a period of two weeks last month after the Commons Standards and Privileges Committee delivered a report which found his conduct to have fallen "below that expected" of an elected representative. Prior to that parliamentary suspension, the Conservative Party had already taken disciplinary action against Mr Sayeed, withdrawing the party whip from him for a month.

Despite the controversies, his local Mid-Bedfordshire Conservative constituency association had voted against a move to deselect him. Mr Sayeed secured 173 of the 299 votes cast by members at the meeting. After the vote, Mr Sayeed addressed only about one-fifth of the association members present, stating that he intended to get on with winning the next general election for the party. However, following the contentious result, the association president Stanley Odell promptly resigned in protest, highlighting deep divisions within the local party.

The Committee's extensive inquiry had initially been launched following a report in The Times newspaper which alleged that a lobbyist had charged clients substantial sums for privileged access to Westminster through Mr Sayeed's parliamentary connections and influence.

Throughout the investigation and subsequent disciplinary actions, Mr Sayeed had consistently denied the core allegations against him. He publicly stated that his parliamentary suspension was "unfair and unjust," although he later made an "unreserved" apology to his fellow MPs in the House of Commons for any distress or damage to the reputation of Parliament. Despite his apology, he continued to insist that the committee's report, which detailed its findings, had contained a "few errors of fact," though he did not specify which points he disputed.

Mohammed Sayeed had served as the Member of Parliament for Mid-Bedfordshire since 1997. He had previously represented the constituency of Bristol East in the House of Commons from 1983 to 1992, before losing his seat.

He said that under a new Labour government, people would face a massive bill to clean up after the election and plug a financial black hole, Mr Howard said. He added that people could see through the chancellor's "sweeteners", which hid real tax rises for hard-working families, he said. Labour's "election campaign" would be characterised by a package of measures, Mr Howard warned. Mr Brown's Budget was not about what was best for the country, but "all about the narrow interests of the Labour party," the Tory leader said after welcoming the chancellor back to the Commons. "Their only answer is to tax, to borrow and to waste - simply to get a vote now and make people pay dearly later." Mr Brown, he claimed, liked to rattle "magical balances conjured out of thin air" in a desperate bid to convince people there was no "hole" in the nation's finances, the Tory leader asserted. "This dodgy government that gave us the dodgy dossier is now publishing a Budget document based on dodgy numbers," he further elaborated. "You propose to borrow, over the next six years, no less than £168 billion of taxpayers' money; so much for fiscal prudence." "The chancellor's figures are no more than the prime minister's political weapons of mass distraction." Mr Brown's council tax rebate for pensioners was £300 less than what the Tories were prepared to offer, Mr Howard stated. There was absolutely nothing in this Budget that would put more police officers on the streets, make our hospitals cleaner or give parents the vital discipline skills they desperately needed in schools. People would face a "stark and clear choice" at the forthcoming election, either "borrowing and ever higher taxes under Labour or lower taxes and true value for money from the Conservatives", Mr Howard declared. "That's the fundamental choice of this election. That's precisely what this election is going to be all about and I say bring it on," he concluded, to loud Tory cheering.

Continental also said that, if it did not make any cuts, it expects to lose "hundreds of millions of dollars" in 2005 in current market conditions. Failure to make cutbacks may also push it to reduce its fleet, the group said. Shares in the fifth biggest US carrier had fallen 6.87% on the news to $10.44 by 1830 GMT. "Without the reduction in wage and benefit costs and a reasonable prospect of future profitability, we believe that our ability to raise additional money through financings would be uncertain," Continental said in its filing to the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)...Airlines have faced tough conditions in recent years, amid terrorism fears since the 11 September World Trade Centre attack in 2001. The company has been working to streamline its operations - and has managed to save $1.1bn in costs without cutting jobs. Two weeks' ago the group also announced it would be able to shave a further $48m a year from its costs with changes to wage and benefits for most of its US-based management and clerical staff.

reconstruction: Indy into India. Irish publishing group Independent News & Media is buying up a 26% stake in Indian media company Jagran worth £25m ($34.1m). Jagran publishes India's top-selling daily newspaper, the Hindi-language Dainik Jagran, which has been publishing for 62 years. News of the acquisition came as the group announced its latest results, confirming they would meet market forecasts. The company reported strong growth across all its major markets globally. Group advertising revenue was up over 10% year-on-year, with circulation revenues also expected to rise by almost 10% year-on-year. This was helped by the positive reception of its "compact" editions in Ireland and the UK, the company said. "2004 has proven to be a particularly important year for Independent News & Media," said chief executive Sir Anthony O'Reilly. "Our simple aim at Independent News & Media is to be the lowest cost producer in every region in which we operate. I am confident that the group will show a meaningful increase in earnings for 2005." Meanwhile, the group made no firm announcement regarding the future of the Independent newspaper despite recent reports that Sir Anthony O'Reilly had held talks with potential buyers of a stake in its daily publication. He denied that the Independent and the Independent on Sunday are for sale. But it is understood that the recent redesign of the main edition of the Independent, which has pushed circulation by 20% to 260,000, has prompted concern from industry rivals, with Daily Mail & General Trust among the most concerned. The loss-making newspaper is still not expected to reach break-even until 2006.
