Support for a ban on fox hunting is 'in decline', a new poll suggests. The survey indicates that less than half of the public now favour a ban, a significant drop from almost two-thirds who supported such a measure in 1999. This data comes from a Mori survey of 2,000 adults, commissioned for BBC One's Countryfile programme.

While the proportion of people actively opposed to a ban has remained relatively constant, there has been a notable shift among the undecided. Those who say they 'neither support nor oppose' the ban have increased by 11%.

The poll also highlights a divergence in opinion based on geographical location. Urban-dwellers continue to show strong support for a ban on fox hunting. However, among rural communities, opinions are much more divided, with people almost evenly split between those who support a ban, those who oppose it, and those who remain undecided.

The polling company Mori carried out both surveys, ensuring consistency in methodology. In 1999, 801 adults were asked if they supported a ban for the Mail on Sunday. For the latest survey, Mori asked 2,234 adults across the country the same question, focusing on their stance on a fox hunting ban.

The 1999 survey found that 63% supported a ban on fox hunting compared with 24% against. In the latest survey, 47% supported the legislation, with 26% against. This marks a clear shift in public opinion.

The programme makers suggest the public are 'divided' because around a quarter say they 'neither support nor oppose' a ban. This growing segment indicates a lack of clear consensus on the issue, contributing to the overall decline in outright ban support.

original: Asia shares defy post-quake gloom..Thailand has become the first of the 10 southern Asian nations battered by giant waves at the weekend to cut its economic forecast...Thailand's economy is now expected to grow by 5.7% in 2005, rather than 6% as forecast before tsunamis hit six tourist provinces. The full economic costs of the disaster remain unclear. In part, this is because of its scale, and because delivering aid and recovering the dead remain priorities. But Indonesian, Indian and Hong Kong stock markets reached record highs on Wednesday, suggesting that investors do not fear a major economic impact...The highs showed the gap in outlook between investors in large firms and individuals who have lost their livelihoods...Investors seemed to feel that some of the worst-affected areas - such as Aceh in Indonesia - were so under-developed that the tragedy would little impact on Asia's listed companies, according to analysts. "Obviously with a lot of loss of life, a lot of time is needed to clean up the mess, bury the people and find the missing. But it's not necessarily a really big thing in the economic sense," said ABN Amro chief Asian strategist Eddie Wong. India's Bombay Stock Exchange inched slightly above its previous record close on Wednesday. Expectations of strong corporate earnings in 2005 drove the Indonesian stock exchange in Jakarta to a record high on Wednesday. In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng index may be benefiting in part from the potential for its listed property companies to gain from rebuilding contracts in the tsunami-affected regions of South East Asia. In Sri Lanka, some economists have said that as much as 1% of annual growth may be lost. Sri Lanka's stock market has fallen about 5% since the weekend, but it is still 40% higher than at the start of 2004...Thailand may lose 30bn baht (£398m; $768m) in earnings from tourism over the next three months, according to tourism minister Sontaya Kunplome...In the affected provinces, he expects the loss of tourism revenue to be offset by government reconstruction spending. Thailand intends to spend a similar sum - around 30bn baht - on the rebuilding work. "It will take until the fourth quarter of next year before tourist visitors in Phuket and five other provinces return to their normal level," said Naris Chaiyasoot, director general at the ministry's fiscal policy office. In the Maldives the cost of reconstruction could wipe out economic growth, according to a government spokesman. "Our nation is in peril here," said Ahmed Shaheed, the chief government spokesman. He estimated the economic cost of the disaster at hundreds of millions of dollars. The Maldives has gross domestic product of $660m. "It won't be surprising if the cost exceeds our GDP," he said. "In the last few years, we made great progress in our standard of living - the United Nations recognised this. Now we see this can disappear in a few days, a few minutes." Shaheed noted that investment in a single tourist resort - the economic mainstay - could run to $40m. Between 10 and 12 of the 80-odd resorts have been severely damaged, and a similar number have suffered significant damage. However, many experts, including the World Bank, have pointed out that it is still difficult to assess the magnitude of the disaster and its likely economic impact.

original: NHS waiting time target is cut..Hospital waiting times for patients in Wales are to be cut, but not to the same extent as those in England...Welsh Health Minister Jane Hutt said no patient would wait more than 12 months for an outpatient appointment by March 2006, against a current target of 18 months. But she said the target for an inpatient appointment would remain at 12 months for March 2006. The announcement came as new monthly waiting figures showed a drop. This current inpatient target was set when the assembly government extended its second offer guarantee scheme, which gives patients the option of having their treatment outside Wales...Details about funding to resource the new targets are expected in the New Year. In England, the current target for inpatients - seeing a consultant to having an operation - is six months. Dr Richard Lewis, Welsh secretary of the British Medical Association (BMA), welcomed the new targets "to make further and faster progress on waiting lists". "However, much remains to be done on waiting lists and waiting times because Wales still lags a long way behind England," he said. "Capacity must be built into the system with sustained investment to ensure that Welsh patients don't receive a worse service than patients over the border." Health analyst Tony Beddow, from the Welsh Institute for Health and Social Care, called the new targets "reasonably impressive"...On Wednesday, Ms Hutt also announced £264m for health services will be spent reducing waiting times, improving key areas and modernising staff pay structures in Wales...Ms Hutt said major achievements had been made in cutting "unacceptably long waits for treatment over the past year". "We are turning the corner on long waits in Wales. Now we need to see those reductions in long waiters being improved again," she said. She added the targets intended to ensure no-one waits more than a year for treatment or to see a consultant. "But let us not forget two thirds of those waiting for treatment now are waiting less than six months, and these targets affect the small minority of patients in Wales that are waiting far too long." Rhodri Glyn Thomas, Plaid Cymru health spokesman said: "It's exactly the same target she set in 1999, with the qualification that it's dependent on a second offer. It's a failed target, from a failed minister..with a failed policy." For the Welsh Liberal Democrats, Kirsty Williams called the new target "hugely unambitious". "It leaves patients in Wales still waiting two years before they're treated." Conservative health spokesman Jonathan Morgan said: "We're spending more money but waiting lists have gone through the roof. "The Audit Commission has said that the money is not being spent efficiently or effectively, and that's quite a criticism." Meanwhile, the latest monthly waiting list figures showed the total number of people waiting more than 18 months as an inpatient in Wales has fallen by 9.8%. Statistics to the end of November showed a decline since October from 785 to 708. The number waiting over 12 months also fell from 7,613 to 6,630, or 12.9%. Ms Hutt said they were "excellent figures". There are 305,775 people on a waiting list of some kind, down from 311,764 last month.

reconstruction:
At the same time, hospital waiting times for patients in Wales are not to be the same as those in England. Minister Jane Hutt said no patient would wait more than 12 months for an outpatient appointment by March 2006, a target that had previously been 18 months. But she said the target for an inpatient appointment would remain at 12 months by March 2006. The announcement came as waiting lists continued to drop. This current target was set when the Welsh Assembly Government extended its second offer guarantee scheme, which gives patients the option of having treatment outside Wales. Further details about the resources that the new targets will require are expected in the New Year. In Wales, the average waiting time for current inpatients - those seeing a consultant or having an operation - is 21 months. Dr Richard Lewis, Welsh secretary of the British Medical Association (BMA), welcomed the new targets, saying they would "make real and faster progress on waiting lists".

"However, much work remains to be done on waiting lists and waiting times, as Wales still lags a way behind England," he said. "Capacity must be built into the investment to ensure that patients don't receive worse treatment than over the border." Health analyst Tony Beddow, from Welsh for Health and Social Care, described the targets as "reasonably impressive" in their scope.

Ms Hutt also announced that £264m in health funding will be spent on reducing waiting lists, with key areas including modernising hospital structures in Wales. Ms Hutt highlighted achievements in tackling "unacceptably long waits for treatment this year".

"We are turning the corner on long waits in Wales. We need to see those currently identified as long waiters being treated again," she said. She stressed that the targets were intended to ensure no-one waits longer than a year for treatment or to see a consultant. "But let us not forget that two thirds of those waiting for treatment now are waiting less than six months, and these new targets specifically affect the minority of patients in Wales who are waiting far too long."

Glyn Thomas, Plaid Cymru spokesman, commented: "It's exactly the same target she set in 1999, with the qualification 'dependent on the second offer'. It's a failed target, from a failed minister, with a failed policy."

For the Welsh Liberal Democrats, Kirsty Williams called the target "meaningless and unachievable". "It means patients could potentially wait up to two years before they are treated."

Conservative health spokesman Jonathan Morgan stated: "We're spending money and waiting lists have gone through the roof." The Audit Commission has clearly said that the money is not being spent efficiently or effectively, and that's quite a damning indictment."

Meanwhile, the latest waiting list figures showed that the total number of people waiting more than 18 months as an inpatient had fallen by 9.8%. Statistics to the end of October showed a decline from 785 to 708. The number of people waiting over 12 months also fell from 7,613 to 6,630, a reduction of 12.9%. Ms Hutt said these were "encouraging figures". Overall, there are now 305,775 people on a waiting list of some kind, down from 311,764 last month.

reconstruction:
Fear, Mr Kennedy warned, voters would have a clear choice between the politics of fear and the politics of hope, said Charles Kennedy, launching his New Year message and sharply attacking both Labour and the Conservatives. He asserted that his party was the one of hope, looking forward with confidence to a general election in 2005. The devastating Asian tsunami had, he noted, revealed the "heartening" generosity being shown by Britons from all walks of life.

Mr Kennedy, speaking as his thoughts were very much with those affected by the humanitarian disaster in Asia, where he had spent Christmas helping coordinate relief efforts, said voters were increasingly turning to the Liberal Democrats as they became disillusioned with the policies and approaches of the other main political parties. A general election, he predicted, would be a "defining moment" for the country, as his party positioned itself as a truly national voice, with the Liberal Democrats ready to challenge Labour on its entire record, he said.

He argued there was a clear philosophical choice now evident in British politics - between the politics of fear and the politics of hope. He claimed that Labour was deliberately counting on the politics of fear, ratcheting up public anxiety with persistent talk of terrorism threats, rising crime rates, and uncontrolled immigration to win support. While the Conservatives, he claimed, were merely re-working their rhetoric about the "menace" of foreign workers and asylum seekers, without offering any real or compassionate solutions to these complex issues.

Mr Kennedy said the government was cynically using the broader climate of fear to try and strip away fundamental civil liberties from ordinary citizens. He highlighted the government's continued use of indefinite detention for terror suspects, despite a recent High Court judgement that this specific policy contravenes basic human rights, he added. He pointed to further alarming legislative proposals, including attempts to introduce trial without jury for certain serious offences, plans to reverse the burden of proof in criminal cases, the curbing of legal aid rights for those in need, increased police stop and search powers without adequate oversight, and the highly controversial national ID card plans. He stated emphatically that people had the right to be secure from harm and danger, but also the equally important right not to face unfair discrimination or a gradual erosion of their freedoms and privacy.

He continued: "But at the same time, the state should not become a dangerous one, encroaching on the legitimate freedoms and privacy of its own citizens," he said. He emphasised that his party "instinctively" understood that "Britain is not a one-party, one-colour country," nor a single monolithic ideology, he added. "We are less deferential than ever before; more inclined to think for ourselves and challenge authority; and much more open about sexuality and equality in all its forms."

"Our national institutions," he stressed, "are changing too, reflecting this vibrant and modern Britain. We are no longer simply a nation of one established church; we are a nation of many faiths, many beliefs, and many cultures. We all live, in our different ways, under the rule of law, and that rule of law must protect everyone's rights and uphold our shared values," he concluded.

He said: "I wouldn't be surprised if nothing had been decided by the last minute of the return leg and the match had to go into extra time. "I have to defend what is mine and the Champions League is mine at the moment. I'm the last manager to have won it." Mourinho never coached Barcelona, assisting both Sir Bobby Robson and Louis van Gaal. But he is not envious, insisting: "I don't have to be jealous about Barcelona because they have 100 years of history and have won the European Cup once..."I have been managing for five years and I have the same amount of Champions League trophies to my name." But Mr Letwin said Britain had fallen from fourth to 11th in the international economic competitiveness league..."Can this country compete, can this country prosper, unless we do something about the burden of regulation and tax on our economy?" he said. "The fact is the very carefully costed, fully funded plans we have laid out for saving £12bn by 2007-2008 are absolutely crucial to delivering an economy that will prosper and provide people with jobs and indeed provide the public services with the money they need on a sustainable long-term basis." New York rockers The Bravery have topped the BBC News website's Sound of 2005 poll, naming them the most promising new act for the coming year.

The Bravery, a synth-pop inspired rock band from New York, have been compared to acts like The Killers and The Strokes, and were the heavily-tipped act in the survey of 110 impartial music industry experts, critics and tastemakers. The Sound of 2004 poll prominently featured acts like The Killers, while US rapper 50 Cent topped the Sound of 2003 list.

Other acts hotly tipped this year included London indie group Bloc Party, who came in second place in the poll. The Bravery played their first gig in 2003, having previously supported established acts like The Psychedelic Furs and Echo and the Bunnymen. Following a flurry of impressive early live shows and demo recordings, they were the subject of a fierce record company bidding war in 2004, and their debut album, Unconditional, created a considerable buzz when it was released in November last year.

Lead singer Sam Endicott said he felt "great" about coming into the year of 2005. "Anyone that doesn't want a zillion screaming fans is a liar," he added, laughing. Paul Connolly, a music critic for The Times newspaper, said he was "in love" with the band's sound. Adam Walton, a DJ and presenter on BBC 6 Music, said the band had "great guitars and a mastery of the synth-pop, new-wave sound, echoing early 80s aesthetics". "The Bravery are proof alone that New York is still home to great new rock and pop, even if the scene is constantly evolving," he added. However, not everyone was entirely convinced by the hype surrounding the band.

The band's first major UK live date with Jools Holland on his popular BBC Two television show saw the group set to appear the day after a gig at a relatively small West London pub. A BBC Radio 1 DJ was among those praising the band, saying: "They are the main package. They have the songs, the look, the attitude and a live band to match, which is what you want to see."

Early reviews from music publications and websites said they were "pretty much the 'new wave' sound personified" and "unusually concise, yearning and epic in the mould of synth-pop legends Duran Duran or indie-rock darlings The Strokes".

Pundits contributing to the extensive annual survey included BBC Radio 1 DJ Jo Whiley, NME editor Conor McNicholas, Top of the Pops presenter Fearne Cotton, Glastonbury organiser Emily Eavis and BBC Radio 2 music editor Jeff Smith.

Elsewhere on the tightly contested top 10 list, second-placed rock band Bloc Party began their ascent after supporting grime artist Kano, who is signed to a major record label and has been championed by Mike Skinner of The Streets. US rapper The Game is another hip-hop artist hotly tipped this year, coming in at number five. The great hope of Leeds, The Kaiser Chiefs, came sixth in the poll with a promise to lead a new wave of vital British rock music.

In last year's Sound of 2004 poll, the winner Keane and other high-profile acts like Franz Ferdinand, The Killers and Joss Stone in the top five all went on to achieve major commercial success, many outside the UK at that time, proving the poll's predictive power. Teenage pop-punk band McFly were eighth, while flamboyant disco-rockers Scissor Sisters, who had the UK's best-selling album of 2004, came in at number seven.

For the poll, the music industry experts were asked to tip up to three acts they believed were most capable of reaching the top in their chosen genre, either in terms of commercial success or critical acclaim. The acts could be from anywhere in the world and from any musical genre, but crucially could not have had a top 20 single in the UK, been a contestant on a TV talent show, or already be famous for doing something else entirely, such as being a soap star. The collective votes were then rigorously compiled to make the final top 10 list.

Hooking up Wi-Fi on the go? Super-speed wireless data networks could soon be used in the UK. The government's wireless regulator, Ofcom, is seeking views on the best way forward for the super-speed wireless data technology known as Ultra Wideband (UWB). Regulators are concerned that UWB-using devices could cause problems for those already using the same part of the radio spectrum.

UWB makes it possible to stream data through the air over short distances. Among its more revolutionary uses, it could make it possible to send DVD quality images to TVs without wires, or let music stream directly to media players from their base station. The technology has the potential to transmit hundreds of megabits of data per second. UWB could be used to create so-called Personal Area Networks that let a person's gadgets quickly swap data amongst themselves. The technology, which operates over a range of 10 metres, uses tiny radio pulses every second to carry data.

At the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas earlier this year, UWB chips built-in to various gadgets got a lot of buzz. However, their use is not currently allowed in UK licencing without significant restrictions. "We're seeking opinion from industry to find whether we are on a path that allows it to be introduced," a spokesman for Ofcom told the BBC News website. The consultation period ends on 24th April. Ofcom is also involved in a pan-Europe body, known as the Conference of Postal and Telecommunications Administrations (CEPT), that is researching harmonisation of UWB standards across the continent.

Early sight of the CEPT's draft work has already caused controversy as some experts think it could severely restrict UWB's potential and limit its benefits to users. According to a preliminary Ofcom report, it would be quite difficult to deploy existing UWB devices in the UK due to potential interference issues. Ofcom said it was considering introducing a "mask" of technical restrictions on UWB-using devices. "This 'mask' would effectively give devices very fine controls so they can operate over a long way or over a short range without causing interference with other services," he added.

There are also wider concerns about the technology being "ahead of its time" and regulatory frameworks not keeping pace. Ubisense, a company specialising in location-based services, has about 40 patents worldwide related to the short-range radio technology, said Theriault, who is also chairman of standards for the UWB Forum. He added that UWB was driving a number of novel applications beyond simple data transfer. "It's like having a 3D mouse all the time, enabling precise location tracking," he said. He said that European regulators were still deliberating on what the exact technical parameters were needed to drive adoption and ensure interoperability.

In addition to being a new and potentially revolutionary way for gadgets and computers to communicate, UWB was originally developed and used for sensing applications. It is used to spot things such as cracks and voids under the surface of runways or to help firemen detect the movement of people through thick walls and smoke.

The world of Bollywood is increasingly opening its doors to global stars. British actress Antonia Bernath is set to make her high-profile debut in Subhash Ghai's epic 'Kisna', marking a growing trend for non-Indian stars to appear in major Bollywood films. This cross-cultural casting reflects a broadening appeal and ambition within the Indian film industry.

Subhash Ghai's latest Bollywood offering, 'Kisna', is a romantic drama set against the opulent backdrop of British colonial India in the 1940s. In the film, Bernath plays Katherine, the cultured and independent daughter of a British army general, who finds herself falling deeply in love with Kisna, a spirited local Indian man, despite the obvious societal divisions and conflicts of the era.

"Reflecting on her experience on set, Bernath shared her impressions of the unique working style. 'I found the whole process of film-making incredibly fluid and dynamic,' she recounts. 'We often improvised a lot on set, which was both challenging and exhilarating.' She adds, 'At first, it was very daunting and a little overwhelming, but Mr Ghai was incredibly patient and supportive. He really helped me understand the nuances of the role and the cultural context of the film.'"

Bernath, who was selected from more than 200 hopefuls at auditions held in London, took the bold step of cutting short her education at Bristol's prestigious Old Vic Theatre School to take up this once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. Industry insiders note that it is highly unusual that somebody so young and with such limited experience gets to play such a significant lead role straight out of drama school. To prepare for the part, she spent several intensive months in India, dedicating herself to learning Hindi and mastering traditional Kathak dance lessons, crucial elements for her character's portrayal.

"Initially, my family and some friends were a bit sceptical about me venturing into a completely new film industry and culture,' she says with a smile. 'But I found the Hindi film industry to be incredibly warm, welcoming, and encouraging. Everyone was so supportive. I even had a few more exciting offers for other projects before the film was officially released, which was a huge confidence boost.'"

Bollywood films are increasingly seen as powerful 'cultural exports' on the world stage. Recent successes, such as Mira Nair's critically acclaimed 'Monsoon Wedding', have not only broken significant box office records internationally but have also successfully broken through established cultural and linguistic barriers, reaching diverse audiences globally. Spurred by this phenomenal success and growing international recognition, Bollywood producers are now actively globalizing all aspects of their film-making process, be it technical innovation, artistic collaboration, or casting choices.

This new global outlook has led to more prominent roles for Western actors. Bollywood productions have previously featured foreign heart-throbs like Nick Moran, known for his role in 'Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels', and supermodel Sophie Dahl. Now, many other non-Indian actors are increasingly eager to seize the most of this expanding opportunity, viewing Bollywood as a vibrant and lucrative alternative to traditional Western cinema markets.

"'Bollywood is now making a concerted and aggressive attempt to woo a non-Asian audience to their cinemas and substantially expand their overseas film market beyond the traditional diaspora'," explains Taran Adarsh, the respected editor of the influential Indian film trade journal 'Trade Guide'. "This strategic shift is aimed at making Indian cinema a truly global entertainment force."

"'To cater specifically to this broader international market, Kisna has been shot simultaneously in both English and Hindi, a significant departure from standard practice. Furthermore, the English version has been meticulously edited and shortened by an hour to accommodate the pacing and preferences of the Western audience,' Adarsh elaborates. 'The film also features a spectacular dance number composed by the legendary AR Rahman and directed by the popular Western choreographer Anthony Van Laast, famously known for his work on the hit stage musical 'Bombay Dreams'. The prominent presence of European or American actors in lead roles can only accelerate this vital step in globalizing Indian cinema even further,' he states."

Beyond 'Kisna', several other significant cross-cultural collaborations are underway. Another accomplished British actress, Caroline Langrishe, known for her television work, plays a pivotal lead role in the upcoming romantic drama 'Dil Jo Bhi Kahey...' (Whatever the Heart Says...), which also prominently stars Bollywood legend Amitabh Bachchan, further cementing the trend of international casting. In a separate ambitious project, critically acclaimed actor-producer Aamir Khan's highly anticipated venture, 'The Rising', is a grand historical drama set against the tumultuous backdrop of the Indian Sepoy Mutiny of 1857, with acclaimed British actor Toby Stephens taking on a key role, adding international gravitas to the ensemble cast.

However, it is Antonia Bernath's breakout role in 'Kisna', which had its premiere and was seen in New York this week, that is being hailed as her major international breakthrough. It is undoubtedly the performance on which other industry eyes are now keenly set, watching to see its impact.

"'Ultimately, whether it's Hollywood or Bollywood, it's the cold, hard box office figures that truly decide whether a new trend is merely passing or whether it has the staying power to become a permanent fixture in the industry,' Adarsh sagely concludes, emphasizing the commercial realities behind artistic innovation. 'Kisna' is scheduled for its much-anticipated release in the UK on 21 January, with high hopes for its international appeal.

Halloween writer Debra Hill dies. Screenwriter Debra Hill, best known for her groundbreaking work on 70s horror films, particularly the iconic Halloween, has sadly died in Los Angeles at the age of 54.

Hill, who had been bravely suffering from cancer, notably co-wrote and produced the seminal 1978 horror film, Halloween, starring Jamie Lee Curtis as a vulnerable babysitter terrorised by a relentless masked killer. Directed with chilling precision by John Carpenter, the film went on to make an astonishing $60m (£31.3m) globally - an unprecedented sum for an independent production at that time.

Beyond Halloween, Hill's creative partnership with Carpenter extended to other memorable projects such as the dystopian action thriller Escape from New York and the supernatural horror The Fog. Hill originally began her illustrious career by diligently working her way up the ranks, starting as an assistant director and progressing to a highly skilled second-unit director, where she was closely collaborating with many emerging filmmakers on set.

She was widely regarded by many as a truly pioneering woman in the male-dominated world of film production, especially since opportunities and significant roles for women in the 1970s were severely limited by prevailing industry attitudes. "When I started in 1974, there were very few women in the industry," she candidly told the BBC in an interview in 2003. "It was mostly make-up and hair, that was pretty much it. I was never automatically assumed to be a writer or producer." She further elaborated: "There weren't many people like me around, there weren't that many women, so I literally had to carve out a place for myself." John Carpenter fondly recalled that working with Hill "was one of the greatest experiences of my entire life." He added that the profound loss would now undoubtedly be followed by a period of deep grief for many. "She was incredibly capable and wonderfully talented," he reflected.

Carpenter and Hill continued their fruitful partnership on a number of subsequent Halloween sequels, which notably included Halloween II, Halloween III: Season of the Witch, and Halloween 4: The Curse of Michael Myers.

Later in her distinguished career, Debra Hill established her own highly successful production company alongside her long-time friend Lynda Obst. Together, they were responsible for making a string of critically acclaimed and Oscar-nominated films, including Terry Gilliam's fantasy drama The Fisher King and the popular comedy Adventures In Babysitting. Hill also independently produced King of the Mountain in 1983 and the much-loved 1985's Clue, a clever mystery comedy famously based on the classic board game.

Throughout the 1990s, she continued to diligently work in the demanding film industry, although she did happily reunite with John Carpenter in 1996 for Escape from LA, which served as the highly anticipated sequel to their earlier hit, Escape from New York. At the tragic time of her death, Hill was actively producing a significant film about the complex search for the last two missing men from the devastated World Trade Towers following the devastating September 11 attacks in 2001. Additionally, she was serving as an executive-producer on a contemporary remake of The Fog, which was widely anticipated and due for release in 2005.

original: US company admits Benin bribery..A US defence and telecommunications company has agreed to pay $28.5m after admitting bribery in the West African state of Benin...The Titan corporation was accused of funnelling more than $2m into the 2001 re-election campaign of President Mathieu Kerekou. At the time, Titan was trying to get a higher price for a telecommunications project in Benin. There is no suggestion that Mr Kerekou was himself aware of any wrongdoing. Titan, a California-based company, pleaded guilty to falsifying its accounts and violating US anti-bribery laws. It agreed to pay $13m in criminal penalties, as well as $15.5m to settle a civil lawsuit brought by the US financial watchdog, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)...The SEC had accused Titan of illegally paying $2.1m to an unnamed agent in Benin claiming ties with President Kerekou. Some of the money was used to pay for T-shirts with campaign slogans on them ahead of the 2001 election. Shortly after the poll, which Mr Kerekou won, Benin officials agreed to quadruple Titan's management fee. reconstruction:
The Mac mini: a mini revolution? Or just another computer? The launch of Apple's latest desktop machine, the Mac mini, was met with much fanfare and excitement last week, generating significant buzz across the technology world.

But the real question is: does it live up to the hype? Let's get a few things dealt with at the outset - yes, the Mac Mini is, visually speaking, another beautifully designed piece of hardware inspired by Apple's renowned aesthetic. It is more than just about 'looks' though, and it is worth remembering that the Mac Mini is just a computer at its core. It packs that G4 processor, a CD/DVD player, a hard drive, some essential bits and bobs, and a robust operating system, all within its incredibly compact casing.

A DVD burner, for example, can be bought at extra cost, as can a wireless keyboard and mouse. Moreover, if you do not already have a monitor, mouse, or keyboard, then you will need to budget to purchase these peripherals also, which can add significantly to the overall price. However, even with these additions, many consider it to be one of the fastest machines for your money, especially if you are looking for something interesting and technically advanced for under £400 - particularly if you are a fan of Apple software. The Mac mini comes bundled with Mac OS X, Apple's acclaimed operating system, and iLife '05, a comprehensive suite of creative software which includes iTunes for music management, Safari as a web browser, iPhoto for photo editing, iMovie for video editing, GarageBand for music creation, and iDVD for DVD authoring.

Many would argue that Windows XP comes a distant second to Mac OS X in terms of user experience and stability... and, of course, there are those running Linux who have their own robust menu of reasons why that's the superior choice. But for people who want to do interesting and creative things with their music, photos, and home videos, the Mac Mini presents an ideal first step into a true digital creative hub. "'It's a surprisingly good machine with a decent amount of power for its size and price, just perfect for the sort of person who doesn't want to worry about the constant threat of viruses and spyware that plague Windows users,' said Mark Sparrow, technical editor of MacUser magazine. He added: 'In effect, it's a powerful computer that's housed in something no bigger than a biscuit tin, and the sheer value that comes bundled with the mini makes any comparable budget PC look sick by comparison.'"

The relatively low price point of the Mac Mini has already encouraged the more technically-savvy computing enthusiasts to experiment with Macs, perhaps for the first time. For instance, one dedicated enthusiast has already built a custom "dock" to seamlessly plug his Mac Mini into his car's entertainment system, creating a mobile computing experience. The incredibly small size of the Mac Mini makes it a practical solution for a myriad of unconventional uses - it's highly portable, adaptable, and remarkably well-designed for tight spaces. Another user, keen to integrate it into their home entertainment setup, has successfully hooked his Mac Mini up to his TV and now controls the entire computer system with a simple wireless keyboard and mouse from his sofa.

When pundits first saw the Mac Mini, many immediately surmised that it was designed to be a sort of stealth media centre - an inconspicuous machine intended to serve up TV programmes, music, films, and photos directly to a living room display. This theory was fueled partly by its sleek, small, and undeniably living room-friendly design. However, upon closer inspection, there are several obvious reasons why this is ultimately not the case - not least the hard drive capacity. Even at 80GB, which is the largest capacity available in the top-end model, it is simply too small to be realistically used as a true, comprehensive media centre for a household's entire digital collection.

While many commercial Personal Video Recorders (PVRs) are currently on the market with 80GB hard drives, it is worth remembering that these devices are specifically designed to highly compress and store only TV content, which takes up significantly less space than other media. A true media centre computer, on the other hand, would need to store entire movie libraries, extensive music files, vast photo collections, and other digital content. For such usage, 80GB seems far too little storage space to be practical. Most dedicated media centre PCs available today typically come with at least 120GB of storage as a minimum, and often much more.

Crucially, without an integrated TV tuner card, a digital audio input, or any kind of dedicated media centre software bundled with the machine, then the Mac Mini must fundamentally be what it is, a compact desktop computer, not what it is not, a fully-fledged media hub. But that practical limitation certainly hasn't stopped some enthusiastic users from turning it into a media centre through aftermarket additions and custom software. 'Is the Mac Mini just another computer or is it a genuine revolution?', asks John Gruber, the insightful editor of Mac Format magazine, who has his own compelling theory. 'It's ultimately just a Mac, but we think it's revolutionary because it's significantly smaller than any other Mac that has come before it, it looks undeniably better than any comparable PC on the market, and crucially, it's the very first Mac designed from the ground up to go head-to-head directly with the notoriously competitive low-cost PC market.'"

The Mac Mini is further compelling evidence of a broader industry trend where computers are becoming far more discreet and integrated into our lives, rather than remaining just big, bulky boxes hidden under desks. There are a growing number of companies who produce small form-factor PCs based on mini-ITX motherboards, offering similar compactness. However, at the moment, these alternative options are either complex custom-build projects for enthusiasts, or pre-built systems that are exclusively built around Microsoft's proprietary Media Center software. But the sheer value the Mac Mini offers, bringing a range of sophisticated and easy-to-use software packages within the reach of more people than ever before, is simply undeniable. For us, here at the BBC, we have to say that the Mac Mini is indeed a revolution - yes, it truly is a revolution.

India trade rules, as its Finance Minister P. Chidambaram attends the G7 leading nations meeting on Friday, is unlikely to be cowed by its newcomer status. In London ahead of the meeting, India's minister lashed out at what he called the restrictive trade policies of the G7. He objected to any suggestions that would prevent developing countries like India from being able to compete fairly in the global marketplace. He specifically called for significant reform of major international financial institutions, including the United Nations, the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) institutions.

Mr Chidambaram, India's finance minister, further argued that the G7 must take into account the evolving new world order, acknowledging India and China's increasing integration into the global economy. He firmly stated that the true solution to current economic challenges lies in embracing globalisation, rather than pursuing disengagement from globalisation.

Mr Chidambaram also took the opportunity to describe the G7 as merely part of the wider G20 group of developing and developed nations, which collectively represents a significant 60% of the world's population and global economic output. At a conference on enterprise hosted by the minister on Friday, he elaborated that he was strongly in favour of flexible exchange rates because they provide a vital mechanism that helps countries cope better with unforeseen economic shocks and market volatility.

"A flexible exchange rate allows for greater adjustment and stability within an economy," he told reporters. "India, along with other major emerging economies such as China, Brazil and South Africa, has to take its rightful place and voice its concerns in the discussions at the G7 meeting in London on Friday and Saturday." He noted that China is currently under renewed pressure to abandon its pegged exchange rate, which the G7 member nations, and in particular the United States, frequently blame for contributing to a surge in cheap exports.

"Some countries prefer to use fixed exchange rates in their economic management. However, I do not believe in such an approach for India's economy," Mr Chidambaram stated. Separately, the India's central bank, the Reserve Bank of India, issued a warning that persistently high oil prices could potentially derail the country's robust economic growth trajectory, which it had previously forecast to be 6.5% for the fiscal year to March 2005. For comparison, in the fiscal year to March 2004, the Indian economy grew by a strong 8.5%.

reconstruction:
Preliminary estimates suggest that claims arising from the devastating Asian tsunami could reach as high as "$10bn," an unprecedented figure for a natural disaster in the region. Global insurers have immediately sought to quantify and face the huge losses emerging after the monstrous tidal waves swept across vast coastal regions, reportedly killing more than 38,000 people in Asia alone, a figure which continues to rise dramatically.

However, despite the immense scale of the human tragedy, major players in the reinsurance market, including the world's two biggest firms, Munich Re and Swiss Re, have indicated that their financial exposure will be less than what they faced for many previous major disasters in other parts of the world. The bulk of these insured costs are likely to be concentrated in wealthier, tourist-oriented countries, and tragically, many of those local residents most directly affected will have little or no insurance coverage, analysts have sadly pointed out. Indeed, some industry experts and financial analysts have cautiously said that total global insured losses are likely to be less than $10bn (£5.17bn), a figure far lower than initial fears had suggested just days after the Boxing Day catastrophe.

Munich Re, one of the industry's leaders and a key barometer for global disaster costs, believes that while the cost would undeniably be substantial, it is unlikely to be in the double-digit billions of dollars, as reported by the Financial Times. The German giant, Munich Re, which is the world's largest reinsurance company, specifically stated that its direct exposure from the catastrophe was less than 100m (£70m; $136m), a relatively modest sum in the context of its overall business.

With over 10 countries affected across the Indian Ocean basin, Sri Lanka, Indonesia, and Thailand are tragically among the worst hit, and these nations are expected to generate the most significant claims for international insurers. Specifically, Thailand's luxury resorts, which are exceedingly popular destinations for millions of Western tourists, are expected to generate a substantial portion of the claimants now coming forward. Lloyds of London, a prominent global insurance market, told the Times newspaper that it expected its primary exposure to be "covering damage to tourist resorts, private properties, travel insurance policies, and marine cargo and hull losses."

A spokesman for Hanover Re, another leading German firm and the world's fifth-largest reinsurance company, indicated that its total tsunami-related losses would be in the "double-digit millions," a figure which they consider manageable within their annual risk assessment. To put this in perspective, the company has previously paid out some $300m (£281m; $400m) to cover damage caused by hurricanes in the US alone in recent years, starkly highlighting the comparative difference in expected payouts for the Asian tsunami.

Currently, many major insurers are not yet releasing detailed economic impact reports, as they are still diligently working through the vast amount of incoming information and claims from the affected regions, a process made difficult by damaged infrastructure. "It's still very unclear, it is just too early to tell the true extent of the damage," said Serge Troeber, deputy head of Munich Re's disasters department in Germany, underlining the immense challenge facing the industry. "There are very complex and often imprecise processes to estimate damages. Unlike the United States, for instance, where sophisticated catastrophe models and extensive historical data exist for natural disasters, there isn't a well-established catastrophe model or an existing framework for natural disasters of this magnitude in Asia." He further anticipated that his own company's insured losses related to the tsunami would be significantly lower than those incurred from recent hurricane seasons, which collectively cost the company over $640m.

Allianz, a leading German insurer with a substantial global presence, also stated it was not yet able to determine precisely what its final financial exposure would be for the Asian catastrophe. However, the tidal waves were certainly expected to have a "significant" impact on its business operations, particularly within the tourism and property sectors in the affected regions. A Financial Times report noted that market analysts could not yet definitively quantify the overall financial ramifications of the disaster, indicating a prolonged period of assessment.

Insurance companies, analysts have consistently noted, have relatively limited exposure in many parts of Asia, especially concerning local populations. On the whole, they tend not to offer specific policies tailored to special catastrophes like tsunamis for the general population, primarily due to low demand and affordability issues. Consequently, insured damage is projected to be merely a small fraction of the "billions of dollars worth of total physical destruction observed in countries such as Sri Lanka, India, Indonesia, Thailand, and the Maldives," said Prudential Equity Group analyst Jay Gelb, emphasising the vast uninsured gap. He added that European insurers are generally expected to have only minimal exposure to minor claims, or even to no losses at all from local policies. "It's likely Bermuda-based [reinsurance] companies might absorb some of the more substantial losses related to tourism infrastructure and major commercial properties," commented David Newsome, a senior analyst at AG&Edwards, a prominent financial services firm.

A significant proportion of the affected populations, as seen in countries like Sri Lanka and the Maldives, do not buy commercial insurance of these kinds, relying instead on community support, government assistance, or simply having no western-based insurance coverage at all.

Estimates from the World Bank and United Nations now place the total amount of international aid needed for comprehensive reconstruction efforts, including vital housing, roads, schools, and restoring local livelihoods, at $5bn (£2.6bn). This staggering figure is comparable to the emergency cash pledged to assist Central America after Hurricane Mitch struck in 1998, a devastating storm which killed 10,000 people and resulted in economic damage of about $10bn that same year.

Beyond these cold financial figures, the true cost of these devastating tsunamis cannot be measured solely by the monetary losses involved. "It is difficult to fathom the immense human cost to the poor and nameless fishermen whose entire villages and traditional way of life have been completely wiped out. Hundreds of livelihoods gone," lamented Jan Egeland, the UN Under-Secretary-General for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, highlighting the profound personal toll.

For Western tourists cutting short their holidays due to the unprecedented scale of the disaster, they too may suffer a considerable financial impact. The Association of British Insurers warned that standard travel insurance policies do not normally cover short holiday cancellations resulting from widespread natural disasters, nor does it typically cover the complete loss of all personal possessions in such events, but they strongly emphasised the crucial importance of carefully examining the fine print of all travel policies before purchase.

original: UK plan to deport terror suspects..Deals are being sought to allow the UK to deport terror suspects to their home countries without risk of them being tortured or sentenced to death...Home Secretary Charles Clarke told the Times he hoped agreement with several countries could be reached. The move follows a Law Lords judgement that the detention of 12 men at Belmarsh prison, London, and Woodhill, Milton Keynes, was unlawful. The 12 affected by the ruling are from Algeria, Tunisia, Egypt and Jordan. The government was told that using anti-terror legislation brought in after 11 September to hold the men indefinitely without charge broke human rights laws...Mr Clarke told The Times: "I think we should be prosecuting much more energetically our ability to deport the individuals concerned to the countries from which they come." He said it was a route that was being pursued in collaboration with Foreign Secretary Jack Straw "in a very positive way". Mr Clarke said that he was seeking "memorandums of understanding" between overseas governments and Britain to ensure suspects would not be subjected to the death penalty on their return. However, he added: "I do not think the solution to the Law Lords' judgement for this government is in deportations, but they will help. "There are other strands that we have to do." But the Liberal Democrat's shadow home secretary, Mark Oaten, accused Mr Clarke of avoiding the main issue with the Belmarsh detainees..."The critical issue that the home secretary is dodging at this stage is to deal with the very principle, to deal with how we tackle this problem in the future," he told BBC News. "And I do want him to grasp those issues and that means looking at how we can actually secure convictions in this country allowing, for example, intercept communications, telephone tapping to be included," Mr Oaten said. "Deportation may tackle this initial problem but I want to see a wider debate urgently about how we can actually get trials and convictions in this country." "Unless we get that, the Liberal Democrats will vote against this measure when it comes for renewal in March."..The BBC's home affairs correspondent, Daniel Sandford, said it appeared Mr Clarke was putting more emphasis on the possibility of deportation than his predecessor, David Blunkett. But he said reaching an understanding with some of the detainees' home countries could be difficult. "Some of these people are accused of very, very serious crimes in their home countries so it's not an easy agreement to get and I think for some of these suspects it won't be the solution." Daniel Sandford said ministers may try to put forward other solutions - such as allowing more secret evidence to be put into normal criminal trials or developing a more secret trials process - in the next few weeks. "The government may try and deport some of them and then those that are left see if they can work out some way of putting them on trial," he said.

The government is pushing ahead with its plan to deport foreign terror suspects. New deals allow the authorities to deport individuals to their home countries without fearing for them facing the death penalty or torture.

Home Secretary Charles Clarke told reporters in London he hoped agreement with several countries could be reached soon. The move comes after a House of Lords judgement that the indefinite detention of 12 suspects, at Woodhill Prison near Milton Keynes, was deemed unlawful. These were 12 men detained by the British government, who were originally from Algeria, Tunisia, and Jordan.

The ruling was that using anti-terror laws specifically designed for detaining foreign nationals after 11 September 2001 to hold the suspects indefinitely without charge or trial broke international human rights laws.

The Times' editorial stated: "We think the government should be prosecuting more energetically or seeking to deport individuals concerned who have come to this country." Mr Clarke indicated that this strategy was already being pursued with Foreign Secretary Jack Straw "in a positive and constructive spirit". He said that the government was actively pursuing "memorandums of understanding" with overseas governments to ensure that suspects would not be exposed to the risk of torture or ill-treatment on return. However, he added: "I do not seek to overturn the Law Lords' ruling, which presents a significant challenge for this government, but they will be fully addressed." "There are many other strands we have to consider and develop."

Liberal Democrat' shadow home secretary, Mark Oaten, strongly criticised Mr Clarke for avoiding the main issue with the remaining Belmarsh detainees.

"The critical issue he is dodging at this crucial stage is how to deal with the very difficult and fundamental deal of how we tackle the terror problem in the long term in this country," he told the BBC. "We do want him to grasp the seriousness of this situation and that means looking at what measures can be put in place to secure fair hearings, allowing all relevant evidence to be presented, and ensuring that evidence obtained under torture is not included," Mr Oaten added.

"Deportation is this initial stop-gap measure but we want a wider and more urgent debate about how we can get trials and convictions in this country without undermining civil liberties." "Unless we find an alternative solution, the remaining detainees will be released against the will of the government by March."

The BBC's home affairs correspondent, Gordon Sandford, commented that Mr Clarke was putting more than a brave face on a very challenging situation, and that reaching an agreement with these foreign governments could prove extremely difficult.

"Some of these individuals are accused of committing very serious crimes in their home countries, and therefore it's an agreement to deport them to face justice there that I think some of these it won't be at all straightforward to secure."

Sandford said ministers would likely try to put forward proposals for such secret bilateral agreements to be put in place, effectively developing a more secret process for dealing with these individuals, involving few public announcements.

"The government may be able to negotiate these deals and deport then those that are currently held in detention, to see if they can persuade these foreign governments to put some of them on trial," he said.

Has your personal computer been recruited into a 'botnet'? More than one million computers across the internet have been pumping out viruses, spam, and other malicious software, according to security experts, spanning more than 100 networks of organisations globally.

The so-called 'bot' networks, extensively spied on by a dedicated research team, made use of over 50,000 hijacked home computers. Comprehensive data was carefully gathered, detailing which countries they originated from and precisely what nefarious uses were made of them.

The research into these 'zombie' or 'hijacked' machines was conducted by the Honeynet Project, a group of security researchers that operates networks of computers designed as 'honeypots' to attract hackers and gather information on how they compromise systems and operate their 'bot nets'. Estimates regarding the widespread nature of these threats are now widely available.

According to detailed information released by the German arm of the Project, the malicious software used to hijack these machines was worryingly easy to install and deploy. The Honeynet Project team discovered that a newly internet-connected machine could become an attack tool in only a few minutes. Indeed, the shortest recorded compromise time for a system was a mere few seconds.

The research found that compromised machines tend to report back via IRC channels to a central 'hacker' control machine for further instructions. Many well-known vulnerabilities in the Windows operating system were systematically exploited by 'bot net' software to gain access and control. Particularly coveted were PCs sitting on always-on broadband connections that were rarely, if ever, turned off.

Months of surveillance revealed that these 'bot nets' - ranging from a few hundred to thousands of machines - were used for a wide variety of illicit purposes. They are often used as relays for spam, to route unwanted email to users, and for other malicious activities.

The researchers also found a range of very different uses. During the observation period, the team saw 'bot nets' used to launch 226 denial-of-service attacks on 99 separate networks. These attacks flood target websites with data in an attempt to overwhelm them and force them offline.

The distributed nature of 'bot nets' across many different networks and nations makes such sustained attacks exceedingly hard to defend against. In one instance, a DDoS attack was used by a company to knock its competitors offline. Other 'bot nets' were involved in perpetrating widespread click fraud, a scam that fraudulently extracts money from search engine advertising schemes.

Some compromised machines were even used to manipulate online polls. Cyber-criminals appear to be starting to employ 'bot nets' for mass identity theft, by systematically trawling websites like those of banks for confidential information to be gathered and used to steal data.

"Leveraging the combined power of several bots, it is entirely viable to take down any website, regardless of its size or security," said a spokesman for the Honeynet Project team.

"In the wrong hands, it is clear that these 'bot nets' are a potent weapon capable of causing immense damage and widespread disruption."

original: Beijingers fume over parking fees..Choking traffic jams in Beijing are prompting officials to look at reorganising car parking charges...Car ownership has risen fast in recent years, and there are now two and a half million cars on the city's roads. The trouble is that the high status of car ownership is matched by expensive fees at indoor car parks, making motorists reluctant to use them. Instead roads are being clogged by drivers circling in search of a cheaper outdoor option. "The price differences between indoor and outdoor lots are unreasonable," said Wang Yan, an official from the Beijing Municipal Commission for Development and Reform quoted in the state-run China Daily newspaper. Mr Wang, who is in charge of collecting car parking fees, said his team would be looking at adjusting parking prices to close the gap. Indoor parking bays can cost up to 250% more than outdoor ones...Sports fans who drive to matches may also find themselves the target of the commission's road rage. It wants them to use public transport, and is considering jacking up the prices of car parks near sports grounds. Mr Wang said his review team may scrap the relatively cheap hourly fee near such places and impose a higher flat rate during matches. Indoor parking may be costly, but it is not always secure. Mr Wang's team are also going to look into complaints from residents about poor service received in exchange for compulsory monthly fees of up to 400 yuan ($48; £26). The Beijing authorities decided two years ago that visiting foreign dignitaries' motorcades should not longer get motorcycle outriders as they blocked the traffic. Unclogging Beijing's increasingly impassable streets is a major concern for the Chinese authorities, who are building dozens of new roads to create a showcase modern city ahead of the 2008 Olympic Games.

Walt Disney Co. settles charges. Walt Disney Co. has settled with regulators over charges that it failed to disclose payments that were made by the company to several of its directors' family members and associated entities. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) ordered the media giant to better inform investors and to refrain from future violations of securities law. The SEC's complaint alleged that between 1999 and 2001, Disney failed to disclose payments to companies owned by three adult children of its directors on its proxy statements. The firm has neither admitted nor denied wrongdoing in the settlement.

The three directors at the centre of the allegations - Bowers, Stanley and Watson - have since retired. Both Mr Stanley and Mr Watson retired from the board in 2003. The companies owned by their children were paid between $60,000 (£30,800) and $150,000 a year. These payments were not disclosed to shareholders as required.

The SEC found that Disney did not adequately disclose a 50% Disney-owned subsidiary company - which was run by the wife of director L. Peter Bryson, Christine Bryson - and that she received more than $1m a year. Mrs. Bryson remains a director for Lifetime Entertainment.

Disney also failed to disclose payments to another company, partly owned by Mr Stanley and a fellow former Disney director. Finally, Disney did not disclose payments of more than $200,000 for office space, secretarial, and leased driver services provided for former director Thomas.

"A lack of accurate and complete information regarding relationships between the company and its directors," said the SEC deputy director of enforcement. "Failure to comply with the SEC's rules in this area impedes shareholders' ability to evaluate the company's corporate governance and the independence of its board."

original: S Korea spending boost to economy..South Korea will boost state spending next year in an effort to create jobs and kick start its sputtering economy...It has earmarked 100 trillion won ($96bn) for the first six months of 2005, 60% of its total annual budget. The government's main problems are "slumping consumption and a contraction in the construction industry". It aims to create 400,000 jobs and will focus on infrastructure and home building, as well as providing public firms with money to hire new workers...The government has set an economic growth rate target of 5% for next year and hinted that would be in danger unless it took action. "Internal and external economic conditions are likely to remain unfavourable in 2005," the Finance and Economy Ministry said in a statement...It blamed "continuing uncertainties such as fluctuating oil prices and foreign exchange rates and stagnant domestic demand that has shown few signs of a quick rebound". In 2004, growth will be between 4.7% and 4.8%, the ministry said. Not everyone is convinced the plan will work. "Our primary worry centres on the what we believe is the government's overly optimistic view that its front loading of the budget will be enough to turn the economy around," consultancy 4Cast said in a report...The problem facing South Korea is that many consumers are reeling from the effects of a credit bubble that only recently burst. Millions of South Koreans are defaulting on their credit card bills, and the country's biggest card lender has been hovering on the verge of bankruptcy for months. As part of its spending plans, the government said it will ask firms to "roll over mortgage loans that come due in the first half of 2005" . It also pledged to look at ways of helping families on low incomes...The government voiced concern about the effect of redundancies in the building trade. "Given the economic spill over and employment effect in the construction sector, a sharp downturn in the construction industry could have other adverse effects," the ministry said...As a result, South Korea will give private companies also will be given the chance to build schools, hospitals, houses and other public buildings. It also will look at real estate tax system. Other plans on the table include promoting new industries such as bio-technology and nano-technology, as well as offering increased support to small and medium sized businesses. "The focus will be on job creation and economic recovery, given that unfavourable domestic and global conditions are likely to dog the Korean economy in 2005," the ministry said.

reconstruction:
A potential future for seamen's identification is being trialled. On board the luxury cruise ship Harmony of the Seas, currently off the coast of Mexico, the serene setting might suggest a typical holiday, but beneath the surface, a significant technological trial is underway. While holidaymakers enjoy the refreshing ocean breezes, a select group of the ship's crew is actively testing a prototype of what could become the world's first widely accepted biometric ID for seafarers, designed to be the definitive equivalent of a national passport. Beyond standard identification details such as the owner's photograph and personal information, the innovative new document incorporates unique biometric features, specifically the holder's fingerprints and facial scans.

These new biometric identity cards are slated to be officially issued by February next year, in full compliance with the revised UN Convention on Seafarers' Identity Documents (Convention 185), which was initially adopted in June 2003. Rigorous tests currently underway are designed to ensure that these new documents, along with their associated machine-readers – which may vary significantly in different countries and ports – are completely interoperable across all international borders. The extensive trials, which actively involve seafarers from a wide range of nationalities and backgrounds, are expected to be thoroughly reviewed and officially approved by the International Labour Organization (ILO) by the end of November, marking a crucial step towards global implementation.

Crystal Cruises, a well-known luxury cruise line which operates vessels such as the Crystal Symphony, has confirmed it is actively exploring the potential use of biometrics for its crew members but has not yet officially committed to a full-scale implementation of the new system. Authenti-Corp, a leading US-based technology firm specializing in secure identification solutions, has been collaborating closely with the ILO, lending its technical expertise and developmental support for the creation and deployment of these advanced biometric cards. "Once you're issued a card in your home country, we want it to work seamlessly and reliably when the ship arrives in any international port where, say, our designated biometric readers are installed," explained a representative for Authenti-Corp, speaking on the BBC's Go Digital programme, emphasizing the need for universal functionality.

France was notably among the very first nations, along with several other pioneering countries, to fully ratify the new convention, indicating a strong commitment to its principles. Many more countries are expected to ratify it in the coming months as global shipping embraces new standards. The primary objective of this new system is to enhance global maritime security, particularly in combating terrorism and illegal activities, whilst simultaneously protecting the fundamental rights and ensuring the unhindered movement of the estimated 1.2 million seafarers worldwide. Furthermore, the convention explicitly highlights the critical importance of shore leave and unimpeded access to land-based facilities as indispensable elements contributing to a seafarer's overall wellbeing, mental health, and social welfare, and, therefore, it says, it indirectly contributes to better environmental practices and cleaner oceans. "By effectively treating the vast expanse of the seas as a secure international border, these new biometric cards will hopefully contribute significantly to reducing the alarmingly high number of piracy incidents observed around the world," stated Ms Natalie Musselman, a senior official with the ILO, underscoring the security benefits. "It should foster a much safer and more secure environment for seafarers to travel and work in," she continued, "and it will be instrumental in protecting their rights by ensuring they have credible, verifiable identification when they are off the ship, in fact, wherever they may need to assert their identity."

reconstruction: Europe asks Asia for euro help, saying that they must let their US dollar to rise against the surging euro. The single currency has been gaining successively against the US dollar over the past few weeks and months. There has been tacit acceptance from the White House regarding the weaker greenback, which could counteract concerns about the persistent US trade deficit and stimulate exports. But Europe feels it has done enough, and insists that Asia must now share some of the responsibility for global currency stability. China, in particular, is seen as the main target of these calls, with 35% of its foreign exchange reserves held in US dollars in 2004 partly on the back of a currency that is effectively pegged to the dollar. "We believe there is a need to engage in greater currency flexibility, particularly in Asian economies," stated French Finance Minister Nicolas Sarkozy, after private talks with his counterpart German Finance Minister Hans Eichel. Markets responded by further strengthening the euro, despite ongoing speculation that the sensitive issue would be unlikely to feature prominently on the agenda of the G7 countries next week's meeting. Early on Tuesday morning, the US dollar had reached a new low of 1.3040 euros. The yen, meanwhile, continued its upward trend, strengthening significantly to 102.975 against the dollar by 0730 GMT.

reconstruction: A US woman has filed a class-action lawsuit over Hewlett Packard's ink cartridges, alleging they are programmed to expire on a predetermined date even when ink remains. The unnamed plaintiff contends that a hidden chip within the cartridge tells the printer that it is empty or expired - even when it is still full or partially used. The lawsuit seeks to represent anyone in the United States who has purchased an inkjet printer from HP since February 2001. HP, the world's biggest printer maker, has yet to publicly comment on the specific allegations of the suit. However, the company has previously stated its ink cartridges incorporate a chip technology designed to alert the user when ink levels are low on ink, prompting the user to change the cartridge for optimal performance. But the suit alleges these chips also cause cartridges to 'expire' based on the date regardless of how much ink is left inside, forcing consumers to buy new ones unnecessarily. 'These so-called smart chips are designed to cause prematurely depletion of ink, or to render a cartridge unusable through use of a pre-set internal expiry date not revealed to the customer,' the court document said. The plaintiff is asking for financial restitution, and significant damages for affected consumers. This legal action mirrors similar complaints and calls for investigations of a similar nature emerging in Europe for the last 18 months. The article highlights the disparity in price, stating that while the initial cost of printers can be as low as £34, the true cost of ownership could escalate to £1,700 in running costs over an 18-month period. This high operational expenditure is primarily due to the frequent replacement of expensive cartridge, often multiple times by the year. Indeed, the broader inkjet printer market has previously been subject of scrutiny and investigation by the UK's Office of Fair Trading (OFT), which notably concluded in its 2002 report that retailers had a responsibility to be far more transparent for consumers regarding the true long-term costs of printer ownership and consumables.

The government has rejected the 60% rise and wants Aguas Argentinas to make an annual investment of 400m pesos ($136m; £72.3m) in improvements. Planning Minister Julio De Vido has offered State help but not for "free"...Mr De Vido said that the Argentine state would not make a contribution "in the form of a subsidy"...He has said a contribution could be made in return for a seat on the company's board. He added that the government is in discussions with Aguas Argentinas about what role it might take in the event that a State contribution is agreed. However, Aguas Argentinas told the Argentine newspaper Clarin it would not accept any change to its legal structure and, in practice, this rules out State participation on its board. The Planning Minister didn't rule out the possibility of cancelling Aguas Argentinas water concession. Yet he added that he didn't like to do "futurology". But last week, Argentine Economic Minister, Roberto Lavagna, told the French media in Paris that the government was considering allowing a 16% increase in tariffs and the possibility of a State contribution to Aguas Argentinas infrastructure investments. Speaking in Buenos Aires, Mr De Vido later denied the possibility of any tariff increase and insisted that the annual investment in water infrastructure was at the centre of the discussions. He added that in the coming weeks the future of Aguas Argentinas would be decided. Suez owns 40% of Aguas Argentinas (39.9%), while Spain's Aguas de Barcelona is its second biggest shareholder with 25.01%. Recently, Suez lost a water concession in Bolivia after mass protests in the city of El Alto (the poorest in the country), with citizens complaining of unfair water charges. This forced the government to cancel the contract...In Argentina, Suez's subsidiary, which has been fined for cutting the supply of water during a recent heat wave and allegedly failing to keep up investment to meet the demand for water, has maintained a tense relationship with the Argentine government. During the last financial crisis in Argentina, the firm sued the state alleging that converting its tariffs from US dollars to pesos, and then freezing them during devaluation, had affected the company and made it difficult for it to meet its contractual obligations. When President Nestor Kirchner of Argentina arrived in power he began to negotiate a solution to the disagreements with international utilities operating in Argentina. But he has rejected any tariff increases, alleging this will impoverish citizens further. He has also asked for more investments to meet the growing demand for water. On May 2004, Aguas Argentinas and the government signed an agreement to renegotiate its Buenos Aires water-concession contract. The firm agreed to invest 242m pesos. The issue has attracted European interest. Last week in Paris, President Kirchner discussed this problem and other issues with French president Jacques Chirac. The Argentine government is also under pressure from European Union countries and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to raise utilities tariffs, because most of the utilities operating in Argentina are European.
