reconstruction:
Water in Argentina row. A major dispute between the Argentine government and water utility Aguas Argentinas, controlled by French group Suez's local unit, is casting serious doubt on the firm's future. The utility firm, which serves the capital, Buenos Aires, and the surrounding province of Argentina, has requested a tariff rise of 60% to fund essential water-supply improvements. The government has vehemently rejected the 60% increase and wants instead to compel Aguas Argentinas to make an immediate investment of 400m pesos ($136m; £72.3m) in its infrastructure. Planning Minister Julio De Vido has publicly ruled out direct State help but called for a solution based on "shared responsibility" between the parties.

Mr De Vido emphasised that the Argentine state would not make any financial contribution "in the form of subsidy". He has said such a contribution could be made only for a seat on the company's board. He added the government was actively engaged in discussions about what steps it would take in the event no agreement was reached.

However, Aguas Argentinas was reported by the Argentine newspaper Clarin as stating it would not accept any change to, in practice, the rules governing its participation. Planning Minister De Vido didn't explicitly rule out revoking the Aguas concession. He stated he didn't want to do "futurology". But last week, a high-ranking French official, Roberto, announced in Paris an agreement allowing a 16% increase in the level of State contribution to Aguas Argentinas' infrastructure. Speaking in Buenos Aires, Mr De Vido later reiterated his firm stance that any increase in tariffs or state aid must be directly linked to new investment in water infrastructure for the residents of Buenos Aires. He added that in the coming weeks the future of the concession would be decided.

Suez owns 40% of Aguas Argentinas (39.9% to be precise), Spain's Aguas de Barcelona is its second biggest shareholder with 25.01%. This situation is not unique for Suez; the French firm recently pulled out of a similar venture in Bolivia in the capital city of La Paz (the poorest city in Latin America), complaining of unfair contractual terms. This subsequently led to the termination of the contract.

Aguas Argentinas's local subsidiary, which has been fined for poor supply of water in recent years and allegedly failing to keep up with demand for water, maintained a strained relationship with the government. Following the major peso devaluation, the firm was forced to convert its tariffs from dollars into local pesos, then freezing them, a move which severely affected the company's ability to meet its financial obligations. President Nestor Kirchner, who took office in 2003, began to negotiate a new framework with international companies operating utility services in Argentina. He has rejected repeated calls for tariff increases, arguing that this would impoverish ordinary citizens. He also asked for more significant investment to meet the growing demand. On October 21, 2004, Aguas Argentinas signed a preliminary agreement with its Buenos Aires water-concession. Under the terms, the government agreed to invest 242m pesos. The long-running dispute however has continued. In February 2005, President Kirchner discussed the problem with senior French government officials, including French President Jacques Chirac. Argentine officials are also facing pressure from European Union countries and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to raise tariffs, a demand that most utilities operating in the country have been making.

The fresh delay came after Polish officials had raised concerns about the law for the second time in two months. But in the end we could not put it on," an EU spokesman told the Reuters agency. He added that no date had been chosen for more discussion of the law...In December, Poland requested more time to consider the issue because it was concerned that the law could lead to the patenting of pure computer software. reconstruction:
New delay hits EU. A controversial proposal has hit new snags, which govern the patentability of computer software. The law was withdrawn from consideration by EU ministers as planned at their Brussels meeting on Thursday, during which it was supposed to have been discussed. The delay came after Polish officials had vetoed the draft law for the second time in two months. Critics argue the current draft would favour large companies over smaller ones and could severely impact the wider software industry.

"There was at one point the hope of having the item discussed today. But in the end, it was not taken up," an EU spokesman told Reuters. He added that no more details could be provided of the reasons for the delay. Poland had requested more time to consider the issue. The issue was that the scope related to the definition of computer software patents was still a point of contention. Its ministers wish to see the phrasing of the text of the Directive on the patentability of computer-implemented inventions changed so that it provides clearer limitations and better safeguards for small businesses. Poland is a large member state, so its agreement on this legislation is vital.

The European Commission says the proposed directive would bring the EU closer to the system prevalent in the US, a move which has caused angry protests amongst many software developers and open-source advocates. In the US, patenting of computer methods is permitted. This means the online retailer Amazon.com holds a patent for its "one-click" checkout system. A similar broad patenting approach in Europe would hurt innovation and independent developers, something many fear. Supporters of a more restrictive patent law argue it should not let big corporations protect basic software concepts for which they have spent little on genuine inventive effort.

reconstruction:
Britain offered to send a contingent of 120 Gurkhas to assist with the relief effort in Indonesia, following the devastating tsunami. The offer also included provision of helicopter support. The troops, from the 2nd Royal Gurkha Rifles' 2nd Battalion, are awaiting deployment details. The Indonesian government indicated the offer was being considered for deployment primarily in the province of Aceh.

Downing Street said a similar offer might be extended to Sri Lankan authorities, but noted logistical issues needed to be dealt with first before such a deployment could take place. A Foreign Office spokesman said: "Following today's daily meeting on the Indian Ocean tsunami relief effort, the UK has offered the Indonesian government the assistance of a company of British Army Gurkhas from the 2nd Royal Gurkha Rifles, totalling 120 personnel, and 120 hours of helicopter flight time." This is in addition to other aid already pledged, and the UK remains committed to the wider relief operation across the Indian Ocean.

Indonesia is by far the country worst hit by the tsunami, with 94,000 of the 140,000 estimated dead worldwide. International Development Minister Gareth Thomas said the offer would most likely focus on the northern province of Aceh. "We have offered the Gurkhas to assist in the relief effort, particularly in Aceh, which is the most devastated region in the Indian Ocean at the moment," he said. "The RAF is playing a crucial role, desperately working to set up truly effective relief operations on the ground in as many affected areas as possible."

The offer comes as Foreign Secretary Jack Straw arrives in Jakarta for meetings regarding the disaster.

Smartphones: Owners of Nokia 7610 handsets are being warned to watch out for a malicious wallpaper program. Users downloading the software are finding that all the 7610 phone functions are 'killed' or rendered inoperable by the malicious software. When this malicious program is installed, it not only kills functions but also impacts many 7610s, making them hard to use and difficult to repair.

The program is the latest in a series of viruses and malicious software to attack mobile phones running the Symbian operating system. The virus, which has been nicknamed 'Skulls', is thought to have surfaced on websites where people can add custom content, such as themes, wallpaper, and ringtones, to their Symbian phones. Symbian officials said it was not entirely sure if the damage caused by Skulls was intentionally malicious or simply a result of poor programming.

The program is being discovered to have originated from internet sites that are known for harbouring and distributing pirated or unauthorised software. The program itself is masquerading as legitimate software, offering a new background for the main screen of the Nokia 7610 phone.

The program, identified as a file named '7610.extended.theme.zip', once successfully installed, replaces the main icons for essential applications, such as 'messaging', 'contacts', and 'calendar', with non-working versions, effectively rendering them almost useless. The only thing the infected phone can still reliably do is make and take calls.

A demonstration was played by the security firm F-Secure, showcasing the malicious program's effects. F-Secure stated that few users would likely fall victim to it, as installation requires users to go through several manual steps, one of which includes disabling a crucial security warning on their device. F-Secure also said the spread of the infection was expected to be limited, as the program cannot replicate or spread from one phone to another by itself.

Finnish phone manufacturer Nokia confirmed it had received sporadic reports of 7610 handsets being affected by Skulls. Nokia advised users to be cautious about what software they download and to only acquire applications and themes from trusted, official sources.

The program is widely thought to have been created by a malicious hacker using the online alias '222'. Similar malicious programs have also been found to infect phones by other manufacturers, including Sony Ericsson, Motorola, Siemens, and Arima, but the 'Skulls' program specifically targets the Nokia 7610 model.

Ethiopia's crop production up 24%. Ethiopia produced 14.27 million tonnes in 2004, 24% more than in 2003 and 21% higher than the average of the past five years, according to a new report. In 2003, production totalled 11.49 million tonnes, a figure jointly released by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the World Food Programme (WFP). Favourable rains and increased use of improved seeds contributed significantly to the rise in output.

Nevertheless, 2.2 million people will still require emergency assistance, the report stated. The report calculated total food aid requirements for 2005 to be 387,500 tonnes. Of that total, 89,000 tonnes of fortified oil, described as "food for survival for children under five, pregnant and lactating women", will be critically needed.

However, pockets of drought continue to cause hardship, with prolonged dry spells draining wells. Last year, a total of 965,000 tonnes of food aid was needed to help seven million people. The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) is recommending that food assistance be bought locally whenever possible. "The purchase of cereals for these programmes is beneficial insofar as it helps domestic farmers," said Henri Josserand, head of the Global Information and Early Warning System (GIEWS) at the FAO.

Agriculture is the main economic activity in Ethiopia, representing 45% of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP). About 80% of the population relies on it directly or indirectly for their livelihoods.

original: Millions to miss out on the net..By 2025, 40% of the UK's population will still be without internet access at home, says a study...Around 23 million Britons will miss out on a wide range of essential services such as education and medical information, predicts the report by telecoms giant BT. It compares to 27 million, or 50%, of the UK, who are not currently online. The idea that the digital divide will evaporate with time is "wishful thinking", the report concludes...The study calls on the government and telecoms industry to come up with new ways to lure those that have been bypassed by the digital revolution. Although the percentage of Britons without home access will have fallen slightly, those that remain digital refuseniks will miss out on more, the report suggests. As more and more everyday tasks move online and offline services become less comprehensive, the divide will become more obvious and more burdensome for those that have not got net access, it predicts...The gap between "have-nets" and "have-nots" has been much talked about, but predictions about how such a divide will affect future generations has been less discussed. BT set out to predict future patterns based on current information and taking account of the way technology is changing. Optimists who predict that convergence and the emergence of more user-friendly technology will bridge the digital divide could be way off mark, the report suggests. "Internet access on other devices tends to be something taken up by those who already have it," said Adrian Hosford, director of corporate responsibility at BT. Costs of internet access have fallen dramatically and coverage in remote areas have vastly improved over the last year but the real barrier remains psychological. "There is a hard rump of have-nots who are not engaging with the net. They don't have the motivation or skills or perceive the benefits," said Mr Hosford...As now, the most disadvantaged groups are likely to remain among low income families, the older generation and the disabled...Those on low incomes will account for a quarter of the digital have-nots, the disabled will make up 16% and the elderly nearly a third by 2025, the report forecasts. Organisations such as BT have a responsibility to help tackle the problem, said Mr Hosford. The telco has seen positive results with its Everybody Online project which offers internet access to people in eight deprived communities around Britain. In one area of Cornwall with high levels of unemployment, online training helped people rewrite CVs and learn skills to get new jobs, explained Mr Hosford. Such grassroot activity addressing the specific needs of individual communities is essential is the problem of the digital divide is to be overcome, he said. "If we don't address this problem now, it will get a lot worse and people will find it more difficult to find jobs, education opportunities will be limited and they'll simply not be able to keep up with society," he said. The Alliance for Digital Inclusion, an independent body with members drawn from government, industry and the voluntary sector has recently been set up to tackle some of the issues faced by the digital refuseniks.

Millions to miss out on the **digital benefits of modern life by** 2025, **with a concerning** 40% of **the UK's** population without internet access **in their own** home, says a **major new report commissioned by telecoms giant BT.** This forecast suggests that up to 23 million Britons will **be excluded from a** wide range of essential services, **from accessing government information and banking to vital** medical **advice.** The report further warns that by 2027, **an estimated** 50% of **the** UK **adults will still not be regular users of the** online **world. The persistent** idea **that the existing** digital divide will simply evaporate with time is "**a dangerous fallacy**", the report concludes. The study **comes** up with new **evidence demonstrating that a substantial segment of the population has effectively** been bypassed **by the rapid advancements of the internet era.** While the **proportion** of Britons **with internet access at** home **has risen** slightly, those that remain refuseniks will miss **out on an ever-increasing number of crucial life opportunities.** As more tasks move **permanently** online and services **become increasingly** less **available offline**, the **resulting digital exclusion will** become more burdensome **for** those that have access, it **starkly warns.**

The **stark disparity** between "have-**nets**" **and** "have-nots" has **long** been much talked **about**, but how such **a profound** divide **impacts different** generations **has rarely** been discussed. **A fundamental shift in how people are** set to taking technology is. **Those** who predict convergence and the **emergence** of **user**-friendly technology will bridge the divide **are wide of the** mark, **the report contends.** "Internet access on **the** other **hand is often taken for granted by those who** already have," **said** Adrian **Hosford, Head of Digital Inclusion and Social** responsibility **at** BT. He noted that "internet access and coverage areas **have seen significant improvements all** over **the country,** but **a substantial social and economic** barrier remains."

"There **are still millions** of have-nots who **are not actively** engaging **with the inter**net. "They don't have the motivation **or the necessary digital** skills **to fully** perceive the benefits," Mr **Hosford said, emphasising the need for targeted support.** "The groups most likely to **be affected are those** among **the lowest** income **brackets, the elderly, and those in remote rural areas.**" The report projects that "Those on **the lowest incomes, and specifically** the disabled will make **up a staggering** 16% **of** the **total digitally excluded population by** 2025," **the report** forecasts. It adds that "Companies **like** BT **have a clear social** responsibility **to actively** tackle **this growing problem.**"

The **report highlights a particularly** positive project which offers internet access in eight communities **across the UK.** In one area **in** Cornwall **where** levels of **digital exclusion were high, the project provided crucial** online training **to help** people **develop skills, create** CVs **and successfully apply** to new jobs," **recounted** Mr Hosford. and very angrily and Gordon Brown reports a significant rift between the two most powerful figures in British politics. A crucial meeting of the Parliamentary Labour Party on Monday evening saw a succession of loyal backbenchers warn that continued feuding at the top of the party could seriously jeopardise Labour's prospects in the upcoming general election, a sentiment echoed by many across the political spectrum. Prime Minister Tony Blair had earlier insisted he would vigorously lead Labour's election campaign, dismissing speculation to the contrary, despite a new and highly anticipated book by respected financial journalist Robert Peston, saying he has reneged on a long-standing pledge to stand aside for his Chancellor, Gordon Brown, before the next poll. Mr Brown himself is scheduled to address the public at the party's major poster launch event on Tuesday, an occasion traditionally designed to project an image of unity and strength. What was desperately hoped would be a clear and unambiguous show of unity, he is nevertheless due to line up alongside Alan Milburn - the party's general election coordinator and a key Blair ally - and the Deputy Prime Minister John Prescott at the event. However, relations between the two are widely reported to have cooled considerably, almost to freezing point, ever since Mr Blair controversially brought back Peter Mandelson to the Cabinet in both 1997 and 2001, reportedly to balance or counter the growing influence of Gordon Brown. Mr Blair told the Parliamentary Labour Party on Monday evening: "I know everyone, in Cabinet and out of it, is absolutely determined to get on with the job of the Labour Party with a unified position that a third term in government desperately needs if we are to win and continue to serve the country."

The prime minister and his chancellor arrived within seconds of each other for the crucial Monday evening meeting of the PLP, attempting to put on a united front for the waiting cameras and for the good of the party, projecting an image of calm despite the swirling rumours. However, the atmosphere of the gathering was undoubtedly overshadowed by sensational claims made in Robert Peston's much-discussed new book, 'Brown's Britain', which explicitly alleges that Mr Blair had gone back on a significant and politically charged pledge to make way for Gordon Brown before the next general election. Veteran Labour MP Paul Flynn, known for his outspoken views and long experience, said Mr Blair and Mr Brown received a "scorching" reception from many MPs, reflecting widespread discontent and frustration within the party ranks: "It was just like the old Parliamentary Labour Party meetings used to be, full of internal dissent and open challenge," he observed, implying a worrying return to factional strife.

Former Labour minister Stephen Byers, a close ally of Mr Blair and a senior figure within the party, had earlier publicly urged those involved in the ongoing disputes to "stop this nonsense, this poisonous briefing and counter-briefing that is damaging the party's reputation". During the emotionally charged meeting, a Labour MP, Mr Campbell, reportedly challenged Mr Blair directly to state publicly and unequivocally that he did not believe the claims of a significant rift with the Chancellor. Several MPs were later heard to complain bitterly after recent reports of persistent infighting and briefing against senior figures had once again dominated the political headlines and diverted attention from the government's policy agenda.

A senior source close to the Prime Minister, speaking anonymously to the BBC, told us clearly, it was important to be telling the truth about the situation: "There were occasional disagreements in government, as there are in any major organisation or indeed any family. But Mr Blair and Mr Brown have consistently been able to work successfully together and have produced greatly improved public services for the country over many years," the source told Radio 4's flagship Today programme on Tuesday morning, attempting to downplay the severity of the claims. The new book specifically claims that Mr Blair hosted a private dinner in late 2003 during which he explicitly told Mr Brown he would stand aside before the next general election if he lost the trust of the party and the public over the controversial Iraq war and its aftermath. However, the book alleges that Mr Blair had decisively changed his mind by June 2004, following direct intervention from senior Cabinet members and a growing suspicion that Mr Brown was actively manoeuvring against him for the leadership, writes Peston. Deputy Prime Minister John Prescott, who was notably also there at the dinner and is seen as a unifying figure, maintained that the discussions were strictly confidential and would remain so. "Of course, I haven't got a waiter's ability to remember everything that was said 10 years on, in precise detail," he quipped, attempting to lighten the mood with a touch of humour. Mr Blair has always steadfastly denied he has done any "deals" over the premiership with his Chancellor, asserting his right to remain as long as he wishes, while Mr Brown has publicly dismissed the book's contents as mere "gossip" specifically designed to distract him from the crucial general election campaign that lies ahead. The opposition Conservatives were quick to capitalise on the turmoil, saying the government is behaving like squabbling children in a playground rather than serious politicians, while the Liberal Democrats say it clearly shows a government driven purely by personal ambition and internal feuds, rather than effective governance for the British people.

reconstruction:
Why We Fight, a potent study of the United States' military engagement over the past 50 years, has picked up one of the main awards at the 2005 Sundance Film Festival in Park City, Utah, US. Revered as a bastion for documentaries, it is the world's leading independent film festival. Director Sean Kirk's The War Tapes, offering an unvarnished look at soldiers serving in war-torn Iraq, received a special jury prize for its powerful depiction of conflict. Both Why We Fight and The War Tapes have been acquired by the BBC and are due to be screened on the BBC later this year.

The Sundance Film Festival, founded by Robert Redford in 1981, concluded its 11-day run on Sunday. This year's event was largely dominated by themes of war and conflict. In the World Cinema Dramatic category, the Angolan film The Hero won the Grand Jury Prize. The film, an Angolan-Portuguese production, tells the story of a veteran who returns home to a new, harsh struggle for survival.

Other notable films competing in categories focused on global conflicts included the Finnish film 3 Rooms of Melancholia, which offers a stark look at the war in Chechnya, and Shake Hands with the Devil: The Journey of a UN Commander, chronicling events in Rwanda during the 1994 genocide. In the World Cinema Documentary category, the Dutch-Indonesian co-production Shape of the Moon - a sensitive study of an extended family in Indonesia - took the top prize.

Meanwhile, the Israeli production The Wall, which bravely examines Israel's controversial security barrier from a Palestinian perspective, received a special jury award for its insightful and balanced portrayal. In the main US Dramatic category, Forty Shades of Blue was named winner of the Grand Jury Prize. The film tells the tale of a complex tug-of-war over love between an older man and his grown son.

Throughout its 24-year history, the Sundance Film Festival has showcased remarkable successes such as Reservoir Dogs, The Blair Witch Project, and The Full Monty. The festival is also well-known for launching recent independent hits like Garden State, Open Water, Napoleon Dynamite, and Super Size Me. The festival is held annually in the picturesque ski resort of Park City, Utah, which sees its population swell dramatically from 7,500 residents to an estimated 45,000 visitors during the event.

When interrogated by a phone, each poster transmits a dedicated number that people can call about the safest options. Sited at busy Tube and train stations, the posters communicate via an infra-red beam directly to a handset. This new initiative is part of Transport for London's (TfL) 'Travel Safe' campaign, which aims to help Londoners, particularly women, avoid potential dangers. In particular, it seeks to reduce the number of assaults reported across the network.

Nigel Harker, head of marketing at Transport for London (TfL), said the posters were proving effective because they worked outside traditional phone networks. "They work in previously inaccessible areas, as underground reception is a huge advantage for a public safety campaign of this sort," said Mr Harker.

The posters will automatically beam information to any phone equipped with a compatible infrared port when it is directed at the poster. "We started with 100 of them, and they are now out there across the network," said Rachel McQueen, a spokeswoman for the technology firm behind the project. "It's truly groundbreaking technology."

There is also a special poster that uses Hypertags short-range technology. Using Hypertags in the display, it does not only pass on a simple contact number, Harker explained, but can pass on almost any information in rich text form, personalised tones and even video clips. He added that no official figures were yet available for how many people are actively using the posters, but the campaign had already racked up an impressive 12,500 downloads.

"Before we launched a major campaign like this, the big question was always: 'Would people engage with it, or would they simply ignore it?' " said Harker. reconstruction:
Intense speculation continues to surround the future of the beleaguered Russian oil giant Yukos. The fate of Russia's key production unit, Yuganskneftegas - the oil firm which has now been sold to a little-known buyer on the back of frantic speculation in Moscow - has been confirmed. A mysterious company, Baikalfinansgroup, emerged as the auction winner, agreeing to pay 260.75bn roubles (£4.8bn; $9.4bn). Russia's state-owned gas monopoly, Gazprom, which had been widely expected to win the highly anticipated auction, did not. The sale has effectively destroyed Yukos, the former owner of Yuganskneftegas, according to its founder Mikhail Khodorkovsky.

"Yuganskneftegas should not have been sold off now, having already been controversially privatised in the 90s," Mr Khodorkovsky was quoted as saying. "They have simply made a Christmas present for a state-backed Russian company," Interfax news agency reported Mr Khodorkovsky as saying via his lawyers.

Gazprom had been the favourite to win but eventually failed to secure a finance deal after a US court barred it from taking part. Last week, Yukos filed for Chapter 11 protection in a US bankruptcy court in Houston - in a desperate attempt to stop the forced sale of Yuganskneftegas, which accounts for 60% of its total oil output. The US court banned Gazprom from taking part in the auction and also explicitly barred international banks from providing financing for the sale.

"They've screwed up badly," commented one analyst at Renaissance Capital. "And Gazprom doesn't simply have that sort of money just lying around that it could easily use for such a large purchase." "It's truly a gift for somebody, but not necessarily for Russia itself," said Oleg Maximov, an analyst at Troika Dialog in Moscow. "We don't really know who owns this company 100% at this point," he added, hinting at the opacity of the deal.

"We'll have to find out who ultimately owns it," he said. "As far as I know, the official papers have not yet revealed the real result of this highly complex and controversial transaction." The sale, however, bought little time for the Russian government to resolve the wider Yukos issue, according to analysts. This current scenario is not supposed to last for more than two weeks, as Yuganskneftegas, currently in the temporary hands of the bailiffs, is set to reach its ultimate buyer very soon. Yukos is not planning on letting go of its critical production unit without a fierce fight and has threatened further legal action against the buyer," a group legal representative said. The company claims that the sale is being politically driven to dismantle it, largely due to the political ambitions of its powerful opponents and its founder, Mikhail Khodorkovsky, who is now facing separate fraud charges. Yukos has been hit by a staggering $27bn in back taxes and crippling penalties, and now that the breakup of the company is fully underway, Yuganskneftegas alone accounts for some 20% of Russia's total oil output.

reconstruction:
Following a furious political attack regarding householders' rights when confronting burglars, Tory shadow home secretary Michael Howard accused the government of performing a series of U-turns on the rules surrounding self-defence, particularly on amending the law, which had been intended to significantly water down the 'reasonable force' provision. He called the government's stance unacceptable, saying: "It is not householders who should be frightened, it is burglars." The Home Secretary said he would keep under active review the law on self-defence, but stressed that it was already robust enough.

The then Metropolitan Police Commissioner, Sir John Stevens, last month said the law needed to be clearer 'so only' householders could 'feel safe and adequately protected' in their own homes and on their property. The mounting public pressure prompted the prime minister to declare that police chiefs and the Crown Prosecution Service would be consulted as part of a wide-ranging review. He told MPs: "In response to legitimate public concern, we, of course, support a change in the law's interpretation, if not its fundamental wording, to provide greater clarity."

Instead, the government announced that no fundamental legislative change to the existing statutes is planned, but new, clearer guidance will be officially issued so people are absolutely clear about what they are legally entitled to do when defending their property and family. On Thursday, Mr Howard told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he believed Mr Brown had initially backed a radical change to the law, then had come full circle to the idea that no significant change was needed again. He blasted: "They've had three different positions in three months and two complete U-turns on this crucial issue." A spokesman for Mr Brown, reportedly taken by surprise, told him bluntly: "There's nothing you could say to that, I believe."

Earlier, Mr Howard had specifically called for the 'reasonable force' test for householders to be matched by a much higher legal hurdle in cases where burglars claimed injury from householders defending their homes and families. The issue first came into the intense public spotlight after the high-profile case of Norfolk farmer Tony Martin, who was jailed for shooting a 16-year-old burglar in 1999 as he ran away from his isolated farm property. But the then home secretary said the law was 'perfectly adequate' and fundamentally sound in its current form, requiring no amendment.

The barrister who successfully represented Tony Martin, Mr Geoffrey Clarke QC, said the rules as they currently stood were "weighted overwhelmingly" in favour of the householder. He added: "The problem there has been the understanding of it - Sir John Stevens was saying one thing and the prime minister making another very different public statement."

Any new official guidance would therefore be welcome on the issue, added Mr Clarke. Separately, the Director of Public Prosecutions, Sir Ken Macdonald, confirmed that only 11 householders or occupants of premises have been prosecuted for using excessive force in self-defence cases in the last 15 years. Those included a man who had specifically waited for a burglar to enter his home, then beaten him severely, he said. Conservative MP Patrick Mercer's Private Member's Bill on self-defence law for householders received a first reading in the House of Commons on Wednesday and now goes to a second debate next month.

reconstruction: Hundreds of thousands of 'mobiles' go online every month. Multimedia phones are showing clear signs of taking off, with more and more people actively using them to go online and access various services. New figures released today from, the Mobile Data Association (MDA), show that the number of mobile phones equipped with GPRS and MMS technology has effectively doubled since this time last year. Users are increasingly able to browse the web, access breaking news, download music and participate in other forms of mobile chat. By the end of 2005, the MDA confidently predicts that 75% of all mobile handsets in circulation will be able to connect to the internet via GPRS. The association says that in the three months leading up to 30 September, mobile data usage was 'well up' on the figures recorded for the same period the previous year. About 53% of the adult population own a mobile phone in the UK, and the MDA reports that almost half of those now have GPRS enabled. GPRS, which is often described as 2.5G - or 2.5 generation - effectively sits between the older 2G and the newer 3G mobile technologies, and is often likened to a 'semi-broadband' experience for mobile phones. With more and more compelling services being offered across mobile networks, a growing number of people are choosing to go online with their handsets. Personalised ringtones are still proving highly popular, as is mobile text chat. The Crazy Frog ringtone was, for example, the biggest ever-selling digital download, according to the MDA, and mobile chat received significant publicity when Prime Minister Tony Blair was seen using it to demonstrate the technology during a public event. Traditional text messaging services are also being looked at with continued interest, with 32% of people in the UK currently able to both send and receive such messages. This represents a significant 14% increase since September's figures were last reported. A new report from Continental Research clearly reflects the continuing battle faced by networks to encourage people to go online and fully use these mobile data services. The report indicates that 36% of mobile users have now successfully sent a multimedia message, or MMS. That's a healthy increase of 7% compared to the figures recorded in 2003. Mobile companies are actively pushing for the adoption of more advanced functions on their phones, particularly multimedia messaging (MMS) and internet access, as this generates significant recurring revenue for them. But critics are quick to say that the technology is often confusing for users and mobile services are still too expensive to consistently use. There have also been ongoing issues over interoperability, with users not always being able to reliably send messages from one mobile phone, perhaps using a particular network, to a different one on another network.

original: Howard rebuts asylum criticisms..Tory leader Michael Howard has gone on the offensive in response to people questioning how a son of immigrants can propose asylum quotas...Mr Howard, whose parents fled the Nazi threat to come to the UK, says the claim would mean no-one from an immigrant family could become premier. His comments come in a BBC documentary called 'No More Mr Nasty'. TV presenter Anne Robinson said as home secretary he gave the impression he would "like to kick your cat". Ms Robinson, a friend of the Tory leader, also revealed that as a Cambridge student Mr Howard was "much loved by women and he was a courteous and kind and rather dashing lover" - although she denied having personal experience. "I wasn't at Cambridge - and it's not personal experience - but I know people who were."..Documentary maker Michael Cockerell was given behind-the-scenes access to Mr Howard for his film portrait. The Tory leader was asked about to respond to people who said that if there had there been a quota on immigration and asylum in the 1930s, his parents might not have been allowed into the country...He replies: "What is the inference of that? "That if you reach the view that you need to control immigration in the interests of the country you're not allowed to put a view forward if you happen to be descended from immigrants? "That seems to me an absolutely extraordinary proposition? It would certainly mean no one from immigrant parents could be prime minister."..Ms Robinson, who presents The Weakest Link tells Cockerell that she despaired at his hardline image when he was home secretary in John Major's government. "I used to have to sit on my hands because he'd get on television and give a passable impression of someone who'd like to kick your cat or would put your baby in prison if he cried. I mean it was very, very Draconian." The film shows Mr Howard laughing at Rory Bremner's impression of him as Dracula, which he calls "good fun", apart from the serious falsehood of a comment suggesting he wants fewer black people in the UK. reconstruction:
Howard asylum criticisms.

Tory leader Michael Howard has come under fire from some people questioning how he, as the son of immigrants, can propose tough new asylum policies for the UK.

Mr Howard, whose parents fled Nazi Germany to come to the UK as refugees, says such a line of attack would mean no-one from an immigrant family background could ever hope to become prime minister.

The film also explores Howard's public persona, including the "No Mr Nasty" label. TV presenter Anne Robinson, interviewed for the programme, revealed that in private he gave the impression he "would like to torture a cat".

Ms Robinson, who described herself as a friend of the Tory leader, also revealed that as a Cambridge student, Michael Howard was "a rather dashing figure" - someone who, she added, had personal "flings" at Cambridge, though she was quick to clarify, "it's not personal - but they were very short-lived."

Veteran BBC journalist Michael Cockerell was given unprecedented, fly-on-the-wall access to Michael Howard for a new documentary film. During filming, the Tory leader was asked about whether he felt people understood that if there had been a similar clampdown on asylum in the 1930s, his own family might not have been allowed into the country.

He responded, clearly exasperated: "Are you suggesting that if you want to control immigration into a country you're not allowed to put a policy in place if you happen to be from an immigrant background?" He continued: "It seems to me an extraordinary suggestion that certainly no immigrant should be allowed to be prime minister, simply because of their background."

Ms Robinson, who the programme revealed had despaired when Michael Howard served as Home Secretary in John Major's Conservative government, was also extensively interviewed.

She elaborated on her feelings during that period: "I had to sit on my hands because I'd give a passable impression of someone who'd like to kick your teeth in prison if he got half a chance. I mean it was, it was Draconian, truly Draconian."

The film attempts to show Howard's lighter side, presenting an image of himself as, he said, "fun", although it noted a serious falsehood in a comment he now wants removed from the final cut of the film. Away from politics, the film shows the leader of the Tory party at home playing with his wife, Sandra, and a model aircraft set.

In one light-hearted moment, when asked by his wife, Sandra, if she'd like a game of table tennis or 'pong', he wryly replied: "Yeah, it would be more enjoyable if I could win, but it's not going to happen."

Former Downing Street communications director Alastair Campbell, now working on Labour's general election campaign, suggested that the "touchy-feely" image being projected does not truly fit Mr Howard. He recalled that Prime Minister Tony Blair was repeatedly mocked by his opponents in early Commons clashes because Mr Howard was perceived to have lacked a clear "strategy" on the war in Iraq.

The Tories, however, dismissed such criticisms as "utterly ridiculous", maintaining that while Labour has been consistent in its overall support for military action, it has been critical of Mr Blair's failure to tell the whole truth about intelligence before the conflict. Seasoned Conservative politician and former chancellor Ken Clarke remarked that Mr Howard has bigger problems with the party's overall direction and appeal than just his personal image. Mr Clarke says improving it is "conceivable" but acknowledged it would be "very difficult".

But he adds, emphatically: "It has got to change itself a bit and widen its appeal to the wider electorate."

The documentary, titled 'Michael Howard: A Life in Pictures', was shown on BBC2 on 12 February 2005.

Standard Chartered Bank seals a significant South Korea-based deal, valued at approximately $3.3bn (£1.8bn). This landmark agreement involves the acquisition of a controlling stake in Korea First Bank (KFB), one of South Korea's main and historically important financial institutions. The move to acquire KFB, a long-term strategic target for Standard Chartered, is understood to have fulfilled a crucial strategic objective of establishing a much bigger and more substantial presence in Asia's dynamic and rapidly expanding economy. This expansion is central to Standard Chartered's long-term growth ambitions across the continent.

To facilitate this substantial investment, Standard Chartered plans to raise approximately 3% in new equity capital. The bank will primarily fund this acquisition through the issuance of new ordinary shares to institutional investors. These shares are expected to be worth around £1bn ($1.8bn), representing an approximate 10% share of the company's existing issued share capital. Looking forward, the bank expects a significant contribution from its new Korean asset, with 16% of the future group's total revenue projected to come from KFB, underscoring the deal's strategic importance.

Furthermore, KFB's operations are anticipated to contribute around 22% of the Standard Chartered group's total earnings. This particular transaction, which comes just over a year after Citigroup successfully acquired KorAm Bank and Standard Chartered itself made an unsuccessful attempt to acquire Korea Exchange Bank, is poised to be the financial sector's biggest takeover deal concluded in South Korea for some time, attracting considerable international attention.

At the time of its announcement, Standard Chartered's acquisition represents the largest overseas investment into Korea's banking sector. KFB is currently Korea's sixth-largest retail bank, serving an impressive 3 million retail customers. It holds a respectable 6% share of the country's competitive banking market and operates an extensive branch network across the nation, providing a strong platform for future growth.

South Korea's financial market is notably robust, estimated to be approximately three times the size of Hong Kong's, with impressive annual revenues reaching $44bn. Standard Chartered, which maintains its global headquarters in London, is renowned for its diverse operations, doing business across key growth markets in Asia, the Middle East, and a substantial portion of the developing financial sectors in Africa.

"We are extremely satisfied with the price agreed for Korea First Bank," stated the group chief executive during a press conference held in Seoul. "A tremendous amount of preparatory work has already been done, and further efforts will continue relentlessly in making sure that this integration is smooth, successful, and delivers the value we anticipate," he added, emphasizing the commitment to the deal's success.

He described KFB as "a strong, well-established bank with a highly skilled and dedicated workforce," further characterizing it as "a very significant and transformative acquisition for Standard Chartered, marking a new chapter in our Asian expansion."

Back in London, news of Standard Chartered's plan to sell 118 million new ordinary shares to institutional investors had a predictable impact on its stock. The share price was pushed downwards in early trading, contributing notably to the FTSE 100 index's overall 0.3% decline on the day.

By midday trading, Standard Chartered's shares were recorded as 28 pence lower, settling at a price of 925p, reflecting investor reaction to the capital raising plans associated with the KFB acquisition.

It was widely reported that rival bank HSBC had also actively queried a potential bid for KFB, underscoring the desirability of the asset. The deal, however, which still requires crucial regulatory approval from both Korean and international authorities, is expected to be formally completed by April 2005, with full operational integration anticipated to conclude by the end of 2006, Standard Chartered confirmed in its statement.

Indeed, banking giant HSBC, operating from its powerful London and Hong Kong bases, was also aggressively running for the prize of KFB. However, Standard Chartered is widely believed to have gained a crucial initiative by putting together a comprehensive and attractive bid package during the quiet Christmas holiday period, catching its rivals somewhat off guard.

"The Standard Chartered team were able to move so quickly and decisively that they caught HSBC entirely unawares," the Financial Times newspaper reported, citing an unnamed analyst based in Seoul. "HSBC will now regrettably have to wait for another opportunity for a bank in Korea to come up for sale - most likely Korea Exchange Bank, which is currently in foreign hands and could be on the market soon," the analyst added.

Standard Chartered emphatically stated it was buying 100% of KFB's equity, a move that would bring an incredibly attractive and robust retail and commercial banking franchise to the bank's expanding global operations, significantly enhancing its footprint in Northeast Asia.

The South Korean government currently owns 51.4% of the bank, a legacy shareholding resulting from past interventions. The remaining significant stakes, along with management control, are primarily in the hands of Newbridge Capital.

Newbridge Capital originally acquired its substantial stake in KFB following the widespread nationalisation of several distressed banks in the immediate wake of the devastating 1997-98 Asian currency crisis, a period which severely crippled South Korea's entire financial sector and necessitated extensive government intervention.

Despite past challenges, South Korea's economy is now robust and is forecast to grow by a healthy 4.5% this year. Once predominantly an export-driven manufacturing economy, South Korea's burgeoning service sector has significantly overtaken manufacturing in terms of contribution to GDP over the last decade or so. Services now account for approximately 40% of the national economy, and domestic consumer spending is growing increasingly strong and important for sustained growth.

In the immediate aftermath of the financial crisis, the South Korean government actively encouraged the growth of credit card usage as a stimulus measure for domestic consumption. However, this policy unfortunately led to a host of bad problems; a major credit card company, which was the country's largest credit card firm, has been struggling desperately to avoid outright collapse for many months, and several other smaller card providers are also in severe financial difficulty.

Despite these challenges, many financial analysts believe that South Korea's financial services industry is ripe for further consolidation and modernization, presenting plenty of attractive opportunities for new, well-capitalised entrants and existing players looking to expand.

Standard Chartered specifically highlighted that it sees "the unique opportunity to create significant value through the introduction and development of more sophisticated products and services, tailored to the evolving needs of the Korean market."

Since 1999, KFB has undergone a strategic transformation, shifting from being predominantly a wholesale-focused bank into a more balanced retail bank. This transformation has focused heavily on expanding its consumer lending portfolio, which now makes up a substantial 45% of its entire loan book, signaling a successful strategic pivot.

Delegates will instead get a spring conference, in what is widely considered a significant move away from the traditional rivalry between the main political parties and their choices of conference locations, usually oscillating between Blackpool and Bournemouth. For Blackpool, the news that the much larger Labour Party gather will not be hosted there is undoubtedly seen as a major blow to the coastal resort. He added the answer represented his view that the war was legal, but was not a summary of his advice to the PM. The government has resisted calls to publish the full advice, saying such papers are always kept confidential...In a statement, Lord Goldsmith said: "I was fully involved throughout the drafting process and personally finalised, and of course approved, the answer." He said the answer had been prepared in his office with the involvement of Solicitor General Harriet Harman, two of his own officials, three Foreign Office officials, a QC, Christopher Greenwood and the then Lord Chancellor, Lord Irvine of Lairg..."No other minister or official was involved in any way." He suggested the claim that Lord Falconer and Lady Morgan had drafted the answer were the result of a mis-transcription of his evidence to the Butler Inquiry into pre-war intelligence. "As I have always made clear, I set out in the answer my own genuinely held, independent view that military action was lawful under the existing (UN) Security Council resolutions," he said. "The answer did not purport to be a summary of my confidential legal advice to government." Former foreign secretary Robin Cook said Lord Goldsmith's admission that his parliamentary answer was not a summary of his legal opinion suggested Parliament may have been misled. "The attorney general may never have presented his answer as a summary, but others certainly did," he said. "What is clear from his statement today is that he does not believe that it was a full, accurate summary of his formal opinion."..Earlier, Tony Blair dismissed questions about the attorney general's advice, and said his Parliamentary statement had been a "fair summary" of his opinion. "That's what he (Lord Goldsmith) said and that's what I say. He has dealt with this time and time and time again," Mr Blair told his monthly news conference in Downing Street. He refused to answer further questions on the issue...On the question of whether such papers have always been kept confidential, Tory MP Michael Mates, who is a member of the Commons intelligence and security committee and was part of the Butler inquiry, told the BBC: "That, as a general rule, is right, but it's not an absolute rule." He said there had been other occasions when advice had been published, most recently regarding Prince Charles's marriage plans. The government could not pick and choose when to use the convention, he said. Mr Mates added: "This may be one of those special occasions... when it would be in the public interest to see the advice which the attorney general gave to the prime minister."..The claims about Lord Falconer and Baroness Morgan's involvement were made in a book published this week by Philippe Sands QC, a member of Cherie Blair's Matrix Chambers. He also says Lord Goldsmith warned Tony Blair on 7 March 2003 that the Iraq war could be illegal without a second UN resolution sanctioning military action...A short statement about Lord Goldsmith's position presented in a written parliamentary answer on 17 March 2003 - just before a crucial Commons vote on the military action - did not suggest this. Former minister Clare Short, who resigned from the government over the Iraq war, said the ministerial answer was the same statement that was earlier shown to the cabinet as it discussed military action. She said the full advice should have been attached, according to the ministerial code, and demanded a Lords inquiry into the matter. The Conservatives and Liberal Democrats say they still want the publication of the full legal advice given by the Attorney General. Lib Dem foreign affairs spokesman Sir Menzies Campbell said Lord Goldsmith's statement still did not clear up the outstanding issues. "If his original advice of 7 March accepted that military action might be illegal, how was it that he resolved any such doubts by the time the Parliamentary answer was published on 17 March?" he said. "Only the fullest disclosure will now do."

reconstruction:
Claims surrounding the Iraq war suggest the Attorney General's advice on the legality of the Iraq conflict was drafted by Downing Street officials, a claim that has caused significant controversy. Lord Goldsmith, Lord Falconer and Baroness Morgan denied taking any part in the drafting process. Lord Goldsmith added the view that the advice he issued was his own legal opinion, but was not a summary of the full range of advice he had given the government previously. The government has consistently resisted calls to publish the full legal advice, arguing that such documents are always kept confidential.

In a detailed statement released on Monday, Lord Goldsmith said: "I was fully involved in the entire process and personally approved, of course, the final answer and its wording." He had his consultations and discussions with the involvement of then Solicitor General Harriet Harman, his own senior legal officials, Foreign Office lawyers, a prominent QC, Elizabeth Greenwood and Lord, Lord Irvine of Lairg. "No other individual or office was involved in any significant way in formulating the final opinion." He rejected completely the claim by Baroness Morgan that his final answer was a misrepresentation of his earlier legal advice provided to the pre-war intelligence committee.

"As I have always made clear in all public statements, I set out my own independently held, considered and firm view that military action was lawful under the existing United Nations Security Council resolutions," he said. "The answer did not in any way represent a change of my legal opinion given to the government at the time." Former Foreign Secretary Robin Cook's previous admission that he had not personally seen *all* of his legal advice should not be taken as a suggestion that his legal team or other officials misled him.

"The former Attorney General presented his final advice as a concise summary, and it certainly did represent his view," he said. "What is apparent from his statement today is that he did not believe that it was a full, accurate reflection of his earlier comprehensive legal opinion."

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Tony Blair quickly dismissed further questions about the Attorney General's statement, stressing that his statement had given a "clear and unambiguous opinion." "That's what he said and that's what I say. He has dealt with this matter fully," Mr Blair said at his regular monthly Downing Street press conference. He refused to answer any more specific questions on the issue.

On the controversial question of why the full legal advice has been kept secret, Tory MP Michael Howard, who is a prominent member of the intelligence and security committee and part of the ongoing Hutton inquiry, told the BBC: "That, as a general rule and a long-standing convention, it's an absolute rule that such advice is kept confidential from the public." He said there had, however, been other instances where legal advice had been published, notably Prince Charles' letters to ministers. And questioning why, in this particular instance, the convention was being rigorously used, he commented: "... it would be of significant public interest to see the full advice which the government received on this crucial matter."

The controversial claims about Lord Falconer and Baroness Morgan's alleged involvement in the advice process were first made public last week by Philippe Sands QC, a respected legal expert and member of Cherie Blair's Matrix Chambers. He specifically claimed that Lord Goldsmith had advised Tony Blair privately on 7 March 2003 that the Iraq war would be illegal without a new United Nations Security Council resolution sanctioning military action against Saddam Hussein's regime.

In short, Lord Goldsmith's final legal position was formally presented in a parliamentary statement to MPs on 17 March 2003 - just before a crucial parliamentary vote on the military action in Iraq. Former International Development Secretary Clare Short, who famously resigned from the government over the Iraq war, said the ministerial statement that was shown to cabinet members as the full advice was a deliberately incomplete summary and misrepresented the full legal counsel. She further said the full advice should have been, according to the ministerial code, placed into the public domain for scrutiny.

Both the opposition Conservative Party and the Liberal Democrats say they still want to see the complete and unredacted full legal advice given by the Attorney General to the government. Liberal Democrat foreign affairs spokesman Sir Menzies Campbell said that Lord Goldsmith's lengthy statement still did not adequately clear up all outstanding issues. "If his original advice of 7 March 2003 genuinely accepted that military action would be deemed illegal without a new UN resolution, then how was it that he managed to overcome such significant doubts by the time his final and definitive answer was published on 17 March 2003?" he questioned. "We believe that the fullest possible disclosure must now take place to understand this disparity fully."

reconstruction:
Manchester United scraped through an FA Cup test against resilient Conference minnows Exeter City in their third-round replay at St James' Park. Cristiano Ronaldo opened the scoring, turning the ball past Exeter goalkeeper Paul Jones after nine minutes, and later added a second, before Wayne Rooney sealed the victory in injury time.

Exeter, who famously held United to a goalless draw at Old Trafford, wasted a host of clear-cut chances to equalise or take the lead at various stages. They were often kept in the game by some great saves from their goalkeeper Jones, but Rooney eventually put the tie beyond all doubt with a very late finish. Despite the scoreline, Exeter continued to press throughout, with two of their most dangerous players, Sean Devine and Andrew Taylor, both forcing United keeper Tim Howard into good saves.

Sir Alex Ferguson, clearly stung by his side's lacklustre 0-0 draw in the first leg at Old Trafford, handed starts to experienced midfielders Paul Scholes and Roy Keane, as well as star attackers Cristiano Ronaldo and Wayne Rooney.

Exeter began brightly, with Sean Devine and Steve Flack seeing plenty of the ball in the opening exchanges. However, it did not take long for United to assert their authority, and the hosts soon found themselves a goal down. A precise cross from Ryan Giggs, delivered to the left side of the six-yard box, was met by the young Portuguese winger, who expertly fired the ball past Jones to give United the crucial early lead.

Exeter had a golden chance to equalise shortly after, with Devine shooting wastefully over from close range. Ronaldo then blasted another effort over from a precise Paul Scholes pass, and a later Wayne Rooney shot was bravely blocked by the Exeter defence, while Ronaldo slammed another promising effort well over from a good position outside the box. Just before the half-time break, Giggs had a clear chance to double United's advantage, but the Welshman fired a left-foot shot badly wide from 10 yards.

In first-half stoppage time, Exeter created their best chance of the half, with Emmanuel Jeannin firing in a dangerous shot from the edge of the area that Devine, after a scramble in the box, somehow touched the ball past Tim Howard's left post, but it was just wide of the target.

The Grecians started the second half in determined fashion, with their defence doing well to collect crosses and deny United further clear-cut chances. After Wayne Rooney had completely messed up a chance to make it 2-0 midway through the second half, Cristiano Ronaldo later showed him how it should be done, his powerful drive forcing a flying save from Jones. The home fans were then baying for a penalty when the ball appeared to strike a United defender's arm inside the box, but Devine's subsequent low shot was well saved by Howard to push it out for a corner, denying an obvious equaliser.

United finally sealed the result in the 87th minute. Ronaldo scored his second goal of the night, latching onto a precise Park Ji-sung pass and firing a low shot past Jones. Earlier, Park himself had seen a shot through the mud, which Jones had raced across his goal to gather on the goalline, preventing an earlier second goal. Moments later, Devine had another clear chance to make himself a hero for the Grecians, but he could only volley Andrew Taylor's inviting cross wide of Howard's left post after an excellent run into the box.

Wayne Rooney eventually rounded Jones with embarrassing ease to score into an empty net in the third minute of injury time, finally putting the tie beyond all doubt and booking a fourth-round tie against fellow Premier League side Fulham.

**Teams:**
**Exeter City:** Preece, Craig Gaia, Emmanuel Jeannin, Gary Fraser, Chris Woodman, Andrew Taylor (Moxey 89), Les Clay (Fitzpatrick 74), Dawson, Steve Flack, Sean Devine (Ampadu 69).
**Unused subs:** Scott Rice.

**Manchester United:** Tim Howard, Gary Neville, Wes Brown, John O'Shea, Quinton Fortune (Mikaël Silvestre 80), Ryan Giggs (Kleberson 70), Roy Keane (Darren Fletcher 66), Paul Scholes, Eric Djemba-Djemba, Cristiano Ronaldo, Wayne Rooney.
**Unused subs:** Ricardo, David Bellion.

**Goals:**
**Manchester United:** Cristiano Ronaldo 9, 87; Wayne Rooney 90+3.

**Attendance:** 9,033.

**Referee:** P Dowd (Staffordshire).

reconstruction:
General Motors (GM) is issuing a major recall alert affecting hundreds of thousands of vehicles in the United States, raising concerns about safety and potentially impacting the company's already strained finances.

The world's biggest carmaker, General Motors (GM), is recalling more than 200,000 US vehicles on critical safety grounds, as announced by federal regulators. This substantial recall highlights ongoing challenges within the automotive industry concerning vehicle reliability and consumer protection.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), the primary US federal agency responsible for vehicle safety, detailed the scope of the recall. It specifically targets 155,465 full-size pick-up trucks, cargo vans, and sport utility vehicles (SUVs), which represent a significant portion of GM's popular models in the US market. This widespread recall has been initiated due to serious concerns regarding possible malfunctions within the vehicles' braking systems. These potential defects could compromise driver control and significantly increase the risk of accidents.

The affected vehicles included in this extensive recall span the 2004 and 2005 model years, a period during which these models were top sellers for the automaker, a spokesperson for General Motors confirmed. Among the models identified as having potential faults are the Chevrolet Avalanche, Chevrolet Sierra, Chevrolet Silverado, and Chevrolet Tahoe, along with the GMC Sierra, GMC Yukon, and Cadillac Escalade. These popular trucks and SUVs are widely used by families and businesses across the country.

Specifically, investigations have revealed that a brake pressure accumulator within these vehicles could potentially develop cracks. Should this occur, it could lead to the forceful propulsion of metal fragments, posing a serious risk of injury to vehicle occupants. Furthermore, such a crack could also allow vital brake fluid to leak from the system. A loss of brake fluid would inevitably make it significantly harder for drivers to bring their vehicles to a stop, or even lead to a complete brake failure, thereby greatly increasing the likelihood of a dangerous collision or a severe crash, GM officials explicitly warned.

In addition to these larger vehicles, GM is also concurrently recalling another 19,924 units, specifically affecting Cadillac XLR luxury roadsters, Cadillac SRX SUVs, and Pontiac Grand Prix sedans, all manufactured in the 2004 model year. This secondary recall addresses a different set of issues. This particular recall for the sedans and roadsters is being implemented because the accelerator pedal assembly may not function correctly when exposed to extremely cold temperatures. Such a malfunction could prevent the driver from accelerating properly or could unexpectedly affect the vehicle's braking capabilities, creating a perilous driving situation.

Moreover, as part of this series of safety actions, GM is recalling 17,815 Buick Rainier, Chevrolet Trailblazer, and GMC Envoy Ascenders from the 2005 model year. The concern here is that the fuel gauge in these vehicles may become unreliable, potentially sticking in an incorrect position or even detaching and falling out of the dashboard, leading to inaccurate fuel readings for drivers.

Despite the gravity of these potential issues, GM has stressed that, at the time of these announcements, it did not have any confirmed reports of injuries or fatalities directly attributable to these specific defects. However, the company is urging all affected vehicle owners to contact their dealerships promptly to arrange for inspection and necessary repairs.

The sheer scale of the recall, announced last week, immediately sparked investor concerns and prompted analysts to predict that GM's financial earnings for the current fiscal year would inevitably be lower than those reported in 2004. This adds further pressure on the automotive giant. Indeed, the world's biggest car maker is currently grappling with a confluence of significant challenges, including persistent financial woes, consistently weak US sales figures, and intensified competition from both domestic and international rivals. The company's market share has been under severe pressure in recent times.

Just in January, General Motors had already issued a cautionary statement, indicating that significantly higher healthcare costs incurred for its employees and retirees in North America, coupled with operational difficulties and financial strain at its automotive financing subsidiary, GMAC, would collectively exert a negative impact on its overall financial performance throughout 2005. This recall only exacerbates those existing pressures, posing additional hurdles for the company's turnaround efforts.

Microsoft, the world's largest software giant, is taking the plunge into the lucrative world of blogging with a new web publishing service to allow users to create and publish personal content online, called Spaces. The new offering is designed to compete directly with services from Google and AOL, which offer to help individuals set up web pages. Blogs, short for web logs, a well-established method for people to share their thoughts and express themselves freely online.

MSN Spaces is a completely free personal publishing platform from MSN. Users will be able to easily choose from a variety of customised designs for the page, images and upload text, video clips and music. The service will be financially supported by banner advertisements placed discreetly on the pages.

"This is a fantastic opportunity for individuals to truly express themselves," said MSN's group product manager for the new service, Blake Irving. "This represents Microsoft's first significant foray into the burgeoning world of personal blogging, which has taken off dramatically as a web phenomenon throughout the entire last year."

Competitors like Google already have a strong presence in the blogging market through its popular Blogger service, while AOL provides its members with access to integrated online journals.

Accurate figures regarding the total number of blogs in existence are somewhat difficult to come by. According to leading blog firm Technorati, the overall number of blogs being created daily has been doubling every five and a half months, and this trend has continued for the last 18 months consecutively. It now estimates the number in existence has exceeded 4. 8 million active blogs globally, and that a quarter are regularly and actively maintained.

The British economy is "facing a tough time'', and the manufacturing sector, in particular, will face "serious challenges" over the next year, the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) has warned. In its latest quarterly economic assessment, the BCC found that manufacturing output had experienced its worst year since 2004, marking a worrying trend over eight years. This downturn, according to the report, largely came as strong sterling exchange rates were being cited as a major factor impacting competitiveness. Across the whole UK economy, the BCC found that overall growth is now set to slow. It forecast that economic growth would fall from more than 3% in 2004 to below 2.5% in both 2005 and 2006, a significant downgrade from earlier projections, signaling a period of sustained economic headwind.

Manufacturers' domestic sales growth fell slightly in the latest quarter, to an index reading of 5,196 points. Employment in manufacturing also saw a decline, with job expectations sinking to their lowest level for a year. "Despite some pockets of positive news, the overall findings from our survey are deeply worrying for the sector's fragile recovery," the BCC said in a statement. "These results cast a shadow of concern over the sector's ability to sustain its tentative recovery amidst challenging global conditions." The outlook for the crucial service sector, while showing some resilience, was also described as "uncertain." Despite a modest increase in sales and orders, as reported by the BCC in its comprehensive survey for the quarter across both service sectors, overall growth nevertheless failed to reach the robust levels seen at the end of 2004. The reduced likelihood of an immediate interest rate rise by the Bank of England had, surprisingly, failed to lead to an anticipated improvement in business confidence or investment. The Bank of England had previously raised interest rates five times between 2003 and this year. However, rates had been kept on hold since the beginning of the year, a decision largely influenced by growing concerns over waning consumer confidence and a noticeable slowdown in overall economic output. "Rising costs across supply chains, severely squeezed profit margins, the burden of relentless regulations, and the cumulative impact of higher taxes are proving to be significant problems for businesses across the country," director Frost commented. "While consumer spending is widely expected to decelerate significantly over the next 12-18 months, it is highly unlikely that business investment and exports will be able to rise sufficiently to pick up the economic slack and avert a more pronounced slowdown."

He didn't say so, but the Tories believe the prime minister is playing the fear card on this one so he can look tough in the run up to the general election And they believe Tony Blair is using the issue to suggest the Tories are soft on terrorism. Why on earth will the prime minister not simply take up the Tories' offer to extend the existing powers temporarily to allow proper parliamentary debate of the laws, he demanded. The prime minister claims this is the clearest indication that it is the Tories who are playing politics with the issue by attempting to score cheap political points in parliament. Is not the opposition against to the proposed laws "in principle", in which case delaying a decision for further debate would be pointless?..What this is really about, believes Mr Blair, is the Tories spotting an opportunity to embarrass, maybe even defeat the government. And that is more important to them than national security. Liberal Democrat leader Charles Kennedy avoided suggesting anyone was playing politics with the issue. He preferred to state that, as with other issues like ID cards, the government's immediate instinct was authoritarian...As is his habit nowadays, the prime minister was less rough with Mr Kennedy than he had been with Mr Howard - he prefers a more exasperated tone suggesting he believes the Lib Dems have, once again, just missed the point. Apart from all that, it was electioneering as usual. The very first question to the prime minister from Derby North's Bob Laxton asked him, in effect, if he would carry on the excellent policy of pouring more resources into schools. Later Birmingham's Sion Simon even went so far as to suggest the Tories were such a shower that we should have the general election now. The prime minister almost blushed. This was not the appropriate place to announce election day, he stammered. But can anyone be in any doubt that that announcement is just days away - an announcement coming in the week beginning 4 April for an election on 5 May is where the big money is in the Commons. And perhaps that simple fact alone means everyone is seen to be playing politics with just about everything at the moment.
