Who, one might legitimately ask of anyone, is truly intent on making politics of the current delicate situation, rather than seeking genuine resolution? The answer, according to many, is clear: no, it's the Prime Minister, who, he claims, is "ramming" through Parliament controversial new legislative proposals and far-reaching reforms without any significant public scrutiny or adequate parliamentary debate.

Yet, for their part, the Tories believe the Prime Minister is demonstrably running scared and cynically attempting to capitalise on public fear on this one, recognising the prospect of a potentially tough and hard-fought electoral contest in the run up to the imminent next general election. And they further believe Blair is using the entire complex issue and ongoing political wrangling to suggest the Tories are simply being obstructionist and uncooperative for purely partisan political gain. Why on earth will the Prime Minister not simply take up the repeated and explicit offer extended by the opposition benches to utilise or amend existing parliamentary procedures and conventions to allow proper debate of the vitally important legislation, ensuring due democratic process?

The Prime Minister, however, presents a starkly different narrative, claiming this is the most egregious and obvious indication that the opposition parties, particularly the Conservative leadership, are merely indulging in opportunistic party politics with this pressing and fundamental issue by deliberately attempting to obstruct, delay, and ultimately derail the government's agenda. He challenges their sincerity, questioning if they are truly not opposed to the laws "in principle", which would surely render any demands for further protracted debate utterly, irrevocably pointless? No, he asserts, it's abundantly clear that this is about, from the vantage point of Mr. Blair and his government, the Tories' opportunity to publicly and humiliatingly embarrass, even defeat the government on a critical and high-profile piece of legislation. For them, it unmistakably represents a crucial, defining battle on the national political stage, a test of will and influence.

Liberal Democrat leader Charles Kennedy, for his part, was typically forthright and quite blunt in suggesting anyone with the ability to critically analyse the current political climate can clearly and unequivocally perceive the underlying truth of the matter. He preferred to unequivocally state, with his customary candour, that indeed, as with other contentious issues like ID cards, mass surveillance, or even curbs on civil liberties, the government's instinct is regrettably always towards the inherently centralising and often authoritarian. As for the Prime Minister's public demeanour, he was observed to be considerably rougher than with Mr Michael Howard, the esteemed leader of the Conservative Party, whom he usually prefers to address with a rather more conciliatory, deferential, and measured tone. He just missed the prevailing public mood and the opposition's strong resolve entirely on this occasion, it would seem. Ultimately and undeniably, all, it is simply calculated and cynical electoral electioneering.

A question to the Prime Minister from Derby North's Labour MP, Bob Laxton, was pointedly and somewhat provocatively asked, about the tangible and potential effect, on the policy of selectively pouring resources into certain key marginal constituencies or strategically important regions, especially with a general election looming. Birmingham's Labour MP Sion Simon even went so as to humorously and rather cheekily suggest that perhaps a cold shower should have been forcefully administered to the Prime Minister himself before he even considered the potentially disastrous idea of calling the election. The Prime Minister, caught off guard, almost blushed. However, it was not a slight or jibe he was prepared to simply absorb or ignore, he replied with a characteristically sharp retort, robustly defending his government's strategies and priorities.

Can anyone truly accurately speculate about a specific polling date these days - an announcement in the very beginning of April for a May 5th general election? The big money is clearly being avidly staked in the Commons on the precise timing of the next ballot and the potential outcomes. And perhaps the most salient and undeniable simple fact is that almost everyone involved in Westminster politics is seen to be overtly and undeniably playing politics with the entire situation at this very contentious and uncertain political moment.

reconstruction:
The Conservative Party today unveiled ambitious plans to blitz what they call 'Labour's bureaucracy', proposing radical reforms. Plans to abolish a total of 162 quangos have been announced as part of a wider drive to show that a future Tory government would dramatically cut back on government red tape and wasteful spending. Numerous other non-departmental public bodies and government units would also be scrapped, the Tories stated. They say these measures would save the taxpayer more than £4.3bn over the course of a parliamentary term. The proposed targets for these significant cuts include all strategic health authorities, various non-ministerial departments, a number of new regulatory bodies, and many university-related quangos.

The aim, they argue, is to create a Tory Britain that is much slimmer in its governmental structures, boasts lower administrative costs, and is significantly more competitive on the global stage. The proposed cuts would affect numerous regional assemblies and various public bodies, such as boards responsible for industrial development, enterprise, and housing. Their powers, the Conservatives contend, would be directly returned to elected local authorities, empowering communities. The Tories specifically highlighted strategic health authorities, claiming they are inefficient and distance decision-making from local people, who they believe should have more direct control over how their local hospitals are run and managed.

A leading Conservative figure stated: "Mr. Blair has completely forgotten the interests of the hardworking majority, and has fundamentally broken the promises made to the British people when he came to power." Far from genuinely improving public services and outcomes, spending billions of taxpayers' money on these ever-growing layers of quangos and agencies has merely led to an explosion of bureaucrats, an increase in stifling regulation and ultimately, ever-higher taxes for ordinary families. The party leader, speaking at a campaign event, argued forcefully that a fundamental change of direction was urgently needed to get a firm grip on the country's public finances and restore accountability.

He continued his attack: "Labour has entirely forgotten the forgotten majority, those diligent people who simply want a fair deal. In the real world, ordinary people are working harder than ever to make ends meet, struggling to support their families. They've seen their hopes and aspirations repeatedly knocked down by government policy. On top of that, they're constantly being hit by ever-increasing taxes. The forgotten majority are paying the steep price of Labour's bureaucratic excess and incompetence."

For their part, the Labour government itself has announced plans to cut 100,000 civil service jobs, arguing these cuts will improve efficiency. But the Chief Secretary to the Treasury, speaking later, strongly attacked the Tory plans as irresponsible and reckless. He stated: "The Conservatives have committed to 'slashing public spending by a staggering £35bn' – a figure that simply does not add up. The required savings for this cannot possibly be found without severely damaging essential front-line public services such as our schools, our hospitals, and crucially, the National Health Service." Meanwhile, the Liberal Democrats have also indicated they would reduce the number of quangos if in power, stating they would ensure any money saved directly reaches frontline public services where it is most needed.

The Information Commissioner, Richard Thomas, says asking Cabinet Office staff to delete e-mails more than three months old and which are not needed for ongoing reference or operational use. Richard Thomas "condemned" the attempts to avoid disclosure of information ahead of new Freedom of Information rules coming into force on 1 January. Government guidance states that e-mails should only be deleted if they have served their administrative purpose and are no longer required for any official record-keeping, Thomas said. The Tories and Liberal Democrats have strongly criticised the timing of the new guidance, fearing it could lead to the destruction of vital government records. Tory leader Michael Howard has written to Prime Minister Tony Blair demanding an urgent explanation of the new rules on e-mail deletion and their implications. On Monday, Lib Dem chairman Alan Beith warned that the deletion of e-mails could potentially conceal key evidence, just like in the high-profile Hutton Inquiry into the death of Dr David Kelly. The timing of the new guidance being issued just before the Act was "too convenient to have been a coincidence", Mr Beith said. But a Cabinet Office spokesman insisted the move was not designed to thwart the incoming Act or to lead to "the destruction of public records". Mr Beith urged the Information Commissioner to look closely at the "e-mail purge" to support the spirit of the Freedom of Information Act. Mr Thomas said: "The new Act on the proper retention of public records will prevent their deliberate and criminal destruction." He said there was clear guidance on document retention and management contained in a Code of Practice issued from the Public Record Office. "As these documents are clearly subject to freedom of information requests, the important thing was the proper retention of all e-mail correspondence", he said. "To retain records has always been a long-standing principle of good governance for government departments and public authorities. It's only when there's absolutely no further operational need for the particular document that it should be lawfully deleted." A deliberate deletion with the full knowledge of the possibility of later public scrutiny is totally unacceptable. The Freedom of Information Act comes into force across England, Wales and Northern Ireland from next January. Similar provisions and legislation are being brought in at the same time in Scotland. It provides the public with a new legal right of access to information held by approximately 100,000 public bodies, including various government departments, agencies, and local authorities. Its implementation is specifically designed to bring much greater transparency to government information and enhance democratic decision-making.

original: New browser wins over net surfers..The proportion of surfers using Microsoft's Internet Explorer (IE) has dropped to below 90%, say web analysts...Net traffic monitor, OneStat.com, has reported that the open-source browser Firefox 1.0, released on 9 November, seems to be drawing users away from IE. While IE's market share has dropped 5% since May to 88.9%, Mozilla browsers - including Firefox - have grown by 5%. Firefox is made by the Mozilla Foundation which was set up by former browser maker Netscape in 1998. Although there have been other preview versions of Firefox, version 1.0 was the first complete official program. "It seems that people are switching from Microsoft's Internet Explorer to Mozilla's new Firefox browser," said Niels Brinkman, co-founder of Amsterdam-based OneStat.com...Mozilla browsers - including Firefox 1.0 - now have 7.4% of the market share, the figures suggest. Mozilla said that more than five million have downloaded the free software since its official release. Supporters of the open-source software in the US managed to raise $250,000 (£133,000) to advertise the release of Firefox 1.0 in The New York Times, and support the Mozilla Foundation. There was a flurry of downloads on its first day of release...The figures echo similar research from net analyst WebSideStory which suggested that IE had 92.9% of users in October compared to 95.5% in June. Microsoft IE has dominated the browser market for some time after taking the crown from Netscape, and its share of users has always stayed at around the 95% mark. Firefox is attractive to many because it is open-source. That means people are free to adapt the software's core code to create other innovative features, like add-ons or extensions to the program. Fewer security holes have also been discovered so far in Firefox than in IE. Paul Randle, Microsoft Windows Client product manager, responded to the figures: "We certainly respect that some customers will choose alternative browsers and that choosing a browser is about more than a handful of features. "Microsoft continues to make significant investments in IE, including Service Pack 2 with advanced security technologies, and continues to encourage a vibrant ecosystem of third party add-ons for Internet Explorer." Firefox wants to capture 10% of the market by the end of 2005. Other browser software, like Opera and Apple's Safari, are also challenging Microsoft's grip on the browser market. Opera is set to release its version 7.60 by the end of the year. OneStat.com compiled the statistical measurements from two million net users in 100 countries.

According to net traffic analysis by OneStat.com, Firefox 1.0, released November 9, seems to be drawing users away from IE. IE's market share has dropped from 93.9% in May to 88.9% in November, a decline of 5 percentage points. Jailed Russian oil tycoon Mikhail Khodorkovsky has transferred his controlling shares in his former oil empire to a business partner, his lawyers have announced. The move follows intense pressure on his Yukos oil group from the Russian authorities.

Mr Khodorkovsky handed his entire 59.5% stake in the company Menatep – which is now controlled by his close ally and former Yukos boss, Leonid Nevzlin – to him. Mr Nevzlin is currently based in Israel, having left Russia to avoid legal proceedings against him.

The handover of the stake followed the controversial and widely criticised forced sale of Yukos's main production unit, Yuganskneftegaz, which was sold off to help settle a giant government tax bill. Yuganskneftegaz was sold in December last year to a state-owned firm for approximately $9.4bn (£5bn), a price many analysts considered to be well below its true market value.

"The sale of Yuganskneftegaz has left little for the business that remains and it's a difficult situation," a statement attributed to Mr Khodorkovsky said, released through his lawyers. It continued: "As for myself, I see my future in activity to build a civil society in Russia." This statement suggests his ongoing commitment to social and political engagement, even from prison.

Mr Nevzlin is now understood to be the largest single shareholder of Menatep. He is living in self-imposed exile, having left Russia amid the escalating legal pressure that crippled Yukos. Yuganskneftegaz, prior to its controversial sale, was a major asset, producing around 1 million barrels of oil per day.

The Russian authorities had claimed colossal government tax arrears against Yukos, amounting to over $27bn. Once widely considered Russia's richest man, with an estimated personal fortune of $15bn, Mr Khodorkovsky is currently on trial for charges of fraud and embezzlement. His high-profile arrest in 2003, which was seen as a major show of force by the Kremlin, sent shockwaves through the Russian business community.

However, critics of the Kremlin's actions argue that the charges against Mr Khodorkovsky are primarily politically motivated. They contend that the prosecution is part of President Vladimir Putin's broader campaign to rein in the influence of the so-called 'super-oligarchs' – powerful businessmen who amassed vast fortunes after the collapse of communism. It also reflects Mr Khodorkovsky's perceived attempts to bankroll political opposition parties and opponents of Mr Putin, a move seen as a direct challenge to the Kremlin's authority and control.

The film follows them as they pull off three heists across Europe. It knocked last week's number one, National Treasure, into second place. The film 'Blade: Trinity', starring Wesley Snipes, was in third place, taking $16.1m (£8.4m). Also in the top five were the animated fable The Polar Express, starring Tom Hanks, and the Christmas comedy Christmas with the Kranks. This marks the first major release since the conclusion of the three films in The Lord of the Rings series. The sequel narrowly beat its 2001 predecessor, Ocean's Eleven, which took $38.1m (£19.8m) on its opening weekend and $184m (£95.8m) in total. A remake of the 1960s film, starring Frank Sinatra and the Rat Pack, Ocean's Eleven was directed by Steven Soderbergh. Soderbergh returns to direct the hit sequel which sees Clooney, Pitt and Julia Roberts return along with Andy Garcia and Elliott Gould. Catherine Zeta-Jones joins the all-star cast. "It's a fun, good film," said Dan Fellman, head of domestic distribution at Warner Bros. US critics were less impressed by the $110m (£57.2m) film, with the Los Angeles Times labelling it 'a disappointment'. A review in the New York Times called the sequel "unabashedly shallow".

reconstruction: The former chief financial officer of a major US telecoms firm WorldCom has finished giving his evidence at the high-profile trial of ex-chief executive Bernard Ebbers. Scott Sullivan admitted to jurors that he had intentionally falsified Wall Street earnings reports. Mr Ebbers, the former CEO, stands on trial for his alleged role in leading WorldCom's collapse in 2002. He pleads not guilty. Mr Sullivan has spent two days on the stand being cross-examined by lawyers representing the former chief executive. Attorney Reid Weingarten attempted to portray Mr Sullivan as a reluctant participant, coerced into the fraud by higher-ups, and on Thursday quizzed him extensively about his controversial decision to inflate WorldCom's reported profit estimates. "At that point in time," Mr Sullivan, referring to the fraudulent accounting entries in 2000, "I knew it was wrong and unethical and knew it went against all company policies and ethical standards, but I would get through in the end and hoped for the best." Mr Sullivan, 42, has pleaded guilty to charges of conspiracy and securities fraud and in Mr Ebbers' ongoing trial, he is appearing as a prosecution witness. Mr Ebbers, 63, vehemently denies he had any personal knowledge or involvement in WorldCom's manipulated finances. The prosecution alleges that the improper accounting practices that led to the company's downfall were between 2000 and 2002 and cost investors billions of dollars. Mr Ebbers could face a maximum sentence of 85 years if convicted of all the charges against he faces. WorldCom's problems are widely understood to have begun with the bursting of the dot-com boom which cut deeply into its internet revenues, impacting the company's profitability and share price. Prosecutors allege Mr Ebbers' direct responsibility for the company's collapse by orchestrating a massive fraud over a period of two years, misleading investors and regulators alike. WorldCom emerged from bankruptcy protection in 2004, and is now known commercially as MCI. On Valentine's Day, 2005, it was formally agreed to be acquired by Verizon Communications in a deal valued at approximately $6.75bn.

original: Wi-fi web reaches farmers in Peru..A network of community computer centres, linked by wireless technology, is providing a helping hand for poor farmers in Peru...The pilot scheme in the Huaral Valley, 80 kilometres north of the capital Lima, aims to offer the 6,000-strong community up-to-date information on agricultural market prices and trends. The Agricultural Information Project for Farmers of the Chancay-Huaral Valley also provides vital links between local organisations in charge of water irrigation, enabling them to coordinate their actions. More than 13,000 rural inhabitants, as well as 18,000 students in the region, will also benefit from the telecoms infrastructure...The 14 telecentres uses only free open source software and affordable computer equipment. The network has been three years in the making and was officially inaugurated in September...The non-government organisation, Cepes (Peruvian Centre for Social Studies) led the $200,000 project, also backed by local institutions, the Education and Agriculture ministries, and European development organisations. "The plan includes training on computers and internet skills for both operators and users of the system," said Carlos Saldarriaga, technical coordinator at Cepes. Farmers are also taking extra lessons on how to apply the new information to make the most of their plots of land. The Board of Irrigation Users which runs the computer centres, aims to make the network self-sustainable within three years, through the cash generated by using the telecentres as internet cafes...One of the key elements of the project is the Agricultural Information System, with its flagship huaral.org website. There, farmers can find the prices for local produce, as well as information on topics ranging from plague prevention to the latest farming techniques. The system also helps the inhabitants of the Chancay-Huaral Valley to organise their vital irrigation systems. "Water is the main element that unites them all. It is a precious element in Peru's coastal areas, because it is so scarce, and therefore it is necessary to have proper irrigation systems to make the most of it," Mr Saldarriaga told the BBC News website. The information network also allows farmers to look beyond their own region, and share experiences with other colleagues from the rest of Peru and even around the world...Cepes says the involvement of the farmers has been key in the project's success. "Throughout the last three years, the people have provided a vital thrust to the project; they feel it belongs to them," said Mr Saldarriaga. The community training sessions, attended by an equal number of men and women, have been the perfect showcase for their enthusiasm. "We have had an excellent response, mainly from young people. But we have also had a great feedback when we trained 40 or 50-year old women, who were seeing a computer for the first time in their lives." So far, the Huaral programme promoters say the experience has been very positive, and are already planning on spreading the model among other farmers' organisations in Peru. "This is a pilot project, and we have been very keen on its cloning potential in other places," underlined Mr Saldarriaga...The Cepes researcher recalls what happened in Cuyo, a 50-family community with no electricity, during the construction of the local telecentre site. There it was necessary to build a mini-hydraulic dam in order to generate 2kW worth of power for the computers, the communications equipment and the cabin lights. "It was already dark when the technicians realised they didn't have any light bulbs to test the generator, so they turned up to the local store to buy light bulbs," recalls Carlos Saldarriaga. "The logical answer was 'we don't sell any', so they had to wait until the next morning to do the testing." Now, with the wireless network, Cuyo as well as the other communities is no longer isolated.

reconstruction:
Wi-fi reaches farmers in remote rural areas, offering the power of digitally linked technology, a helping hand that promises to transform their livelihoods. The project, centred in the Chancay-Huaral Valley, 80 kilometres north of Peru's capital Lima, aims to offer a 6,000-strong agricultural community up-to-date information on agricultural practices, market prices, weather forecasts and trends. This Information Project for Farmers in the Chancay-Huaral Valley is considered vital for improving communication between local residents and those in charge of critical resources, particularly water management, thereby enabling them better to coordinate their efforts and maximize efficiency. More than 13,000 inhabitants, as well as 18,000 in the region, will benefit from this advanced telecoms infrastructure and the opportunities it presents. The 14 telecentres are equipped with only open source equipment. The network has three in full operation since being launched officially last September, with plans for more to come online soon.

The project is spearheaded by the non-governmental organisation, Cepes (Peruvian Centre for Social Studies), which secured the $200,000 funding, a sum backed by local institutions, including the Ministries of Education and Agriculture, and various other community organisations. "Our primary goal is to ensure that computers and internet users become commonplace among the farming communities," said Carlos Zelada, the technical coordinator. Farmers also attend regular training lessons to learn how to apply new information to improve the overall management of their daily operations and productivity of their farms. Irrigation schedules are now often managed or optimized through the computer, and the overall project aims to make the telecentres financially self-sustainable, through the cash generated from various services offered, such as internet access, printing, and phone calls.

One of the core components of the initiative is the Agricultural Information System, with real-time data and expert advice to equip farmers for better decision-making, as well as crucial information topics ranging from pest and crop plague to the latest market prices and optimal planting seasons. The system also enables residents of the Chancay-Huaral Valley to better monitor and manage their vital water supply and distribution systems. "Water is the essential resource that all life depends on. It is a precious commodity in Peru's coastal region, where it is often so scarce, and therefore it is imperative that we have proper irrigation systems to make the absolute most of every drop of it," Mr Zelada told the BBC. The network also allows farmers to connect to distant markets outside their region, and the wider country, and even to global agricultural networks.

The active involvement and engagement of local farmers has been key in the project's remarkable success. "Throughout the initial implementation years, the people have actively provided a project; they feel it completely belongs to them," said Jorge Saldarriaga, the project director. "Training sessions, attended by both men and women, have been the backbone of our community engagement. We have witnessed a truly enthusiastic response, young people are particularly quick to adopt the new technologies. But we have also had a very encouraging feedback when we trained 40 or 50-year-olds, seeing the positive impact it has had on their lives over a short period of time."

So far, the programme organizers say the experience has been very positive, and they are already planning on spreading the model among other farmers' organisations in other parts of the country. "This is a pilot, and we are very keen on cloning this successful model in other places," added Saldarriaga. Cepes encountered significant challenges during what was initially conceived as a straightforward installation for a single 50-household village with no electricity, ultimately requiring the complex construction of the site. There it was imperative to build a mini-dam in order to generate 2kW worth of power for the computers, the wireless network, and lighting for the entire facility. "It was already getting dark when technicians realised they didn't have any light bulbs, so they turned up at a local store to buy light bulbs," Saldarriaga recounted with a chuckle. "The logical answer from the team was 'we can't possibly work in the dark, we need light', until someone ingeniously improvised a solution to get the job done." Now, with the wireless network, providing reliable connectivity to other communities is no longer an insurmountable obstacle.

original: Macy's owner buys rival for $11bn..US retail giant Federated Department Stores is to buy rival May Department Stores for $11bn (£5.7bn)...The deal will bring together famous stores like Macy's, Bloomingdale's and Marshall Field's, creating the largest department store chain in the US. A duo have been convicted in what is believed to be the first major prosecution of its kind in the US against internet spammers. A man, Jeremy Jaynes, in the US has been found guilty of sending millions of unsolicited e-messages to computer users across the country and around the world.

It is the prosecution's first major victory against unsolicited commercial email, often referred to as spam, on the internet. Jurors in Virginia recommended that the principal defendant, Jeremy Jaynes, be sentenced to nine years in prison and that his sister, Jessica DeGroot, be fined $7,500 for their roles in the vast spamming operation.

They were found guilty, with prosecutors arguing that the bulk e-mails were fake and designed to mislead recipients into fraudulent schemes. They will be formally sentenced next year, with the judge having the final say on the penalties.

A third defendant, Richard Rutkowski, had previously pleaded guilty to similar charges. Prosecutors said Jaynes was a "snake oil salesman in a new format", using the internet to hawk his wares, the Associated Press reported.

One of the products promoted was an "Ex-Processor" supposed to allow people to earn $75 from the sale of an "eraser". His sister helped him process these transactions. The operation amassed a fortune of $24m, prosecutors said.

'He's been successful ripping people off for all these years,' AP prosecutor Paul McGuire was quoted as saying.

The court found that a Virginia state law prohibits the sending of more than 100,000 unsolicited emails in a 30-day period. Virginia Attorney General Jerry Kilgore reportedly hailed the verdict.

Prosecutors had asked for 15 years in prison for Jaynes, and for his sister to face similar severe penalties. Jaynes' lawyers called the nine-year sentence recommended "excessive" and believed he was being unfairly targeted.

The defence pointed out that three of the accused lived in North Carolina and were therefore outside the direct jurisdiction of Virginia's anti-spam law. Spam messages are estimated to account for 60% of all emails sent worldwide.

**British triple jumper Ashia Hansen has ruled out a return to competition until 2006, confirming a significant setback in her long recovery from a troublesome knee injury, reports BBC Sport. Hansen, the former world indoor and reigning European champion, has been sidelined from all major events since the World Cup in June 2004.**

**It had been hoped that Hansen would be able to return to action earlier than this, but the process of recovery from her persistent injury has unfortunately been very slow to heal. Her coach, Keith Antoine, gave an update to The Times newspaper, indicating the need for a realistic outlook on her return.**

**"We're now looking at 2006, which is realistic for a triple jumper like Ashia given the nature of the injury," Antoine stated. He suggested that while Hansen might potentially be able to return to competitive sprinting in the near future, there was absolutely no short-term prospect of her competing again in her specialist triple jump event, which inherently places immense stress on the affected joint.**

**Detailing the ongoing challenges, Antoine said: "The wound was making good progress and seemed to be healing well a couple of months back, but that positive trajectory has now regrettably stalled." He further explained the careful plan for her return: "It will undeniably be a very long and demanding process for her to regain full fitness as a top-level athlete. She will initially start by participating in some low-key meetings as a measured introduction to competitive action, rather than jumping straight into major events."**

**Despite the extended layoff, Antoine expressed his unwavering belief that Hansen possesses the determination and skill to make it back to the very highest level of international competition. However, he also acknowledged that it is now highly improbable she will be sufficiently ready in time for the Commonwealth Games, scheduled for Melbourne next March, by which point Hansen will have celebrated her 34th birthday.**

**"It's unquestionably been an incredibly difficult and frustrating time for her, particularly at this crucial stage of her distinguished career, but I can assure you it has certainly not broken her spirit or diminished her desire to achieve success once more," Antoine concluded.**

original: Brown to outline presidency goals..Next year will be "make or break" for development in poorer countries Gordon Brown will say as he sets out UK goals for its EU and G8 presidencies...The chancellor is due to outline a series of key targets the government will be judged on in 2005. They will include doubling aid from donor countries and eliminating debt owed by the poorest nations. Mr Brown also wants other G8 nations to match his target for overseas aid - spending 0.7% of national income...He also wants the richer countries to do more to help the development of vaccines for Aids and malaria. The chancellor is travelling to America next week as part of his persuasion drive over the issue. He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "We need more resources allied to progress on trade and progress on debt relief if we are going to make an impact on the problems of ill health, of illiteracy, of poverty, particularly in Africa but right through the developing countries."..His proposals were effectively a new "Marshall Plan" for the world, including an international finance facility, which would issue bonds in an attempt to double global aid cash to $100bn a year. Agreement in the Doha development talks could also give developing nations the trading ability they needed, he argued. The European Union's Common Agricultural Policy had caused aggravated trade problems, he said, but there was now an agreement to end export subsidies...Mr Brown said much had been achieved on issues such as debt relief in the last seven years. But with 30,000 children were dying unnecessarily every day more was needed, including 100% debt relief multilaterally. "That is why next year is a test," he said. "If after five years of making promises the world is not prepared to honour them, then people will be justified in saying they promised but they did not produce results." The Catholic aid agency Cafod will host Mr Brown's speech on Wednesday...Cafod wants Britain to use its influence to pressure countries like the US to make firm commitments to tackle global poverty. Mr Brown said America too needed to take more action but defended President George Bush for guaranteeing resources to countries which introduced reforms to tackle corruption. Oxfam's Paying the Price report this week said 45 million children will die needlessly before 2015 and aid budgets are half their 1960 levels. The charity's director, Barbara Stocking, said: "2005 offers the chance for an historic breakthrough, but unless world leaders act now the year will end in shameful failure." The report said the G8 of top industrialised nations had agreed in 1970 to spend 0.7% of their incomes on aid...But 34 years later none of the organisations members had reached this target and many had not yet set a timetable. Mr Blair, who has described Africa as a "scar" on the world's conscience, has already said tackling world poverty would be one his G8 priorities along with climate change and the Aids epidemic. But Band Aid founder Bob Geldof in July said he was sick of hearing "guff" about scars on the world. It was pathetic that Britain was the 4th richest country in the world but only the 11th most generous aid donor, he added. Conservative shadow international development secretary Alan Duncan accused Mr Brown of missing his target on providing anti-retroviral drug treatment to three million Africans by 2005. Instead, only 500,000 people would benefit, he said. "There's no point in him demanding praise and adulation for setting a whole new raft of targets when he has so woefully failed to meet the ones he already has," added Mr Duncan.

reconstruction:
Brown calls the coming year "make or break" for development in the world's poorest countries. Gordon Brown is set to say he will commit the UK to achieving ambitious goals during its G8 presidency next year. The chancellor is expected to outline key criteria by which Britain's progress will be judged during 2005. He will say that the success of donor countries will ultimately be judged by the world's poorest nations. Mr Brown wants other G8 nations to match the long-standing UN target for spending on aid - 0.7% of gross national income. He will also urge the richer countries to help fund the development of a new vaccine for malaria. The UK is preparing to host the G8 summit next year as part of a major drive to galvanise international action over the issue. He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "More resources on trade justice and progress on debt relief are going to make a massive and lasting impact on problems of poor health, of illiteracy, of hunger and disease, in Africa."

He is expected to reiterate his proposals for a "Marshall Plan", including a significant increase in international finance, aimed at helping to double global aid flows to $100bn. Agreement in the Doha talks would significantly improve the ability of developing countries to trade their way out of poverty, he emphasised. The European Union's Common Agricultural Policy has long aggravated trade problems, the chancellor said, calling for an urgent agreement to phase out controversial agricultural export subsidies. Mr Brown said much had been achieved in the last few years. But 30,000 children were unnecessarily dying every single day, he added, and still much more was needed, including 100% debt cancellation for the poorest nations through multilaterally agreed channels. "That is why next year will be such a test," he declared. "If after five years promises have not been properly prepared or delivered, then people in developing countries will feel they were promised a great deal but they did not produce results." Aid agency Cafod issued a statement welcoming Mr Brown's speech on international development. It wants Britain and other G8 countries like the US to deliver on their collective commitments to tackle global poverty. A spokesman for Cafod said that while America too needed to take more decisive action, it defended President George W Bush's initiatives for guaranteeing resources which some aid critics feared could be susceptible to corruption. Its latest report, 'Paying the Price of Poverty', said 45 million children across the globe will die needlessly before 2015 because international aid budgets are half 1960 levels. The charity's director, Chris Bain, said: "2005 represents our greatest chance, but leaders must seize this opportunity now if the year is not to end in failure." G8 industrialised nations agreed back in 1970 to spend 0.7% of their gross national income on overseas aid. But 34 years later, many have still not met that pledge and a timetable for doing so is long overdue. Prime Minister Tony Blair, who has taken tackling global poverty as a "mission" on his personal conscience, has already said tackling world poverty would be one of the UK's top G8 priorities, along with climate change and fighting Aids. Concert organiser Live 8 founder Bob Geldof said he was sick of hearing "guff". He said it was pathetic that Britain, the 4th richest country in the world, was but the 11th most generous in terms of aid spending, he added. Conservative shadow development secretary Alan Duncan accused Brown of missing his own government's target for providing life-saving anti-retroviral drugs to Africans by 2005. "As a direct result, 500,000 people would die unnecessarily every year," he said. "There's absolutely no point in standing up and setting a whole new raft of aid targets when you're failing to deliver on the ones he already has," added Mr Duncan.

original: Super Size Me wins writers' award..Super Size Me director Morgan Spurlock has won the Writers Guild of America's award for documentary feature writing...The Oscar-nominated film followed Spurlock as he ate only McDonald's fast food for an entire month. Spurlock was given the award at a special ceremony at the Roosevelt Hotel in Hollywood on Tuesday. Organisers said the rising popularity of documentary films led them to honour a writer for a documentary screenplay for the first time...Producer Brian Grazer presented the award to Spurlock and the film's backers, Roadside Attractions, Samuel Goldwyn Films and Showtime Independent Films. Spurlock set out to discover the effect of living on nothing but McDonald's for a month, upgrading to supersize portions when offered. Arash Sigarchi and Mojtaba Saminejad are in prison. They are just trying to be free to publish their thoughts and opinions. The Iranian authorities have been cracking down on bloggers for some time. "I hope this day will focus people's attention," said Jeremy Hopkins, chairman of the Committee, speaking to BBC News.

The actions people can take are simple and local. The Committee has designated Tuesday as "Free Mojtaba and Arash Day" as part of its ongoing campaign. It is calling on the wider internet community of bloggers to do what it can to help raise awareness of the plight of Mojtaba and Arash, as well as other "citizen journalists". "If you have a blog, then there is nothing to stop you putting something on about Arash," said Mr Hopkins. "That would mean you could, for even just one day alone, light the way for them."

"If you don't have a blog, find one dedicated to the cause - it takes 30 seconds." A search engine like Technorati tracks and confirms that 12,000 new blogs are active online. It is estimated that this year alone, 5.8 million new blogs will come online. It is a fundamental shift, says Jeremy Hopkins, chairman of the Committee to Protect Bloggers, a Washington-based think-tank.

The Committee to Protect Bloggers, started by UK blogger Jeremy Hopkins, counts freedom of speech advocate Ellen Hume as a deputy director. She has since started the International Bloggers' Rights of Passage campaign, a petition to protect bloggers at the UN. Although it is not the only website committed to issues relating to freedom of expression by, for, and about bloggers and their speech, it aims to be a strong voice.

The Committee, now five years old, aims to be a focal point for these issues in the future, and will operate as a non-profit foundation for independent media. "It's just this weird phenomenon. You can see it as one thing or another, depending on your point of view," said Mr Hopkins. "You think of columnists, of pundits, of journalists, some of whom have a private blog which is just a platform. But bloggers do not have a constituency and they do not have the backing of a major media organisation."

It is not only countries like Iran, which have a track record of restricting media, that are of concern to the Committee. Journalists in Western countries also have to face challenges. The recent cases in which traditional journalists have been sacked for what they have said on their own platforms is disturbing and has received much press recently. This, coupled with the rise of often anonymous blogs, has highlighted that the blogsphere currently represents a complex challenge to traditional media ethics and employment.

"It's a messy argument," said Mr Hopkins. "It is such a new way of doing things, there will be legal challenges." He added: "The way to sort these things out is through the courts, but that is part of the whole messy situation."

"If you haven't already got a blog in your company, you will have them soon - and if you aren't a blogger now you had better start looking into having one. The fact is that the blogsphere is doubling in size every five months, and it takes little expertise to create a blog."

"Everyone does it - mums, politicians, radicals, teenagers," he said. Many companies now offer services - often for free - to help people create a blog in minutes and become part of a global community. "This is the real difference," said Mr Hopkins. "What I like about the software is that it gives every single person on Earth the chance to have a voice. You don't even have to own a computer to participate."

reconstruction:
Former Conservative minister Sir Nicholas Scott dies aged 71.
Sir Nicholas Scott, a former Northern Ireland Secretary, has died at the age of 71, his family announced. The former Conservative MP for Kensington and Chelsea passed away after a long illness. He was Northern Ireland Minister from 1981 to 1987 during the premiership of Margaret Thatcher.

In Northern Ireland he dealt with issues relating to education and later security. He famously spoke out against IRA terrorism from the pulpit of a church in 1983.

In his education brief, he oversaw school closures and considered the future of the teacher training colleges. He also merged the New University of Ulster and the Ulster Polytechnic to create the University of Ulster. Sir Nicholas's approach to the Anglo-Irish Agreement was unpopular in some unionist and SDLP circles. Some experienced unionists, some of whom dubbed him "Minister of Misery", were particularly critical.

After leaving Northern Ireland in 1987, he became a UK disability minister. However, he later lost his seat as a Member of Parliament for Kensington to Alan Clark, after being deselected by his constituency party in 1996. His deselection followed a number of embarrassing incidents, including being found slumped in a car by police during the Conservative party conference in Bournemouth and subsequently being taken back to his hotel.

Sir Nicholas claimed he had a strong constitution but reacted badly to a small amount of alcohol, which he said caused the incidents. After his deselection and sacking, he bitterly said that despite the widespread support of John Major and many backbenchers, Eurosceptics in his constituency were "absolutely determined to get me out".

reconstruction:
Few people 'trust politicians' - with nine out of 10 voters saying they do not believe politicians tell the truth, a new poll suggests.
Some 87% of the 1,000 people quizzed by ICM for News 24 said politicians did not deliver on the promises they made. This comes after Foreign Secretary Jack Straw said rebuilding trust would be "the key" issue in the next general election. Both the government and the opposition parties are keen to address a perceived lack of public trust, particularly in the wake of claims over Iraqi weapons of mass destruction.

According to a separate BBC poll, 61% said the Iraq war made no difference to their voting intention or, more widely, to how they will vote on May 5. The poll also looked at where the public tend to lay the blame for this lack of trust. Some 87% said politicians do not keep their promises before an election, and 92% said they do not tell the public "straight". Interestingly, three-quarters (73%) said they considered themselves to be dishonest too.

Mr Straw told voters in Blackburn on Thursday that they would have to look very carefully at the parties and decide which party "best deserves" their "trust". He declared that trust would be "the key choice at the next election." He acknowledged that the Labour government, he suggested, could indeed persuade people to "re-engage their trust with us" if they could successfully overcome attempts to breed cynicism in politics. Mobile phones are celebrating their 20th anniversary this weekend, reflecting on two decades of widespread use. Britain's first official mobile phone call was made on 1 January 1985 by veteran comedian Ernie Wise. In the 20 years since, mobile phones have become an indispensable part of daily life, with almost 90% of Britons now owning a handset. Indeed, mobiles are so popular that for many, their handset is their only phone, and landlines are rarely used anymore. While the first ever call over a truly portable phone was made in 1973 in New York, it took a further 10 years for the first commercial network to be properly launched. Britain was among the first nations in the world to establish mobile networks in 1985. The historic call was placed from St Katherine's dock to Vodafone's headquarters in Newbury, with Ernie Wise making the call from a local curry house. For nine initial days of 1985, Vodafone was the sole operator with a network in the UK. Then, on 10 January, Cellnet (now O2) launched its competing service.

John Caudwell, a pioneer in the industry, said that when the first devices were launched, they were the equivalent of a staggering £2,000, and had a battery life of less than 20 minutes. "They were seen as hugely aspirational in the mid-80s," he recalled. "They became a yuppy must-have business accessory." There was also the fact that the initial analogue technology used was cumbersome and prohibitively expensive, which made it difficult for mobile phones to truly catch on with the wider public. Indeed, it took years to sign up the first million customers, yet only 18 months for them to get the second million.

"It's easy to forget that in 1983 we put a bid document forecasting that the market would only be one million," he noted. "Yet Cellnet was forecasting half that figure." Now, Vodafone alone has 14 million customers in the UK, highlighting the dramatic growth of the sector.

Vodafone and Cellnet were the dominant mobile phone operators in the UK until 1993, when One2One (now T-Mobile) was launched. Orange followed with its UK network in 1994. Both newcomers notably operated digital networks from the outset, a standard which now all operators universally use. The spectrum previously used by the older analogue phones has since largely been re-allocated to accommodate newer technologies. The technology called Global System for Mobile communications (GSM), for example, is now the most widespread mobile phone technology on the planet, and more than 1.2 billion people make calls on it globally. The advent of digital technology helped to introduce other innovative features, such as text messaging and further data services, which have made mobiles so ubiquitous and essential to modern life.

reconstruction:
Liberian economy is set to grow significantly, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has projected. The Liberian economy started to show signs of recovery in 2004, but "sustained and deep reform efforts" are crucial to ensure long-term economic stability and prosperity, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said in its latest review. An assessment made in its report, published on October 10, specifically talks about the country's economic outlook.

The IMF, according to official data provided by the Liberian government, the nation's GDP rose by 2% in 2004, a significant turnaround from a 31% contraction recorded in 2003. This growth signifies a crucial step in recovering from a devastating 14-year war that came to an official end in late 2003. The current Transitional National Government of Liberia will remain in office until January 11, when the nation will hold its first democratic presidential and parliamentary ballots since the end of the conflict.

Liberia's economic performance started to grow last year largely attributed to a "recovery in key sectors like agricultural production, manufacturing and ongoing local post-conflict reconstruction" efforts. Despite these positive indicators, the IMF remains cautious about what it sees as a persistent lack of transparency in certain government actions. In particular, it pointed to the continuing mystery surrounding the status of diamond and timber stockpiles and the alleged disappearance of related logging and concession permits. These matters are being actively investigated by the Liberian authorities and the IMF urges that their findings be made fully public.

The IMF said it was actively working with the World Bank, and other international partners, to ensure that the country's nationally managed finances are put on a sound basis and that the country's large external debt can be addressed in a sustainable manner. "The IMF stands ready to provide further technical assistance and policy advice to the government in all these critical areas," the report said. "With the upcoming crucial elections and the subsequent inauguration of a new democratically elected government, there will be significant new challenges, particularly concerning the future fiscal management of the state. The IMF expresses its unwavering support for Liberia's ongoing transition."

In Europe, cameras on mobiles can take 1.3 megapixel images. But in Japan and Asia Pacific, where camera phone technology is much more advanced, mobiles have already been released which can take 3.2 megapixel images. Japan still dominates mobile phone technology, and the uptake there is huge. By 2008, according to Gartner, 95% of all mobiles sold there will have cameras on them...Camera phones had some teething problems when they were first launched as people struggled with poor quality images and uses for them, as well as the complexity and expense of sending them via MMS (Multimedia Messaging Services). This has changed in the last 18 months. Handset makers have concentrated on trying to make phones easier to use. Realising that people like to use their camera phones in different ways, they have introduced more design features, like rotating screens and viewfinders, removable memory cards and easier controls to send picture messages...Mobile companies have introduced more ways for people to share photos with other people. These have included giving people easier ways to publish them on websites, or mobile blogs - moblogs. But the report suggests that until image quality increases more, people will not be interested in printing out pictures at kiosks. Image sensor technology inside cameras phones is improving. The Gartner report suggests that by mid-2005, it is likely that the image resolution of most camera phones will be more than two megapixels. Consumer digital cameras images range from two to four megapixels in quality, and up to six megapixels on a high-end camera. But a lot of work is being done to make camera phones more like digital cameras. Some handsets already feature limited zoom capability, and manufacturers are looking into technological improvements that will let people take more photos in poorly-lit conditions, like nightclubs. reconstruction:
The Conservative Party has today unveiled comprehensive plans to introduce significantly tougher health checks on all immigrants entering the United Kingdom, should they win the upcoming General Election. The detailed proposals, outlined in a new policy document, focus specifically on individuals coming to live in Britain from countries outside the European Union. Under the new regime, any applicant who plans to stay for a period of six months or more, and originates from a country identified as having high rates of infectious diseases, particularly tuberculosis (TB), would be required to undergo a compulsory chest X-ray and potentially further medical screening if deemed appropriate by health professionals.

Furthermore, the proposals stipulate that all people from outside the European Union who wish to secure a visa to work, study, or permanently settle in the UK will be compelled to undergo a full and thorough medical examination. This examination would explicitly test for serious communicable diseases, including Tuberculosis, various forms of Hepatitis, and HIV. The policy document clearly states that a positive test result for an active infectious disease like TB could lead to the visa application being automatically turned down. Other, less severe, health conditions would be carefully assessed and dealt with on a case-by-case basis by specialist medical practitioners, taking into account individual circumstances and potential risks.

Applicants would be mandated to demonstrably prove they possess good health and that their presence would pose no significant danger to public health within the UK. Moreover, they would need to show they would not impose an unreasonable or unsustainable burden on the National Health Service (NHS). The party's plans also suggest that, where deemed appropriate, individuals would be screened in relation to the specific work or study activities they intend to undertake in Britain, particularly if these roles involve vulnerable populations. For instance, people seeking entry to Britain for longer than six months would face more rigorous medical assessment if they intended to work in sensitive sectors such as health care, childcare, or education. Children, specifically those under 16, wanting to settle permanently in Britain would also be required to have a chest X-ray to screen for TB, and would undergo tests for hepatitis and HIV as part of a comprehensive health check.

The Conservative document indicates that asylum seekers fleeing persecution or conflict would not be automatically denied entry to Britain solely on the grounds of poor health. However, rigorous health checks would still be conducted upon their arrival to ensure that any conditions are identified and that they receive appropriate treatment, while also mitigating any potential public health risks to the wider community. The party claims that recent government figures reveal the number of TB cases has alarmingly increased by 25% across the UK over the last 10 years, and that nearly three-quarters of all individuals diagnosed with the disease in Britain during this period were born overseas. They also argue forcefully that there is an urgent need for stricter controls and more robust screening over who comes into the country, specifically to prevent individuals from posing a health risk to the existing population. The Conservatives assert that these proposed measures will not only protect the health of the public but also help to alleviate the increasing pressure on the NHS.

Under the new proposals, a significant change would see applicants prevented from applying for a visa while already physically present in the country. Instead, all applications for entry visas would need to be made from outside the UK. Asylum seekers, however, would be screened for TB and other conditions upon their arrival in the UK, once their asylum status is in the process of being established. The current Home Office Minister, Des Browne, highlighted existing measures, stating that the UK already routinely checks people for TB when they come into the UK for more than six months or a year. He pointed out that medical professionals currently carry out approximately 175,000 such checks annually, with about 10,000 specific screenings conducted at Gatwick Airport alone. From these existing tests, approximately 100 cases of active TB were identified and addressed last year.

However, the Tories are advocating for a much broader and more comprehensive application of these types of health checks, extending them to all categories of immigrants. The Conservative Party has extensively studied and drawn inspiration from the established health screening procedures for immigrants in other developed nations, including Australia, Canada, and the United States. A party spokesperson noted that their proposals are considered "quite similar" to the robust health screening system currently in place in New Zealand.

Meanwhile, the Labour Party has sharply criticised the Conservative policy, characterising it as a cynical "attempt to derail Labour's own three-year plan" for managing immigration and public health effectively, a plan which was itself publicly released last year. Labour's existing policy advocates for TB screening that specifically focuses on applicants originating from high-risk countries *before* any visas are granted. Under Labour's framework, individuals diagnosed with an active form of the disease would be required to complete a full course of treatment in their home country before being permitted to travel to the UK. Adding to the criticism, the Liberal Democrats have accused the Tories of using immigration as a divisive 'wedge issue', stating emphatically that they were "of pandering to prejudice rather than challenging it directly through reasoned policy."

reconstruction:
Today, Yahoo! celebrates its 10th anniversary. Yahoo, one of the net's pioneering giants, is celebrating its 10th this week, marking a decade of influence on the web. The web has undergone a remarkable change since the company was founded by David Filo and Jerry Yang in a university trailer. These two Stanford graduate students wanted a simple system of keeping track of their ever-growing list of favourite websites. From this simple need, they devised hundreds of categories and links, and quickly saw business in their idea to create a comprehensive directory.

Originally dubbed "Jerry's Guide to the World Wide Web," the fledgling company adopted the moniker "Yahoo!" because its founders defined the term as rude, unsophisticated, and boorish, reflecting their anti-establishment attitude. This was also an informal reference to the "Yahoos" in 18th Century Jonathan Swift's classic, 'Gulliver's Travels.' 'We were very much "not civilised" at the time,' commented Mr Yang ahead of the anniversary, officially on 2 March.

They did not, however, lack astute business brains, and by April 1995 prestigious venture capitalists Sequoia, then key investors in Apple Computer, stepped forward to fund Yahoo to the $2m (£1.04m) valuation. Further rounds of funding followed swiftly in the autumn, and the company floated successfully in 1996 with just over 50 employees, marking a significant milestone.

Now, the 7,600 workers globally continue to embrace its iconic dot-com culture of "work hard, play hard" still. In spite of just about surviving the tumultuous dot-com crash, it now faces intense rivalry from formidable competitors such as Google, MSN and AOL.

Mr Yang, who remains the firm's visionary co-founder and 'Chief Yahoo!', is proud of what the company has achieved and become. "'In essence, the internet now provides the consumers just about everything - it's a truly rich and wonderful experience,' he said. 'After all, we build products to serve our users' aspirations and needs, but it's even more - it's the profound opportunity of enabling people to discover, get more information, connect with communities, and ultimately, enrich their lives.'"

original: Brazil approves bankruptcy reform..A major reform of Brazil's bankruptcy laws has been approved by the country's Congress, in a move which it is hoped will cut the cost of borrowing...The bill, proposed in 1993, has finally been approved by the leadership of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. The old law, dating from 1945, gave priority first to workers, second to tax revenue and finally to creditors. The new legislation changes this, giving priority to creditors and limiting payments to workers. The new regulations will limit payments to workers to 150 times the minimum monthly salary, which is currently $94. The law also makes it more difficult for a company to declare bankruptcy. However, when a firm is declared bankrupt it will gain protection from creditors for 180 days while a recovery plan is worked out...The proposals were opposed in the past by leftist parties, including Mr Lula's Worker Party. They considered that they undermined workers' rights. But President Lula became a defender of the reforms, arguing that the country's bank lending margins were among the highest in the world and were damaging the economy. According to Andreas Adriano of Latin Trade Magazine, the new bankruptcy law will help in reducing the spread - difference between the interest rates of the banks and federal bonds. reconstruction:
Brazil approves bankruptcy reform. A major reform of Brazil's bankruptcy laws has been approved by the country's Congress, in a move hoped to cut the cost of borrowing. The reform, proposed back in 1993, has been signed into law by President Luiz Inacio da Silva.

Under the previous law, dating from 1945, priority was given to workers, second to tax authorities, then to creditors. Under the new legislation, this priority is reversed; priority is now given to creditors and limiting the compensation for workers. The new law will cap payouts at 150 times the national minimum wage, currently valued at around $94.

The aim is to make it more attractive to file for company bankruptcy. However, when a firm is declared bankrupt, workers will gain from payments covering up to 180 days of wages worked. The changes were opposed by leftist parties, including some within President Lula's own Workers' Party. They considered that it undermined workers' protections.

But President Lula defended a compromise version of the bill, arguing that the country's previous bankruptcy law was one of the worst in the world and its rigidity was damaging the economy. According to Andreas Adriano of Standard & Poor's, in reducing the spread – the difference between the rates of corporate debt and federal bonds – the new law is a positive step. However, Mr Adriano also called for lower interest rates from the Central Bank to complement its policy, focusing not only on inflation but also on growth.

Scotland head coach Gregor Williams says he has never quit anything in his life, passionately reiterating his commitment to the national rugby team despite growing pressure. In a defiant public statement, he insisted he will not quit as coach following what many are calling his slump to a new low with the recent crushing defeat to Italy at Murrayfield. The 31-29 loss marked a significant setback for the Scots, further exacerbating the team's poor run of form in the ongoing Six Nations Championship. The atmosphere around the squad has been tense, with fans and pundits alike questioning the team's direction and Williams's leadership. Should their fortunes not turn around, the result would now leave the Scots as favourites to win the dreaded Wooden Spoon this year, a stark and unwelcome prospect for a nation that had harboured hopes of a much stronger campaign.

"I never quit in life, maybe painting," Williams told BBC Sport in an exclusive interview conducted after a contentious post-match press conference. He appeared visibly emotional but steadfast in his resolve. "My commitment to this team, to Scottish rugby, is absolute and unwavering," he added, directly addressing the swirling speculation about his tenure. "I have given my whole time here 100%," Williams asserted, defending his performance and the effort he has put into the role. "Every day, every training session, every match, I have given everything I have. There is no question of a lack of effort or dedication from myself or my staff."

Despite his unwavering commitment, Williams has yet to experience an overall Six Nations Championship victory after four frustrating attempts at the helm of the Scottish squad. Indeed, the statistics paint a grim picture: the team have lost 12 of their 14 matches under his leadership, a record that has understandably fuelled calls for change among sections of the supporter base. However, Williams vehemently rejected some sources drawing parallels between his current predicament and that of former Scotland football manager Berti Vogts, who faced severe criticism during his tenure for a poor run of results and a perceived lack of connection with the Scottish sporting public. Williams bristled at the comparison, seeing it as unfair and irrelevant to his situation.

"How can a German football manager and I, a rugby coach, possibly have in common?" Williams rhetorically asked, his voice betraying a hint of indignation. He argued that the sports, the contexts, and the individual circumstances were vastly different. "That is a flawed analogy. It is so absurd it borders on being insulting," he continued, visibly annoyed by the media narrative. "I am focused on rugby, on this team, and on building for the future, not on historical comparisons from another sport."

"I am revelling in this kind of pressure," Williams declared, adopting a more assertive tone. "This is what elite sport is all about. It's challenging, it's intense, but it's also where you learn the most about yourself and your team." He suggested that this difficult period was a proving ground. He indicated that he was now in his second major coaching role, implying prior experience with high-stakes environments and the demands of national team management, perhaps even a "second bite at the cherry" type scenario.

"Success is not beyond the realms of possibility for this team, even now," Williams asserted, attempting to inject a dose of optimism into the conversation. "We have shown glimpses of what we are capable of, and we need to build on that." "There's nothing much between the top teams and ourselves in terms of raw talent, so we must go into the next games against them with belief and conviction," he added, referencing the competitive nature of the Six Nations. "Every match is an opportunity to prove ourselves and turn our season around."

"I really enjoy seeing how the players cope with such a coach," Williams mused, reflecting on the psychological aspect of leadership during adversity. "It tests their character, their resilience, and their willingness to fight." "It helps the team grow and helps me massively as a coach to understand what works and what doesn't under intense scrutiny," he explained. "These difficult moments, though painful, are invaluable for development."

"We won one game and now have a disheartening string of defeats, but we were confident in our performances during those first games of the campaign and we are confident we can recapture that initial promise and turn our fortunes around too," Williams concluded, looking ahead with a glimmer of hope despite the current gloom surrounding the squad. His determination remains unshaken, even as the pressure mounts.

original: Boris opposes mayor apology..Ken Livingstone should "stick to his guns" and not apologise for his "Nazi" comment to a Jewish reporter, Tory MP Boris Johnson has insisted...Mr Johnson also claimed Tony Blair's intervention in the row was "an attempt to reassure Jewish voters". London mayor Mr Livingstone says he is "standing by" his remarks which likened an Evening Standard journalist to a "concentration camp guard". But the prime minister says it is time for Mr Livingstone to say sorry...Labour's Mr Livingstone has said his comments may have been offensive but were not racist, and said earlier this week he would not apologise even if Mr Blair asked. Later the prime minister said: "A lot of us in politics get angry with journalists from time to time, but in the circumstances, and to the journalist because he was a Jewish journalist, yes, he should apologise."..However, Mr Johnson, who was forced to apologise last year for an article in the magazine he edits about Liverpudlians grieving over the death of British hostage Ken Bigley, said Mr Blair "should butt out of" the row. "I don't see why the prime minister has to get involved in this," The Spectator editor told BBC Radio 4's Today programme. "It's a dispute between Ken Livingstone and a reporter on the Evening Standard." Mr Johnson, MP for Henley-on-Thames, Oxfordshire, said he suspected Labour was now trying to reassure Jewish voters "because of this curious way in which Labour seems to be trying to curry favour with disillusioned Muslim voters who may be disillusioned about the war"..."Ken doesn't think he's got anything to say sorry for and if that's really his feeling, then I think that he should stick to his guns," he said. Mr Johnson apologised last October for perpetuating an "outdated stereotype" of Liverpool in the leader article on the death of Mr Bigley. The article in the magazine suggested grieving Liverpudlians were wallowing in their victim status. It also attributed blame to drunken Liverpool football fans for the 1989 Hillsborough disaster in which 96 died. Mr Johnson told Today: "It's perfectly true that I got into the grovelling game myself and when I apologised there were some things that I felt I ought to say sorry for ... there were also other things I didn't think I should apologise for," he said. "But here's old Ken - he's been crass, he's been insensitive and thuggish and brutal in his language - but I don't think actually if you read what he said, although it was extraordinary and rude, I don't think he was actually anti-Semitic."

Hitachi's 1.3m (4.2ft) tall Emiew was presented as the 'fastest-moving robot yet'. Its two prototypes, named Pal and Chum, eloquently introduced themselves at a press conference held in Tokyo. This significant unveiling comes ahead of the World Exposition 2005 in Aichi, Japan, where many companies will showcase their latest robots to demonstrate significant developments in electronics and robotics technology.

Last year, Yamaha also notably stepped into the rapidly developing robotics field and unveiled its impressive trumpet-playing humanoid robot.

Mobile takes off in India, where the country is witnessing rapidly growing activities among tech-savvy consumers, particularly in the urban centres. The mobile gaming market generated an estimated $26m (£13.8m) by the end of 2004, according to leading industry analysts In-Stat/MDR. In October, mobile users grew by 1.4 million to reach a total of 44.9 million, overtaking fixed-line connections for the first time, said the Telecom Authority of India. Analysts suggest that youth is driving the market. With a large proportion of under-25s, many in cities and towns are fast adopting mobiles as a must-have technology and lifestyle accessory. India's mobile gaming revenue will bring in $336m (£178m) by 2009, and the overall market is projected to explode in the next few years.

Around 220 million will be mobile phones by 2009, generating significant revenue for value-added services other than just voice calls. Revenues collected by operators in India have, as a direct result of the rapid rise in subscribers, grown exponentially. "The phenomenal growth of this market has attracted publishers, developers, designers, musicians, and ultimately is stimulating the entire content creation ecosystem," said Clint Chau, director of In-Stat/MDR's broadband access service. "Mobile gaming is not just fun; it represents one element of a rich, diverse digital content offering and a substantial market opportunity for both local and international players."

Currently, India is witnessing a surge in big games and four mobile platforms that specifically cater to their diverse user base, said Mr. Chau. According to In-Stat/MDR, the country is to take up the most important position in the mobile market within the broader Asia/Pacific region of the world. In 2003, there were only 10 million mobile subscribers in India. Many rural areas in the vast country still remain unconnected to mobile networks. Despite this, penetration is still far lower than 20% of India's total population having access to a mobile phone, compared to well over 50% in many developed countries. The trend for the uptake of mobiles is rapidly developing, which allows a growing number of people to opt to leapfrog slower and often less reliable, more state-run fixed-line services altogether.
