'Keep your powder dry,' he says with characteristic intensity. 'When you talk about the pursuit of glory, keeping your gunpowder dry is an absolutely essential part of the preparation. That's the unwavering mantra we preach.' Ireland coach Eddie O'Sullivan appears to have quite successfully run his meticulously planned player conditioning programme this season. After the gruelling and somewhat disappointing 2003 World Cup campaign, the entire squad has been afforded a comprehensive and timely conditioning period much earlier in the year. That intensive programme concluded with a demanding 10-week period leading directly into this pivotal Six Nations championship campaign. This proactive and somewhat unconventional approach seems to have demonstrably annoyed some quarters, and in particular segments of the Welsh media and coaching staff, who clearly perceive it as a subtle act of perceived disrespect towards the established, traditional rhythm and calendar of the game. 'We will say nothing of the constant suggestions about ''poaching'' of players that faced them on Sunday, or the somewhat thinly veiled criticisms made about their preparation and dedication,' he states firmly, knowing full well his subject matter, particularly when you talk about the revered national side and the immense pride and passion that goes with representing your country at the very highest level. The Irish Rugby Football Union (IRFU) has robustly thrown their considerable weight behind this bold strategy, and must in the main, ensure there is a fully functioning and equitable system of centrally-contracted players, which demonstrably helps manage their workload, fitness, and overall availability for both club and international duties.

Shane Gleeson returning from a period on the sidelines nursing broken bones, is a welcome sight in Eddie O'Sullivan's squad, which is now poised and ready to launch this season's formidable challenge. You won't hear O'Sullivan openly gloat about the meticulous handling and preparation of his players. He's simply not that sort of individual. However, when you consider how overworked and injury-hit other squads, notably France, have seen their key players suffering, then he has every right to quietly pat himself on the back. But despite the evident physical freshness, there is still the crucial question of stepping up mentally and transferring that palpable freshness into concrete results when the referee finally blows the whistle for the start of a demanding international game. Ireland are widely considered favourites for the Grand Slam, and indeed they harbour strong ambitions to hog all the success and major accolades this season. It would be a monumental achievement, marking their first Grand Slam since they completed a historic sweep way back in 1948. With the iconic fixtures against England and France both scheduled to take place at Lansdowne Road for the very last time before the old darling of Irish rugby is pulled down and rebuilt, everything looks perfectly placed for a truly memorable campaign. But the days of frightened men in green jerseys are emphatically over for the modern Irishman. Under the shrewd leadership and astute coaching of Eddie O'Sullivan, they have fundamentally changed their approach and their mindset. Just take the celebrated Triple Crown-winning side of 1985 under the late Mick Doyle. They were expected to raise the ante for a further Grand Slam, the first in their history. What happened then in 1986? They were whitewashed. You simply can't assume anything in this sport; they still have to prove it on the pitch against formidable opposition. This is a different kind of beast, a different era entirely. O'Sullivan's current side are very capable of proving that crucial point. For the first time in what feels like 19 long years, if they can truly live up to their burgeoning success and take a definitive step up the ladder of international rugby. His unwavering faith in his players, they have repaid in spades with committed performances. And there is undoubtedly much more potential there to come. He keeps his dogs of war close to his squad, ready for action, and he brings to this current team a truly different box of tricks, a new-found verve to succeed at the highest level. They absolutely can succeed, but for now, let's just whisper it.

It is his second number one in a row. The show used Presley photos last week. Presley will feature in the charts for several more months as all 18 of his original UK chart-toppers are reissued...A Top of the Pops spokesperson said: "It's a very special number one as it's the UK's 1,000th. Kombou is likely to appear on the show again next week as the next Presley re-release, A Fool Such As I, is on course to give him his third number one in three weeks. Kombou plays Vince Everett in Jailhouse Rock - the same role Presley played in the 1957 film of the same name.

original: Lifestyle 'governs mobile choice'..Faster, better or funkier hardware alone is not going to help phone firms sell more handsets, research suggests...Instead, phone firms keen to get more out of their customers should not just be pushing the technology for its own sake. Consumers are far more interested in how handsets fit in with their lifestyle than they are in screen size, onboard memory or the chip inside, shows an in-depth study by telecommunications company Ericsson. "Historically in the industry there has been too much focus on using technology," said Dr Michael Bjorn, senior advisor on mobile media at Ericsson's consumer and enterprise lab. "We have to stop saying that these technologies will change their lives," he said. "We should try to speak to consumers in their own language and help them see how it fits in with what they are doing," he told the BBC News website...For the study, Ericsson interviewed 14,000 mobile phone owners on the ways they use their phone. "People's habits remain the same," said Dr Bjorn. "They just move the activity into the mobile phone as it's a much more convenient way to do it."..One good example of this was diary-writing among younger people, he said. While diaries have always been popular, a mobile phone -- especially one equipped with a camera -- helps them keep it in a different form. Youngsters' use of text messages also reflects their desire to chat and keep in contact with friends and again just lets them do it in a slightly changed way. Dr Bjorn said that although consumers do what they always did but use a phone to do it, the sheer variety of what the new handset technologies make possible does gradually drive new habits and lifestyles. Ericsson's research has shown that consumers divide into different "tribes" that use phones in different ways. Dr Bjorn said groups dubbed "pioneers" and "materialists" were most interested in trying new things and were behind the start of many trends in phone use. "For instance," he said, "older people are using SMS much more than they did five years ago." This was because younger users, often the children of ageing mobile owners, encouraged older people to try it so they could keep in touch...Another factor governing the speed of change in mobile phone use was the simple speed with which new devices are bought by pioneers and materialists. Only when about 25% of people have handsets with new innovations on them, such as cameras, can consumers stop worrying that if they send a picture message the person at the other end will be able to see it...Once this significant number of users is passed, use of new innovations tends to take off. Dr Bjorn said that early reports of camera phone usage in Japan seemed to imply that the innovation was going to be a flop. However, he said, now 45% of the Japanese people Ericsson questioned use their camera phone at least once a month. In 2003 the figure was 29%. Similarly, across Europe the numbers of people taking snaps with cameras is starting to rise. In 2003 only 4% of the people in the UK took a phonecam snap at least once a month. Now the figure is 14%. Similar rises have been seen in many other European nations. Dr Bjorn said that people also used their camera phones in very different ways to film and even digital cameras. "Usage patterns for digital cameras are almost exactly replacing usage patterns for analogue cameras," he said. Digital cameras tend to be used on significant events such as weddings, holidays and birthdays. By contrast, he said, camera phones were being used much more to capture a moment and were being woven into everyday life.

These are exciting times for Arsenal."..The 55-year-old Frenchman told Arsenal's website www.arsenal.com: "My intention has always been clear. I love this club and am very happy here." Wenger has won the title and the FA Cup three times each during his reign. Chairman Peter Hill-Wood said: "We are absolutely delighted that Arsene has signed an extension to his contract. "We currently have a fantastic crop of young players coming through the ranks together with a number of world-class players who are playing a wonderful brand of football." Meanwhile, Arsenal director Danny Fiszman is looking for Wenger to stay beyond 2008. "When we come towards the end of his contract we will both review the situation. I'm sure we will want him to stay on and I hope he will too," said Fiszman.

But what you will not find is much Spanish-language hip-hop...Hip-hop and rap are actually quite popular in the Spanish-speaking world, but local artists are having trouble marketing their work abroad. But now, a US company is bringing rap and hip-hop en espanol to computer users everywhere. Los Caballeros de Plan G are one of Mexico's hottest hip-hop acts. They have a devoted fan base in their native Monterrey. But most Mexican hip-hop fans, not to mention fans in most of the Spanish-speaking world, rarely get a chance to hear the group's tracks on the radio..."You can't really just go on the radio and listen to hip-hop in Spanish... it's just not accessible," says Manuel Millan, a native of San Diego, California. "It's really hard for the Spanish hip-hop scene to get into mainstream radio. You usually have a very commercialised sound and the groups are not really known around the country or around the world." Millan and two friends set out to change that - they wanted to make groups like Los Caballeros de Plan G accessible to fans globally...Mainstream radio stations were not going to play this kind of music, and starting their own broadcast station was economically impossible. So, Millan and his friends launched a website called latinohiphopradio.com. The name says it all: it is web-based radio, devoted to the hottest Spanish language rap and hip-hop tracks. The site, which is in both in English and Spanish, is meant to be easy to navigate. All the user has to do is download a media player. There are no DJs. It is just music streamed over the net for free. Suddenly, with the help of the website, Los Caballeros de Plan G are producing "export quality" rap...The web might be just the right medium for Spanish language hip-hop right now. The genre is in what Millan calls its "infant stage". But the production values are improving, and artists such as Argentina's Mustafa Yoda are pushing to make it better and better. Mustafa Yoda is currently one of the hottest tracks on latinohiphopradio.com. "He's considered the Eminem of Argentina, and the Latin American hip-hop scene," Millan says. "He really hasn't had that much exposure as far as anywhere in the world, but he's definitely the one to look out for as far as becoming the next big thing in the Spanish-speaking world." Currently, the Chilean group Makisa is also in latinohiphopradio.com's top 10, as is Cuban artist Papo Record. "Every country's got it's own cultural differences and they try to put those into their own songs," Millan says. Latinohiphopradio.com has been up and running for a couple of months now. The site has listeners from across the Spanish speaking world. Right now, Mexico leads the way, accounting for about 50% of listeners. But web surfers in Spain are logging in as well - about 25% of the web station's traffic comes from there. That is not surprising as many consider Spain to be the leader in Spanish-language rap and hip-hop. Millan says that Spain is actually just behind the United States and France in terms of overall rap and hip-hop production. That might be changing, though, as more and more Latin American artists are finding audiences...But one Spaniard is still firmly in latinohiphopradio.com's top 10. His name is Tote King and Manuel Millan says that he is the hip-hop leader in Spain. On his track Uno Contra Veinte Emcees, or One Against 20 Emcees, Tote King shows he is well aware of that fact. "It's basically him bragging that he's one of the best emcees in Spain right now," Millan says. "And it's pretty much true. He has the tightest productions, and his rap flow is impeccable, it's amazing." Latinohiphopradio.com is hoping to expand in the coming year. Millan says they want to include more music and more news from the world of Spanish language hip-hop and rap...Clark Boyd is technology correspondent for The World, a BBC World Service and WGBH-Boston co-production.

original: Yukos sues four firms for $20bn..Russian oil firm Yukos has sued four companies for their role in last year's forced state auction of its key oil production unit Yuganskneftegas...Yukos is claiming more than $20bn (£11bn) in damages after Yugansk was sold in December to settle back taxes. The four companies named in the law suit are gas giant Gazprom, its unit Gazpromneft, investment company Baikal, and state oil firm Rosneft. Yukos submitted the suit in Houston, where it filed for bankruptcy. As well as suing for damages, Yukos has asked the US court to send its tax dispute with the Russian government to an international arbitrator. It also has submitted a reorganisation plan as part of its Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing...The clash between Yukos and the Kremlin came to a head last year when Yukos was hit with a bill of more than $27bn in back taxes and unpaid fines. To settle the bill, Russia forced Yukos to sell off Yuganskneftegas...Yukos called the sale illegal and has turned to courts in the US in an effort to regain control of the oil production business. It also has vowed to use all legal means at its disposal to go after any firm that tries to buy or take control of its assets. Earlier this month it sued the Russian government for $28.3bn. Analysts have questioned whether a US court has any jurisdiction over Russian companies, while Moscow officials have dismissed Yukos' legal wrangling as meaningless. In Houston, bankruptcy Judge Letitia Clark will start a two-day hearing on 16 February to hear arguments on whether a US court is the proper forum for the case...The threat of legal action from Yukos and its bankruptcy filing in Houston did have an effect on last year's auction, however. Concerned that it would be caught up in a court battle, Gazprom and Gazpromneft withdrew from the auction, and Yuganskneftegas was sold to little-known investment firm Baikal Finance Group. A few days later, Baikal gave control of the company to state-run oil group Rosneft for $9.3bn. Rosneft, meanwhile, has agreed to merge with Gazprom, bringing a large chunk of Russia's very profitable oil business back under state control. Yukos claims that the rights of its shareholders have been ignored and that is has been punished for the political ambitions of its founder Mikhail Khodorkovsky. Mr Khodorkovsky, once Russia's richest man, is in prison, having been charged with fraud and tax evasion and repeatedly denied bail.

Yukos sues for $20bn. Russian firms have been accused for their role in the contentious state auction of its main oil unit.

Yukos is claiming more than $20bn (£11bn) in damages after its former main production unit, Yuganskneftegas, was sold in December last year to settle back taxes. Named in the suit are gas giant Gazprom, its joint venture Gazpromneft, and the state-controlled oil firm Rosneft.

Yukos submitted its lawsuit in Houston, Texas, where it earlier filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. As well as suing for significant damages, Yukos has asked the US court to send its ongoing tax dispute with the Russian government to an independent arbitrator. It has also filed a comprehensive reorganisation plan as part of its Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing.

The dispute between Yukos and the Kremlin came to a head last year when Yukos was hit with a massive demand of $27bn in back taxes and penalties. To settle the mounting bill, Russia forced Yukos to sell its main production unit, Yuganskneftegas.

The company has now turned to the US courts in an attempt to regain control of its production business. It hopes to use the US legal system to go after those who bought or took control of its key assets. Earlier, the Russian government also filed a claim for an additional $28.3bn against Yukos.

Analysts have questioned whether US courts have any jurisdiction over Russian companies, and Russian officials have categorically dismissed the legal action as meaningless. In Houston, US bankruptcy Judge Kevin J Clark will start a two-day hearing on 16 February to hear whether a US court is the proper venue for the case.

Initially, a consortium including gas giant Gazprom and its unit Gazpromneft withdrew from the auction, reportedly due to unspecified investment risks. A few days later, however, a newly-formed shell company sold Yuganskneftegas to state-run Rosneft for $9.3bn. This move, it has been widely agreed, brings a significant portion of Russia's valuable oil industry back under state control. Critics argue that the government's actions have ignored due process and have punished political opponents. Yukos's founder, Mikhail Khodorkovsky, once Russia's richest businessman, is in prison, having been charged with fraud and tax evasion repeatedly.

My memories of Bob Marley... On the 60th anniversary of the birth of reggae legend Bob Marley, Rob Partridge - Marley's former head press-man - lifts the lid on the scenes behind the music. Partridge worked closely with the legendary Jamaican musician from 1977 until his untimely death in 1981.

"I joined Island Records in 1977 and in the very first week I was there, I worked on his ground-breaking show at the Rainbow Theatre in London. It was one of the only major dates he did in London at that time."

"The Exodus album came out in 1977 and that truly established his global appeal and cemented his place as an international superstar. By 1979 he was a massive touring attraction. You could see him playing dates in cities like Paris and Turin and Barcelona."

"Bob was one of the most mesmeric performers I ever had the privilege to witness. He must have known he was special, destined for greatness. Bob was a very spiritual and profound man. What I realised from the very start was the incredible power that was manifest within him, a power that he graciously shared with the world. He didn't suffer fools gladly at all. He wasn't afraid of stating the obvious, no matter how uncomfortable, he was a very intuitive and deeply insightful writer and perhaps the best lyricist I've ever come across. He saw things far ahead of his times."

"I remember vividly in 1978 he came to London for Top of the Pops and a Daily Mirror journalist was half-an-hour late for his scheduled interview. It was for a rehearsal session. He went back into his dressing room to resume playing football, but there was a World Cup qualifying match on television. He sat down directly in front of the TV and after about 10 minutes wasn't going to move for anyone. It was a rather truncated interview, to say the least. The last time I saw him perform was in 1980. I went to see him play four-a-side football indoors in Paris, where he was touring."

"He was a seriously committed and very gifted player. His rules for the game are Jamaican-style rules, very physical and fast-paced. He was an exceptional, truly natural player. His team was spontaneously assembled wherever he played gigs, picking up local talent. We played in London against some renowned FA Cup-winning team, which was quite a challenge."

"It was always a challenge for him to truly connect with Black America. Reggae didn't really correspond with the overwhelming popularity of disco in the 70s, which dominated the airwaves there. But by the 1990s the emergence of icons like the Fugees and Wyclef Jean's classic album The Score saw Third World music finally cross over into the mainstream. In 1991, exactly ten years after his death, his greatest hits records were, at the time, his biggest sellers ever. It saw a whole new generation taking their first steps into his incredible music."

"He, worldwide, is probably the greatest music star there's ever been. If you go anywhere in Africa he would be everywhere, his face and music iconic, in places where John Lennon or Elvis wouldn't necessarily be known. No disrespect to those legendary artists, but Bob Marley truly made his unique mark as the greatest, most enduring and influential artist in popular music history."

"1981 was to be the pivotal year he toured Africa with the great Stevie Wonder. He had only performed in Gabon and Zimbabwe before this ambitious tour. If the full 1981 tour had actually happened, the whole continent would have undoubtedly embraced him as a returning prophet. One can only speculate what more he could have achieved, but he was at the absolute height of his creative powers, just 36 years old. He had no limits to his artistic or social potential."

"He talked endlessly about Africa and its eventual spiritual return to greatness. He realised that nothing was going to stop him or his message. He had total, unwavering belief in the power of music and the resilience of the people. I'm sure if he was alive today he would have seen Africa firstly become a truly unified and powerful continent and be the antidote to the global epidemic of inequality and injustice."

"His final album - Uprising - released in 1980, featured some of the most enduring classics of all time, solidifying his legacy."

With his party's previous pledge to increase taxes by one penny in the pound to spend on public services already adopted by the government, he has switched tack. Now he is promising to levy a "modest" increase of the same amount on earnings over £100,000 a year to allow him to finance a series of pledges. On policy, Charles Kennedy has sought to reassure voters that his party will be "honest" in its approach to the general election. With the two big parties battling for overall control, the Liberal Democrats, led by Mr Kennedy, are going into the election pledged to raise taxes and seeking to ensure they are seen as a distinct choice from the other two main parties.

While his party's previous policy was to increase by a penny the basic rate of income tax to spend on public services funded by the state, he has now made a significant shift. The new proposal is to introduce a "modest" tax on the amount of earnings over £100,000 a year to fund a specific series of pledges. These pledges are aimed at abolishing student tuition fees, providing long-term care for the elderly, and reforming local council tax. That particular policy would also see about 3% of the working population paying more, with higher-earning pensioners in particular, being significantly affected.

Both Labour and the Conservatives have vehemently attacked these proposals as being unrealistic and not properly costed. Both of the larger parties insist there is no need to raise taxes in order to invest adequately in public services. The Tories, for their part, claim they can achieve up to £35bn in efficiency savings across government departments, while Labour has only offered £22bn and has yet to map out any significant new tax proposals, meaning there is little chance they will propose any before the election. In many ways, the argument between the Lib Dems and the others over the best approach to tax and spending echoes the heated debate that raged between Labour and the Conservatives in the 1980s and early 1990s. But, unlike the traditional Tory-Labour debate, the Lib Dems are presenting themselves as "modest" on the amount of money actually needed to invest in and improve public services. Their approach, they argue, is backed by recent polls suggesting that the public would rather pay for improved public services through taxation than accept further cuts to vital provisions.

However, there is also a distinct and somewhat different tone to the Lib Dem approach to immigration, with Mr Kennedy specifically attacking Labour for trying to "foment artificial" concerns over immigration for short-term electoral gain. Once again, the other main parties are singing similar songs on immigration, generally stressing more restrictive or less liberal approaches than that of his own party. Mr Kennedy also struck a remarkably confident mood over his party's election chances, stating emphatically that they expect to be "significant players" in the event of a hung parliament, holding the balance of power.

He explicitly pledged not to do any back-room deals or make secret pacts with either of the two main parties after the election. He also refused to rule out the possibility of bringing down a minority government with a "vote of no confidence" in a future Tony Blair's government, should it fail to gain a clear majority. This strongly suggests the Lib Dem leader believes he could well find himself in a highly powerful king-making position, even in a vastly altered and fragmented political landscape. His party has often been overlooked and underestimated in the past, but Mr Kennedy clearly feels this election could be different.

The UK's adoption of digital services and broadband has helped make it one of the most digitally connected nations across Europe, a report by Jupiter Research has indicated. But the United Kingdom still lags in overall terms of average internet speeds to its European counterparts. The most digitally sophisticated Europeans, those exhibiting higher rates of ownership of goods such as digital media players, digital TV, net cameras, are Scandinavians. More than 14 million households in the UK, representing approximately 60%, currently subscribe to digital TV, according to the independent communications regulator, Ofcom. The least digital of the European nations was found to be Italy, ranked 17th, on the overall Digital Life Index. However, even between the leading countries such as Sweden, and Norway, there remain some distinct trends. The Life Index demonstrates that while many key digital services are common today, but across Europe there is still no single uniform pattern of consumer adoption," said Ian Fogg, a lead Jupiter analyst. "This means that individual groups of people adopt services in quite distinct ways." Although there remain significant differences between different European nations, the overall pace of technology adoption is steadily increasing, the Jupiter Research report concluded. The projected demand for innovative new digital products and technologies, including digital video recorders (DVR), Internet Protocol television (IPTV) services, and video-on-demand platforms, will only continue to substantially increase. More households now have a greater number of multiple digital devices. By the middle of 2005, it was confidently estimated that 50% of all UK net users will be accessing the internet via broadband connections. The introduction of much faster broadband (Subscriber) ADSL2+ technology will give speeds of 18Mbps compared to the current speeds which are usually around 1Mbps or up to 2Mbps. Telecommunications giant BT has announced plans to trial the technology later this year. Such super-fast broadband will be necessary to adequately cope with the rapidly increasing demands of high-definition (HD) video-on-demand, and this technology is also set to be rolled out rapidly across other European countries. A separate report, released by global market research firm GfK, last week further revealed that, across all key markets, people's appetite for the latest digital gadgets continues unabated. The extensive poll of 20,000 consumers conducted in 20 countries worldwide found that 59% wanted to purchase new consumer electronics items. The most popular item requested was "a new digital TV" amongst so-called gadget people (75%). The second most desired item overall (67%), was the mobile phone, which was closely followed by a digital camera, desired by 54%. Digital TV was clearly the popular choice gadget of 2005, the GfK survey revealed, with 40% of consumers expressing a preference for it over wireless networking equipment and home DVR technologies. Approximately 25% of Britons said a new digital camera would be their top purchase priority for the upcoming year. A new games console, 22%, said they were planning on buying one of that particular sort. Forty-eight percent were looking into buying something "innovative and exciting". This might include music players, such as iPods, or global positioning system (GPS) devices. The Nintendo DS and Sony's PlayStation Portable (PSP) both went into the shops in 2005, with the next wave of generation games, including the much-anticipated Xbox 360 console, set to be released later in the year. Jupiter Research's index is calculated from more than 40 different factors and metrics, across users' overall connectivity, wireless and mobile phone use, online activity, and digital content consumption.

reconstruction:
US state takes action to stop 'spammers'. The US state of Texas has taken a significant step in the ongoing battle against unsolicited commercial e-mail, commonly known as spam. In a major lawsuit filed this week, Texas authorities are targeting two individuals identified as among the world's most prolific spammers, seeking millions of dollars in damages. The Texas Attorney General's office alleges that the companies operated by these individuals have consistently flouted federal anti-spam legislation. While the companies named in the lawsuit have vehemently denied any wrongdoing, stating their full compliance with all relevant regulations, the state's action represents a concerted effort to curb the pervasive nuisance of spam. Specifically, the lawsuit names Ryan Pitylak, a University of Texas graduate, and Lance Trotter, who resides in California. Both men are described as key executives within a network of firms, principally PayPerAction LLC. and Leadplex LLC., which are accused of orchestrating and facilitating the transmission of many millions of unwanted e-mail messages across the internet.

"Spam must be stopped," declared Greg Abbott, the Texas Attorney General, during a press conference announcing the legal action. He underscored the severe impact of spam on everyday internet users, stating, "It is one of the most annoying and pervasive problems facing consumers today, clogging inboxes, wasting bandwidth, and often leading to fraud and deceptive practices." His remarks highlighted the widespread frustration experienced by individuals and businesses alike due to the relentless barrage of unsolicited electronic communications.

The attorney general's detailed complaint alleges that Mr Pitylak and Mr Trotter's companies have engaged in systematic violations of several critical pieces of legislation designed to protect consumers from spam. These include the federal 2003 Controlling the Assault of Non-Solicited Pornography and Marketing Act, widely known as the CAN-Spam Act, which sets stringent requirements for commercial e-mail. Furthermore, the lawsuit cites breaches of the Texas Mail and Electronic Mail Act, specific to the state's jurisdiction, and the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act, which prohibits false, misleading, or deceptive acts or practices in commerce. Collectively, these three powerful laws confer significant statutory penalties for each violation of their terms, allowing for substantial fines. Should the men be found guilty of the alleged offenses and the maximum penalties under each applicable statute be applied, the financial implications could be severe, with the potential for them to face a bill running into the millions of dollars.

The core of the state's case revolves around the deceptive tactics allegedly employed in the e-mails. Prosecutors contend that the messages were intentionally designed to mislead recipients, primarily by using misleading subject lines that obscured their commercial nature. Crucially, these e-mails were often not clearly identified as advertisements, a key requirement under anti-spam laws. Moreover, many of these unsolicited communications offered a range of goods or services, frequently related to health products, financial schemes, or adult content, which the companies allegedly had no proper licence or authority to market and sell within the state of Texas. In response, lawyers representing the alleged spammers have swiftly dismissed the lawsuit as baseless and groundless. They have publicly stated their intention to mount a robust defence, vowing to vigorously protect their clients' reputations and operations against all accusations.

A spokesperson for the defendants, speaking on behalf of Mr Pitylak and Mr Trotter, reiterated their position, asserting, "Leadplex and PayPerAction engage in legitimate affiliate marketing practices that are in full compliance with all relevant state and federal laws and regulations." This ongoing legal battle in Texas unfolds amidst broader efforts by US authorities to crack down on spam. The move by the Texas Attorney General comes shortly after the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC), the nation's primary consumer protection agency, took its own decisive action. The FTC recently secured a court order for a preliminary injunction against a separate group of companies specifically implicated in sending vast quantities of sexually explicit e-mail. The FTC's action explicitly details how the messages sent by these other companies violated several critical parts of the CAN-Spam Act. In particular, the commission highlighted that the pornographic messages failed to clearly identify themselves as containing sexually explicit material, a clear violation. Furthermore, they were found to have employed deceptive subject lines to lure recipients, failed to include valid opt-out mechanisms for consumers to stop receiving future mail, and failed to include a valid physical postal address for the sender, all mandatory requirements under federal law. The court order in the FTC's case immediately stops the targeted companies from sending further e-mails and also freezes their assets, pending a final decision on a permanent injunction, demonstrating the severe consequences faced by those who breach anti-spam legislation.

The plan forms part of a wider Lib Dems policy to encourage first time buyers and those on lower incomes into the market...Under the proposals, the average saving for a new buyer would be more than £1,000, according to Mr Cable. "First time buyers are being squeezed out of the housing market not only by higher house prices but also by being swept into the stamp duty net," he said. "By failing to uprate the stamp duty threshold Gordon Brown has hit first time buyers and those on low incomes the hardest. "By pledging to increase the threshold to £150,000, the Liberal Democrats will make it possible for many first time buyers to buy a property without facing this tax." Lib Dems' Pledge to target stamp duty for first-time buyers.
Liberal Democrats are making a key announcement ahead of the general election, as they seek to court first-time buyers at a difficult time for the housing market.
Vince Cable, the party's Shadow Chancellor and Treasury spokesman, said the party's proposal to raise the stamp duty threshold to £150,000 would prevent 400,000 home-buyers from paying the charge.
He argued that first-time buyers were being increasingly squeezed out of the housing market by rising prices and the current tax regime.
Liberal Democrats propose to fund this cut by increasing stamp duty on properties worth more than £1m. The move forms part of a wider package of measures to encourage first-time buyers and those struggling to get a foot into the property ladder.
Under the new Liberal Democrat proposals, a typical first-time buyer would save more than £1,000, according to Mr Cable.
"First-time buyers are being effectively priced out of housing not only by house prices but also by being swept into the stamp duty tax net," he stated in an interview.
"By failing to consistently uprate the stamp duty threshold in line with inflation, the government has hit first-time buyers and those on low incomes hardest," he added.
"By increasing the threshold to £150,000, the Liberal Democrats believe they will make it possible for many first-time buyers to acquire a property without having to pay any stamp tax."
Paul Murphy MP, Labour's Shadow Chief Secretary to the Treasury, responded by saying: "The Lib Dems' financial sums just don't add up. They can have absolutely no credibility at all if they cannot demonstrate how they can fund their tax proposals and other spending commitments."
Mr Cable is expected to publish the Liberal Democrats' full alternative "Budget" document for the upcoming general election on Monday.

Concerns are growing over the future of ballet in the UK. Fewer children are following in the dainty footsteps of ballet dancers, and fewer are carving out a career as a professional ballet dancer. Research from the Royal Academy of Dance (RAD) shows that over a third of 10-year-olds attending ballet classes stop taking part in them. The Academy blames the decline in the popularity of ballet on other changes in children's lifestyles. And there are fears that if this decline is not reversed, there could be a crisis for ballet in the future. The RAD report further states that overall participation drops by 70% by the time children reach the age of 10 or 11.

Diana Trew, a veteran dance teacher who has taught for 48 years, told BBC News she had observed a 'vast' change in attitudes over the years. She squarely blamed the significant fall in ballet attendance on children having far too many other recreational activities. 'I think many children have so many hobbies now vying for their attention,' she commented. 'The wide array of options available to them, with computers, wide-screen televisions, and everything else, means that there is significantly less time or inclination spent on ballet.'

Hazel Gilbert, 23, an information manager from Newcastle, who personally gave up ballet at the age of 10, is cited as typical of the problem the industry faces. 'It's very cool to do until you go 'big' and you have to be very focused on ballet to keep going,' she said, recalling her own experience. 'I used to love it very much, but it became a bit too disciplined and prescriptive for me, and I didn't want that kind of commitment at a young age.' She added, 'I preferred other things, like swimming and kickboxing, and ballet just wasn't something I wanted to do any longer.' Ms Trew, who passionately runs her own dance school, admitted that it would be 'very difficult indeed' to reverse the current trend. She stressed that dancers have to be truly willing to make the significant sacrifices necessary to succeed in such a demanding art form. 'You have to commit to it wholeheartedly and you have to be very dedicated from a young age,' she reiterated. 'It is a career path that you have got to truly want, because it's such hard work and requires immense discipline.' She concluded, 'Children have got so many things demanding their time these days... ballet is very demanding and perhaps not seen as fun enough for many young people.'

Currently, only five out of the 16 principal dancers at the Royal Ballet - including the celebrated Darcey Bussell - are British, a stark contrast to the 16 out of 21 in 1985. A spokeswoman for the English National Ballet told BBC News that although six out of their 12 principal dancers were British, a significant proportion, nearly a third, of the company's entire roster of dancers were from outside the UK. She added emphatically that the competition for places in London's premier ballet companies was unequivocally 'the strongest in the world'. In response to these worrying trends, both the RAD and leading professional companies have collectively launched new initiatives designed to reverse the decline in ballet participation and interest. Dame Antoinette Sibley, president of the RAD, for instance, launched the prestigious Nureyev Scholarship scheme earlier this month. Aimed specifically at talented 10 to 13-year-olds, it is earnestly hoped that this programme will help keep ballet thriving and evolving for future generations. A spokeswoman for the RAD elaborated, saying: 'It aims to help nurture young dancers for the long-term future of ballet in this country. We want to provide them with a comprehensive framework and a clear goal to work towards, alongside dedicated support and coaching in an environment where their inherent talent can truly flourish.' Perhaps, more than just offering the mere opportunity to experience a 'performance', this innovative initiative aims to reignite a profound and lasting passion for ballet in young people, rather than simply giving them the fleeting thrill of an isolated performance.

"BT has a critical role to play, and today we are making a set of far-reaching proposals towards that framework," he said. BT wants lighter regulation in exchange for the changes, as well as the removal of the break-up threat...The group is to set up a new Access Services division - with a separate board which would include independent members - to ensure equal access for rivals to the "local loop", the copper wires that run between telephone exchanges and households. reconstruction:
BT has set out a package of proposals designed to offer improved access for rivals to its network. The company has made a series of concessions, including a pledge to cut wholesale broadband prices and open its entire local network to competitors. The announcement comes after telecom regulator Ofcom warned in November that the firm must fundamentally offer 'access to its phone network', or face being legally broken up, meaning BT the telecommunications giant could be split into two. The company had carried out a strategic review aimed at fostering greater competition in the sector. However, critics argue that it still leverages its telecoms monopoly and effectively limits access for many customers who wish to use its retail broadband services. Its latest submission was delivered ahead of a crucial deadline for review of its future structure and operations.

Central to the proposals are plans for BT to lower its prices for wholesale broadband services and make them more transparent, along with ensuring highly-regulated access to BT's local network, the company said in a statement. 'This addresses concerns regarding its perceived monopoly.' 'The United Kingdom is in danger of falling behind in the telecoms world,' BT chief executive Ben Verwaayen said. 'BT has a vital role to play, and we are making far-reaching proposals to achieve that aim,' he added. BT wants changes, well short of the break-up advocated by some industry players.

The group is to set up a new Access division with its own board, the majority of whose members would be independent from BT, to manage access for rivals to the fundamental network infrastructure, including the copper wires that run between exchanges and customer premises. BT plans to reduce prices for its most popular broadband products, such as its ADSL offerings, by about 8% from this summer, in response to increasing demand from consumers.

It added it plans to invest £10bn in the next five years to create a '21st Century' network capable of delivering next-generation services. To help meet the growing demand for high-speed internet, BT announced in April plans to recruit 4,000 new engineers from the UK. Telecom regulator Ofcom broadly welcomed the move, stating that BT 'had covered a lot of ground' in its latest proposals.

The big question now is whether the rest of the industry, particularly Ofcom's vocal critics, feel these proposals go far enough. 'This represents an important stage in the negotiation,' said Tony Lavender, a telecoms analyst from consultancy Ovum. Internet service provider (ISP) Plus.net also backed the proposals, saying 'it would be entirely reasonable if Ofcom chose to accept them'.

'If BT has been willing to play fair, then they will introduce a much-needed new era of competition. The scenario now is to carefully evaluate these plans as an improvement in service,' said Plus.net chief executive Richard Tang. Meanwhile, Chris Panayis, managing director of ISP Freedom2surf expressed optimism, saying that it would make the market situation clearer. 'It's the first productive dialogue we've had with BT,' he commented, adding that there was still a need to ensure a level playing field.

'However, according to Ofcom, unless BT fundamentally changes the dynamics of the broadband market, the opening up of the local telephone network to competition remains fragile,' a spokesman said. 'For sustained success, BT needs to fully commit to broadband service improvements and provide more local loop unbundling if consumers are to see the benefits of competition and infrastructure investment.'

More than 100 telecom companies, and other interested parties are expected to make submissions to Ofcom during the consultation period. Ofcom is expected to spend the next few weeks examining the proposals before making an announcement on its final decision in a few months.

reconstruction:
Operating profit at US media giant Time Warner jumped by 76% to $1.13bn (£600m) for the three months to 31 December, from $639m a year earlier.

The company, which is now one of the most favoured among institutional investors, benefited from strong growth in high-speed internet subscriptions and higher advertising sales. Time Warner's fourth quarter sales rose by 2% to $11.1bn from $10.9bn in the corresponding period of the previous year.

The overall profits figure was boosted by some significant one-off gains, which helped to offset a reported profit dip at its Warner Bros. film division, and continued subscriber losses at its struggling online arm, AOL.

Time Warner also stated that it now accounts for 8% of the US search-engine market. Its internet business, AOL, had, as previously reported, lost a further 464,000 subscribers in the quarter. While overall profits for the division were lower than in the preceding period, the company's underlying internet advertising revenues showed an increase of 8%.

It hopes to reverse this negative trend by offering a free service to its remaining dial-up users and trying actively to sign up its existing customers to broadband connections.

Time Warner also faces the prospect of having to restate its financial results for 2000 and 2003 following an ongoing inquiry by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), which is investigating its accounting practices.

Time Warner's film division fared slightly better than analysts had expected. Its movie arm saw profits rise by 27% to $284m, helped by strong box-office performances from films like Alexander and Catwoman. This was, however, in sharp contrast to the year earlier, when the third and final instalment of the hugely popular Lord of the Rings trilogy boosted results considerably.

For the full year to December 31, Time Warner posted a net profit of $3.36bn, an increase of 27% from 2003, while total revenues grew by 6.4% to $42.09bn. "Our financial performance was strong, meeting or exceeding all our full-year objectives and greatly improving our financial flexibility," said chief executive Richard Parsons in a statement. For 2005, Time Warner expects its operating income to grow by around 5%, and also expects higher advertising revenues and wider operating margins across its businesses.

Time Warner is also facing continued scrutiny over its accounting practices as part of an ongoing inquiry into AOL by US federal regulators. It has already offered to pay $300m to settle the case, but the proposed deal is still under review by the SEC. The company further said it was forced to set aside new reserves for potential legal costs, which now stand at $500m. It also intends to restate the way it accounts for German media firm Bertelsmann's purchase of a stake in AOL Europe, as previously reported. As a result, it will book more of its share of the value of that stake.

reconstruction:
Winn-Dixie, the US grocery store chain, has today announced it has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, citing intense pressure from rivals. The US group Winn-Dixie has been struggling for some time, finally succumbing to stiff competition in a retail market dominated by giants like Wal-Mart.

Winn-Dixie, which remains among the largest US supermarket operators, said the Chapter 11 protection would provide the necessary breathing room to allow it to restructure its operations and emerge successfully as a viable business.

The company confirmed that 920 stores would remain open during the restructuring process, but acknowledged it would likely have to sell off a significant number of underperforming sites in order to streamline its operations and improve profitability.

The Jacksonville, Florida-based grocery giant has reported total debts of an estimated $1.87bn (£980m). In its bankruptcy filing, it listed its largest unsecured creditor as the US food giant Kraft, to which it currently owes a substantial $15.1m.

Analysts say Winn-Dixie has simply not kept pace with rivals' rapid changes and aggressive pricing strategies. They also highlight that the company has been heavily burdened by the considerable cost of upgrading its ageing stores and distribution network, struggling to find the capital required.

A previous 10-month restructuring effort, aimed at revitalising the ailing business, was widely considered a failure. Following the announcement of a larger-than-expected quarterly loss earlier this week, Winn-Dixie's formal move into bankruptcy proceedings was widely expected by financial markets.

The company's management said Winn-Dixie intended to fully utilise the Chapter 11 breathing space to "take decisive action to turn itself around" and regain its competitive edge in the highly challenging retail sector.

"This comprehensive strategy includes significant cost reductions across the entire organisation, a renewed focus on improving the overall customer service experience, and generating sustainable growth in sales," commented Philip Lynch, an analyst at Gimme Credit. "However, it's not an ideal situation," said Mr Lynch, "as the news of bankruptcy would inevitably put off a certain segment of loyal customers."

"The company desperately needs to win over customers over the next one or two critical quarters. Now they are fighting for every single customer and must make every effort to reassure all customers that this is their preferred local store," he added, emphasising the uphill battle ahead for the beleaguered retailer.

All eyes are on London this evening as the film world truly gears up for the 2005 British Academy Film Awards. Stars from across the globe are preparing to walk the illustrious red carpet, arriving in their finest attire, for this year's highly anticipated award ceremony, a definitive highlight in the international cinematic calendar. The atmosphere is buzzing with excitement and widespread speculation ahead of what promises to be an unforgettable night of celebration and recognition.

The prestigious 2005 Bafta Awards ceremony is being held at the grandeur of the Odeon Leicester Square, located in the very heart of London. This iconic venue will once again play host to an assembly of the industry's most celebrated talents. Hollywood A-listers, including the critically acclaimed Cate Blanchett, the ever-popular Leonardo DiCaprio, and the screen legend Richard Gere, are among the many luminaries expected to attend, adding a touch of international glamour to the proceedings. The evening's proceedings will be skillfully hosted by the inimitable Stephen Fry, widely known for his sharp wit and elegant stage presence. For those unable to be present at the ceremony in person, it will be broadcast live on BBC One, commencing promptly at 20:10 GMT, offering a front-row seat to the glamour and excitement for millions of viewers across the country and beyond.

A stellar line-up of performers and filmmakers, many of whom are nominated for the biggest accolades in UK film, will grace the event. Among the confirmed attendees and nominees are the talented Gael García Bernal, fresh from his acclaimed role in The Motorcycle Diaries; the esteemed British actress Imelda Staunton, a strong favourite for Best Actress; the striking Diane Kruger; the versatile Jamie Foxx, nominated for his transformative performance in Ray; the legendary Anjelica Huston; the regal Helen Mirren; and none other than former James Bond himself, Pierce Brosnan, adding a touch of classic charm to the red carpet proceedings.

Martin Scorsese's epic blockbuster The Aviator, starring Leonardo DiCaprio in a career-defining portrayal of eccentric billionaire Howard Hughes, leads the nominations with an impressive 14 nods. This includes the highly coveted prizes for best film, best director, and best actor, positioning it as a strong favourite to sweep a number of categories on the night. Its meticulous period detail and compelling performances have captivated critics and audiences alike, making it a standout of the year.

The Aviator faces fierce competition in the Best Film category from a distinguished slate of critically acclaimed movies. It is up against the imaginative and moving Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, the enchanting and poignant Finding Neverland, and the evocative The Motorcycle Diaries. Additionally, Mike Leigh's powerful and deeply resonant British film, Vera Drake, has garnered significant attention, securing an impressive 11 nominations. This makes it a formidable contender, particularly in the British film categories and the acting races, reflecting its critical success.

In the highly competitive Best Actress category, British favourite Imelda Staunton is widely considered one of the frontrunners to win the prestigious award for her truly gritty and heart-wrenching performance as a small-time abortionist in Vera Drake. Her nuanced portrayal has earned widespread critical acclaim and resonated deeply with audiences. She faces formidable competition from a stellar line-up of international talent. Among her rivals are the compelling Charlize Theron, recognised for her transformative and harrowing role in Monster; the graceful Zhang Ziyi, praised for her breathtaking work in House of Flying Daggers; and the celebrated British actress Kate Winslet, who remarkably has two nominations to her name this year, for her captivating performances in both Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind and Finding Neverland, highlighting her exceptional versatility and range.

The Best Actor category also promises a thrilling contest, with nominations going to the charismatic Gael García Bernal for his portrayal of young Che Guevara in The Motorcycle Diaries; the powerhouse Jamie Foxx for his extraordinary embodiment of Ray Charles in Ray; the often-comedic but deeply dramatic Jim Carrey for his poignant turn in Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind; and the ever-versatile Johnny Depp for his whimsical yet heartfelt performance in Finding Neverland. Each actor delivered a standout performance, making this one of the hardest categories to call with any certainty.

British actor Clive Owen is hoping to repeat his recent Golden Globe success, where he triumphed in the Best Supporting Actor category, for his intensely compelling performance in the drama Closer. His Closer co-star, the equally talented Natalie Portman, is also nominated in the Best Supporting Actress category. She is up against a formidable quartet of actresses: Meryl Streep for her chilling role in The Manchurian Candidate, Virginia Madsen for her nuanced work in Sideways, Sophie Okonedo for her powerful performance in Hotel Rwanda, and Cate Blanchett for her exquisite portrayal of Katharine Hepburn in The Aviator. The competition here is exceptionally strong, promising a tense moment when the winner is finally announced.

Finally, the prestigious Best Director award will be fiercely contested by some of cinema's most celebrated visionaries. Nominees in this category include Mike Leigh for Vera Drake, Martin Scorsese for The Aviator, Michael Mann for Collateral, Michel Gondry for Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind and Marc Forster for Finding Neverland. The suspense will build throughout the evening to see who takes home the iconic Bafta masks, recognising outstanding cinematic artistry and directorial skill. The stage is truly set for an unforgettable night of celebration and recognition of the finest achievements in film.

He commented that it was the 'last one not for children'. Mr Lucas told US television show 60 Minutes the latest instalment would be the darkest and most disturbing of the series. Camera phones are becoming 'must-haves' for many consumers. Four out of five new mobiles sold will come with cameras built into them by 2004, a significant jump from just one in five last year, according to market analysts. Globally, the number of camera phones shipped in 2003 reached 159 million units, an impressive increase of 104% from the previous year. The report further forecasts that nearly 70% of all mobile phones sold worldwide will have a built-in camera by 2008. Improving imaging technology and ease of use are making camera mobiles an even greater "must-have" buy for consumers.

In Europe, camera mobiles typically take images at resolutions of 1.3 megapixels. But in Japan, where consumers are often early adopters of advanced technology, many handsets already have cameras that can capture images at higher resolutions, often up to 3.2 megapixels. NTT DoCoMo dominates the Japanese market, and the uptake of camera phones there is huge. By 2008, according to research firm Gartner, 95% of all handsets sold there will have cameras built in.

When camera phones first emerged some years ago, people struggled to easily share images from them, due to the complexity of uploading and sending them via MMS (Multimedia Messaging Services). But now, the 18 major handset makers have concentrated on making camera phones much simpler to use. They have enabled users to share photos in a variety of easier ways, and have introduced more user-friendly design features, like rotating viewfinders, removable memory cards and more intuitive controls.

Mobile images are primarily for sharing with other people, a social rather than a purely photographic activity. Manufacturers have been giving users easier ways to publish them directly to personal websites, or even create mobile-specific weblogs - commonly known as moblogs. However, until the image resolution increases more significantly, the average consumer will likely not be interested in printing pictures at dedicated kiosks.

The quality of the image sensor inside camera phones is constantly improving. By mid-2005, it is likely that the resolution of most new camera phones will be greater than one megapixel. In comparison, dedicated digital cameras currently range from two to six megapixels in quality for consumer models, with high-end versions offering up to eight megapixels. But there is still a lot of work to be done to make camera phones truly compete with dedicated digital cameras in terms of image quality and features.

Some handsets already feature basic video recording capability, and manufacturers are actively looking into improvements for taking pictures in challenging low-light conditions, like dimly lit nightclubs. Other developments include wide-angle modes, self-timer features, and enhanced sensors and processors for capturing better quality video clips.

Mobile phone images have even made it into the art world. An exhibition next month in London, in aid of a leading charity, will feature works taken from the phones of top artists. The show, which is yet to be formally titled, will feature contributions from renowned photographers, as well as celebrated artists like Nan Goldin, and Sir Peter Blake, Tracey Emin and David Shrigley. Concerns for their potential misuse, however, have worried many organisations.

In the UK, for instance, the Home Office and the Ministry of Defence have, for example, banned camera phones from government buildings and sensitive sites to prevent the leaking of sensitive information and classified data. Meanwhile, schools across the country have also raised concerns about privacy issues and potential misuse. The Information Commissioner has also issued a code of practice concerning how camera phones can be used ethically and legally in public places.

But not everyone is worried by these concerns; indeed, for many, the 'profits are rolling in' for handset makers like Sony Ericsson, who are benefiting hugely from the accelerating demand for new camera phones. Over 60% of all Sony Ericsson phones sold during the last quarter were camera phones, a trend driven primarily through the popularity of their latest models.

Almost immediately in the 48th minute, a powerful 25-yard shot from Paul Scholes took a deflection off Tony Hibbert, but Nigel Martyn dived full-stretch to save brilliantly, pushing the ball wide. Martyn came to Everton's rescue later to deny Wayne Rooney's big moment as he raced through on goal, once again the veteran keeper proving outstanding with a brave block. Paul Scholes' initial shot took a deflection, Martyn could only parry it out into the path of an oncoming player, and Cristiano Ronaldo reacted first to score easily, tapping home into an empty net. Everton's plight worsened further when their goalkeeper sustained an injury just minutes after the goal. There may indeed be serious trouble ahead for Everton after goalkeeper Nigel Martyn received lengthy treatment for an injury, having conceded the second goal. Wayne Rooney was a constant threat and focal point on his return to Everton, looking determined to impress. Martyn's injury-enforced exit briefly halted the game, but once again, Rooney was denied a goal by the excellent goalkeeping of the England international before his departure, frustrating the striker.

The UK's trade deficit narrowed in November, on a 7.5% rise in exports outside the European Union, official figures showed. According to the Office for National Statistics, the difference between what was exported and imported, the goods trade deficit, was £3.1bn ($5.8bn), down from £3.6bn in the preceding month. Overall - including trade in both goods and services - exports rose by more than 3.2% to £24.8bn, while imports rose again to a total value of £27.9bn. The deficit for goods alone stood at £4.6bn, a reduction from October's £5bn.

In November alone, the UK exported £16.9bn worth of goods, and imported £21.5bn. The cumulative deficit for the first eleven months of 2004 now stands at £36.3bn, some £4.5bn higher than the same period in 2003, highlighting persistent challenges. This overall improvement comes with an encouraging rise in export sales to both the European Union and the rest of the world, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS). EU exports specifically rose by 2%, a gain fuelled by an increase in demand. Non-EU exports were significantly up by 7.5%, with robust growth observed across a range of manufacturing sectors, including chemicals. The service sector also saw a 1% rise in exports. However, service imports rose 3%, while overall economic growth in the UK slowed to 0.5% during the period.

The UK's trade deficit with non-EU countries narrowed to £1.9bn from £2.1bn, while the shortfall in trade with EU countries also narrowed to £2.7bn from £2.9bn in October. The country's traditionally strong surplus on trade-in-services remained impressively steady at £1.5bn for the fifth month in a row. Dales, UK Economics, said the results represented a positive development, offering some relief, but he stressed that the long-term prognosis for the economy was still challenging. "The figures were a lot better than expected, but the underlying trend of the UK's trade balance still remains a concern," he added. "There are very encouraging signs that UK export recovery is beginning to take hold. But there is a real danger it will be constrained by the ongoing strong domestic demand on imports."

The Scottish Environment Protection Agency (SEPA) presented stark and detailed evidence to the Scottish Parliament's Environment, Climate Change and Land Reform Committee regarding the Scottish Government's current progress and future challenges in tackling environmental change.

Officials indicated that while substantial investment in wind power infrastructure may prove to be one of the more effective and better options available for trying to combat global warming, other significant recommendations put forward by conservationists include drastically reducing internal air travel and substantially boosting the development and use of electric trains across the country.

The evidence heard during the committee's comprehensive inquiry on the critical issue of climate change in Scotland highlighted SEPA's urgent call for drastic cuts to global greenhouse gas emissions, particularly stressing the concern as emissions from the transport sector continue to relentlessly increase. It was also strongly suggested that the public, and particularly local communities, may have to accept "significant intrusion" from large-scale new wind farm developments if the nation's challenging climate targets are to be successfully met, as such vital infrastructure is deemed needed for many decades to come.

Meanwhile, alarming reports indicated that Scotland's west coast has already experienced more devastating and extreme weather events across the last month alone, with experts now predicting that storms will become not only more frequent but also significantly more intense in the years ahead.

Researchers from the University of the Highlands and Islands, in collaboration with the University of Southampton, have been diligently looking at historical climate patterns and fluctuating sea levels over the last several decades. The extensive research project, which involved key contributions from the Environmental Research Institute in Thurso, the University of the Highlands and Islands (UHI) Institute, and the distinguished National Oceanography Centre in Southampton, carried out a series of detailed and rigorous studies. These investigations specifically included the innovative use of advanced wave buoys to accurately monitor sea conditions around the entire Scottish coast and the wider North Atlantic region.

reconstruction: The US trade gap widened by more than expected in October, reaching record levels as significantly higher prices for imports pushed the overall trade shortfall to $55.5bn (£29bn). This figure represented an increase of 9% from September's revised total, the Commerce Department announced. That brought the cumulative 10-month deficit for the year to $500.5bn, establishing a new record. Imports of goods and services rose by 3.4%, while US exports managed to increase by only 0.6% over the same period. The weaker value of the US dollar also increased the cost of imports, and this factor helped drive stronger consumer and business demand for foreign products. 'It's certainly getting worse, but it's not entirely unexpected given current economic circumstances,' said David Wyss, chief economist at Standard & Poor's in New York. 'The fundamental problem is that when the dollar goes down, it inevitably raises the price of imports, making them more expensive for American buyers.' He further added that the US was also experiencing a noticeable slowdown in international export orders due to global economic weakness. 'Things are, unfortunately, going to get worse before they get better in terms of our national trade balance.' Concerns, however, continue to remain prominent among economists and policymakers as to how the US will effectively fund its substantial twin deficits – both trade and budget – especially should they continue to widen at the current alarming rate. Another pressing problem frequently cited by analysts is the ongoing situation with China, which has consistently been accused of artificially keeping its national currency, the yuan, weak in order to significantly boost its own exports onto the global market. The US imported almost $20bn worth of goods from China during October alone, while exporting a little under $3bn in return, illustrating the imbalance. 'It seems that the key worry that has long existed over the valuation of the Chinese currency still remains a major concern for US trade policy,' said Anthony Chan, a respected bond strategist at Tabak in New York. He further added that this trend of a widening trade deficit would undoubtedly continue 'going forward' into the next year. These latest trade figures are likely to add to further widespread expectations that the Federal Reserve will indeed raise interest rates for a fifth consecutive time this year. Borrowing costs across the economy are widely tipped to rise by a quarter of a percentage point, bringing the federal funds rate target to 2.25% at the Fed's next policy meeting, scheduled for Tuesday.

original: Band Aid 20 single storms to No 1..The new version of the Band Aid song Do They Know It's Christmas? has gone straight in at number one in the UK singles chart...The charity record is also tipped to be this year's Christmas number one. It features vocals from the likes of Chris Martin, Dido, Robbie Williams and the Sugababes. The original version - which was the Christmas number one in 1984 - sold 750,000 copies in its first week and 3.5 million in total. It was released in the US, and reached number 13 in the singles chart. However, Band Aid 20 is not going to be released in the US, despite being sold in many countries around the world. US record shops are stocking an import version of Do They Know It's Christmas, which is said to be selling very well in Los Angeles and New York...British stars who appear on the current recording, such as Dido and Coldplay's Chris Martin, are well known to music fans across the Atlantic, along with U2 frontman Bono. Record company Universal is responsible for the global distribution of the single, which will be available across Europe, Asia, South America and Canada. But music fans in the US are still able to access the song and download it on Band Aid 20's official website. In 1985, a group of high-profile American stars known as USA For Africa came together to record their own fund-raising single, We Are The World. The song was written by Lionel Richie and Michael Jackson, with Quincy Jones as producer...It topped the US charts for three weeks and went on win Grammy awards for best record and song. Dionne Warwick, Diana Ross and Tina Turner were among the line-up of performers. Proceeds from the sales of the Band Aid 20 single will go towards aid relief in Africa, in countries such as Ethiopia and Sudan. The money raised will also be used to help combat HIV and Aids across the continent. The Band Aid Trust which was set up 20 years ago, when the original single was released, handed out $144m (£75m) to famine relief projects across Africa between January 1985 and November 2004.

original: US economy still growing says Fed..Most areas of the US saw their economy continue to expand in December and early January, the US Federal Reserve said in its latest Beige Book report...Of the 12 US regions it identifies for the study, 11 showed stronger economic growth, with only the Cleveland area falling behind with a "mixed" rating. Consumer spending was higher in December than November, and festive sales were also up on 2003. The employment picture also improved, the Fed said..."Labour markets firmed in a number of districts, but wage pressures generally remained modest," the Beige Book said. "Several districts reported higher prices for building materials and manufacturing inputs, but most reported steady or only slightly higher overall price levels." The report added that residential real estate activity remained strong and that commercial real estate activity strengthened in most districts. "Office leasing was especially brisk in Washington DC, and New York City, two of the nation's strongest commercial markets," the Fed said.

original: Berlin cheers for anti-Nazi film..A German movie about an anti-Nazi resistance heroine has drawn loud applause at Berlin Film Festival...Sophie Scholl - The Final Days portrays the final days of the member of the White Rose movement. Scholl, 21, was arrested and beheaded with her brother, Hans, in 1943 for distributing leaflets condemning the "abhorrent tyranny" of Adolf Hitler. Director Marc Rothemund said: "I have a feeling of responsibility to keep the legacy of the Scholls going." "We must somehow keep their ideas alive," he added...The film drew on transcripts of Gestapo interrogations and Scholl's trial preserved in the archive of communist East Germany's secret police. Their discovery was the inspiration behind the film for Rothemund, who worked closely with surviving relatives, including one of Scholl's sisters, to ensure historical accuracy on the film. Scholl and other members of the White Rose resistance group first started distributing anti-Nazi leaflets in the summer of 1942. They were arrested as they dropped leaflets at Munich University calling for a "day of reckoning" with Adolf Hitler's regime. The film focuses on the six days from Scholl's arrest to the intense trial which saw Scholl initially deny the charges and ended with a defiant appearance. It is one of three German films vying for a top prize at the Festival...A South African film version of Bizet's tragic opera Carmen shot in Cape Town in the Xhosa language has also premiered at the Berlin Festival. The film is entitled U-Carmen eKhayelitsha or Carmen in Khayelitsha after the township in which the story is set. It is performed by a 40-strong music and theatre troupe in their debut film performance. The film is the first South African feature in 25 years and only the second to be nominated for a Golden Bear Award.

Agriculture Minister, Mallam Adamu, announced the scheme aimed to significantly boost output levels from an expected 180,000 tonnes this year to a target of 600,000 by 2008. The government will invest a substantial sum of 154m Naira ($1.1m; £591,000) into farming chemicals and other crucial inputs, such as improved seedlings and training. Nigeria is currently the world's fourth-largest cocoa producer, a position it hopes to improve significantly. Cocoa had been the main export crop in the 1960s. But with the coming of oil, the government started paying less attention to the sector, leading to a decline from a peak of about 400,000 tonnes a year in 1970. The minister, speaking at a press conference in the south-western city of Ibadan, Mr. Bello, reiterated that the primary aim of the programme was to actively encourage cocoa farmers to expand their operations and thereby lift overall production. He also stated that 91m Naira out of the funding had been earmarked specifically for establishing new, high-yield cocoa plantations across the country. The country hopes to draw inspiration from and emulate the success of Ghana, which produced around 490,000 tonnes last year, although some farmers expressed reservations about the feasibility of the new strategy. "People who are not wealthy or well-connected enough often find it difficult to participate in such schemes," said Joshua Osagie, a local farmer speaking to Reuters. "Many farmers in the village see this new initiative primarily as a benefit for bigger landowners and those with political ties," he further commented. At the same time as its new initiative, neighbouring Ghana - the world's second largest cocoa producer by volume - announced record revenues for its thriving cocoa industry, which had broken all previous performance benchmarks. Ghana saw an impressive $1.2bn-worth of beans exported during the 2003-04 marketing season. Ghana's national Cocoa Board, Cocobod, said high-yield techniques and crop management strategies had led to this remarkable growth, successfully pushing production levels far beyond those achieved in the 1960s when Ghana was considered the world's leading grower.

The state of the Economy'' is set to be a key issue in the upcoming general election. UK businesses are bracing themselves for further interest rate rises this year, according to a report published today. Optimism among businesses is currently at its highest since 1997 and business will reap the benefits from a significant rise in public spending, say researchers at accountancy firm BDO. The Bank of England is expected to keep interest rates on hold this week - but they could go up later this year. Rates are widely anticipated to increase after the anticipated general election in the spring of 2005.

The BDO optimism index - a crucial indicator of economic growth in the coming quarters ahead - climbed sharply in January to 102.5, from 102.2. The rise is due, in large part, to a projected strong increase in global demand and increased acquisition activity among firms, reflecting greater business confidence. "It is only this year left before there will be a general election," BDO said, highlighting the political backdrop to economic sentiment.

Its BDO's output index - which also remained at 100.8 in January, implying GDP growth of 2.9% in the second quarter of 2005 - suggests that the output gap is back, even despite sterling's strength against major currencies and persistently high oil prices, the group noted.

Furthermore, the BDO inflation index, which has risen over the last 8 months, now stands at 110.0 compared with 108.0 last year, indicating a gradual upward pressure on prices.

"The economy is looking in good shape going into the general election, but it will still need a substantial jolt ahead as the Bank of England reacts to continuing global economic growth," commented Peter Hemington, partner at BDO St Hayward. "However, if global growth were to slow by the end of 2005, it is unlikely that we will see higher interest rates or a sustained increase in consumer demand."

It is hoped her dedicated new training regime will pay significant dividends at the championships, which are set to take place on 5-6 March.
