Gordon Brown sought to bat off economy fears today, as he announced a package of measures.
Mr Brown gave the go-ahead to petrol duty increases, a £1bn tax rises boost and new, extended maternity leave plans. He said tough borrowing targets would still be met. The chancellor also claimed he had overseen the longest period of sustained economic growth in UK "history", and denied he was "complacent about the future". But Oliver Letwin, for the Shadow Cabinet, attacked government red tape, dubbing Mr Brown "Wastealot".

Mr Brown's "golden rules" for public borrowing had been effectively broken, critics said, with total government borrowing predicted to top over £170bn. Mr Letwin added: "The wrong tide is going on the British economy. He is spending, taxing more and more so he is not getting value for the taxpayer's money."

Mr Matthew Vincent, for the Liberal Democrats, accused the Chancellor of ducking tough economic choices. He insisted: "Last week the minister gave us the politics; this chancellor has comprehensively ignored the difficult economics of the situation." There are challenges ahead from the global economic slowdown and the rapid downturn in the housing market amid soaring levels of personal debt. Yet they are failing to address them properly.

Mr Brown rejected the 'call' to set up an independent economic Audit, saying financial judgments and assessments should continue to be made by the Treasury. Many leading economists say his latest calculations for the public finances are based on nothing more than wishful thinking. BBC economic editor Evan Davis said the latest borrowing figures were plausible but also contained considerable uncertainties and risks. This package, he suggested, "was a pointed rebuttal" to a recent public warning from new European Commissioner Peter Mandelson.

In his Pre-Budget Report, he set a 10-year comprehensive childcare strategy if Labour wins the next general election. It includes a £285m injection of funds to extend paid maternity leave from six months to nine, and making it possible for fathers to be able to transfer leave to their partners. He also pledged to increase free nursery places for three-and four-year-olds to 15 hours a week by 2007. New funding will be provided to help keep schools open from 0800 to 1800 GMT daily, to look after pupils while parents work. Taken as a whole, the proposals would make the UK "truly family-friendly for the first time in a generation", said Mr Brown.

He announced cash-payments and other benefits for pensioners, with a one-off payment of £50 for over-70s as an extra top-up to their annual winter allowance. In a controversial move to curb council tax rises to just 5% for the next financial year, the chancellor said there would be an extra £1bn for local councils. The money is expected to come from tough new cuts across other government departments and fresh efficiency savings.

Mr Brown said he was fully sticking to his tough economic fiscal rules - namely, to borrow only for investment and keep national debt "low" - both in this parliamentary term and the next. Borrowing for 2003/04 is now forecast at £35bn - £2.5bn lower than the £37.5bn in his last March's budget, announced the Chancellor for the current financial year. It is now tipped to fall to just £31bn by 2005/06 - but even this figure is £2bn more than Mr Brown predicted back in his March budget. The Treasury's forecast for economic growth would be 1.75% this year and rise to 2% in the next, according to Mr Brown. An extra £105m will be committed to increasing security measures and fighting anti-terrorism activities.

Business leaders welcomed efforts to improve UK competitiveness in skills and innovation. However, there were widespread concerns about the additional costs of more family-friendly policies for employers. Stephen Alambritis, from the Federation of Small Businesses, said: "The latest measures were clearly made with the upcoming general election in mind and with far too little thought to their potential impact on small businesses."

original: Big war games battle it out..The arrival of new titles in the popular Medal Of Honor and Call of Duty franchises leaves fans of wartime battle titles spoilt for choice...The acclaimed PC title Call of Duty has been updated for console formats, building on many of the original's elements. For its part, the long-running Medal of Honor series has added Pacific Assault to its PC catalogue, adapting the console game Rising Sun. Call of Duty: Finest Hour casts you as a succession of allied soldiers fighting on World War 2 battlefronts including Russia and North Africa. It is a traditional first-person-viewed game that lets you control just one character, in the midst of a unit where cohorts constantly bark orders at you. On a near-identical note, Medal of Honor: Pacific Assault does all it can to make you feel part of a tight-knit team and plum in the middle of all-out action. Its arenas are the war's Pacific battles, including Guadalcanal and Pearl Harbour. You play one character throughout, a raw and rather talkative US soldier...Both games rely on a carefully stage-managed structure that keeps things ticking along. When this works, it is a brilliant device to make you feel part of a story. When it does not, it is tedious...A winning moment is an early scene in Pacific Assault, where you come under attack at the famous US base in Hawaii. You are first ushered into a gunboat attacking the incoming waves of Japanese planes, then made to descend into a sinking battleship to rescue crewman, before seizing the anti-aircraft guns. It is one of the finest set-pieces ever seen in a video game. This notion of shuffling the player along a studiously pre-determined path, forcibly witnessing a series of pre-set moments of action, is a perilous business which can make the whole affair feel stilted rather than organic. The genius of something like Half Life 2 is that it skilfully disguises its linear plotting by various means of misdirection. This pair of games do not really accomplish that, being more concerned with imparting a full-on atmospheric experience...Call of Duty comes with a suitably bombastic score and overblown presentation. Finest Hour has a similar determination, framing everything in moody wartime music, archive footage and lots of reflective voice-overs...Letting you play a number of different roles is an interesting ploy that adds new dimensions to the Call of Duty endeavour, even if it sacrifices the narrative flow somewhat. The game's drawback could be said to be its format; tastes differ, but these wartime shooters often do seem to work better on PC. The mouse control is a big reason why, along with the sharper graphics a top-end computer can muster and the apparent notion that PC games are allowed to get away with a bit more subtlety. Call of Duty on PC was more detailed, plot-wise and graphically, and this new adaptation feels a little rough and ready. Targeting with the PS2 controller proved tricky, not helped by unconvincing collision-detection. You can shoot an enemy repeatedly with zero question as to your aim, yet the bullets will just refuse to hit him. Checkpoints are so few and far between that when you get shot, which happens regularly, you are set harshly far back, and will find yourself covering vast tracts of scorched earth again and again. The game wants to be a challenge, and is, and many players will like it for that. It is as dynamic a battlefield simulator as you will experience and even if it is not as refined as its PC parent, the sense of being part of the action is thoroughly impressive...Both of these games feature military colleagues who are disturbingly bad shots and prone to odd behaviour. And in Pacific Assault in particular, their commands and comments are irritatingly meaningless...But the teamwork element in titles like this is superficial, designed to add atmosphere and camaraderie rather than affect the gameplay mechanics at all. Of the two games, Pacific Assault gets more things right, including little points like auto-saving intelligently and having tidier presentation. It engages you very well and also looks wonderful, making the most of the lush tropical settings that are reminiscent of the glorious Far Cry, although we had to ramp up the settings on a high-spec machine to get the most out of them. Finest Hour is by no means bad, and it is only because the PC original was so dazzling that this version sometimes feels underwhelming. Those looking for a wartime game with plenty of atmosphere and a hearty abundance of enemies to shoot will be contented. But they will also have a niggling puzzlement as to why it does not break a little more ground rather then just being competent.

original: Court mulls file-sharing future..Judges at the US Supreme Court have been hearing evidence for and against file-sharing networks...The court will decide whether producers of file-sharing software can ultimately be held responsible for copyright infringement. They questioned if opening the way for the entertainment industry to sue file-sharers could deter innovation. They also said that file-trading firms had some responsibility for inducing people to piracy...The lawsuit, brought by 28 of the world's largest entertainment firms, has raged for several years. Legal experts agree that if the Supreme Court finds in favour of the music and movie industry they would be able to sue file-trading firms into bankruptcy. But if the judge rules that Grokster and Morpheus - the file-sharers at the centre of the case - are merely providers of technology that can have legitimate as well as illegitimate uses, then the music and movie industry would be forced to abandon its pursuit of file-sharing providers. Instead, they would have to pursue individuals who use peer-to-peer networks to get their hands on free music and movies. The hi-tech and entertainment industries have been divided on the issue. Intel filed a document with the Supreme Court earlier this month in defence of Grokster and others, despite misgivings about some aspects of the file-sharing community. It summed up the attitude of many tech firms in its submission which states that its products "are essentially tools, that like any other tools, capable of being used by consumers and businesses for unlawful purposes"...Asking firms to second-guess the uses that its technologies would be put to, and to build in ways of preventing illegitimate use, would stifle innovation, it said. The Electronic Frontier Foundation, a civil rights watchdog, is also defending StreamCast Networks, the company behind the Morpheus file-sharing software. The case raises a question of critical importance at the border between copyright and innovation, it said. It cites, as do many, the landmark ruling in 1984 which found that Sony should not be held responsible for the fact that its Betamax video recorder could be used for piracy. Defenders remain optimistic that the judges will rule in favour of the peer-to-peer networks, upholding the precedent set by the Sony Betamax case. A small band of supporters were outside the court as the lawyers entered, wearing "Save Betamax" t-shirts. "The Betamax principles stand as the Magna Carta for the technology industry and are responsible for the explosion in innovation that has occurred in the US over the past 20 years," said Gary Shapiro, chief executive of the Consumer Electronics Association. Supreme Court Justice Stephen Breyer said that inventions from printing to Apple's iPod could be used to illegally duplicate copyrighted materials but had, on balance, been beneficial to society. He said that while file-trading software can be used to illegally trade movies and music, conceptually the technology had "some really excellent uses"...Based on Tuesday's hearing it seems unlikely that the Betamax ruling will be overturned but file-sharing firms might still be held responsible for encouraging or inducing piracy. Grokster's lawyer argued that the company should be judged by its current behaviour rather than what it did when it first set up. But this argument was dismissed as "ridiculous" by Justice David Souter. CEA boss Mr Shapiro thinks the case is the most important that the Supreme Court will hear this year. "It's about preserving America's proud history of technological innovation and protecting the ability of consumers to access and utilise technology," he said. The case has already been heard by two lower courts and both found in favour of the peer-to-peer networks. They ruled that despite being used to distribute millions of illegal songs, file-sharing could also be used to cheaply distribute software, government documents and promotional copies of music.

reconstruction:
The US Supreme Court mulls file-sharing liability. Judges at the Supreme Court have been hearing arguments and evidence for and against file-sharing services, grappling with complex issues of copyright in the digital age. The highest court in the land will now decide whether the producers of peer-to-peer file-sharing software can ultimately be held liable for the copyright infringement committed by their users.

Those defending the file-sharing technology argue that the aggressive way the entertainment industry wants to sue these companies could severely deter technological innovation. They concede, however, that file-trading firms had some responsibility for inducing copyright infringement by actively promoting the exchange of copyrighted material. This particular lawsuit, brought by 28 of the largest entertainment companies including major film studios and record labels, has raged through lower courts for several years. The plaintiffs argue that if the Supreme Court rules in their favour, they would be able to effectively shut down these businesses and potentially drive them into bankruptcy, thereby protecting their intellectual property.

However, if the rules governing file-sharing liability in this case merely acknowledge that a technology can have legitimate as well as illegitimate uses, then the music and movie industry would be forced to abandon their current pursuit of file-sharing companies. This is a crucial point of contention, with the tech industry emphasizing the dual-use nature of their software. Instead, the entertainment industry would then have to resort to targeting individual users who exploit peer-to-peer networks to obtain music and movies free of charge. The ongoing battle between the hi-tech sector and the entertainment industry has been a central issue for legal scholars and technologists alike.

The Supreme Court is currently hearing the consolidated cases of MGM v. Grokster and Arista Records LLC v. StreamCast Networks, Inc., putting the spotlight on these particular file-sharing services. This legal challenge has drawn significant attention, despite misgivings from some segments of the file-sharing community who fear potential shutdowns. A core tenet of the defense, reflecting the attitude of many in the technology industry, is the assertion that software products "are tools, that like any other tools, consumers and businesses can use for lawful or unlawful purposes." Asking the courts to second-guess how a technology would be put to use by its users, and to build in prohibitions on its potential future use, would severely stifle innovation, it is strenuously argued by tech advocates.

The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), a prominent civil liberties watchdog group, is actively involved in the case, representing StreamCast Networks, the maker of the Morpheus file-sharing software. Their involvement underscores the civil liberties implications of the ruling. This high-profile case raises questions of fundamental importance at the border between copyright protection and technological innovation, it is widely agreed. It echoes, for many legal observers, the landmark 1984 Supreme Court ruling in the Sony Betamax case, which held that Sony Corporation could not be held responsible for the copyright infringement that its video cassette recorder (VCR) was sometimes used for, as it also had substantial non-infringing uses.

Many in the technology sector hope that the judges will rule in favour of the peer-to-peer networks, upholding the precedent set by the Sony Betamax decision and allowing for the continued development of new technologies. Outside the Supreme Court building, a small band of supporters for the file-sharing companies were present as lawyers entered, some of them notably wearing "Betamax" t-shirts, drawing a direct parallel to the historic case. "We view the Betamax case as the Magna Carta for technology and for innovation that has flourished over the last 20 years," said Gary Shapiro, president and CEO of the Consumer Electronics Association (CEA), emphasizing the importance of a favourable ruling for future tech development.

During oral arguments, Justice Stephen Breyer alluded to Apple's popular iPod music player, noting that while it could be used to illegally duplicate copyrighted music, it had, on balance, been overwhelmingly beneficial to society by facilitating legitimate music consumption and management. He further suggested that while file-sharing technology can indeed be used to illegally copy music, it conceptually had "some really valuable uses" that were entirely legitimate. However, on Tuesday's hearing, it seems that a ruling on file-sharing might lean towards finding companies responsible for actively encouraging or inducing piracy, a legal concept known as 'inducement liability'.

Lawyers for the entertainment industry argued that the software in question should be judged on its current dominant use as a tool for widespread copyright infringement, rather than what it did or claimed to do when it first set out. This argument was reportedly echoed by Justice David Souter, indicating a possible shift in judicial perspective. The CEA boss reiterated his belief that "this is the most important Supreme Court case to hear this year for the technology industry," underscoring the potential long-term implications for innovation and consumer rights. "It's about America's tradition of technological innovation and protecting the ability of consumers to use technology in ways that benefit them, without undue restrictions," he added, framing the debate as a fundamental choice about the future of technology.

The case has already been through lower courts, specifically the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals, which found in favour of the file-sharing networks, applying the Sony Betamax standard. Supporters of file-sharing argue that in addition to being used to distribute millions of illegal songs, file-sharing could also be legitimately used to distribute open-source software, public domain documents, and promotional copies of music, among other lawful applications.

reconstruction:
Mobile phones are collecting like a mountain of lost property in the nation's lost and found offices. They are cheaper, smaller, and more common than ever, making them an indispensable part of modern life for millions. But this ubiquity also means they are just more likely to be left behind, misplaced, or forgotten. Over the past twelve months alone, more than 63,000 mobile phones have been lost in London's black cabs, according to a new study that highlights the growing problem of forgotten gadgets. This translates to an astonishing rate of about three phones being left behind every hour.

The problem isn't confined to just phones. Over the same period, the study found that 5,000 laptops and 5,800 PDAs, such as Palms and other handheld PCs, were also left in taxis. While the numbers paint a picture of forgetfulness, the good news is that many of these valuable items are eventually reunited with their beloved owners, thanks to the diligence of cab drivers and efficient lost property systems.

However, some lost items have more glamorous stories. Jemima Khan reportedly left her mobile phone, not just her purse, in a London taxi. After contacting the lost property office, she eventually asked for it to be returned to her, only for the driver who brought it back to turn out to be her then-partner, Hugh Grant, making for a rather star-studded reunion.

As technology has become increasingly intertwined with our daily routines, and as we trust more of our lives and personal information to these devices, we seem to be forgetting them in ever larger numbers. The trend is stark: the numbers of laptops left behind in taxis leapt by a significant 71% over the last year. This, by the way, serves as a crucial reminder and highlights the importance of regularly backing up personal data, a key recommendation from organisations such as the Association of Chief Police Officers and data security experts, who consistently stress the need for robust data backup strategies to prevent distress and inconvenience.

London's black cabs seem to be particularly prone to becoming unwitting repositories for lost gadgets. More items are left in London's iconic black cabs than in nine other major global cities combined, including New York, Paris, Munich, Tokyo, Copenhagen, and Sydney. These are the locations where the research on lost property and gadgets was carried out for comparison. By contrast, Danes were found to be the most disciplined; they were least likely to be losing phones, or being less likely to leave them in a cab, and notably more effective at retrieving them if they did. This suggests cultural differences in vigilance or perhaps more streamlined lost property services.

Top of the range phones and smartphones can store an enormous amount of personal information and valuable data. Often, they contain enough to hold a person's entire address book, an extensive history of calls and messages, contact details, personal photographs, and even financial information. Given how reliant people have become upon their mobile devices, it is a fair assumption that they carry them around everywhere they go, making their loss even more impactful. You could lose a fair chunk of your life in a lost phone, and this is not just because of the contact numbers stored on the phone, but because so much of your digital life and precious memories might not have been backed up anywhere else. Equally, a lost phone can sever connections, as it acts as a gateway to your social network, making it difficult for people to retrieve their friends' details or reconstruct their social circles if they need to.

This growing problem of losing expensive and data-rich gadgets partly explains the rise of alternative solutions, such as Retrofone, a company which lets you buy an old-school, simpler mobile phone to replace the tiny, fragile, and often very expensive smartphone one might have lost. These less complex devices offer a low-cost, low-stress alternative for those who simply need basic communication.

Britons' love affair with mobile phones has also led to the development of initiatives like the Mobile Equipment National Database (MEND). This database allows individuals to register their phone's unique IMEI number, which can be invaluable in helping to trace and return your device to you in the event of it being stolen or lost. The issue of phone loss and theft has serious implications beyond mere inconvenience. According to police statistics, a staggering 50% of all street robberies and other related offences now involve mobile phones, making them a prime target for criminals.

Millions of lost and found items are now logged in comprehensive databases which Transport for London and other authorities consult when trying to unite owners with their beloved gadgets. For cab drivers, finding a mobile phone in the back of their cab is often one of the more pleasant things many have found during their working lives, a sentiment shared when compared to some of the more bizarre items. Indeed, a recent survey of items left in taxis across the UK has revealed a truly eclectic range of unusual objects, including a harp, a pet hamster, a prosthetic leg, and even a large wedding cake. Such findings certainly add a touch of eccentricity to the everyday drama of lost property.

Jagran publishes the country's top-selling newspaper, the Hindi-language Dainik Jagran, which has been published continuously for 62 years. Independent News & Media, the Irish-based international media group, announced its full-year financial results would meet market expectations. The company reported increased revenue across all its major markets and regions, indicating strong performance. Group revenues were up over 10% year-on-year, the group said, with overall newspaper circulation expected to rise by almost 10% year-on-year across its various titles. This was also significantly helped by the positive impact of its new 'Metro' free daily editions in Ireland, where it has expanded successfully and gained market share. 'Indeed, 2004 has been an excellent year for the group overall,' said Sir Anthony O'Reilly, chairman and chief executive of Independent News & Media. 'Our aim is to be a leading player wherever we operate. I am confident we will have an equally strong year in 2005.' Sir Anthony O'Reilly, however, made no direct comment about the ongoing speculation that he recently held talks with potential buyers over a significant stake in the Daily Express newspaper. He has consistently denied suggestions that the Independent and Independent on Sunday newspapers were actively up for sale. It is understood that the recent free edition of the Independent, which has increased its circulation by 20% to 260,000 copies, has taken significant circulation from rival publications, with Associated Newspapers (publishers of the Daily Mail and Metro) being the most likely to have been affected. The Independent newspaper is expected to break-even only by 2006, according to company forecasts and internal projections.

reconstruction:
Asian share markets have shown resilience post-tsunami impact. Thailand has become one of the 10 Asian nations battered by giant waves at the weekend, and its economy's growth is now expected to slow to 5.7% in 2005, rather than the 6% forecast before the disaster hit its southern provinces. Concerns about the economic outlook remain. In part, this is because of the sheer scale of the devastation, and the ongoing challenges in delivering humanitarian aid and recovering the dead remain significant. But, in financial centres like Singapore and Hong Kong on Wednesday, analysts suggested that investors do not anticipate a major long-term impact on the wider regional economy. The stark disparity between investors, large firms, and the millions of individuals who lost their homes and livelihoods, seemed to suggest to some observers that many of the most affected areas – such as parts of Indonesia – were relatively less developed, and therefore the disaster would have little impact on 'blue-chip' companies, according to one report.

"Obviously there's a tremendous loss of life, and a lot of money is needed to clean up the mess, bury the dead and reconstruct infrastructure. But it's not necessarily a really big thing from a macroeconomic perspective," said ABN Amro chief Asian economist Eddie. Meanwhile, India's Bombay Stock Exchange inched slightly up on Wednesday. Optimism about economic prospects for 2005, surprisingly, drove the Indonesian stock market in Jakarta to a record high. In fact, many companies may even be benefiting from their listed exposure to the massive rebuilding efforts that will be required across tsunami-hit South East Asia.

In Sri Lanka, however, the economic outlook is more sombre, with some economists warning that as much as 1% of annual economic growth may be lost. The country's stock market has fallen about 5% since the weekend, though it is still 40% higher than at the close of 2004, indicating underlying strength. Thailand alone has lost an estimated 30bn baht (£398m; $768m) in potential revenue from tourism this year, according to its Tourism Minister Sontaya. In the affected provinces, he stated that the priority for funds will be for immediate relief, to be followed by extensive government-led reconstruction efforts. Thailand intends to allocate a similar amount - approximately 30bn baht - towards the rebuilding of vital infrastructure and tourist facilities. "It will likely take until well into the next year before visitors feel confident enough to return to Phuket and other southern provinces," said Naris Chaiyasoot, director general at the ministry's fiscal policy office. The sheer scale of reconstruction costs, however, could seriously impede economic recovery and potentially wipe out recent economic gains, according to a government spokesman.

"Our primary focus here is immediate recovery and long-term rebuilding," said the chief spokesman for the Maldives government. He estimated the economic damage to be in the tens of millions of dollars, a crippling blow to the small island nation. The Maldives has a relatively small gross domestic product of just $660m annually. "It wouldn't be at all surprising if the total cost of the damage far exceeds our entire annual GDP," he said grimly. "Over the past few years, we had made great progress in raising our standard of living and developing our tourism sector - something the United Nations had recognised. Now this progress can disappear, in a few short weeks," he lamented. Shaheed noted that in a single major island, where tourism is the absolute mainstay of the economy, damage could reach as high as $40m. Between 10 and 12 of the 80-odd tourist resorts in the archipelago, which were directly in the path of the waves, have suffered significant structural damage. Overall, international experts, including those from the World Bank, have found it extremely difficult to accurately assess the full long-term extent of the disaster's true economic impact across the region.

reconstruction:
**Tautou film tops prize nods despite eligibility row**

The French film *A Very Long Engagement*, starring Audrey Tautou, has received a leading 12 nominations for France's prestigious Cesar film awards, despite a recent legal battle over its eligibility. The epic romance, directed by Jean-Pierre Jeunet, who previously directed Tautou in the international hit *Amelie*, had faced a challenge that threatened its status as a fully "French" production.

A French administrative court had ruled that the film was "too American" in its financing to qualify for full state subsidies and to be eligible for certain French film festivals. This ruling, which was partially backed by a commercial court, sparked considerable debate within the French film industry. Associations of French producers had challenged director Jeunet's right to receive full state subsidies, arguing that the film had substantial American financial backing, specifically from Warner Bros.

Despite being entirely filmed in France and utilising predominantly French technicians, cast, and crew, the significant foreign investment prompted the legal dispute. However, the organisers of the Cesar awards, France's equivalent of the Oscars, swiftly modified their rules to ensure the acclaimed film could compete for the country's top cinematic honours.

Alain Terzian, president of the Academie des Arts et Techniques du Cinema, which organises the Cesars, said the new rules, which allow films of "French expression" to compete, were made three months prior to the court decision specifically concerning *A Very Long Engagement*, thereby enabling its participation.

*A Very Long Engagement* leads a strong field of contenders for the Best Film award. Other major nominees in this hotly contested category include Olivier Marchal's gritty police drama *36, Quai des Orfèvres*, Arnaud Desplechin's intricate family drama *Rois et Reine (Kings and Queen)*, Abdellatif Kechiche's critically acclaimed coming-of-age story *L'Esquive (Games of Love and Chance)*, and Christophe Barratier's surprise 2004 box-office hit *Les Choristes (The Chorus)*.

In the acting categories, nominations for Best Actor include Daniel Auteuil for his role in *36, Quai des Orfèvres*, Mathieu Amalric for *Rois et Reine*, and Benoit Poelvoorde for the comedy *Podium*. Philippe Torreton also received a nomination for his performance in *L'Equipier (The Teammate)*.

For Best Actress, Audrey Tautou is nominated for her leading role in *A Very Long Engagement*. She will compete against Emmanuelle Devos for *Rois et Reine*, and Karin Viard for *Le Rôle de sa vie (The Role of Her Life)*.

The Best Foreign Film category features a strong international line-up, including Michael Moore's controversial documentary *Fahrenheit 9/11*, Sofia Coppola's critically lauded *Lost in Translation*, Michel Gondry's surreal romance *Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind*, Alejandro González Iñárritu's intense drama *21 Grams*, and Pedro Almodóvar's evocative *Bad Education*.

The 30th Cesar awards ceremony will be held on Saturday, February 26th, at the historic Théâtre du Châtelet in Paris. This year, honorary Cesars will be presented to several international and French cinema figures. Hollywood actor Will Smith, known for blockbusters like *I, Robot* and *Independence Day*, will receive an honorary award, along with acclaimed American actress Susan Sarandon, and veteran French singer and actress Jeanne Moreau.

original: Hague 'given up' his PM ambition..Former Conservative leader William Hague says he will not stand for the leadership again, having given up his ambition to be prime minister...Mr Hague, 43, told the Daily Telegraph he would now find a life dominated by politics too "boring" and unfulfilling. Mr Hague, who stepped down after his party's 2001 election defeat, does not rule out a return to the front bench. He also told the paper he hopes to remain MP for Richmond, North Yorks, and start a family with wife Ffion. Mr Hague, who recently had published the biography of William Pitt the Younger, also said he wanted to continue writing books and speech-writing...He told the newspaper: "I don't know whether I will ever go back on to the front, but don't rush me." Asked if he would stand for the leadership again, Mr Hague replied: "No. Definitely not." reconstruction:
NHS waiting times in Wales are set to be significantly cut following a new announcement from the Welsh Assembly Government. Welsh Health Minister Jane Hutt has announced that no patient will have to wait more than 12 months for an inpatient or outpatient appointment by March 2006, significantly improving on an earlier target of 18 months for all types of treatment. She added that the maximum waiting time for an initial outpatient appointment would remain 12 weeks until March 2006, specifically underlining her commitment to maintaining short waiting times for initial consultations. The announcement comes as the latest waiting figures show a welcome drop. This commitment follows a current government guarantee scheme, previously introduced to ensure patients are offered the option of having their treatment outside Wales if their wait exceeds certain stipulated limits. However, concerns have been strongly raised by opposition parties and medical professionals about the potential resource implications for implementing these ambitious new targets in the New Year. In England, for comparison, the current target for treatment is seeing a patient within 18 weeks. Dr Richard Lewis, secretary of the British Medical Association (BMA) in Wales, commented that while the targets "would certainly help to ensure and deliver faster progress on reducing waiting list burdens", he also cautioned that more fundamental changes were urgently needed across the health service.

"However, much more concrete action needs to be taken on addressing waiting lists and waiting times because Wales still lags a long way behind England," he added. "Sufficient capacity needs to be built into the entire system to truly ensure Welsh patients receive a first-class service that meets their needs," he stressed. Independent health analyst Tony Field, from the Social Care Workforce Research Unit at King's College London, called the new targets "reasonably stretching" but ultimately achievable if proper investment and planning were put in place. On Wednesday, Ms Hutt had previously announced an extra £264m investment for health services right across Wales, specifically earmarked for reducing waiting times, improving key frontline services, and crucially, modernising staff pay and conditions to boost morale.

Ms Hutt emphasised that major achievements had already been made in cutting "unacceptably long treatment times over the last few years right across Wales. Now we need to build decisively on those reductions in the number of people waiting for treatment," she stated. She added that these new targets were specifically intended to ensure no-one in Wales waits more than a single year for either urgent treatment or an initial hospital appointment. However, Ms Hutt also pointed out during her statement: "But let us not forget that two-thirds of those currently waiting for treatment have waited less than six months, and these are certainly not the small proportion of patients in Wales who have been waiting too long; we are addressing the longer waits specifically."

Jocelyn Thomas, Plaid Cymru's shadow health spokesman, sharply criticised the announcement, saying: "'This new target is not the one she originally set in 1999, which was only met with the qualification that it applied to a second referral or a secondary waiting list.' 'This has clearly failed, minister. This is a failed policy and amounts to nothing more than a political fudge.'" For the Liberal Democrats, health spokeswoman Kirsty Williams described the new target as "woefully unambitious". "'It still leaves many patients waiting for up to two years'," she added, expressing concern. Conservative health spokesman Jonathan Morgan was equally critical of the government's approach, stating: "'They are simply spending more money but are plainly not cutting lists fast enough and moving patients efficiently through the system, leaving many in limbo.'"

The recent report by the Welsh Audit Commission indicated that public money is currently not being spent effectively across the NHS in Wales, and that's quite a serious criticism that needs to be addressed immediately. Meanwhile, the latest official figures released show the total number of people waiting more than 18 months has fallen by 9.8% across Wales. Statistics compiled to the end of December showed a significant drop since October from 785 to 708 patients. Furthermore, the number of patients waiting over 12 months has also fallen from 7,613 to 6,630, representing a commendable drop of 12.9%. Ms Hutt stated that these figures were "very encouraging" and demonstrated progress. Overall, there remain 305,775 people currently on a waiting list of some kind across Wales, a figure which is notably down from the 311,764 recorded last month, indicating some positive movement in overall waiting numbers.

original: Peer-to-peer nets 'here to stay'..Peer-to-peer (P2P) networks are here to stay, and are on the verge of being exploited by commercial media firms, says a panel of industry experts...Once several high-profile legal cases against file-sharers are resolved this year, firms will be very keen to try and make money from P2P technology. The expert panel probed the future of P2P at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas earlier in January. The first convictions for P2P piracy were handed out in the US in January. William Trowbridge and Michael Chicoine pleaded guilty to charges that they infringed copyright by illegally sharing music, movies and software. Since the first successful file-sharing network Napster was forced to close down, the entertainment industry has been nervous and critical of P2P technology, blaming it for falling sales and piracy. But that is going to change very soon, according to the panel...The music and film industries have started some big legal cases against owners of legitimate P2P networks - which are not illegal in themselves - and of individuals accused of distributing pirated content over networks. But they have slowly realised that P2P is a good way to distribute content, said Travis Kalanick, founder and chairman of P2P network Red Swoosh, and soon they are all going to want a slice of it. They are just waiting to come up with "business models" that work for them, which includes digital rights management and copy-protection standards...But, until the legal actions are resolved, experimentation with P2P cannot not happen, said Michael Weiss, president of StreamCast Networks. Remembering the furore around VCRs when they first came out, Mr Weiss said: "Old media always tries to stop new media. "When they can't stop it, they try to control it. Then they figure out how to make money and they always make a lot of money." Once the courts decided that the VCR in itself was not an illegal technology, the film studios turned it into an extremely lucrative business. In August 2004, the San Francisco-based US Court of Appeals ruled in favour of Grokster and StreamCast, two file-sharing networks. The court said they were essentially in the same position that Sony was in the 1980s VCR battle, and said that the networks themselves could not be deemed as illegal...P2P networks usually do not rely on dedicated servers for the transfer of files. Instead it uses direct connections between computers - or clients. There are now many different types of P2P systems than work in different ways. P2P nets can be used to share any kind of file, like photos, free software, licensed music and any other digital content. The BBC has already decided to embrace the technology. It aims to offer most of its own programmes for download this year and it will use P2P technology to distribute them. The files would be locked seven days after a programme aired making rights management easier to control. But the technology is still demonised and misunderstood by many. The global entertainment industry says more than 2.6 billion copyrighted music files are downloaded every month, and about half a million films are downloaded a day. Legal music download services, like Apple iTunes, Napster, have rushed into the music marketplace to try and lure file-sharers away from free content. Sales of legally-downloaded songs grew tenfold in 2004, with 200 million tracks bought online in the US and Europe in 12 months, the IFPI reported this week. But such download services are very different from P2P networks, not least because of the financial aspect...There are several money-spinning models that could turn P2P into a golden egg for commercial entertainment companies. Paid-for-pass-along, in which firms receive money each time a file is shared, along with various DRM solutions and advertiser-based options are all being considered. "We see there are going to be different models for commoditising P2P," said Marc Morgenstern, vice president of anti-piracy firm Overpeer..."Consumers are hungry for it and we will discover new models together," agreed Mr Morgenstern. But many net users will continue to ignore the entertainment industry's potential controlling grip on content and P2P technology by continuing to use it for their own creations. Unsigned bands, for example, use P2P networks to distribute their music effectively, which also draws the attention of record companies looking for new artists to sign. "Increasingly, what you are seeing on P2P is consumer-created content," said Derek Broes, from Microsoft. "They will probably pay an increasing role in helping P2P spread," he said. Looking into P2P's future, file sharing is just the beginning for P2P networks, as far as Mr Broes is concerned. "Once some of these issues are resolved, you are going to see aggressive movement to protect content, but also in ways that are unimaginable now," he said. "File-sharing is the tip of the iceberg."

Peer-to-peer (P2P) networks, and indeed their users, are on the verge of being exploited by hackers, according to a leading security expert. There have been several high-profile cases filed this year where malicious software, or malware, is found to be very specific to and spread through P2P. Dr. Phil Smith, head of P2P security at the Institute of Electronics, highlighted this pervasive threat in January, warning that new forms of malware specifically designed for P2P systems are easily handed in by unsuspecting users.

William Duffy and several other individuals have pleaded guilty to copyright infringement, and were subsequently fined heavily for illegal downloads. Since file-sharing systems first came into widespread common use, the entertainment industry has been at loggerheads with P2P proponents, feeling it has to fight vigorously for its very survival, according to the powerful Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA). Both the music and film industries have launched widespread legal campaigns against P2P networks – claiming they fundamentally facilitate illegal downloading – and individuals accused of illegally distributing copyrighted material over these networks.

But P2P is a powerful technology that's here to stay, asserts Travis Kalanick, co-founder and chairman of P2P firm Red Swoosh. 'The industry is going to want a piece of the action eventually,' he predicted. 'They are going to have to come up with innovative "business models" that truly work, which includes allowing consumers to easily access content and being far more flexible in their approach, with less focus on costly legal action, and more on creative experimentation,' Kalanick said. 'P2P is not just going away,' added Wayne Rosso, president of Grokster Networks. Remembering the early days around when Napster first came out, Rosso reflected: 'It was a truly great business model that just didn't work for the entrenched incumbents. They found out they couldn't make money off it directly and it quickly became a major source of contention and extensive legal battles.' The courts initially found P2P itself was inherently illegal, but later this stance turned into something extremely difficult to legally regulate and enforce.

In August 2004, a federal judge notably ruled in favour of P2P services Grokster and StreamCast, two companies vigorously sued by the entertainment industry. The court specifically stated it was not in a position to arbitrarily make a new law, and that the existing applicable law was the 1980s Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), which deemed illegal the act of creating technology that primarily facilitates copyright infringement. However, the judge emphatically noted that the services themselves were not inherently illegal, only their use for illicit purposes. P2P networks do not usually rely on a central server for operation. Instead, it allows individual computers to connect directly to each other, forming a distributed network. There are now many types of P2P systems that operate in fundamentally different ways. P2P can be used to share any type of digital data, from documents to free software, to music files, videos or other digital content.

The BBC decided the only way it could safely use P2P for content distribution was if it could distribute them in a carefully locked format. The content itself would be encrypted or otherwise locked to a specific playback programme, making it significantly easier to control its subsequent use and prevent unauthorised copying. The entertainment industry vigorously believes more than 2.6 billion copyrighted files are downloaded illegally every month, an alarming average of 86 million every single day. This massive scale of unauthorised sharing has pushed the industry into trying to find innovative ways to lure file-sharers away from free, and often illegal, downloads and towards legitimate paid services. Legally, the industry has started suing individual file-sharers in an unprecedented number of cases. In 2004, with over 200 million registered users online in some form of P2P network in the previous 12 months, the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) revealed this week that downloads of its members' music had dropped slightly, but illegal file-sharing still remained prevalent. But new services are continually emerging on P2P networks, offering at least the promise of a truly legal alternative to illegal file-sharing.

These enterprising companies hope that several new business models will turn P2P into a viable revenue stream for content creators. These include 'pay-per-download' models, 'subscription models', and various forms of advertising-supported file-sharing, where a small fee or portion of advertising pass-through revenue the firms receive when content is shared, or offering other integrated solutions and advertiser-funded applications, or indeed all of the above." "There are many different, often competing, approaches to for commoditising P2P," said Alex Mironovich, vice-president of technical operations at Overpeer, a company that actively monitors P2P networks for copyright infringement. "The major labels are certainly hungry to discover new revenue models," he added.

But users will not simply submit to the industry's inherently controlling nature on content they feel they have a right to access freely, or P2P users who want to share their own creative creations. The key is to create robust systems that allow for legitimate use of P2P for music and other media effectively, which means artists can get paid fairly and still sign up to such networks without fear of exploitation." "P2P is not just about piracy anymore," said Derek Burney, senior product manager at Microsoft. "We see a promising future where people will willingly pay in P2P, through micro-payments or subscriptions for access to high-quality content." Looking into P2P's immense potential, the ongoing challenge is to make it work financially for P2P networks and content owners, and that is indeed the focus of much current development. "Some of these proposed models are very exciting, others are part of an aggressive movement by the industry to fiercely protect its traditional revenue streams, in ways that are not always user-friendly or consumer-centric," he concluded. "The future of P2P, and indeed digital distribution, is still being written."

"If we lose 2-0 we are out but I think we can score in Germany - certainly one, and that will make all the difference." And the Liverpool boss is looking forward to having skipper Steven Gerrard, who was suspended for the Anfield leg, back for the return in Germany..."Steven Gerrard is a key player for us," said Benitez. "When he is on the pitch he makes everyone else play better - and the opposition pay special attention to him - which gives space for others. "Steven is one of the best players in the world, but I need a team that is not about just one player. There must be 11 players on the pitch all doing well."

"But it wasn't just about him; nobody's individual contribution mattered more than the collective effort of the entire team. We would have considered that a worthy outcome against formidable European opposition."

Benitez was also very happy with the performance of goalkeeper Jerzy Dudek, highlighting his crucial saves at key moments during the encounter. Discussing the significance of the 3-1 scoreline compared to other potential results, Benitez remarked: "A 2-0 lead, I think, would have been a good advantage, but that difference can still feel quite precarious. The 3-1, especially with three goals scored ourselves, provides a much more significant and comfortable difference for us heading into the return leg."

The Liverpool manager, whose team secured this valuable lead in front of their home fans during the Anfield leg, reiterated his consistent philosophy on the importance of teamwork and shared responsibility. "When a player is on the pitch and performs exceptionally well, he naturally draws the attention and focus of the opposition's defenders," Benitez explained further. "This in turn gives more space and opportunities to others, which is vital in these big games." At the Conservative Party conference in Brighton, party chairman Liam Fox officially opened proceedings, launching a robust defence of the Conservatives' own record in government. Mr. Fox set the tone for what was anticipated to be a combative conference, eager to present a united front against the government. All eyes were keenly watching for the impending address by party leader Michael Howard, who was due to speak later in the day, expected to outline a clear alternative vision for Britain's future and rally the party's grassroots ahead of the next general election.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Tony Blair, speaking separately, reaffirmed the Labour government's commitment to its long-term agenda, stating unequivocally that Labour would continue to deliver on its promises to the British people. He emphasised the progress made across various sectors, even while acknowledging the persistent challenges the nation faces. Blair's comments sought to project confidence and stability amidst the opposition's vocal critiques, underscoring the government's determination to press ahead with its reform programme.

However, the economic arguments remained central to the Conservative critique. Opposition figures pointed to what they described as a worrying trend, noting that Britain had slipped to 11th in the international economic league tables, a position they argued was unacceptable for a leading global economy. "Can we make something more of our economy?" one prominent Tory MP asked rhetorically, challenging the government's stewardship and demanding more ambitious growth strategies. The question underscored the core of their economic argument, stressing the need for fundamental changes to boost national competitiveness.

The Conservative critique continued, with speakers highlighting that if the country is truly to take on the great challenges of the modern era – those posed by fierce global competition, rapid technological advancement, and the imperative for sustainable growth – then decisive action on the economy is paramount. "We have got to do something substantive about the fundamental structure of the economy," another Conservative spokesperson asserted, calling for tax cuts, deregulation, and greater private sector involvement to spur innovation and job creation. This formed a key pillar of their platform, promising a revitalised economic approach.

In response, Labour robustly defended its fiscal plans, detailing its very comprehensive spending commitments for the forthcoming financial years. The government confirmed that substantial allocations, amounting to £12bn for 2007-2008, are specifically designed to provide essential public services with the stability and long-term basis they require. This investment, Labour insisted, was crucial for sustained improvements in areas like health and education. Labour officials further contrasted their record with the Conservatives' past performance, asserting that the previous Tory rule had been notoriously characterised by periods of "lost trust and abject failure." The historical context was invoked to bolster Labour's claim as the more reliable and competent party to lead the country through its present and future challenges.

The band, whose sound has been compared to seminal bands like The Cure and Joy Division, were heavily-tipped by the 110 impartial music industry experts and critics who participated in the extensive survey. The poll has a strong track record of identifying future stars; previous winners include the acclaimed indie-rock band Keane, who topped the Sound of 2004, and hip-hop sensation 50 Cent, who was named the Sound of 2003.

Other new acts making a significant impact on this year's list include London-based electro-punk stalwarts Bloc Party, who secured a strong second place. The Bravery first emerged on the New York club scene in 2003 and quickly gained a reputation for their energetic live shows, drawing comparisons to classic post-punk bands such as Echo & the Bunnymen and the more contemporary sounds of The Killers. They subsequently signed a major record deal in 2004 and their highly anticipated debut album is expected to be a huge hit upon its release in spring 2005, cementing their status as a band to watch. Lead singer Sam Endicott expressed his delight at the news, telling the BBC that the band felt "greatly honoured and excited" to be highlighted in the prestigious Sound of 2005 list.

"We don't want to be seen as a bunch of screaming jackasses just making noise," he added, emphasising their focus on songwriting and melody. Speaking about The Bravery, one of the top music critics involved in the tipping process, who regularly presents the 'In Pop' show on BBC Radio 6 Music, commented that the band possessed "the raw energy and rebellious spirit of The Clash, but with a thoroughly modern sensibility". "The ultimate proof, of course, will still be in the records they release and the live shows they play," he cautiously concluded.

Alison Howe, a BBC TV producer and key member of the panel that compiled the list, was effusive in her praise after catching one of their electrifying performances in London recently. "I wouldn't be surprised if they're headlining the main stage at Glastonbury within a couple of years," she enthusiastically predicted. "They have a truly great sound, fantastic hooks, and a really strong, infectious attitude when they play live," she added.

Early critical reviews of The Bravery's singles have consistently highlighted their distinctive sound, comparing them to "an unusually melodic version of The Killers, blended with the synth-pop flair of Duran Duran or the garage-rock coolness of The Strokes". The comprehensive survey was compiled from tips submitted by a diverse panel of 110 influential music industry experts. This esteemed panel included prominent BBC Radio 1 DJs, senior NME editors, Top of the Pops producers, Glastonbury Festival organiser Emily Eavis, and BBC Radio 6 Music presenter Colin Martin, among many others.

Beyond The Bravery and Bloc Party, the top 10 list also features grime artist Kano, who secured an impressive third place with his critically acclaimed debut record 'Home Sweet Home'. The talented young rapper from East London is frequently heralded as a Dr. Dre protege, indicating high hopes for his future. Meanwhile, the energetic Leeds indie group Kaiser Chiefs rounded out the top five, landing in fifth position. The Bravery now join a distinguished lineage of acts that have been catapulted into the spotlight by the annual Sound of poll. This includes former winners and highly-placed artists such as the emotive rock band Keane, indie darlings Franz Ferdinand, and soul sensation Joss Stone – many of whom were relatively unknown to the wider music-loving public when they first appeared on the prestigious list, demonstrating the poll's predictive power.

Boy, the success of acts like Scissor Sisters, whose self-titled debut album was widely named best album of 2004 by numerous music publications and critics, provides a strong benchmark for the kind of impact these tipped artists could achieve. The panel of experts rigorously assessed hundreds of potential candidates, ultimately selecting artists they believed were reaching for something truly innovative, something that would resonate profoundly with audiences and define the sound of the coming year. The specific criteria for inclusion in the Sound of 2005 list stipulate that acts must not have released an album prior to 1 January 2005. However, they are permitted to have released up to 20 singles or EPs, or to already possess a degree of public recognition from other media ventures, such as appearing in a popular television soap opera. All individual tips submitted by the panel were then meticulously counted and compiled to form the definitive top 10 list of artists to watch in the coming year.

original: Souped-up wi-fi is on the horizon..Super high-speed wireless data networks could soon be in use in the UK...The government's wireless watchdog is seeking help on the best way to regulate the technology behind such networks called Ultra Wideband (UWB). Ofcom wants to ensure that the arrival of UWB-using devices does not cause problems for those that already use the same part of the radio spectrum. UWB makes it possible to stream huge amounts of data through the air over short distances. One of the more likely uses of UWB is to make it possible to send DVD quality video images wirelessly to TV screens or to let people beam music to media players around their home. The technology has the potential to transmit hundreds of megabits of data per second. UWB could also be used to create so-called Personal Area Networks that let a person's gadgets quickly and easily swap data amongst themselves. The technology works over a range up to 10 metres and uses billions of short radio pulses every second to carry data. At the recent Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas products with UWB chips built-in got their first public airing...Currently, use of UWB is only allowed in the UK under a strict licencing scheme. "We're seeking opinion from industry to find out whether or not we should allow UWB on a licence-exempt basis," said a spokesman for Ofcom...Companies have until 24 March to respond. In April the EC is due to start its own consultation on Europe-wide adoption of UWB. The cross-Europe body for radio regulators, known as the European Conference of Postal and Telecommunications Administrations (CEPT), is carrying out research for this harmonisation programme. Early sight of the CEPT work has caused controversy as some think it over-emphasises UWB's potential to interfere with existing users. By contrast a preliminary Ofcom report found that it would be quite straight-forward to deploy UWB without causing problems for those that already use it. The Ofcom spokesman said it was considering imposing a "mask" or set of technical restrictions on UWB-using devices. "We would want these devices to have very strict controls on power levels so they can not transmit a long way or over a wide area," he said. Despite the current restrictions the technology is already being used. Cambridge-based Ubisense has about 40 customers around the world using the short-range radio technology, said David Theriault, standards and regulatory liaison for Ubisense. He said that UWB was driving novel ways to interact with computers. "It's like having a 3D mouse all the time," he said. He said that European decisions on what to do with UWB allied with IEEE decisions on the exact specifications for it would help drive adoption. Prior to its adoption as a way for gadgets and computers to communicate, UWB was used as a sensing technology. It is used to spot such things as cracks under the surface of runways or to help firemen detect people through walls.

reconstruction:
New Ultra-Wideband (UWB) wireless data networks, capable of transmitting vast amounts of data over short distances, could soon be available for widespread use in the UK. However, the government's approach to the way it will regulate these behind-the-scenes networks, which industry leaders believe are crucial for future digital innovation, has been called into question by leading technology firms and a global industry body.

The industry urgently wants to accelerate the arrival of UWB technology, which operates by using a previously underutilised part of the radio spectrum to stream immense amounts of data through the air. One of the most touted and likely uses for UWB is to enable seamless streaming of high-definition TV programmes, digital pictures, and music content around the home, letting people easily stream this rich media content to various devices without cables. The technology boasts the potential for speeds reaching up to hundreds of megabits per second, far exceeding current wireless standards for some applications. Beyond entertainment, UWB could also be used to create spontaneous, ad-hoc networks that let' gadgets and computers within close proximity easily swap large files and information between themselves without manual configuration.

The underlying technology works by sending a multitude of very short radio pulses, often millions of them every second, to create a very wideband signal that is robust and interference-resistant. Already, at the recent Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas, products with UWB chips built-in have started to appear and have got a significant amount of attention from both the media and potential manufacturers, indicating a strong market interest in this burgeoning technology.

Currently, UWB is not widely allowed to operate commercially in the UK due to regulatory uncertainties. 'In our opinion, we should absolutely allow UWB to operate on a licence-exempt basis, which would enable rapid deployment and innovation,' stated a spokesman for the UWB Forum, an international trade organisation representing the industry. The Forum has formally called for Ofcom, the UK's independent communications regulator, to make a definitive decision on UWB's status by 24 May. This move is also closely linked to a broader Europe-wide decision on the future regulatory framework of UWB, which is keenly anticipated by manufacturers across the continent.

Across Europe, the European Conference of Postal and Telecommunications Administrations (CEPT), the body responsible for harmonising spectrum use, is actively carrying out this crucial consultative work to determine common rules. Many voices within the industry strongly think UWB's existing regulatory framework is overly restrictive and is stifling innovation. A favourable Ofcom report, aligning with industry desires, would essentially allow UWB devices to go straight to market, enabling companies to deploy new products and services quickly without needing individual site-by-site licences, thus speeding up adoption.

However, an Ofcom spokesman voiced concerns about the potential for UWB devices to "mask" or interfere with existing licensed radio services, such as those used for emergency services or critical infrastructure. 'We want these devices to be very low power so they transmit over a very small area, thereby minimising any potential interference,' he explained, providing justification for the current, cautious restrictions. Despite these concerns, approximately 40 countries around the world already allow UWB for various short-range radio communications applications, highlighting a disparity in global regulations, said the UWB Forum. The Forum's chairman further elaborated on UWB's potential, stating that UWB was 'like a 3D radar in real-time, offering unprecedented spatial awareness capabilities,' he explained. A harmonised European decision on what frequencies and power levels to allocate for UWB would undoubtedly help to significantly drive adoption across the continent. Such wider adoption would pave the way for numerous other innovative applications and services, including revolutionary concepts such things as mapping the interior surface of rooms in precise detail to help people 'see' through walls, locating objects hidden behind solid obstacles, or even creating advanced gesture control systems for smart homes.

original: Halloween writer Debra Hill dies..Screenwriter and producer Debra Hill, best known for her work on the 70s horror classic Halloween, has died in Los Angeles aged 54...Hill, who had been suffering from cancer, co-wrote the 1978 film, which starred Jamie Lee Curtis as a babysitter terrorised by a psychopath. Directed by John Carpenter, it made over $60m (£31.3m) worldwide - a record for independent film at that time. Hill also worked with Carpenter on Escape From New York and The Fog. Born in New Jersey, Hill began her career as a production assistant and worked her way through the ranks, becoming an assistant director and second-unit director before she began collaborating with Carpenter...She was regarded by many as a pioneering woman in film, taking on jobs in the 70s that were more commonly taken by men. "Back when I started in 1974, there were very few women in the industry," she said in 2003. "I was assumed to be the make-up and hair person, or the script person. I was never assumed to be the writer or producer." "I took a look around and realised there weren't that many women, so I had to carve a niche for myself." Carpenter said that working with Hill was "one of the greatest experiences of my life". "The ground that she trailblazed in the beginning can now be followed by anyone. She was incredibly capable and talented," he said. Carpenter and Hill collaborated on a number of Halloween sequels, including Halloween II, Halloween: Resurrection and Halloween: The Curse of Michael Myers...Later in her career, Hill formed a production company with her friend Lynda Obst, making a string of hit films including Oscar nominee The Fisher King and teen comedy Adventures In Babysitting. Other films included the Stephen King adaptation The Dead Zone in 1983 and 1985's Clue, a comedy based on the board game Cluedo. In the 90s she pursued work in TV, although she was reunited with Carpenter in 1996 for Escape From LA, the sequel to Escape From New York. At the time of her death she was working on a film about the last two men pulled from the rubble of the Twin Towers following the 11 September terror attacks in 2001. She was also co-producing the remake of The Fog, which is due for release early next year.

reconstruction:
Debra Hill, the acclaimed film producer and screenwriter who co-wrote and produced the seminal 1978 horror classic Halloween, has tragically died at the age of 54. Hill, a pivotal figure in the creation of the iconic independent film, worked closely with director John Carpenter to bring to life the terrifying story of a babysitter terrorised by the relentless, masked killer Michael Myers. The film, which captivated audiences upon its release, went on to make over $60m (£31.3m) at the box office - an astounding figure that made it the most successful independent film of that year, launching a new era for horror cinema. Beyond Halloween, Hill's fruitful collaboration with Carpenter extended to other memorable films, including the atmospheric chiller The Fog (1980) and the dystopian action thriller Escape From New York (1981).

Born in Haddonfield, New Jersey, a location that would later inspire the setting for Halloween, Hill began her professional journey in the film industry as a diligent production assistant. She steadily climbed the ranks, gaining valuable experience as a unit publicist, before her groundbreaking partnership with Carpenter truly blossomed. Hill frequently recounted how many crucial creative and production decisions made during the 1970s were often spearheaded or commonly taken by her. "I started in the industry in 1974, with a very clear vision," she stated in an insightful interview in 2003. "It was not to make up hair, or be a publicist or a script supervisor. My singular ambition was to be a producer." She further elaborated, adding, "I looked around and realised there wasn't a pre-existing path for me to follow, so I simply had to carve my own way." Hill was widely recognised as one of the very few prominent female producers of her era, effectively paving the way for future generations. "The innovative template that she so boldly created at the very beginning of her career is now widely followed by almost anyone capable, independent, and ambitious," reflected a close colleague.

Carpenter and Hill continued their successful partnership on a number of direct sequels and related films to the original Halloween, further cementing the franchise's legacy. These included Halloween II (1981), Halloween III: Season of the Witch (1982), and Halloween: The Curse of Michael Myers (1995). Throughout her extensive and impactful career, Hill meticulously produced a string of other critically acclaimed and commercially successful films. Among these were the Oscar nominee The Fisher King (1991), the cult favourite comedy-mystery Clue (1985), and several Stephen King adaptations. Other significant films in her diverse portfolio included The Dead Zone (1983) and the action-comedy Big Trouble in Little China (1986). In the 1990s, her prolific output continued with films such as The Frighteners (1996) and The Adventures of Pluto Nash (2002).

At the unfortunate time of her passing, Debra Hill was deeply engrossed in a poignant documentary project, focusing on the last harrowing days of the World Trade Center amidst the rubble following the devastating September 11, 2001 attacks. In addition to this significant work, she was actively planning to produce a contemporary remake of The Fog, another of her earlier collaborations with John Carpenter, which was poised to be her very next cinematic project. Her untimely death leaves a void in the film community, but her enduring legacy in horror and independent cinema remains profoundly influential.

A potential acquisition would further consolidate Pernod Ricard's position in the global spirits market, adding significantly to its existing premium offerings. Allied Domecq's diverse portfolio includes popular brands such as Malibu rum, Mumm champagne, and Ballantine's whisky. Beyond spirits, Allied Domecq also owns a substantial casual dining and fast-food business, encompassing prominent brands like Dunkin' Donuts and Baskin-Robbins ice cream. original: Mac Mini heralds mini revolution..The Mac Mini was launched amid much fanfare by Apple and great excitement by Apple watchers last month. But does the latest Macintosh justify the hype? Let us get a few things dealt with at the outset - yes, the Mac Mini is really, really small, and yes, it is another piece of inspired Apple design. There is more to be said on the computer's size and design but it is worth highlighting that the Mac Mini is a just a computer. Inside that small box there is a G4 processor, a CD/DVD player, a hard drive, some other technical bits and bobs and an operating system. A DVD burner, wireless and bluetooth technologies can be bought at extra cost. And if you do not have a monitor, keyboard or mouse then you will need to purchase those also...It is not the fastest computer for the money but for under £400 you are getting something more interesting than mere technical specifications - Apple software. The Mac Mini comes bundled with Mac OS X, the operating system, as well as iLife 05, a suite of software which includes iTunes, web browser Safari, iPhoto, Garage Band and iDVD. original: India calls for fair trade rules..India, which attends the G7 meeting of seven leading industrialised nations on Friday, is unlikely to be cowed by its newcomer status...In London on Thursday ahead of the meeting, India's finance minister, lashed out at the restrictive trade policies of the G7 nations. He objected to subsidies on agriculture that make it hard for developing nations like India to compete. He also called for reform of the United Nations, the World Bank and the IMF...Palaniappan Chidambaram, India's finance minister, argued that these organisations need to take into account the changing world order, given India and China's integration into the global economy. He said the issue is not globalisation but "the terms of engagement in globalisation." Mr Chidambaram is attending the G7 meeting as part of the G20 group of nations, which account for two thirds of the world's population. At a conference on developing enterprise hosted by UK finance minister Gordon Brown on Friday, he said that he was in favour of floating exchange rates because they help countries cope with economic shocks. "A flexible exchange rate is one more channel for absorbing both positive and negative shocks," he told the conference. India, along with China, Brazil, South Africa and Russia, has been invited to take part in the G7 meeting taking place in London on Friday and Saturday. China is expected to face renewed pressure to abandon its fixed exchange rate, which G7 nations, in particular the US, have blamed for a surge in cheap Chinese exports. "Some countries have tried to use fixed exchange rates. I do not wish to make any judgements," Mr Chidambaram said. Separately, the IMF warned on Thursday that India's budget deficit was too large and would hamper the country's economic growth, which it forecast to be around 6.5% in the year to March 2005. In the year to March 2004, the Indian economy grew by 8.5%.
