reconstruction: Calls for fair rules to govern the global economy, which the G7 industrialised nations are increasingly being challenged by dynamic new economic powers from the developing world. In London on Thursday, ahead of their crucial annual summit meeting, the finance ministers of the G7 industrialised nations are expected to focus much of their attention on calls for greater fairness in international trade. The G7 nations will also be urged to take concrete steps to reduce their substantial agricultural subsidies that make it extremely difficult for developing nations like Brazil, India, and many African countries to compete in global markets. The President of the World Bank, James Wolfensohn, speaking on the eve of the G7 talks, urged leaders to give serious consideration to the demands of developing countries. He stated that 'we need a global trading system that is truly equitable for all nations, not just the wealthy ones.' He added that he is not against globalisation but believes it must be managed on 'fair and inclusive terms' for everyone. He went further, suggesting the G7, comprising only the wealthiest economies, should broaden its membership to include the wider G20 group of nations, arguing this would better reflect the economic realities and represent a much larger proportion of the world's population. Speaking at a separate meeting of developing nations' finance ministers also held in London, UK Chancellor Gordon Brown confirmed that he was floating a new proposal for an international fund designed specifically to help poorer countries cope with unexpected economic shocks and natural disasters, providing a much-needed financial safety net. "A flexible exchange rate regime, where currencies are allowed to float freely according to market forces, is vital for global economic stability," the Chancellor further emphasised. "It allows economies to adjust more smoothly to external pressures." Key emerging economies including India, Brazil, China, and Russia were invited to take part in an expanded session of the G7 meeting in London, underscoring their growing influence on the global economic stage. China's currency policy, which currently sees its yuan pegged at a fixed rate to the US dollar, has been a contentious issue. G7 finance ministers, in the past, have repeatedly called for Beijing to allow its currency to appreciate, arguing that its undervaluation gives Chinese exports an unfair price advantage, contributing to a significant surge in Chinese exports into their markets. "It is evident that some countries have historically tried to use their currency valuations as a deliberate tool to gain an advantage in international trade. However, I am not making any judgements about any particular nation at this moment," Mr Brown stated diplomatically. Separately, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) released its latest assessment of the Chinese economy, highlighting that its current account surplus was projected to reach an exceptionally high 6.5% of its Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in 2005. This followed an impressive economic performance in 2004, when the Chinese economy had expanded by 8.5%.

reconstruction:
The initial estimates for the insurance industry's exposure to the devastating Asian tsunami are starting to emerge, with predictions suggesting total claims could reach up to **'$10bn'**. Authorities across the affected region **have sought to calm fears** and coordinate relief efforts in the wake of the powerful **earthquake** and subsequent tidal waves that have tragically claimed the lives of **at least 38,000** people across South East **Asia**. Major global insurers and reinsurers are now assessing the unprecedented scale of the disaster. **Swiss Re**, one of the **world's biggest** reinsurance companies, has confirmed it will **have exposure** to claims arising from the multiple **disasters**. However, insurance payouts **are likely to be considerably lower than** the total economic damage, particularly in many affected **countries** where **many people do not have** adequate insurance **cover**, experts **said**. In a widely reported initial assessment, **Munich Re**, the world's largest reinsurer, **has said** that total industry **claims** for the catastrophe are **likely to be around $10bn (£5.17bn)**. Separately, **Swiss Re** indicated that its own specific **cost would be in the low to mid three-digit million** dollar range, according to reports in the **Financial Times**. Meanwhile, **Munich Re**, **the world's** largest **reinsurance company**, has itself estimated a net loss of approximately **100m euros (£70m; $136m)** from the catastrophe, a figure that is still subject to change as more information becomes available from clients.

**At least 10 countries have been** severely affected by the tsunami, including **Sri Lanka**, Indonesia, Thailand, India, and **the Maldives**. The **region's many tourists are expected to be among the main claimants**, with personal injury, property damage, and travel disruption leading to a significant number of claims. Reinsurers like Swiss Re typically have **exposure to** a broad range of related policies, including marine, property, **"personal accident, and travel risks"**. A **spokeswoman for Swiss Re** indicated that this event would rank as 'one of their **fifth-costliest natural catastrophes**' in the company's history, yet it would still be considered 'in the **low-end of** their estimates' for a major annual loss. She further explained that the **company has** a remaining capacity of **300 million euros (£281m; $400m) to cover** natural catastrophe losses for the current year, **after accounting for four major hurricanes** that struck the **US** earlier in the season. This indicates that while significant, the tsunami losses are manageable within their existing provisions.

However, **insurers are quick to stress that their payouts will not reflect the full economic cost of the damage and destruction** witnessed in the region. Many claims **are still coming through**, and the assessment process is complex. 'These **are, of course, just early** estimates, as the claims notification and assessment **processes are still very much underway**,' said one industry expert. '**Unlike the** situation with hurricanes, where **you have** established wind storm **models** to help with forecasting losses, **you don't have a similar model** for tsunamis, making the evaluation process more challenging.' Meanwhile, Lloyd's of London chairman, Lord Levene, had earlier **anticipated that his** market's total **claims then** would stand **at $640m**. European insurance giant **Allianz, Europe's largest insurer, said it did not yet know how large its claims would be**, but stated that the devastating **tidal wave was unlikely to significantly impact its** overall profitability or earnings targets. **Financially, they** added, **they** are generally in a strong position, having maintained **heavy** reserves for such events, and many **insurers also do** set aside **a proportion of their profits into special funds** to absorb major catastrophe losses. 'The **insured damage will represent a mere fraction** of the true economic **worth in** terms of infrastructure, livelihoods, and rebuilding costs **in these affected countries**,' commented **Jay** Wason, an analyst at **Prudential insurance** Group, highlighting the vast gap between insured and uninsured losses.

Crucially, **many countries** in the region, **including** Indonesia, Thailand, and **the Maldives**, **buy little or no catastrophe insurance** for public infrastructure or private assets. This significantly contributes to the large disparity between insured losses and total economic damage. The **World Bank estimates the overall economic damage to the affected region, including** Indonesia, **India, Sri Lanka**, and Thailand, could be **about $5bn (£2.6bn)**, a figure **similar to** the economic impact of Hurricane Mitch in **Central America**. Hurricane **Mitch** killed approximately **10,000 people** and caused economic damage **of $10bn** in **1998**. 'However, the scale of the human tragedy, and the number **of individuals involved** in this disaster, is far greater,' said a spokesperson for the UN. '**We are talking of very poor societies, fishermen and farmers, who have lost everything that they have**. There are hundreds of **thousands** of people displaced and in need of urgent aid,' stated **Jan** Egeland, UN Under-Secretary-General **for** Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator. 'The long-term recovery **of their** communities **may take a generation**.' For individuals concerned about their personal losses, **The Association of British Insurers (ABI) warned that home insurance policies would not normally cover** damage to **overseas possessions, but stressed the importance of checking travel policies** for specific coverage related to personal belongings, accident, or medical expenses.

original: Have hackers recruited your PC?..More than one million computers on the net have been hijacked to attack websites and pump out spam and viruses...The huge number was revealed by security researchers who have spent months tracking more than 100 networks of remotely-controlled machines. The largest network of so-called zombie networks spied on by the team was made up of 50,000 hijacked home computers. Data was gathered using machines that looked innocent but which logged everything hackers did to them...The detailed look at zombie or 'bot nets of hijacked computers was done by the Honeynet Project - a group of security researchers that gather information using networks of computers that act as "honey pots" to attract hackers and gather information about how they work. While 'bot nets have been known about for some time, estimates of how widespread they are from security firms have varied widely...To gather its information the German arm of the Honeynet Project created software tools to log what happened to the machines they put on the web. Getting the machines hijacked was worryingly easy. The longest time a Honeynet machine survived without being found by an automatic attack tool was only a few minutes. The shortest compromise time was only a few seconds. The research found that, once compromised machines tend to report in to chat channels on IRC servers and wait instructions from the malicious hacker behind the tools used to recruit the machine. Many well-known vulnerabilities in the Windows operating system were exploited by 'bot net controllers to find and take over target machines. Especially coveted were home PCs sitting on broadband connections that are never turned off...The months of surveillance revealed that the different 'bot nets - which involve a few hundred to tens of thousands of machines - are used for a variety of purposes. Many are used as relays for spam, to route unwanted adverts to PC users or as launch platforms for viruses. But the research team found that many are put to very different uses. During the monitoring period, the team saw 'bot nets used to launch 226 distributed denial-of-service attacks on 99 separate targets. These attacks bombard websites with data in an attempt to overwhelm the target. Using a 'bot net of machines spread around different networks and nations makes such attacks hard to defend against. One DDoS attack was used by one firm to knock its competitors offline. Other 'bot nets were used to abuse the Google Adsense program that rewards websites for displaying adverts from the search engine. Some networks were used to abuse or manipulate online polls and games. Criminals also seem to be starting to use 'bot nets for mass identity theft, to host websites that look like those of banks so confidential information can be gathered and to peep into online traffic to steal sensitive data. "Leveraging the power of several thousand bots, it is viable to take down almost any website or network instantly," said the researchers. "Even in unskilled hands, it should be obvious that 'bot nets are a loaded and powerful weapon."

Is your PC part of a global network of compromised computers? More than a million machines have already been hijacked by cybercriminals to launch various attacks and send vast quantities of spam. This huge number of infected machines was recently uncovered by dedicated security researchers, with some active botnets continuously operating for more than 100 days. The largest single 'zombie' team identified in their research was made up of an astonishing 50,000 computers, with the criminals using them to carry out a wide array of illicit activities.

A deeper look at one such 'botnet' was diligently carried out by a specialized group of researchers who employed sophisticated honeypots to attract and carefully gather information about exactly how they operated. They were thus able to gain crucial insights about these nefarious networks, which are often hidden from public view, by collecting data from widely distributed compromised sources.

To gather specific, actionable information, a German arm of the security firm installed discreet monitoring software onto machines they had successfully compromised. The infected machine, without the legitimate user being aware of the intrusion, effectively became a powerful tool for the botnet operators. Once a machine was thoroughly compromised, it would secretly report back to its designated IRC (Internet Relay Chat) servers to receive updated instructions, along with any additional malicious tools to be deployed on that machine. Many of these sophisticated bots are well-known to specifically infect Windows machines by exploiting unpatched software vulnerabilities and frequently using various social engineering techniques to trick users. The vast majority of these infections were found on consumer home broadband connections, which were then unknowingly turned into active participants in criminal enterprises.

Different types of botnets typically involve thousands of individual machines – these are then used for a wide variety of nefarious tasks. They can be employed to re-route PC traffic, act as robust spam launch platforms, or indeed be put up for rent on highly active underground forums for other criminals to use.

During the extensive period of study, these observed 'botnets' launched an astonishing 226 denial-of-service (DoS) attacks, an alarming 99 of which were specifically designed to completely overwhelm their targeted servers and websites. Using a distributed botnet, criminals can launch attacks of such a large scale that they are incredibly difficult for individuals, smaller firms, or even nations to adequately defend against. Many of the reported DDoS attacks were seemingly commissioned by rival firm competitors, while others were used for outright extortion or simply to cause widespread disruption. These malicious networks were also frequently used to manipulate online polls and surveys, or to spread vast amounts of spam or politically motivated disinformation. Furthermore, cybercriminals are increasingly starting to rent out their botnets for mass identity theft campaigns, to host large databases of stolen confidential information, and to surreptitiously inject malicious content into unsuspecting online traffic streams.

Looking at the intricate operations of these bots, it is abundantly clear to anyone paying close attention that this is a rapidly growing and constantly evolving threat to cybersecurity. It should be obvious that these 'botnets' are becoming ever more sophisticated, increasingly loaded with new and dangerous features, and consequently ever more powerful.

Twelve terror suspects currently at home pose a potential risk to national security, Home Secretary Charles Clarke has warned. The Law Lords recently ruled that the indefinite detention of 12 foreign nationals without trial, including those held in Belmarsh prison in London, and the radical cleric Abu Qatada in Milton Keynes, was unlawful. The 12 individuals directly affected by the landmark ruling included nationals originally from countries such as Tunisia and Jordan. The government's anti-terror laws, which were controversially introduced after the 11 September attacks in the US, allowed for the indefinite detention of foreign nationals without charge or trial, a measure which the Law Lords determined was a breach of fundamental human rights laws.

Mr Clarke told The Times newspaper in an interview: "I think our new proposals are yet to come." He explained that it was a diplomatic strategy being actively pursued by the Foreign Office as "a matter of urgent national security". Mr Clarke said he had sought and received an "understanding" with foreign governments that terror suspects deported from Britain would not be subjected to torture or ill-treatment on their return. He added: "I am actively seeking a comprehensive solution to the Law Lords' judgement on deportations, and where deportations are possible, they will significantly help us to achieve that objective."

The suspects, many of whom are accused mainly with involvement in international terrorism and links to al-Qaeda, are now effectively under house arrest. A senior BBC political correspondent observed that "the main problem the Home Office is currently facing is how to effectively deal with this immediate situation, and crucially, how to deal with it in the long-term future." He elaborated: "He wants to get these individuals off the streets and secure convictions. That means looking at how you can actually secure convictions in this country, perhaps by allowing intercept evidence, or phone tapping, to be used in court, something currently not permitted," he explained. "The initial problem for the government is to see how this new approach is going to be implemented and how effective it will prove to be, especially given that the Liberal Democrats will be pushing vigorously for a sunset clause when the anti-terror laws come up for renewal in March."

She said French, Jordanian and Nigerian nationals would be the first seafarers to get the new ID cards since their countries have already ratified the convention. It aims to combat international terrorism whilst guaranteeing the welfare the one million seafarers estimated to be at sea. Europe asks for international help as its leaders demand other major economies adjust their currencies to ease the mounting pressure on the euro. Concerns are mounting in the Eurozone that the strong single currency is harming export competitiveness, thus limiting the upside for economic recovery across the bloc. While European nations tackle domestic issues like rising house prices and persistent budget deficits, a global move towards currency revaluation is seen as paramount for stability. European officials argue that Europe has largely reformed its own economies, and now Asia must contribute more substantially to global economic rebalancing.

China's yuan is widely seen as the central problem. Critics argue its fixed exchange rate policy distorts international trade; in 2004, an estimated 35% of global commerce was believed to operate under such inflexible currency policies. French Finance Minister Hervé Gaymard and German Minister Hans Eichel have been particularly vocal in strongly advocating for greater currency flexibility from Beijing.

This intense rhetoric, reflecting significant economic pressure felt by several nations, is unlikely to ease at the upcoming G7 finance ministers and central bank governors' meeting later this week. Ministers will likely address the issue directly and seek a coordinated approach to global currency imbalances.

On Tuesday, the euro was trading higher against the dollar, reaching 1.3040 euros. The Japanese yen, meanwhile, strengthened to 102.975 against the dollar by 0730 GMT. Markets keenly await the G7 outcomes on currency policy and any potential shifts.

The woman, whose legal action is aimed at HP's US operations, states that a specific microchip embedded inside the ink cartridges effectively renders them useless, either by requiring a reset or by actively preventing users from refilling them, even when a substantial amount of ink may still be present within the reservoir.

The legal complaint, which seeks to gain class-action status on behalf of many affected consumers, was originally launched against US HP in February 2001. HP, widely recognised as one of the world's leading manufacturers of computer printers, is accused of intentionally designing its proprietary cartridges with these sophisticated electronic chips. These chips, the lawsuit claims, are programmed to deactivate the cartridge at a predetermined usage threshold or a set time, irrespective of the actual volume of ink remaining inside. This mechanism, it is argued, compels users to frequently purchase costly new replacement cartridges, even if their existing ones are not genuinely empty.

"This systematic design dually and prematurely renders a cartridge of no further use, even when not genuinely depleted of ink," the detailed legal document asserts. The lawsuit is seeking substantial financial damages and appropriate compensation for all consumers who have been negatively impacted by these alleged anti-consumer practices. While a single basic ink refill can occasionally be found for as little as £34, the cumulative and ongoing expenditure on replacement cartridges for a typical user could surprisingly accumulate to as much as £1,700 over an 18-month period, according to a significant report published by Computeractive Magazine last year.

A fresh delay in the implementation of controversial EU laws concerning the patenting of computer software has been announced. The proposed legislation, which has been the subject of intense lobbying and public debate, has a controversial basis and has not been able to gain final approval.

This fresh delay came after Polish concerns that the law, at this time, was not appropriately framed and would and could impact open-source software development negatively across the continent. A European Commission spokesperson confirmed the postponement, stating that further discussions were needed to address member states' concerns.

'There were some significant sticking points regarding the scope and definitions of patentable inventions,' a source close to the negotiations told the BBC. 'We're still working on the finer details to ensure a balanced outcome for all stakeholders.' They added that there would be no more immediate discussion on the directive for the time being, largely because there was significant concern over the broad scope of the proposals and how it could profoundly affect the future of computer innovation and software development. Its fundamental challenge is the interpretation of the Directive on Computer-Implemented Inventions, which deals specifically with the complex area of computer-patenting.

The European Union has consistently reaffirmed its backing for this legislation, arguing that it is essential for the single market. The EU says the directive is crucial to bring in a harmonised and clear approach to software patents across member states, thereby fostering innovation and protecting intellectual property rights. However, its proposals have caused some considerable debate among critics, including open-source advocates, academics, and many small to medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) who fear it could stifle competition and innovation.

In the US, by contrast, the patenting of computer-implemented methods is widely permitted, reflecting a different legal tradition and a more expansive view of what constitutes an invention. This US model often holds a broader interpretation of what constitutes a patentable invention, encompassing many software-related concepts.

Critics in Europe, however, say a similar broad approach would severely hurt small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and independent developers, which often do not have the legal or financial resources of larger companies to navigate complex patent disputes. They also argue that such laws could lead to a proliferation of trivial patents, hindering genuine innovation and forcing developers to pay royalties for basic functionalities. Proponents of the directive, primarily from large corporations and patent offices, say the current European law, which is a patchwork of national interpretations, does not adequately protect many software inventions, leading to legal uncertainty and making it difficult for companies to recoup the significant research and development capital spent on creating new technologies. They argue that without clear patent protection, companies are less likely to invest in cutting-edge software development.

The UK is stepping up its efforts to help victims of the Asian tsunami, announcing a significant commitment of military personnel and equipment. "We have offered a company of 120 personnel to assist the relief efforts," a spokesman for Downing Street said. The offer comes as international aid agencies struggle to deliver vital supplies, with Indonesia bearing the brunt of the catastrophe.

The troops would be from the 2nd Battalion Royal Gurkha Rifles, a highly regarded unit known for its expertise in challenging environments. They will provide crucial logistical and engineering support. "They would have the full co-operation of the Indonesian government in Aceh, where much of the devastation is concentrated," a government spokesman in Jakarta said. This underscores the growing military involvement in the humanitarian operation.

Discussions highlighted the immense difficulties faced by aid organisations on the ground. Mr Stott made it clear that a particular logistical challenge in Indonesia, stemming from severe infrastructure damage, was something the Gurkhas would be able to assist with using their specialised skills. The remote and inaccessible nature of many affected areas has hampered earlier attempts to deliver aid effectively.

A Ministry of Defence spokesman further elaborated on the UK's commitment, stating: "Following today's meeting with the Indonesian authorities, the UK has formally offered the Indonesian Army a company from the 2nd Battalion Royal Gurkha Rifles, comprising 120 personnel, and two helicopters." These helicopters are critical for accessing isolated communities and airlifting supplies to cut-off areas. In addition to personnel and helicopters, more ships and aircraft have also been committed to the humanitarian effort, bolstering the UK's presence in the disaster zone. These assets are already en route or being prepared for deployment.

Indonesia was the country most severely affected by the Boxing Day tsunami, with official estimates of between 94,000 and 140,000 deaths, although the true figure is feared to be much higher. The scale of destruction, particularly in the northern province of Aceh, is almost unimaginable. "We need to assist in scaling up the relief effort rapidly, particularly in the area of the coast at the capital, Banda Aceh, where entire towns have been obliterated," he said. "We have a significant amount of equipment which we need to get in place in order to make a truly meaningful impact on the ground." It compares to 27 million, or 50%, of the UK, who are not currently online. The idea that the digital divide will evaporate with time is "wishful thinking", the report concludes...The study calls on the government and telecoms industry to come up with new ways to lure those that have been bypassed by the digital revolution. Although the percentage of Britons without home access will have fallen slightly, those that remain digital refuseniks will miss out on more, the report suggests. As more and more everyday tasks move online and offline services become less comprehensive, the divide will become more obvious and more burdensome for those that have not got net access, it predicts...The gap between "have-nets" and "have-nots" has been much talked about, but predictions about how such a divide will affect future generations has been less discussed. BT set out to predict future patterns based on current information and taking account of the way technology is changing. Optimists who predict that convergence and the emergence of more user-friendly technology will bridge the digital divide could be way off mark, the report suggests. "Internet access on other devices tends to be something taken up by those who already have it," said Adrian Hosford, director of corporate responsibility at BT. Costs of internet access have fallen dramatically and coverage in remote areas have vastly improved over the last year but the real barrier remains psychological. "There is a hard rump of have-nots who are not engaging with the net. They don't have the motivation or skills or perceive the benefits," said Mr Hosford...As now, the most disadvantaged groups are likely to remain among low income families, the older generation and the disabled...Those on low incomes will account for a quarter of the digital have-nots, the disabled will make up 16% and the elderly nearly a third by 2025, the report forecasts. Organisations such as BT have a responsibility to help tackle the problem, said Mr Hosford. The telco has seen positive results with its Everybody Online project which offers internet access to people in eight deprived communities around Britain. In one area of Cornwall with high levels of unemployment, online training helped people rewrite CVs and learn skills to get new jobs, explained Mr Hosford. Such grassroot activity addressing the specific needs of individual communities is essential is the problem of the digital divide is to be overcome, he said. "If we don't address this problem now, it will get a lot worse and people will find it more difficult to find jobs, education opportunities will be limited and they'll simply not be able to keep up with society," he said. The Alliance for Digital Inclusion, an independent body with members drawn from government, industry and the voluntary sector has recently been set up to tackle some of the issues faced by the digital refuseniks.

By 2025, up to 40% of the UK's population could be without even basic access to the internet, or the fundamental skills to use it effectively, according to a new and comprehensive study. Around 23 million people will struggle to access a wide range of essential digital services such as online banking, applying for jobs, and even basic communication through telecoms, warns BT, who commissioned the research. This figure is projected to rise rapidly, to 27 million, or 50% of the entire population, if current trends continue unabated, leaving a huge segment of society effectively cut off from modern life and truly online. This growing "digital divide", the report concludes, poses a significant threat to social equality and economic growth. The study highlights the increasing disparity between those who are comfortable and proficient in the digital realm, and those who are excluded by a lack of access or skills. Although many people believe that technology is inherently inclusive and that everyone will eventually get online, the report suggests that the opposite is true for a significant proportion of the population. As society relies on more tasks being performed digitally, the more disadvantaged those without these skills will become, not less, it predicts.

The persistent gap between "haves" and "have-nots" in the digital sphere has been much talked about, but the profound impact this will have on future generations is far less discussed. BT carried out this in-depth research, based on an extensive analysis of its own customer data and a robust account of demographic shifts and technological advancements, providing a stark look at the trajectory the nation is heading in this way.

Optimists often predict that the rapid advancement of technology and the increasing prevalence of more user-friendly interfaces will bridge the digital gap naturally over time, but the BT report suggests this view is overly simplistic and dangerously complacent. "Merely providing broadband access is not sufficient; many other complex factors and societal trends must be acknowledged and solutions actively taken by those with influence and foresight," said Gavin Hosford, director of corporate social responsibility at BT.

"While internet coverage in the UK might have seen significant improvements year on year, the real challenge for the nation lies beyond mere infrastructure. There is a growing segment of have-nots who either don't have the fundamental motivation or skills necessary to fully engage with, or even to properly perceive the tangible benefits of, being online and participating in the digital world," said Mr Hosford, speaking at the launch of the report.

Those most at risk of being left behind are likely to be those with low incomes, older members of society, and individuals with disabilities or specific learning needs. Those on low incomes, who are digitally excluded, could make up 16% of the entire working-age population and a staggering third of the elderly population by 2025, potentially exacerbating existing inequalities across the country, the report suggests.

This alarming trend is seen as a significant barrier to social mobility and economic prosperity for the UK as a whole, the report said. However, there have been some very encouraging and positive developments seen in communities around the country, demonstrating that local initiatives can make a real difference. "For example, one successful project involves pairing mentors with individuals needing basic IT training, CVs preparation, and job application skills," Mr Hosford explained. "Such grassroot level initiatives are absolutely crucial to helping the country collectively overcome this pressing societal challenge."

"If we don't address this growing societal problem, it will not only lead to greater inequality but will also mean a lot of people are excluded from the modern workforce, while at the same time more jobs will be created that require digital proficiency, but they won't have the fundamental skills to take them up," he said, underscoring the urgency of the situation. The Department for Digital Inclusion, an important governmental body established to address these very issues, has recently acknowledged the scale of the challenge and outlined its strategy to boost digital literacy nationwide.

Security experts have clarified that 'Skulls' is not a traditional virus that self-replicates. Instead, it operates as a Trojan horse program. Experts have said that users would have to go through a complex and time-consuming process to remove it, which often includes a factory reset or reformatting of the phone's memory. This ensures the complete eradication of the malicious software and the restoration of full functionality, though it can lead to the loss of personal data if not backed up.

There is concern that the spread of this program is likely to travel to other devices if users share infected files or download content from the same compromised sources. The virus lab at leading mobile security firm F-Secure has been actively investigating the 'Skulls' program, confirming the threat specifically impacting the 7610. Users will need to diligently follow removal instructions to restore their phones to working order again.

The production figure for 2003 totalled 11.49 million tonnes, and the government has been encouraging farmers to use fertilizers and other modern methods for improved production. Nevertheless, 2.2 million people across the country still need urgent food assistance.

The calculated emergency food requirements for 2005 stand at 387,500 tonnes of grain. On top of this general requirement, an additional 89,000 tonnes of food is specifically required for vulnerable groups like severely undernourished children and lactating mothers.

In various regions of Ethiopia, prolonged drought conditions have severely damaged crops and wells have completely dried up. As a consequence, an estimated 965,000 people are currently facing severe food shortages and require immediate food aid. The Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) is therefore calling for international assistance.

The FAO suggests that the best way to purchase cereals is as much as possible from domestic markets and local producers. This not only ensures efficient distribution but also supports the local economy, says the latest assessment from the Global Information and Early Warning System on Food and Agriculture. Agriculture in Ethiopia remains the backbone of the economy, accounting for 45% of the country's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and employing over 80% or even more of the total population.

Mexican director Alfonso Cuarón, known for his critically acclaimed work on "Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban," has signed a multi-year deal with Hollywood studio Warner Brothers, trade magazines reported this week.

Cuarón, who masterfully directed "Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban," a film released in 2004, was extensively lauded for successfully infusing a more profound, darker, and emotionally mature tone into what was already a globally recognized mainstream franchise.

"We really wanted a director with his unique vision for Harry," a studio source reportedly commented. "His other highly regarded works include his seminal 2001 Spanish-language drama titled "Y tu mamá también," which compellingly portrays two adolescent boys who embark on an unexpected road trip adventure with an older, somewhat mysterious and attention-grabbing woman."

This particular critically acclaimed film garnered numerous prestigious awards and significant nominations, notably an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Screenplay, an honor he shared with his talented brother Carlos Cuarón, his frequent writing partner and collaborator. Cuarón's remarkable artistic flexibility and his consistent ability to effectively transcend both cultural and linguistic barriers are widely considered a defining hallmark of his remarkably diverse and impactful filmography.

"This exceptional level of distinct artistry, and the proven capacity to successfully craft such compelling and varied narratives across widely different genres and diverse cultures, is truly a rare and invaluable talent," stated Mr. Toby Emmerich, who serves as the chairman of Warner Bros. Pictures Group, in an official comment regarding this new exclusive deal. Cuarón's impressive body of earlier work also notably includes the beloved 1995 Warner Brothers family classic, "A Little Princess."

This particular film beautifully tells the poignant story of a resilient young girl who is abruptly sent to a stern boarding school, notably located in New York, after her father, having been widowed, is tragically presumed dead. Despite the vastly different and more mature nature of his previous critically acclaimed work like "Y tu mamá también," Cuarón was initially perceived as a somewhat surprise choice to helm and direct the third installment of the Harry Potter film series. However, his distinctively darker and more nuanced interpretation of the globally beloved book was overwhelmingly praised by both astute critics and devoted fans alike, ultimately reinvigorating and deepening the entire series.

A new economic cooperation and deal has been forged between Egypt and Israel. In a significant development of relations in both Egypt and Israel, the two countries have officially ratified an agreement, allowing Egyptian goods greater access to the Israeli market.

The new trade protocol, signed in Cairo, is expected to significantly boost bilateral trade in Egypt. It grants numerous Egyptian products duty-free access to the Israeli market, provided at least 35% of their value originates in Egypt. This accord is being hailed as the most important economic agreement between Israel and Egypt in decades. The protocol establishing this deal has been formally approved by both governments after extensive negotiations.

However, there remains deep sensitivity about any form of co-operation between Israel and Egypt, as the wider Arab-Israeli peace process remains largely blocked. The political climate in the region has been particularly strained in recent weeks. Just this month, with eight convicted individuals facing legal action in security-related cases, tensions have remained high, highlighting the delicate environment.

Despite these challenges, the deal has progressed. Israeli Prime Minister Ariel Sharon described the agreement as the best way to achieve greater economic stability and to foster a more constructive relationship with Egypt, signalling a focus on practical cooperation despite political impasses.

Cairo now views Prime Minister Sharon as moving towards the political centre from his former hard-line positions. The Egyptian government believes that this shift, alongside the trade agreement, is more than just a pragmatic search for short-term economic gains. It suggests a potential for broader engagement.

But at its economic core, the new trade agreement is undeniably about practical benefits and tangible growth. It is expected to give huge impetus to bilateral trade flows, and to gradually drop existing various regulations over the course of the coming year. The long-term aim is to significantly strengthen the economies of both nations and enhance regional stability.

original: Blair and Brown criticised by MPs..Labour MPs have angrily criticised Tony Blair and Gordon Brown amid renewed reports of a rift between the two men...A meeting of the Parliamentary Labour Party saw a succession of normally loyal members warn that feuding could jeopardise Labour's election hopes. The PM insisted nothing would derail Labour's campaign, despite a new book saying he has upset his chancellor by backing out of a pledge to stand aside. Mr Brown will again be in the public eye at the party's new poster launch. In what the party had hoped would be perceived as a show of unity, he is due to line up alongside Alan Milburn - the man controversially appointed as the party's election supremo - and deputy leader John Prescott for the event in London on Tuesday. Relations between Mr Brown and Mr Milburn are widely reported to be cool ever since Mr Blair brought the latter back into the Cabinet to run Labour's election campaign, a role successfully carried out by Mr Brown in both 1997 and 2001...Mr Blair told the Parliamentary Labour Party on Monday: "I know from everyone here, in Cabinet and government, nothing is going to get in the way of a unified Labour Party with a unified position and winning the third term people desperately need."..The prime minister and his chancellor arrived within seconds of each other for the meeting of the PLP and were seemingly in good spirits as it started. New speculation about the state of their relationship was sparked by claims in Brown's Britain, by Sunday Telegraph journalist Robert Peston, which suggested Mr Blair went back on a pledge to make way for Mr Brown. Labour's Paul Flynn said Mr Blair and Mr Brown had a "scorching" from MPs adding: "It was a Parliamentary Labour Party meeting like no other."..Backbencher Stephen Pound said some MPs had threatend to expose those fuelling the reports if Mr Blair and Mr Brown did not "stop this nonsense, this poisonous briefing". Lord Campbell-Savours, a former MP, challenged Mr Brown to deny reports that he had told the prime minister he did not believe anything he said. Mr Prescott said MPs were entitled to complain about discipline after reading recent press reports..."They told us very clearly, it was the troops telling the leaders: get in line," he told BBC Radio 4's Today on Tuesday. Mr Prescott said there were occasional disagreements in any government. But he argued Mr Blair and Mr Brown could work successfully together and had produced a strong economy and better public services...The new book claims Mr Prescott hosted a dinner in November 2003 where the prime minister told Mr Brown he would stand down before the next election because he had lost trust over the Iraq war. He had then changed his mind in June 2004, following intervention from Cabinet allies and suspicion that the chancellor was manoeuvring against him, writes Mr Peston. Mr Prescott said there was a dinner but the discussions were confidential. "Of course as a waiter for 10 years I have a professional ability here," he joked. Mr Blair has insisted he has done no deals over the premiership while Mr Brown says he will not let "gossip" distract him from helping a unified election campaign. The Conservatives say the two men are behaving like squabbling schoolboys and the Liberal Democrats claim personal ambition is obstructing good government.

**London, UK** - Labour have angrily criticised **Chancellor Gordon** Brown **following** renewed reports **of** a rift **between him and Prime Minister Tony Blair at the very top of the party**.

A Labour Party **spokesperson swiftly dismissed the speculation, stating emphatically that the reports were merely an attempt to create a division within the party** that **would ultimately fail**. The Prime Minister, **Tony Blair,** insisted **that these persistent reports would not** derail **the government'**s **crucial legislative agenda**, saying his **absolute priority was to deliver for the people of Britain**. Mr **Brown** will **take a prominent role** in the party's **forthcoming local elections campaign**. **He will be campaigning extensively**, lining up alongside - controversially, as **was the case during the 2001 general** election - John Prescott for **many of the key events across the country**. Relations between **Mr Blair and Mr Brown** are to **be as strained as** ever. Mr **Prescott, the former Deputy Prime Minister, has often spoken publicly about the unenviable role he played in mediating between the two leaders during their intense Cabinet run's, a role he carried** out by both **men between** 1997 **and** 2001.

Mr **Blair told a meeting of the** Labour Party: "**We must move forward decisively** from **this unhelpful and distracting speculation**, in **a united and purposeful** way **to win the next general** election and **secure a historic** third term **in government for the Labour Party**."

**Immediately following** his **address, Mr Brown** arrived **at a separate meeting** of other PLP **(Parliamentary Labour Party) members, which reportedly helped to lift their** spirits. New speculation **about the precise** state of their **relationship was further fuelled when Robert** Peston, **the BBC's respected political editor,** suggested Blair went to **see Mr Brown for a private, conciliatory meeting to try and resolve their ongoing differences**. Paul **Tyler, the Liberal Democrat spokesman, quickly seized upon the growing disarray, issuing** a **statement saying there was a clear message** "" from MPs: "**that a Parliamentary vote of** no **confidence in the Prime Minister was now a very real possibility**."

**Sources close to Mr Blair** said **he felt he was being** threatened **by** those **who were engaged in 'poisonous and divisive' attacks, urging them to** "stop, **these poisonous tactics immediately**". **Meanwhile**, a **spokesman for Mr** Brown **moved quickly to** deny the **reports that** he **was not loyal to the Prime Minister or was involved in any undermining activities**. **Mr** Prescott **was also pressed by reporters** about recent reports...

**One political analyst, speaking anonymously on a background briefing, observed: "This is** clearly, **the Prime Minister's loyal** troops telling **potential rebel** leaders: 'get **back in** line,' **he** told BBC **Radio** 4'. **However, Mr** Prescott said there **was no fundamental disagreement or bad blood between Mr** Blair **and himself. He maintained that they had worked closely** together and had produced a strong economy **for the nation over many years**.

**A new** book claims **that Mr** Prescott **had privately urged Mr Blair to step** down **as Prime Minister in** 2003 **before the 2005 general** election **to avoid a potential defeat for Labour**. **The publication also delves into Mr Blair's growing concerns, detailed in** his **memoirs, about events in** 2004, following Cabinet suspicion that **Gordon Brown's inner circle was actively briefing** against **his policies and leadership from within the government**."

**Mr Blair** said **that a recent private** dinner **with Mr Brown had been 'difficult' but that the disagreement was now fully resolved**. "Of course **we have had our disagreements over the years, but I have always held the utmost respect for** his professional ability," he **added during a press conference**. **He** insisted he **had always** done **his best to manage the delicate succession process** over **the years** while let**ting Mr Brown take on increasingly significant responsibilities within the government. He dismissed attempts by critics to undermine the party, comparing them to 'schoolboys obstructing' progress, with a particular dig at the Liberal Democrats obstructing **the vital work of government**.

Brian O'Driscoll is set to lead a star-studded IRB Rugby World XV team in a special exhibition match organised to raise money for a crucial appeal. The Irish legend will captain a side featuring some of the biggest names in international rugby from both hemispheres, promising an exhilarating encounter for a charitable cause.

The roster boasts an impressive array of talent, including Australian icon George Gregan, one of the most prolific scrum-halves of his generation, and legendary All Blacks centre Tana Umaga. South African flanker Schalk Burger has successfully shaken off a recent knock to take his place in the starting line-up, a welcome boost for the World XV. Joining him will be Springbok stalwarts John Smit, the formidable hooker and captain, powerful prop Cobus Visagie, and towering lock Victor Matfield, among other renowned players, ensuring a powerful contingent from the southern hemisphere.

However, the team has been hit by a few withdrawals from Northern Hemisphere players. Scotland's astute scrum-half Chris Cusiter and France's formidable lock Fabien Pelous are notable absentees, having been withdrawn due to club commitments or minor injuries. These changes, however, have opened up an exciting opportunity for Leicester and England centre Ollie Smith to impress coach Clive Woodward, who will be taking charge of the World XV side. Woodward commented on Smith's inclusion, stating: "I think Ollie has a fantastic chance here," he told the Leicester Mercury, acknowledging the young centre's potential. "He probably hopes to seize this opportunity and show us all what he's capable of at this elite level." Also featuring for the World XV will be dynamic Wales scrum-half Dwayne Peel, known for his blistering pace and astute decision-making.

Woodward expressed his immense enthusiasm for the project, saying, "I'm really looking forward to working with these top-class players from around the world. It's a great chance to showcase the game and, importantly, we get to raise significant money for a very deserving cause. It’s a win-win situation for everyone involved, especially the fans who will witness a truly unique spectacle."

The Welsh contingent has also seen changes, with the unfortunate withdrawal of Wales wing Rhys Williams, who was originally scheduled to play but has been called up for a crucial Celtic League match with his regional side. original: Beastie Boys win sampling battle..US rappers Beastie Boys have won their long-running battle over the use of a sample in their song Pass the Mic...The punk-rappers used three notes of music from flautist James Newton's Choir in their track from 1992. Although the group had paid a licence fee for the sample, Mr Newton said his copyright had been infringed. But the US Court of Appeal upheld its original decision that the group did not have to pay an additional fee to license the underlying composition. The Beastie Boys - Michael Diamond, Adam Horowitz, and Adam Yauch - are considered to be one of early pioneers of sampling music...Sampling, now a standard practice among musicians, involves taking a segment of one track and using it in a different song. A three-judge panel of the court held in 2003 that the band had abided by copyright protections by paying a licence fee for a sample of Mr Newton's recording. That finding upheld a lower-court dismissal of the case in favour of the Beastie Boys. "We hold that Beastie Boys' use of a brief segment of that composition, consisting of three notes separated by a half-step over a background C note, is not sufficient to sustain a claim for infringement of Newton's copyright," Chief Judge Mary Schroeder wrote in her opinion. Mr Newton is a critically acclaimed jazz and classical flutist, composer, performer, and university professor. Mr Newton and the Beastie Boys were not available for comment.

**Beastie Boys win battle over music samples in landmark ruling**

**The influential hip-hop group Beastie Boys have won a significant legal battle concerning the use of brief musical samples in their work, a decision that could have wide-ranging implications for the music industry.**

Beastie **Boys** have long **been celebrated for** their **innovative and pioneering** use of sample**s in** their **groundbreaking** music, **which has helped shape a generation of hip-hop. The recent legal dispute, which attracted considerable attention, centred on** three **short notes, a mere three-second fragment of** music from James Newton's 1992 **composition 'Choir'.**

The case, **which was brought by Tuf America, a company claiming to own the underlying copyright to the composition, alleged that the Beastie Boys had infringed their copyright when they sampled the track for their 1992 hit 'Pass the Mic'.** Although **the Beastie Boys had already licensed** the **master recording of 'Choir' from ECM Records, Tuf America** said **in their legal challenge that the initial agreement was insufficient and sought a new court** decision that **the** group pay an additional **royalty for the specific three-note sequence used.**

Michael **Diamond, known to fans as Mike D, one of the three surviving members of the Beastie Boys, spoke out after the ruling. He emphasized that the band** are pioneers **in the art of using** music **samples, and hailed the verdict as a crucial victory for artistic freedom and innovation in the industry.** The case, among **other complex legal questions**, involves **the nuanced debate surrounding how to properly** track a song **or small parts of a composition when only a very brief segment is incorporated into a new work, and whether such use constitutes infringement.**

**US District** judge **Alison Nathan presided over the case in Manhattan. In her ruling, she referenced** the 2003 protections **for 'de minimis' use – a legal principle stating that trivial amounts of copying do not constitute copyright infringement. Judge Nathan ruled that requiring an additional** fee for **such a tiny snippet**'s **inclusion would unduly stifle artistic expression and place an unreasonable burden on creators.** That finding **was ultimately instrumental in deciding** the case in favour **of the** Beastie Boys.

"'**The** use of **such a small segment** of, **in this instance, less than** three half-**seconds, is not** sufficient **to establish a valid** claim of copyright **infringement**,' **stated intellectual property expert, Chief Mary Williams.** Chief Mary Williams **is a critically acclaimed** jazz composer, **musician, and** professor. **She believes** the **ruling could have significant implications for how musical works** were **traditionally protected, and that the debate over fair use will continue.**"

original: Tories attack burglar 'U-turns'..Tory leader Michael Howard has accused Tony Blair of performing U-turns over rules on using force against burglars...The government has ruled out amending the present law, which allows "reasonable force" in self defence. Mr Howard branded the decision unacceptable, saying: "It is not householders who should be frightened, it's the burglars." Home Secretary Charles Clarke said ministers had kept to their pledge to review the law...Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir John Stevens last month backed a Tory attempt to change the law so only householders using "grossly disproportionate" force could be prosecuted. The pressure prompted the prime minister to say the police and Crown Prosecution Service would be consulted as part of a review of the law. He told MPs: "If we get the right response from those people, we will, of course, support a change in the law." Instead, the government has decided no change is needed but there will be a publicity campaign so people are clear they are entitled to defend themselves. On Thursday, Mr Howard told BBC Radio 4's Today programme Mr Blair had initially refused the law change, then had come round to the idea and was now backtracking again. He said: "We've had three policy positions in three months and two U-turns. "It's not surprising Gordon Brown told him: 'There's nothing you could say to me now that I could ever believe.'"..Mr Howard said the "grossly disproportionate" test matched the hurdle ministers had introduced for civil cases where burglars where claimed compensation from householders. The issue entered the public spotlight when Norfolk farmer Tony Martin was jailed for shooting dead a 16-year-old burglar in 1999 as he ran away from the farm. But the home secretary said Mr Howard was wrong to say the law was biased in favour of burglars. The barrister who had represented Mr Martin had said the rules were "weighted overwhelmingly" in favour of the householder, said Mr Clarke. He said: "The problem is there has not been enough understanding of it - that was the point Sir John Stevens was making and the prime minister was making." The new guidance would help ensure clarity on the issue, added Mr Clarke. The director of public prosecutions, Ken Macdonald, says only 11 householders or occupiers of business premises have been prosecuted in the last 15 years. Those cases included a warehouse manager who had waited for a burglar, tied him up, beat him and set him alight, he said. Tory MP Patrick Mercer's private member's bill to change the law received a first reading in Parliament on Wednesday and goes to a full debate next month.

reconstruction:
The government was performing a significant U-turn on the contentious issue of householders' use of force against burglars. This move followed sustained pressure from, among others, opposition leader Michael Howard, who had consistently called for greater protection for homeowners. Prime Minister Tony Blair's government, in what it now described as a 'reasonable' decision, was adopting a new, more sympathetic stance towards those who defend their homes. 'This is for householders, it's a decision they have been waiting for, and a common sense approach,' a government spokesman stated.

Indeed, the government had in the previous month appeared to back a Tory attempt to bolster the rights of householders using 'reasonable force' to defend their property and persons, aiming to prevent them from being unfairly prosecuted. The immense public and political pressure on the Prime Minister to act decisively was considerable and growing. The Director of Public Prosecutions would, it was understood, play a pivotal part in interpreting any new guidelines or amendments to the law, and had previously stated publicly: 'Those people who, in fear, defend their homes and families, we will support and robustly defend.'

However, in a somewhat contradictory move, the government decided that existing law already clearly stipulated that people were legitimately entitled to use reasonable force when confronted by an intruder. Mr Blair, speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, steadfastly refused to acknowledge any fundamental shift or law change, though he had previously, then again, and now again appeared to subtly adjust his position. He declared, perhaps ironically, 'We've had three U-turns.' This statement proved surprising to many political commentators, especially as he had previously told reporters that 'nothing has changed now' regarding the existing legislation governing self-defence in the home.

Mr Blair also indicated that ministers would be urgently reviewing the operational guidelines for both police and prosecutors on how to handle cases where householders might have used force. The highly contentious case of Tony Martin, a Norfolk farmer who controversially shot dead a 16-year-old burglar in 1999, had consistently ran from the headlines for years, sparking fierce public and parliamentary debate about the rights of homeowners. The Home Secretary, Mr Clarke, was understood to be personally in favour of clarifying the law further to protect those defending their homes. He had, in a notable intervention, represented himself in a personal capacity, publicly stating that the law as it currently stood was 'weighted' against the innocent householder. Mr Clarke said: 'There has been a very valid and pertinent point Sir John Stevens was making, and the government wholeheartedly agrees with the spirit of it and intends to act upon it.'

The new guidelines, which are widely anticipated and expected to be unveiled soon, are specifically designed to ensure greater clarity and reassurance on the issue for both police forces and the general public. According to detailed figures released by the Director of Public Prosecutions, Ken Macdonald, a remarkably low number of only 11 householders have been prosecuted in the last 15 years for actions taken against burglars within their homes. Those specific cases invariably involved householders who had clearly used excessive or unlawful force, including one instance where a householder had set a spring gun, another who had used disproportional and gratuitous violence, and a further case involving one who had deliberately laid a dangerous booby trap. Paul Mercer, whose persistent and high-profile campaign for a change in the law had received widespread public and political support, expressed his satisfaction, stating that 'it goes a long way towards reassuring householders and providing clarity where it's desperately needed.'

His comments come in a BBC documentary called 'No More Mr Nasty'. TV presenter Anne Robinson said as home secretary he gave the impression he would "like to kick your cat". Ms Robinson, a friend of the Tory leader, also revealed that as a Cambridge student Mr Howard was "much loved by women and he was a courteous and kind and rather dashing lover" - although she denied having personal experience. "I wasn't at Cambridge - and it's not personal experience - but I know people who were."..Documentary maker Michael Cockerell was given behind-the-scenes access to Mr Howard for his film portrait. The Tory leader was asked about to respond to people who said that if there had there been a quota on immigration and asylum in the 1930s, his parents might not have been allowed into the country...He replies: "What is the inference of that? "That if you reach the view that you need to control immigration in the interests of the country you're not allowed to put a view forward if you happen to be descended from immigrants? "That seems to me an absolutely extraordinary proposition? It would certainly mean no one from immigrant parents could be prime minister."..Ms Robinson, who presents The Weakest Link tells Cockerell that she despaired at his hardline image when he was home secretary in John Major's government. "I used to have to sit on my hands because he'd get on television and give a passable impression of someone who'd like to kick your cat or would put your baby in prison if he cried. I mean it was very, very Draconian." The film shows Mr Howard laughing at Rory Bremner's impression of him as Dracula, which he calls "good fun", apart from the serious falsehood of a comment suggesting he wants fewer black people in the UK. The film shows the private side of the Tory leader watching television at home or playing table tennis with his wife, ex-model Sandra. Asked if she enjoys a game of ping pong she confesses: "Yeah, it would be more enjoyable if I could win occasionally too, but otherwise it's quite fun."..Former Downing Street communications chief Alastair Campbell, now working on Labour's election campaign, says a "touchy-feely" image does not fit Mr Howard. He says Tony Blair was not worried by his opponents' early performance in their Commons clashes because Mr Howard lacked a "big strategy", including on issues like Iraq. The Tory leader brands such criticisms as "absolutely rubbish", arguing that he has been consistent on his support for the war but critical of Mr Blair's failure to tell the truth on intelligence. Former Tory chancellor Ken Clarke says Mr Howard has a bigger problem changing perceptions of the Tory party than his personal image. Mr Clarke says the party is improving and it is "conceivable" it could win the next election. But he adds: "It has got to change itself a bit and broaden its appeal."..- Michael Howard: No More Mr Nasty is being shown on BBC2 on Saturday 12 February at 2005 GMT.

reconstruction:
Conservative leader Michael Howard has been making a concerted effort to reshape his public image as a general election looms, with recent media appearances providing fresh insights into his character and political strategy. After years of being perceived as a stern, even "nasty" politician, Mr Howard and his team are attempting to project a more relatable and empathetic persona, while simultaneously reaffirming his uncompromising stance on key issues like immigration and asylum. This balancing act is under intense scrutiny as polls suggest a challenging path for the Conservatives to regain power.

A recent high-profile interview on the BBC has sparked considerable debate about Mr Howard's public presentation. During the encounter, **Anne** Robinson, the veteran broadcaster, described Mr Howard as giving her **the impression** of a **"frightened cat"**. This candid observation, made during a programme focusing on his character, quickly became a talking point across the political spectrum. **Ms** Robinson, **the** host of 'Room 101' and known for her probing interview style, **revealed** a contrasting perspective offered by **a student Mr Howard was** mentoring. According to the student, **he was "rather a kind"** person – a description that Ms Robinson admitted **she** found herself **not having**. Reflecting on the interview, Robinson stated: **"I try not to be too personal, but you know, there were"** moments that provided unexpected glimpses into his personality.

Howard's tough rhetoric on immigration and asylum has long been a cornerstone of his political platform, a position he often links to his own family history. A new **film portrait** offering unprecedented access **to Howard** seeks to explore this connection and present a more rounded picture of the man behind the headlines. In the documentary, **The Tory leader** recounted how his **parents** were immigrants who came to this **country** in the 1930s. He draws parallels between their experience and his views on controlled immigration, stating: "My parents came to this country in the 1930s. They were people that had faced a quota on immigration." He then challenged critics with a series of rhetorical questions: **"What's wrong with that? What's wrong if you take the view that we need immigration control so that the country is allowed to view itself as a cohesive whole? What's wrong with that? That doesn't mean no one from an immigrant background could ever become prime minister."** His comments underline his belief that a firm immigration policy is not incompatible with Britain's historical role as a haven for those in need, but rather a necessity for social cohesion.

Further insights into Mr Howard's character come from those who have worked closely with him. Isabel **Cockerell**, his former private **secretary in John Major's government**, offered a revealing perspective on his drive and ambition. She characterised his uncompromising nature, recounting an observation about his determination: "He's not going **to sit on my hands because** he'll **get** frustrated, **and you're in prison.** It's **draconian**." This suggests a leader who abhors inaction and feels deeply constrained by obstacles. Cockerell also offered a lighter anecdote, describing **him as** a highly **serious** politician who, **apart** from his political work, enjoys simple pleasures. Recalling her observations of **the Tory** leader **at his** Kent home, she mentioned his fondness for table tennis, adding **"if she enjoys ping-pong, she says it's more enjoyable occasionally. 'It's fun.'"** This small detail contrasts with his often austere public image, hinting at a more relaxed private persona.

The Conservative Party's **communications** team is acutely aware of the need to refine Mr Howard's public **image** ahead of the upcoming **election**. The push for a more **"touchy-feely"** approach is a deliberate attempt to broaden his appeal beyond the party's traditional base. Mr Howard himself has been keen to portray Tony Blair as avoiding direct confrontation. He suggested that **Tony Blair was not** engaging **in clashes because** he lacked a convincing argument, dismissing claims of a **"big strategy"** behind the Prime Minister's reluctance to engage in head-to-head debates. Instead, Howard implied that Blair was holding back because he had little new to say. He also used recent platforms to rally his core **support**, urging them not to dwell on past electoral **failure**, but to focus on the future.

Even within his own party, there are voices urging Howard to cultivate a broader appeal. **Ken** Clarke, **Mr** Howard's former leadership rival and a prominent moderate, weighed in on the party's prospects. Clarke **says** he believes that **the bigger** Michael Howard can make **his image** as a credible and serious leader, the more likely the Conservatives **could win** the next general election. However, Clarke also sounded a note of caution, adding: **"It** is essential **to broaden its appeal."** This reflects a long-standing concern within the party that its messaging and policies need to resonate with a wider segment of the electorate, beyond its traditional heartlands, if it is to overcome Labour's dominance. The task facing Mr Howard is therefore two-fold: to maintain his reputation as a decisive leader while simultaneously presenting a more compassionate and inclusive vision for Britain.

As the election campaign intensifies, Michael Howard finds himself at a critical juncture. His efforts to soften his image, while maintaining a tough stance on core issues, will be crucial in determining the Conservative Party's fortunes. The insights from his interviewers, his former colleagues, and his own family history are all contributing to a more complex public understanding of the man who hopes to lead the country. The success of this image reconstruction will ultimately be judged by the electorate.

The **documentary**, titled **'Michael Howard: No More Nasty', is on BBC2 at 12:00 BST on 25 May 2005**.

original: UK bank seals South Korean deal..UK-based bank Standard Chartered said it would spend $3.3bn (£1.8bn) to buy one of South Korea's main retail banks...Standard Chartered said acquiring Korea First Bank (KFB) fulfilled a strategic objective of building a bigger presence in Asia's third largest economy. Its shares fell nearly 3% in London as the bank raised funds for the deal by selling new stocks worth £1bn ($1.8bn), equal to 10% of its share capital. Standard Chartered expects about 16% of future group revenue to come from KFB...The South Korean bank will also make up 22% of the group's total assets. The move, a year after Citigroup beat Standard Chartered to buy Koram bank, would be the South Korean financial sector's biggest foreign takeover. This time around, Standard Chartered is thought to have beaten HSBC to the deal. KFB is South Korea's seventh largest bank, with 3 million retail customers, 6% of the country's banking market and an extensive branch network...The country's banking market is three times the size of Hong Kong's with annual revenues of $44bn. Standard Chartered has its headquarters in London but does two thirds of its business in Asia, and much of the rest in Africa. "We're comfortable with the price paid...the key here has been speed and decisiveness in making sure that we won," said Standard Chartered chief executive Mervyn Davies at a London press conference. Standard Chartered said KFB was a "well-managed, conservatively run bank with a highly skilled workforce" and represented a "significant acquisition in a growth market". In London, Standard Chartered's sale of 118 million new shares to institutional investors pushed its share price down, and contributing to the FTSE 100's 0.3% decline. Standard Chartered's shares were 28 pence lower at 925p by midday. Some analysts also queried whether Standard Chartered had overpaid for KFB. The deal, which requires regulatory approval, is expected to be completed by April 2005 and to be earnings accretive in 2006, Standard Chartered said...Rival banking giant HSBC, which is based in London and Hong Kong, was also in the running. Standard Chartered is believed to have gained the initiative by putting together a bid during the Christmas break. "They were able to move so quickly it caught HSBC by surprise," the Financial Times newspaper quoted an insider in the talks as saying. HSBC will now have to wait for the next South Korean bank in line to be sold off - thought likely to be Korea Exchange Bank, also currently in the hands of a US group. Standard Chartered said it was buying 100% of KFB, an agreement that would bring an end to the bank's complex dual ownership. The South Korean government owns 51.4% of KFB, while the remaining shareholding, and operational control, are in the hands of US private equity group Newbridge Capital. Newbridge bought its stake during the government's nationalisation of several banks in the wake of the 1997 Asia-wide currency crisis which crippled South Korea's financial institutions...South Korea's economy is expected to grow by 4.5% this year. Although often thought of an export-driven economy, South Korea's service sector has overtaken manufacturing in the last decade or so. Services now make up roughly 40% of the economy, and consumer spending and retail banking have become increasingly important. In the aftermath of the Asian financial crisis, the government encouraged the growth of consumer credit. Bad loan problems followed; LG Card, the country's biggest credit card provider, has been struggling to avoid bankruptcy for months, for instance. But analysts believe South Korea's financial services industry is still in its infancy, offering plenty of scope for new products. Standard Chartered sees "the opportunity to create value by the introduction of more sophisticated banking products". Since 1999, KFB has been restructured from a wholesale bank into a retail bank focused on mortgage lending, which makes up 45% of its loans.

But Downing Street said Mr Blair should be judged by results not his style...Lord Butler said Mr Blair bypassed the Cabinet and relied instead on small, informal groups of advisers to help him make decisions. The prime minister's official spokesman said the Cabinet was still used to achieve a consensus on important issues. But he added: "You cannot, in a modern government, take every decision in Cabinet. It's just not possible."..Lord Butler said the government had too much freedom to "bring in bad Bills" and "to do whatever it likes" and it relied too much on the advice of political appointees. The former cabinet secretary said in an interview with The Spectator magazine: "I would be critical of the present government in that there is too much emphasis on selling, there is too much central control and there is too little of what I would describe as reasoned deliberation which brings in all the arguments." Mr Howard described Lord Butler's intervention as "very important". "This is from someone who was an insider at the very heart of the Blair government. "It is certainly the most damaging testimony I can ever remember from someone in such an eminent position."..Lord Butler's report earlier this year into Iraq intelligence said the government's September 2002 weapons dossier did not make clear intelligence about claims that Saddam Hussein had stockpiles of chemical and biological weapons was "very thin". The reason for this is that it would have weakened ministers' case for war, Lord Butler said in his Spectator interview, which was conducted by the magazine's editor, Conservative MP Boris Johnson. He said: "When civil servants give material to ministers, they say these are the conclusions we've drawn, but we've got to tell you the evidence we've got is pretty thin. "Similarly, if you are giving something to the United Nations and the country you should warn them."..Asked why he thought the warnings were not there Lord Butler said: "One has got to remember what the purpose of the dossier was.
