Lord Butler, the former top civil servant, launched a scathing attack on Tony Blair's way his government operates, accusing it of being obsessed with headlines and spin rather than a robust and collegiate decision-making process. He warned that the prime minister's style risked undermining the integrity of government.

He suggested that 'the intelligence on Iraq was not as robust as presented' and questioned the claims made in the notorious 2002 dossier. He revealed that the intelligence committee, which he chaired, had heard "damning testimony" from senior officials that could further damage public confidence in the handling of the pre-war intelligence. Lord Butler argued that Downing Street should be more open and transparent in its dealings, rather than operating in an opaque manner. He said Mr Blair often bypassed formal cabinet processes, preferring instead to rely on informal advice and a small inner circle of confidantes, which led to a lack of proper scrutiny.

A former senior minister's official, speaking anonymously, echoed these concerns. But added, with exasperation: "You cannot just ignore inconvenient facts. You just can't always 'put a positive spin' on everything. There is too much pressure to 'bring in good news' and ignore 'bad news', or to 'do whatever' it takes to push a particular agenda, leading to 'too much political interference' in what should be impartial processes." In a wide-ranging interview with The Spectator magazine, the former cabinet secretary further elaborated: "At present there is too much emphasis on selling a policy, there is too little of what I describe as genuine deliberation which brings all the facts to the table, allows for dissenting voices, and encourages proper, open discussion before crucial decisions are made."

Lord Butler's report, published earlier this year, was the result of an inquiry chaired by 'someone who was an insider, very much at the heart of the British establishment and its intelligence community'. One senior Whitehall source, reflecting on the period, commented: "I remember such an atmosphere of pressure and an almost evangelical zeal to present a particular narrative, rather than a balanced assessment."

Lord Butler's report earlier this year into the intelligence on Iraq specifically said the government's 2002 dossier, claiming Iraq had weapons of mass destruction, did not make it clear that intelligence on chemical and biological weapons was 'sporadic and unverified' and 'less certain than presented'. He questioned the 'reason that we have ministers for' if their role in scrutinising intelligence is diminished. In a separate Spectator interview, the then Shadow Cabinet member, MP Boris Johnson, offered his own insights: "We ought to be able to say to ministers, 'Look, this is what we've got, these are the facts, but we've got to be utterly transparent about it and lay it bare'. The United Nations, the international community, you should be honest with them and not cherry-pick information."

Mr Johnson added: "One has to ask what the real purpose of the dossier was – to inform or to persuade? British intelligence on Iraq was very good, but the way it was presented to the public and Parliament was highly selective." When pressed on why such issues persist in government, Mr Johnson replied: "Well, we are not having a proper, serious debate about how government should be conducted, and that is a fundamental flaw." He continued: "We should move away from the current tendency to bring in so much of, and rely upon, huge regulation and bureaucracy for every single decision. Whatever happens, and whatever people like or dislike, we must consider what will be the lasting legacy on the future of government in this country."

Lord Butler's assessment was strongly backed by a highly respected former Cabinet Secretary, Lord Armstrong of Ilminster, who told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "From what I have observed and read, it doesn't appear there was a sufficient exercise of collective judgement to bear upon making those decisions, particularly in foreign policy, to which ministers are entitled." Liberal Democrat deputy leader Menzies Campbell also weighed in, saying he thought 'the Prime Minister's highly centralised and personalised style of leadership' was 'detrimental to sound governance and democratic accountability'. Speaking on the first anniversary of Labour's re-election, when the issue was particularly salient, he stated on Radio 4's Today programme: "The inaccurate presentation of intelligence and the misleading nature of the claims made cannot be taken politically out of context; it fundamentally shaped public opinion and parliamentary debate leading to war."

original: Labour chooses Manchester..The Labour Party will hold its 2006 autumn conference in Manchester and not Blackpool, it has been confirmed...The much trailed decision was ratified by Labour's ruling National Executive Committee in a break with the traditional choice of a seaside venue. Blackpool will get the much smaller February spring conference instead in what will be seen as a placatory move...For years the main political parties have rotated between Blackpool, Bournemouth and Brighton. And the news the much larger annual conference is not to gather in Blackpool will be seen as a blow in the coastal resort. In 1998 the party said it would not return to Blackpool but did so in 2002. The following year Bournemouth hosted the event before the party signed a two year deal for Brighton to host the autumn conference...Colin Asplin, Blackpool Hotel Association said: "We have tried very hard to make sure they come back to Blackpool. "Obviously we have failed in that. I just hope Manchester can handle the crowds. "It amazes me that the Labour Party, which is a working class party, doesn't want to come to the main working class resort in the country." The exact cost to Blackpool in terms of lost revenue for hotel accommodation is not yet known but it is thought that block bookings will be taken at the major Manchester hotels after the official announcement.

original: Goldsmith denies war advice claim..The attorney general has denied his statement to Parliament about the legality of the Iraq war was drafted by Downing Street officials...Lord Goldsmith said Lord Falconer and Baroness Morgan played no part in drafting the answer. He added the answer represented his view that the war was legal, but was not a summary of his advice to the PM. The government has resisted calls to publish the full advice, saying such papers are always kept confidential...In a statement, Lord Goldsmith said: "I was fully involved throughout the drafting process and personally finalised, and of course approved, the answer." He said the answer had been prepared in his office with the involvement of Solicitor General Harriet Harman, two of his own officials, three Foreign Office officials, a QC, Christopher Greenwood and the then Lord Chancellor, Lord Irvine of Lairg..."No other minister or official was involved in any way." He suggested the claim that Lord Falconer and Lady Morgan had drafted the answer were the result of a mis-transcription of his evidence to the Butler Inquiry into pre-war intelligence. "As I have always made clear, I set out in the answer my own genuinely held, independent view that military action was lawful under the existing (UN) Security Council resolutions," he said. "The answer did not purport to be a summary of my confidential legal advice to government." Former foreign secretary Robin Cook said Lord Goldsmith's admission that his parliamentary answer was not a summary of his legal opinion suggested Parliament may have been misled. "The attorney general may never have presented his answer as a summary, but others certainly did," he said. "What is clear from his statement today is that he does not believe that it was a full, accurate summary of his formal opinion."..Earlier, Tony Blair dismissed questions about the attorney general's advice, and said his Parliamentary statement had been a "fair summary" of his opinion. "That's what he (Lord Goldsmith) said and that's what I say. He has dealt with this time and time and time again," Mr Blair told his monthly news conference in Downing Street. He refused to answer further questions on the issue...On the question of whether such papers have always been kept confidential, Tory MP Michael Mates, who is a member of the Commons intelligence and security committee and was part of the Butler inquiry, told the BBC: "That, as a general rule, is right, but it's not an absolute rule." He said there had been other occasions when advice had been published, most recently regarding Prince Charles's marriage plans. The government could not pick and choose when to use the convention, he said. Mr Mates added: "This may be one of those special occasions... when it would be in the public interest to see the advice which the attorney general gave to the prime minister."..The claims about Lord Falconer and Baroness Morgan's involvement were made in a book published this week by Philippe Sands QC, a member of Cherie Blair's Matrix Chambers. He also says Lord Goldsmith warned Tony Blair on 7 March 2003 that the Iraq war could be illegal without a second UN resolution sanctioning military action...A short statement about Lord Goldsmith's position presented in a written parliamentary answer on 17 March 2003 - just before a crucial Commons vote on the military action - did not suggest this. Former minister Clare Short, who resigned from the government over the Iraq war, said the ministerial answer was the same statement that was earlier shown to the cabinet as it discussed military action. She said the full advice should have been attached, according to the ministerial code, and demanded a Lords inquiry into the matter. The Conservatives and Liberal Democrats say they still want the publication of the full legal advice given by the Attorney General. Lib Dem foreign affairs spokesman Sir Menzies Campbell said Lord Goldsmith's statement still did not clear up the outstanding issues. "If his original advice of 7 March accepted that military action might be illegal, how was it that he resolved any such doubts by the time the Parliamentary answer was published on 17 March?" he said. "Only the fullest disclosure will now do."

The protracted controversy surrounding the legal advice provided by then Attorney General Lord Goldsmith on the legality of the Iraq war deepened further today, with senior figures defending their actions and facing renewed scrutiny. Lord Falconer, a prominent figure in Tony Blair's government at the time, firmly denied persistent allegations that Lord Goldsmith's initial and more cautious legal advice to the government, particularly concerning the necessity of a second United Nations resolution, was in fact drafted or significantly influenced by officials within Downing Street. These claims have been central to criticisms suggesting that the independent legal opinion was unduly influenced by political considerations from the outset. Critics had strongly asserted that Lord Falconer, who served as Lord Chancellor during the lead-up to the war, played a significant and potentially inappropriate role in the drafting and shaping of the Attorney General's final public statement that declared military action to be lawful. He was widely acknowledged as a close personal friend and powerful political ally of Prime Minister Tony Blair, a relationship that has frequently fuelled accusations of political interference in what should have been an impartial legal assessment. The Labour government, led by Tony Blair, has faced persistent accusations from opposition parties and former cabinet members of exerting considerable pressure on Lord Goldsmith to alter his initial, more circumspect legal opinion to one that unequivocally supported the legality of military action without a new UN Security Council resolution. Addressing these serious allegations directly, Lord Falconer stated: "There was a robust and thorough process that led to the Attorney General's final advice being formulated, and personally, as Lord Chancellor at the time, I was fully aware of all stages of that process and the extensive deliberations involved." This statement, however, has been met with further scrutiny by opposition parties and legal commentators alike, who continue to press for greater transparency regarding the precise sequence of events and the evolution of the legal advice.

Lord Falconer further elaborated on the circumstances surrounding the preparation of the crucial parliamentary answer provided by the Attorney General. He confirmed that the drafting of this answer was undertaken in the presence of the Solicitor General, Harriet Harman, a number of senior legal officials, a Queen's Counsel (QC) who was part of the legal team, and ultimately, the Prime Minister himself. Lord Falconer added, defending the procedure: "That was the entirely proper and established way such important advice to Parliament was drawn up and vetted." He then critically addressed a specific claim suggesting that both Lord Falconer and Lady Morgan had directly drafted the parliamentary answer given by the Attorney General, asserting that such a claim constituted a serious misrepresentation of the evidence that had been provided to the Intelligence and Security Committee. He implied that the committee had been given a clear account, and this narrative was being distorted.

For his part, Lord Goldsmith himself has consistently sought to defend the integrity and independence of his final legal opinion. He reiterated his position firmly, stating: "I have made it unequivocally clear, and set out in detail within my answer to Parliament, my genuinely held legal opinion that military action against Iraq would be lawful under the existing United Nations Security Council resolutions." He underscored the importance of this legal determination, adding: "This legal position continues to be the definitive stance of my government and underpins its actions."

The debate over the legal basis for the war was reignited by a significant admission from Former Foreign Secretary Robin Cook, who resigned from the government over the Iraq war. Cook had previously made a candid admission that parliamentary legal opinion provided to MPs had not been the full and unvarnished advice, leading to the grave implication that Parliament may, in fact, have been misled about the precise legal justification for military action. This admission, from such a senior and respected figure, added considerable weight to calls for greater disclosure.

However, Lord Goldsmith robustly countered the suggestion that he had ever intentionally misled Parliament or the public. He insisted: "The attorney general himself never gave a false impression or presented an inaccurate picture, but I acknowledge that others certainly did, perhaps unintentionally, through selective interpretation or partial disclosure." He emphasized that the statement he personally made to Parliament was, to the best of his ability, a full and accurate summary of his formal and comprehensive legal advice, reflecting his final, considered view on the matter.

Responding to the ongoing controversy and the intense media interest, Lord Goldsmith's spokesman, speaking at a news conference at Downing Street, affirmed that the Attorney General had been "fair" and comprehensive in dealing with the mounting criticism and questions surrounding his advice. "He has answered time and time and time again, patiently explaining his position," the Prime Minister's official spokesman told the assembled journalists at Downing Street. The spokesman, however, steadfastly refused to comment further on the broader policy issue of whether such sensitive legal advice to the government should always be kept confidential, citing longstanding convention. Michael Mates, a former Conservative MP who was a prominent member of the independent Butler inquiry into the intelligence on Iraq, offered his perspective on the matter. He told the BBC: "Legal advice given to the government, and particularly to the Attorney General, is generally treated as confidential under our system, but that confidentiality is not absolute. There are clear precedents." Mates continued, highlighting instances where the public interest had overridden the need for secrecy. "There have been occasions when such advice has indeed been released, most recently regarding Prince Charles's lobbying efforts, where the government ultimately disclosed details. The government has not released the full legal advice in this instance, and it should be reconsidered," Mr Mates said. Mr Mates added that, "On a number of occasions throughout our constitutional history, it would clearly be in the overwhelming public interest to see the advice which the minister has been given, especially when it concerns matters of war and peace."

Adding further fuel to the debate, Lady Morgan's controversial comments and revelations regarding the advice were made public in her highly anticipated and widely discussed book, "Cherie's Matrix," which offered an insider's perspective on the Blair years. Crucially, it emerged that Lord Goldsmith's initial, unvarnished opinion on 7 March 2003, had been that a new, specific UN Security Council resolution would be necessary to legalise military action against Iraq under international law. This position, however, appeared to undergo a significant transformation, as his subsequent and much-publicised legal advice, presented in a written answer to Parliament on 17 March 2003, unequivocally declared the war to be lawful under existing resolutions - a crucial and highly contentious shift in his documented advice just days before military action began. Clare Short, a former cabinet minister who famously resigned from the government over the Iraq war, confirmed that the content of the crucial parliamentary answer regarding the legality of the war was indeed discussed in detail within government circles shortly before its publication. She forcefully reiterated her long-standing belief that the full legal advice, in its entirety, should have been published to Parliament and the public, and she demanded a full, independent inquiry into the precise circumstances surrounding the evolution and finalisation of Lord Goldsmith's advice. Both the Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats echoed these calls, demanding that the comprehensive legal advice given by the Attorney General be immediately published for public scrutiny. Shadow foreign secretary Sir Malcolm Rifkind pressed Lord Goldsmith rigorously on the specific timeline of his legal advice and the crucial issues surrounding the perceived changes in his opinion.

Sir Malcolm Rifkind pressed Lord Goldsmith with a direct and pointed question: "If his original advice on 7 March accepted military action to be unlawful without a further UN resolution, how was that fundamental issue resolved in such a short time before his categorical answer on 17 March, which stated the war was lawful?" he said. "Only the fullest and most comprehensive disclosure of all the legal advice, including all drafts and associated communications, will now satisfy the public and ensure accountability on such a momentous decision."

The critically acclaimed Russian drama 'The Return' has been named the winner of the prestigious Best Film award at the British Independent Film Awards (BIFA) ceremony. The powerful film, directed by Andrey Zvyagintsev, tells the poignant story of two adolescent brothers forced to adjust to a new and unsettling regime when their strict, enigmatic father unexpectedly returns after a 10-year absence and takes them on a mysterious trip.

Zvyagintsev's masterpiece previously garnered significant international acclaim, having won the coveted 2003 Golden Lion award at the Venice Film Festival, cementing its status as a major cinematic achievement. Its triumph at BIFA further solidifies its reputation as an impactful independent film.

The awards ceremony took place in central London, hosted with his usual wit and charm by television presenter Jonathan Ross. The event brought together talent from across the British and international film industries to celebrate outstanding independent cinema.

The selection of 'The Return' was the result of extensive deliberations by a distinguished judging panel. This year's panel included acclaimed actress Gillian Anderson, respected film critic Kim Clarke, and Jonathan Ross himself, who is also the long-serving presenter of BBC's Film 2005. Their collective expertise guided the final decisions.

A strong shortlist of six outstanding films from around the world had been rigorously chosen from a vast pool of submissions. Among the other highly regarded nominees for Best Film were Walter Salles' 'The Motorcycle Diaries,' and Zhang Yimou's visually spectacular martial arts epic 'Hero'. Interestingly, 'Hero' had previously topped a public poll' related to the awards, securing an impressive 32% of audience votes, though the critical consensus ultimately favored 'The Return'.

The production of 'The Return' was particularly lauded for its powerful, understated storytelling, exceptional cinematography, and the remarkable performances delivered by its young lead actors, filmed over an intense 15-week period in challenging, remote locations.

Alongside the main prize, the winner of the Award for Best Animated Film was also announced earlier in the evening, recognizing creative excellence in animation.

Manchester United faced a truly stern test in their FA Cup third round replay, but ultimately avoided a potential banana skin and an embarrassing upset by eventually seeing off a hugely spirited and determined Exeter City side at St James Park. The score finished 3-0 to the Premier League giants.

Manchester United took a deserved early lead through a clinical finish from Cristiano Ronaldo, firing home from close range, though Exeter goalkeeper Paul Jones' string of truly heroic saves kept his spirited side in contention for much of the gripping FA Cup tie. United did not, however, make the result fully safe until a late flurry of goals ensured victory. Exeter had their own clear-cut opportunities to score, with powerful striker Sean Devine volleying wide on two occasions and Tim Howard making a particularly crucial acrobatic save for United from a fierce shot. Sir Alex Ferguson was taking absolutely no chances after the surprising and frustrating 0-0 draw in the first game, and he consequently opted to field a very strong, near full-strength side, starting key attacking players such as Paul Scholes and star striker Wayne Rooney. Devine and Flack of Exeter constantly pressed and harried United's defence, and with one particularly incisive attacking move, a lively and pacey winger broke clean in to the dangerous area just inside the side of the penalty box and almost scored with a curling effort. However, United's second goal came from a familiar and well-practised combination, with Paul Scholes providing a pinpoint through-ball assist for the clinical Wayne Rooney.

Wayne Rooney now had another shot blocked over from a good cross by Ronaldo, showing his attacking intent. Moments later, on a quick counter-break, Giggs had a glorious opportunity to double United's lead, but dragged a left-footed shot badly wide of the post. Cristiano Ronaldo had opened the scoring for the visitors in the 10th minute with a low drive that snaked past Jones. Exeter had one significant attacking chance left to them before the interval, but failed to capitalise on a promising free-kick just outside the box. They came out after the break with renewed determination and energy, putting United under sustained pressure and diligently searching for an equalizer, with many dangerous crosses sent into the penalty box. The Grecians might have scored from a goalmouth scramble, but the ball seemed to get stuck in the heavy St James Park mud, preventing a clear strike. Exeter captain Paul Jones also made a crucial goalline block to deny United a third goal from a swift counter-attack, keeping his side's hopes alive. Exeter forward Sean Devine then found himself in a good position to be a local hero, but his powerful volley went brilliantly wide from an unmarked position at the back post, much to the dismay of the home crowd. United eventually sealed the victory when Wayne Rooney picked the ball up around 20 yards out and unleashed a stunning drive from distance, which flew past the Exeter keeper and into the top corner, leaving Jones with no chance. Exeter, however, had a goal-bound effort of their own which found its way into the net, beating Tim Howard all ends up, but the assistant referee's flag meant the effort was eventually ruled out for offside, much to the frustration of the Grecians. Wayne Rooney rounded off the scoring, tapping the ball home with an easy finish after another precise pass from Scholes, to make it 3-0 and send United comfortably through to the next round of the FA Cup.

The British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) reported that business confidence picked up in the last months of 2004, reaching its best level in eight quarters. Despite this rise, the group found the whole economy still faced "major risks" and warned against complacency.

The BCC is forecasting economic growth of 3% in 2004, but anticipates a slowdown to little more than 2.5% in both 2005 and 2006. This suggests a period of more constrained expansion for the UK.

Furthermore, the balance for service exports in the quarter, according to the BCC, increased overall at the end of 2004, contributing positively to trade figures.

Despite these positive signals from services, the BCC highlighted a growing concern. The threat of further interest rate increases has intensified, largely due to improved economic data and underlying inflationary pressures. This follows a period of significant monetary tightening by the Bank of England, which raised interest rates five times between 2003 and 2004. These cumulative hikes have placed considerable pressure on households and businesses since their implementation, contributing to a noticeable slowdown of overall consumer activity across the country.

Businesses continue to grapple with fundamental challenges. "Squeezed profit margins, the relentless increase in input costs, and the burden of higher taxes all remain serious problems for our members," the BCC warned. These factors are impacting profitability and hindering investment across various industries.

While the overall outlook for the UK economy over the next 12-18 months remains mixed and uncertain, there is a clear hope that sustained strength in exports will continue to help buoy up the economy's performance and provide a much-needed impetus for future growth in the coming year, the BCC concluded.

original: Ireland win eclipses refereeing 'errors'..The International Rugby Board may have to step in to stop frustrated coaches and players from publicly haranguing referees when things go belly-up...It may have to go the whole way and have NFL-style video cameras all over the field, or slap the vociferous perpetrators over the knuckles. What the IRB does not want is a football scenario where the verbal slanging matches often overshadow the game itself. Sunday's explosive Six Nations clash at Lansdowne Road was a good example as Ireland took another step towards their first Grand Slam since 1948. The game was as exciting as it comes, with a much-improved England side enraged at a few decisions that did not go their way. One can understand that frustration. There was no doubt that Ireland had the rub of the green in their 19-13 victory, but the reaction from the England camp may not have endeared them to the sport's "blazers". Referee Jonathan Kaplan was not perfect by any means and two decisions in particular made him the villain of the piece. I doubt whether Kaplan would have been too pleased at the comments made. After all, he has no public recourse to criticism...It was the same for Simon McDowell, the touch judge who was heavily criticised by Scotland coach Matt Williams after their defeat against France. As far as England were concerned, there were queries over Mark Cueto's first half-effort when he went over in the corner from a Charlie Hodgson kick...England coach Andy Robinson referred to a similar case at Ravenhill in January when Ulster were playing Gloucester in the Heineken Cup. On that occasion, David Humphreys kicked to Tommy Bowe, who touched down in the corner only for the try to be wiped out. But you cannot have cameras at every conceivable angle to pick up such anomalies. Perhaps Robinson was right to say the referee should have gone upstairs when Josh Lewsey was driven over the Irish line near the end...Lewsey claims he touched it down and was in full control. However, one has to credit Ireland flanker Johnny O'Connor for cleverly scooping the ball away and blocking any evidence of a touchdown. But in rugby, everything tends to even out over the 80 minutes. The referee also missed England's Danny Grewcock taking out Ronan O'Gara off the ball to allow Martin Corry a Sunday stroll to the line. Those were the stand-out moments in a classic game between the two old foes...But there were many more, and one should not take away from those. Brian O'Driscoll's winning try was as well-conceived as they come, while Charlie Hodgson's brilliant kicking display was another highlight. And Ronan O'Gara's tremendous ability to control the game was also a crucial component. But the defining moments came with Ireland under the cosh in the final 15 minutes. Two outstanding pieces of defensive play denied England and allowed Ireland to hold on. The first was Denis Hickie's brilliant double tackle in the right-hand corner. He gobbled up Cueto from another Hodgson cross-field kick, then regained his feet to stop Lewsey from scoring a certain try. Ireland's second-row colossus Paul O'Connell was equally superb. England had turned Ireland one way then the other, and the defence cordon was slowly disintegrating. England prop Matt Stevens ran in at full steam to suck in a few more tacklers. Unfortunately he ran into O'Connell who hit him hard - very hard - and then wrestled the ball away for a crucial turnover. That spoke volumes about Ireland's back-foot display, with defensive coach Mike Ford taking a bow at the end. To win a game like that showed that Ireland have moved forward. It may be tries that win games, but it is defence that wins championships.

Players and coaches have to be frustrated from publicly criticising referees when things go wrong and major controversies flare up after matches, often overshadowing the performance of the athletes. This trend is becoming increasingly problematic and threatens to undermine the integrity of the game, affecting the way matches are officiated across the entire field, or when perpetrators of blatant foul play go unpunished over and over again, leading to accusations of inconsistency. The sport's governing body, the International Rugby Board (IRB), does not want this to become a verbal slanging game, fearing it could severely damage rugby's global reputation and deter new fans from the sport.

Yet, despite these pervasive concerns about officiating standards, this explosive Six Nations championship has been as good as any we have seen in recent memory, and took another significant step forward last weekend with a truly thrilling encounter that captivated audiences worldwide. Indeed, Sunday's pivotal game was as exciting as ever, perhaps even more so given the stakes, and with a marked improvement in how teams react to decisions that go against them, even if some contentious calls still generate significant debate and post-match analysis. That frustration, no doubt, was keenly felt by the Irish contingent after their narrow 19-13 loss to England, a result heavily influenced by some questionable refereeing decisions that swung momentum, and the subsequent reaction in the victorious England camp, where there was little sympathy for their opponents' plight, only served to compound their disappointment and sense of injustice. The errors by the officials in particular made him, presumably the Irish coach or captain, incandescent with rage. Andy Kaplan, a prominent IRB figure, had been pleased by comments made earlier in the week regarding improved player discipline, but Sunday's events would surely have tested his patience and faith in the process.

It was Simon, whose touchline comments, broadcast widely, touched heavily on the perceived injustices suffered by his side throughout the match. As were the numerous controversial calls, there were several first-half incidents that drew the ire of the Irish support, notably when England's first try was controversially awarded after a clearly forward pass from Jonny Hodgson to Josh Lewsey went undetected. This decision felt eerily familiar to many, echoing events back in January against Ulster at Gloucester, where a similar official oversight occurred. On that occasion, Ulster's Tommy Bowe kicked the ball ahead and chased, scoring a try that was allowed to stand despite clear evidence to the contrary. But the television cameras at the ground clearly showed he was offside, a fact inexplicably missed by the officials on the day. It's right to say the referee upstairs, Josh, was probably not over the moon about the decision to allow the try to stand, knowing it was flawed. Indeed, England's Josh Lewsey knew he had it full on, and had to credit Ireland for playing with such conviction and spirit despite the apparent injustice of some crucial decisions going against them. In everything out of the 80 minutes, the referee also missed an obvious penalty call for England being 'off their feet' at a crucial breakdown, allowing England to continue their attack unimpeded, which directly led to further points shortly after.

Despite the controversies, the game itself was a pulsating encounter, filled with drama and moments of breathtaking skill from both sides. The stand-out moments in the game were shared evenly between the two formidable foes, showcasing the immense talent on display and the fierce rivalry. But none more so than a moment of individual brilliance, and one from Ireland's talismanic captain, Brian O'Driscoll, was particularly well-taken, demonstrating his unparalleled class under immense pressure. England's fly-half Charlie Hodgson's display was also strong and influential, orchestrating much of his team's attacking play with precision and tactical acumen. O'Driscoll's ability to control the game's tempo and direction, often against the run of play and under relentless English pressure, was also crucial to keeping Ireland firmly in the contest until the final whistle. Under the cosh for much of the game, Ireland's heroic 15 men denied England a try through sheer willpower and dogged defence, often putting their bodies on the line, but they couldn't deny the scrum's relentless dominance which yielded crucial penalties and field position. For example, the Hickie-led England pack gobbled up another chance to score near the line, only for Ireland to regain their feet and miraculously stop them scoring the try, a testament to their never-say-die attitude and incredible resilience. Ireland's scrum was struggling badly under immense pressure throughout the second half, and their disintegrating prop, under severe duress, ran to suck in a tackle, drawing in multiple defenders to create space elsewhere and buy his team time. Paul O'Connell, typically industrious and a towering presence, hit hard - very hard - in defence and impressively stole the ball back for Ireland, igniting a desperate counter-attack and relieving pressure. That was a key defensive moment, soon followed by a superb last-ditch tackle from England's Ford, preventing a certain score that would have sealed the game. It seemed tries were coming thick and fast in the frantic closing stages, but it was not to be that day for England, as Ireland held on for a morale-boosting, if not winning, performance.

The Tories and the Lib Dems have questioned the timing of the new rules...Tory leader Michael Howard has written to Tony Blair demanding an explanation of the new rules on e-mail retention. On Monday Lib Dem constitutional affairs committee chairman Alan Beith warned that the deletion of millions of government e-mails could harm the ability of key probes like the Hutton Inquiry. The timing of the new rules just before the Freedom of Information Act comes into forces was "too unlikely to have been a coincidence", Mr Beith said. But a Cabinet Office spokeswoman said the move was not about the new laws or "the destruction of important records". Mr Beith urged the information commissioner to look at how the "e-mail regime" could "support the freedom of information regime"...Mr Thomas said: "The new Act of Parliament makes it very clear that to destroy records in order to prevent their disclosure becomes a criminal offence." He said there was already clear guidance on the retention of e-mails contained in a code of practice from the lord chancellor. All e-mails are subject to the freedom of information laws, but the important thing was the content of the e-mail, said Mr Thomas..."If in doubt retain, that has been the long-standing principle of the civil service and public authorities. It's only when you've got no further use for the particular record that it may be legitimate to destroy it. "But any deliberate destruction to avoid the possibility of later disclosure is to be totally condemned." The Freedom of Information Act will cover England, Wales and Northern Ireland from next year. Similar measures are being brought in at the same time in Scotland. It provides the public with a right of access to information held by about 100,000 public bodies, subject to various exemptions. Concerns regarding government e-mail retention policies have sparked new **probes into e-mail** management within Whitehall departments. These investigations follow revelations suggesting efforts to limit public access to official electronic communications.

Internal **information suggests a senior official was urgently asking the Cabinet Office for guidance on how to delete e-mails rather than retain old ones**, potentially to avoid their future disclosure. This has ignited a political storm, with critics arguing such advice could severely undermine public accountability.

Liberal Democrat MP Paul Thomas was quick to voice strong criticism. He stated: "The **deletion of e-mails would prevent their being subject to Freedom of Information** requests – and that practice **should only be** permissible in very specific and transparent circumstances. To deliberately obscure government workings from public scrutiny is unacceptable and a grave disservice to public trust."

Questions **have been raised about the timing of the** alleged guidance, particularly as it coincides with sensitive ongoing inquiries. Conservative Party leader **Michael Howard has written to the Prime Minister, Tony Blair, demanding immediate clarification on the rules** for managing government **e-mails**. On **Monday, the Liberal Democrat constitutional committee** also issued a strong warning that widespread deletion **of e-mails could significantly harm probes** like the ongoing **Hutton** Inquiry into the death of weapons expert Dr David Kelly. The committee stressed that all relevant evidence must be meticulously preserved to ensure the integrity of such investigations.

Speaking yesterday, Liberal Democrat MP Alan **Beith said** that the **new Freedom of Information Act**, which is due to come **into** force shortly, appears to **have been** undermined **too** easily by these reported practices. He expressed deep fears that the very spirit of transparency intended by the landmark legislation was being jeopardized. In response to the growing criticism, **a Cabinet Office spokeswoman** denied any wrongdoing, stating that **the guidance was about the "proper management of** electronic information and the efficient use of public resources," rather than any attempt to deliberately withhold data from the public.

However, critics remain unconvinced by the government's explanation. Mr. **Beith** reiterated his concerns, stating that such actions "could seriously erode public trust and ultimately compromise the very foundation of **freedom of information** in this country." In a separate but related comment, Mr. **Thomas** warned of potential legal ramifications. "There is an **Act of Parliament in** place to ensure that the destruction of public records is not a **criminal offence** in certain defined circumstances. However, if e-mails are deleted to avoid scrutiny, that could constitute a serious breach of public duty. The deletion of **e-mails are part of the wider problem of** a lack of transparency and accountability that we are currently seeing within government," **said Mr. Thomas**, calling for urgent and independent investigations into the alleged directives.

This controversy highlights the critical importance of robust records management **in** modern government and its potential impact on the **long-term** credibility of the civil **service** and other public **authorities**. Experts stress the importance of clear, published guidelines, stating: "It's about having robust policies for **when to retain and when to destroy** documents and electronic data appropriately." However, they added: "But to simply **avoid the** issue altogether by deleting emails before they can be legitimately requested **is totally** unacceptable and runs counter to the very purpose of open government." The impending **Freedom of Information Act** in the UK, which became law in **Ireland last year**, is **being brought in** at roughly **the same time**. It will hold approximately **100,000 public bodies** to greater scrutiny, granting the public enhanced rights to access information, albeit with specified **exemptions**. The full **implementation** of this landmark legislation, however, is expected to be a phased and complex process, making the current debate over email retention all the more significant as departments prepare for a new era of transparency and public accountability.

While Microsoft's Internet Explorer (IE) still accounts for approximately 90% of surfers, figures from web analytics firm OneStat indicate a shift. OneStat, a prominent source for browser statistics, reports that the new Firefox 1.0 browser has already captured 5% of the market. This gain for Firefox means Internet Explorer's market share has fallen to 88.9%, representing a decline of 5 percentage points. Firefox is developed by the Mozilla Foundation, an open-source organisation whose roots trace back to the Netscape Navigator project of 1998. While there have been other versions and beta releases, the 1.0 edition was the first complete, official program intended for a wide, mainstream audience.

Many people are increasingly moving away from Microsoft's Internet Explorer towards alternatives like Mozilla Firefox. The open-source browser, available from mozilla.com, has garnered significant attention, particularly from tech-savvy users and those concerned about security. Some reports, including figures from analytics firm WebSideStory, suggest Firefox 1.0 has reached 7.4% of the market in certain regions, indicating an even faster uptake than OneStat's global average. Mozilla said that its official open-source software project was backed by strong community support and over $250,000 (£133,000) in donations for the Firefox 1.0 launch. The browser achieved millions of downloads in its first few days, highlighting its immediate and widespread appeal. Further figures from analyst firm WebSideStory showed Internet Explorer's US market share fell from 95.5% in January to 92.9% by October, illustrating a clear trend of decline. IE had dominated the browser market for some time after it took the crown from Netscape Navigator, which itself once commanded over 95% of the market in the late 1990s. Firefox's appeal also lies in its open-source nature, which means the 'core' code is freely available for public inspection. This transparency is often credited with contributing to a more secure program. Indeed, significantly fewer critical security vulnerabilities have been discovered so far in Firefox than in Internet Explorer, the dominant client browser. This trend suggests that users will increasingly be choosing browsers based more about security and features than simply sticking with a default option.

Microsoft continues to address security concerns in IE. The release of Windows XP Service Pack 2 introduced several new security technologies aimed at bolstering protection for its browser. However, many users are still opting for third-party add-ons and security solutions for additional safeguards. Industry analysts predict Firefox could capture 10% of the browser market by the end of 2005. Other alternative browsers, like the Norwegian-developed Opera, are also actively challenging IE's dominance, though with smaller market shares. Opera, currently in its 7.60 version, continues to offer a compelling and feature-rich alternative. OneStat, the firm providing these figures, collects its statistical data from millions of internet users across more than 100 countries, providing a comprehensive global snapshot.

"The plan includes training on computers and internet skills for both operators and users of the system," said Carlos Saldarriaga, technical coordinator at Cepes. Farmers are also taking extra lessons on how to apply the new information to make the most of their plots of land. The Board of Irrigation Users which runs the computer centres, aims to make the network self-sustainable within three years, through the cash generated by using the telecentres as internet cafes...One of the key elements of the project is the Agricultural Information System, with its flagship huaral.org website. There, farmers can find the prices for local produce, as well as information on topics ranging from plague prevention to the latest farming techniques. The system also helps the inhabitants of the Chancay-Huaral Valley to organise their vital irrigation systems. "Water is the main element that unites them all. It is a precious element in Peru's coastal areas, because it is so scarce, and therefore it is necessary to have proper irrigation systems to make the most of it," Mr Saldarriaga told the BBC News website. The information network also allows farmers to look beyond their own region, and share experiences with other colleagues from the rest of Peru and even around the world...Cepes says the involvement of the farmers has been key in the project's success. "Throughout the last three years, the people have provided a vital thrust to the project; they feel it belongs to them," said Mr Saldarriaga. But we have also had a great feedback when we trained 40 or 50-year old women, who were seeing a computer for the first time in their lives." So far, the Huaral programme promoters say the experience has been very positive, and are already planning on spreading the model among other farmers' organisations in Peru. "This is a pilot project, and we have been very keen on its cloning potential in other places," underlined Mr Saldarriaga...The Cepes researcher recalls what happened in Cuyo, a 50-family community with no electricity, during the construction of the local telecentre site. There it was necessary to build a mini-hydraulic dam in order to generate 2kW worth of power for the computers, the communications equipment and the cabin lights. "It was already dark when the technicians realised they didn't have any light bulbs to test the generator, so they turned up to the local store to buy light bulbs," recalls Carlos Saldarriaga. reconstruction:
A pioneering initiative to bridge the digital divide and empower rural communities has reached Peru. A groundbreaking network of community computer centres, leveraging modern technology, is actively helping poor farmers and their families access vital information and improve their livelihoods across the Huaral Valley.

In the heart of this fertile region, approximately 80 kilometres north of the bustling capital Lima, these innovative telecentres are making a tangible difference. They currently offer invaluable information and services to a community of 6,000-strong farmers, providing them with critical data that was previously out of reach. The ambitious project, dubbed the 'Information Project for Farmers,' aims to revolutionise agricultural practices by supplying real-time data on crucial aspects such as water distribution schedules, market prices for crops, and effective pest control actions. This empowers farmers to make informed decisions, optimising their resources and improving their yields significantly.

The reach of this pioneering endeavour extends beyond the initial group, with projections indicating that over 13,000 families, encompassing approximately 18,000 individuals, will ultimately benefit from the services offered by these facilities. The network currently comprises 14 fully operational telecentres, strategically located within the valley to ensure accessibility for even the most remote communities. Each centre is equipped with robust, yet affordable, computer hardware and runs on open-source software, making the technology sustainable and cost-effective. The project has been making substantial progress since its inception and was officially launched with significant fanfare last year. Spearheaded by a local non-governmental organisation with support from international donors, the entire initiative represents an investment of over $200,000, meticulously allocated to infrastructure, training, and ongoing support.

"These centres are much more than just internet cafes; they are vital hubs that include computers and offer tailored resources for users of the farming community," explained Carlos Saldarriaga, a key coordinator for the project. "Farmers can not only access weather forecasts and market trends but also learn about new, sustainable farming techniques, obtain guidance on crop diversification, and even get assistance with important administrative tasks like registering their land ownership, which is crucial for legal security and access to credit."

Beyond the immediate utility of the computer screens, the vision for these telecentres is to foster vibrant community spaces. Many of the centres are designed to be inviting and comfortable, with some even making space for small, informal cafes where farmers can gather, share experiences, and discuss agricultural challenges over a cup of coffee. The underlying philosophy, according to project leaders, is that the key to sustained success lies in providing farmers with comprehensive, practical tools and support. This enables them to find tailored solutions to a wide range of farming issues, from optimising planting schedules and soil management to disease prevention and effective crop rotation strategies. The centres are designed to be dynamic resources, constantly adapting to the evolving needs of the local agricultural landscape.

A significant component of the project focuses on enhancing the efficiency of the Huaral irrigation system, a lifeline for the valley's agriculture. The telecentres provide farmers with access to data on water levels, flow rates, and distribution schedules, allowing for more equitable and efficient water usage. This collective management approach minimises waste and ensures that water, a scarce resource, is allocated optimally across the entire farming community. "This project is vitally important because it empowers the farmers to take ownership of their future and make informed decisions about their practices. Therefore, it is inherently sustainable as it builds capacity from within the community," Mr. Saldarriaga told BBC News during a recent visit. The readily available information also allows farmers to share their own unique experiences, learn from the successes and challenges of their colleagues across the vast Huaral region, and even access global best practices and agricultural innovations.

Mr. Saldarriaga repeatedly emphasised that robust community involvement is absolutely key to the long-term viability and success of the entire project. "The three core principles we established from the outset – accessibility, relevance, and community ownership – have provided a vital framework to guide our efforts and empower them directly," he explained. Beyond simply providing technology, the project places a strong emphasis on education and skills development. Regular training sessions, often held several times a week at the telecentres, have been met with overwhelming enthusiasm and participation. These sessions cover everything from basic computer literacy to specific agricultural software applications.

"It's truly incredible to witness the impact these sessions have on people. We have seen such an amazing transformation," Mr. Saldarriaga recounted. "People, especially older farmers who might never have touched a keyboard before, have shown great aptitude and enthusiasm. It's particularly rewarding to see someone aged 40 or 50 confidently using a computer for the first time in their lives; it opens up a whole new world of possibilities for them and their families."

The initial feedback on the programme has been overwhelmingly positive, with local communities reporting significant improvements in farming efficiency and economic stability. Inspired by this early success, project coordinators are already planning further expansion and deeper integration of services among participating communities. "We have seen firsthand the transformative power of this model," Mr. Saldarriaga underscored, "and we have very strong intentions and are actively working on cloning and replicating this successful approach in other rural regions across Peru, where similar challenges persist."

A testament to the spirit of community ownership can be found in the remote village of Cepes Cuyo, nestled high in the Andean foothills, approximately 50 kilometres from the main Huaral Valley hub. Here, the construction of the local telecentre site was a truly collective endeavour. Facing chronic electricity shortages, the community decided not to wait for external power lines. Instead, with guidance from engineers and a collective effort, they ingeniously built a small hydraulic dam on a nearby stream. This mini-hydro power plant generates a crucial 2 kilowatts of electricity, sufficient to power the centre and provide basic lighting for homes. The self-sufficiency of this project is remarkable, demonstrating how local ingenuity can overcome significant infrastructure hurdles. The dam, alongside the necessary electrical equipment and installation, represented a substantial investment, estimated to be worth thousands of dollars in labour and materials, much of it contributed by the villagers themselves.

The story of the Cepes Cuyo centre is full of inspiring anecdotes that highlight the community's commitment. "When they first completed the installation of the generator, the technical team realised they didn't have any light bulbs to connect to the new electrical system, so they asked the villagers if they could provide some bulbs," Mr. Saldarriaga recalled with a smile. "The immediate and honest answer from the project team on site was 'we don't have any spare ones right now.' So, without hesitation, the community members themselves sprung into action. They went to their homes and brought back their own light bulbs, ensuring the centre could be illuminated and operational from day one."

This simple act of collective responsibility perfectly encapsulates the spirit driving the entire initiative. Each of the 14 telecentres is also equipped with modern wireless internet connectivity, breaking down geographical barriers and connecting these previously isolated communities not just to vital agricultural information, but also to the wider world. This crucial link is transforming educational opportunities, enabling remote healthcare consultations, and fostering a new sense of possibility and empowerment among communities where basic infrastructure was once a distant dream. The project stands as a powerful example of how targeted technological intervention, combined with strong community engagement, can profoundly impact rural development and improve lives.

The combined entity will operate around 1,000 stores, with annual sales of $30bn. It will face intense competition from discounters like Wal-Mart.

This acquisition marks the latest consolidation trend in the US retail sector, as other retailers as well seek to gain economies of scale and compete more effectively in a challenging market.

Federated expects the acquisition to significantly boost its earnings per share by 2007, anticipating substantial cost synergies. However, it also anticipates approximately $1bn in integration costs over the next two years as it combines operations and rebrands many of May's stores.

Such strategic moves have been widely taken across department store companies, creating larger, more efficient enterprises with greater geographic scope and increased purchasing power.

The chairman of Federated hailed the merger as a transformative step, stating, "We are creating a powerful new national retailer, and we are confident that the combined strengths of our companies will allow us to grow and move up." Ulster's Stephen Ferris is one of the new faces in Ireland's expanded 40-man provisional RBS Six Nations squad, which aims to build on recent promising performances. The squad was announced today by coach Eddie O'Sullivan, featuring a blend of experienced internationals and exciting young talent. Ferris, a powerful back-row forward, has impressed consistently for his province this season, earning him a richly deserved call-up to the national setup.

His Ulster colleagues, including fellow back-row Bryan McCormack, along with Leinster's prominent duo Bernard Jackman and Shane Horgan, have all been included despite recent injury concerns. Jackman, a hooker, and Horgan, a versatile wing, have both been battling back injuries, but O'Sullivan clearly values their experience and potential contribution. "A lot of effort was put into selecting this squad," coach Eddie O'Sullivan told BBC Sport. "We've been monitoring players closely across all four provinces, and also those based in England and Wales. The Six Nations is always a demanding tournament, and we need depth in every position to compete at the highest level."

O'Sullivan particularly highlighted the inclusion of several uncapped players. "Flanker Peter Campbell was just one of the uncapped players who has really caught our eye," O'Sullivan added. "He has been very impressive and fully deserves his place in this provisional squad. It's a testament to the hard work he's put in at provincial level." The coach acknowledged the difficulty of the selection process, noting, "There were many deserving players just on the fringes, and it was tough to leave some out. But we believe this squad offers the right balance for the challenges ahead."

The competition for places in the back-row is especially fierce, with established internationals David Wallace and Victor Costello vying for selection alongside Alan Quinlan, the promising Roger Wilson, veteran Simon Easterby, Munster stalwart Anthony Foley, the dynamic Denis Leamy and the inspirational Paul O'Connell. The half-back positions also feature strong competition, with experienced fly-halves David Humphreys and Kevin Maggs named. Simon Best leads the Ulster contingent, making it the province's biggest representation in terms of the panel for the upcoming campaign. Paddy Wallace and Shane Horgan are strong contenders to wear 12 and 11 respectively in the opening fixtures, offering both creativity and power in the midfield and wing roles. The sole Connacht representative, Gavin Duffy, a robust full-back or wing, is also named, underscoring the wider provincial contribution to the national team. Several British-based players, whose club form has been exceptional, are also prominent in the selection, bringing further experience to the group.

Bryan McCormack expressed his delight at the call-up. "I'm shocked but absolutely thrilled to be included," McCormack told reporters. "It's every player's dream to represent their country, and I'm really looking forward to getting involved with the training camp and pushing for a place in the matchday squad." He added, "I've played alongside many of the lads at Ulster and Leinster, both in provincial derbies and in European competition, and I know we can do well on the international stage. I'm confident with our prospects and believe we have the talent and determination to challenge for the championship this year."

original: US duo in first spam conviction..A brother and sister in the US have been convicted of sending hundreds of thousands of unsolicited e-mail messages to AOL subscribers...It is the first criminal prosecution of internet spam distributors. Jurors in Virginia recommended that the man, Jeremy Jaynes, serve nine years in prison and that his sister, Jessica DeGroot, be fined $7,500. They were convicted under a state law that bars the sending of bulk e-mails using fake addresses...They will be formally sentenced next year. A third defendant, Richard Rutkowski, was acquitted. Prosecutors said Jaynes was "a snake oil salesman in a new format", using the internet to peddle useless wares, news agency Associated Press reported. A "Fed-Ex refund processor" was supposed to allow people to earn $75 an hour working from home. Another item on sale was an "internet history eraser". His sister helped him process credit card payments. Jaynes amassed a fortune of $24m from his sales, prosecutors said. "He's been successful ripping people off all these years," AP quoted prosecutor Russell McGuire as saying. Jaynes was also found guilty of breaking a state law which prohibits the sending of more than 100,000 e-mails in 30 days, Virginia State Attorney General Jerry Kilgore reportedly said. Prosecutors had asked for 15 years in jail for Jaynes, and a jail term for his sister. But Jaynes' lawyer David Oblon called the nine-year recommended term "outrageous" and said his client believed he was innocent. He pointed out that all three of the accused lived in North Carolina and were unaware of the Virginia state law. Spam messages are estimated to account for at least 60% of all e-mails sent.

reconstruction:
Morgan Spurlock, the director behind the critically acclaimed and Oscar-nominated documentary 'Super Size Me', has been honoured with a prestigious Writers' Guild of America award. The film, which captivated audiences globally with its exploration of the fast-food industry's impact on health, was lauded for its compelling narrative and significant cultural influence. Speaking about the recognition, Mr Spurlock expressed his gratitude, stating that the enduring popularity of 'Super Size Me' and its continued ability to provoke discussion was an honour for him and his team. The award ceremony was a high-profile event, presented at the revered Samuel Goldwyn Theater in Los Angeles, an evening that also featured other cinematic attractions and was broadcast on Showtime.

The documentary follows Spurlock's personal experiment, in which he consumed only McDonald's food for 30 days straight. The film unflinchingly chronicled the alarming physical and psychological deterioration he experienced, including a significant weight gain of 25lb (11kg) and substantial damage to his liver, among other serious health concerns. His journey served as a stark warning about the potential dangers of a diet reliant on fast food. The film's release sparked widespread debate about corporate responsibility in the food industry and individual dietary choices. In what was widely perceived as a direct response to the documentary's powerful message and the resulting public pressure, McDonald's announced the discontinuation of its "supersized" meal options last year. This move was celebrated by health advocates and many consumers as a victory for public awareness, attributing the change to the potent effect of Spurlock's investigative film.

Coincidentally, on the very day of Mr Spurlock's award, another significant development unfolded in a separate, long-running legal battle involving the fast-food giant. A High Court in London delivered a ruling concerning two environmental activists who had been embroiled in a protracted libel case brought against them by McDonald's. Helen Steel and David Morris, both from north London, became famously known as the 'McLibel Two'. Their marathon legal fight, which began in the 1990s, became one of the most protracted libel cases in English legal history. McDonald's had originally sued them over a leaflet they distributed, which made various allegations about the company's labour practices, environmental record, and the nutritional value of its food. While the High Court in London had initially ruled largely in favour of the company, awarding McDonald's damages of £60,000 against Ms Steel and £40,000 against Mr Morris, the judgment was not entirely one-sided. Crucially, the court also found that several claims made in the activists' leaflet, particularly concerning certain aspects of McDonald's food and advertising to children, were demonstrably true. This mixed outcome meant that despite the financial awards to McDonald's, the activists were able to claim a partial victory in exposing some of the company's less favourable practices, thereby raising critical questions about corporate power and free speech.

Twenty years have passed since Britain's first commercial mobile phone call, marking a significant milestone in communication history. The 20th anniversary of that pioneering 'brick' phone call was on 1 January 1985, a date vividly recalled by a network veteran who helped launch the service.

Twenty years since, mobile phones have transformed from luxury status symbols into an indispensable part of daily life for millions. Today, they are an intrinsic part of how we live, work, and communicate, with over 90% of adults in the UK now owning a mobile device. While the concept of a mobile phone was first demonstrated by Martin Cooper of Motorola in 1973 in New York, it took another 10 years for the first commercial mobile phone networks to be established in the UK, truly ushering in the mobile era.

Britain, surprisingly, was far behind the rest of the world in setting up its own commercial mobile phone infrastructure. It was in 1985 that the first official call was made on the newly launched Vodafone network. The historic moment, when Sir Ernest Harrison, then chairman of Racal Vodafone, called his son Gerry, walking through the streets of London, is etched in the memory of those involved. Katherine Scott, who was then a key figure at Vodafone, serving as its head of public affairs at the time, vividly remembers the excitement. She recalls that on January nine 1985, her firm, Vodafone, alongside Cellnet, became the inaugural mobile phone network operators in the UK.

Alongside Vodafone, Cellnet (which later became O2) also launched its service in January 1985. A spokesman for Vodafone, reflecting on those early days, highlighted the stark differences compared to today's sleek devices. He noted that when the networks first went live, the initial handsets were notoriously bulky, often nicknamed 'bricks'. They could cost up to £2,000, an astronomical sum at the time, and offered a battery life of little more than 20 minutes of talk time. 'These colossal devices were incredibly expensive and cumbersome, yet they quickly became a popular status symbol for those who could afford them in the mid-to-late 80s,' he said, smiling at the memory.

This rapid embrace of the new technology occurred despite the fact that early mobile phones operated on analogue networks, which made them prone to interference, call dropping, and even security concerns where calls could be easily intercepted. The early growth was slow but steady. A representative for one of the pioneering networks said it took almost nine years for them to rack up their first million subscribers. In stark contrast, they now acquire that many new customers in just a matter of months, sometimes even 18 days for significant promotions. 'It's easy to look back now with hindsight,' the representative mused, 'but in 1983, when we put the bid document together for the licence, we were forecasting that the total number of mobile phone users in the entire UK would be no more than 10,000 people. Today, my company alone boasts over 14 million subscribers in the UK alone.'

For nearly a decade, Cellnet and Vodafone remained the only two mobile operators in the UK, enjoying a duopoly that shaped the nascent industry. This changed dramatically in 1993 when One2One (later T-Mobile, and now part of EE) launched its service, bringing fresh competition and innovation to the market. Orange followed swiftly in 1994, further intensifying the competitive landscape. These newcomers operated on entirely digital networks, a significant technological leap that offered clearer calls, better security, and opened up new possibilities for mobile communication. This digital revolution paved the way for services like text messaging (SMS), which is to this day the most widely used feature on mobile phones globally, with more than 1.2 billion messages sent daily worldwide. A technology analyst, Mr. David Woodcock, said digital technology allowed for many other new things, such as mobile internet access, picture messaging, and affordable international roaming, making these devices immensely popular and integral to modern life, far beyond what the pioneers of 1985 could have ever imagined.

In fact, many of the items that are traditionally sold in high street stores can now also be conveniently found and purchased online, often with better prices and delivery options.

An estimated 85% of the UK's 18 million active internet users are predicted to gift online this Christmas, according to comprehensive industry reports. Each online shopper, on average, will spend approximately £220 this Christmas, a substantial sum leading to a significant boost for the burgeoning e-commerce sector across the country. Almost 29% of British shoppers who intend to spend money this Christmas will do so online, a stark contrast compared to only 4% of traditional high street buyers registered in the year 2000, underscoring the rapid adoption of online retail. Consumers are now much more confident to buy - not just smaller, traditional online items like books and CDs, but also significant big ticket items like plasma televisions and high-end digital cameras, reflecting a growing trust in online transactions.

Mr Roper from the online retail association, a leading industry body, advised people to shop safe and ensure they receive their ordered presents for Christmas in good time, especially with potential delivery delays. He also strongly advised them to give themselves plenty of time to order so as to avoid any last-minute disappointment or stress. A survey conducted by the web hosting company Hostway shows that men online often avoid the perceived embarrassment of buying certain personal and intimate items, such as lingerie, for their partners and sometimes even clothes or toys for their children, preferring the anonymity of the internet. This impulse buying and anonymous shopping is often done, much to the chagrin of their unsuspecting partners, very late on Christmas Eve, according to comprehensive research compiled by prominent retail analyst John Saint.

original: Voters 'don't trust politicians'..Eight out of 10 voters do not trust politicians to tell the truth, a new poll conducted for the BBC suggests...And 87% of the 1,000 adults quizzed by ICM for BBC News 24 said politicians did not deliver what they promised. The poll comes after Foreign Secretary Jack Straw predicted trust would be "the key choice" at the next election. Both the Tories and the Lib Dems are keen to emphasise a perceived lack of trust in Tony Blair, following his claims over Iraqi weapons...But according to the BBC poll, 61% said the issue of trust made no difference to whether or not they would vote at the next election, widely expected on 5 May. The poll also looked at what lay behind the lack of trust in politicians. Some 87% said politicians did not keep the promises they made before elections, while 92% said they never gave "a straight answer". Just under three-quarters of respondents (73%) said politicians had shown themselves to be dishonest too often...Mr Straw told activists in Blackburn on Thursday that voters would have to decide at the next election which party "best deserves" their "future trust". "That in the end is the key choice at the next election."..He acknowledged that the public had lost faith in Labour, but suggested it could persuade people to "reinvest their trust with us" if the party could overcome Tory attempts to spread cynicism in politics. The Conservatives are keen to highlight the trust issue. During his response to Gordon Brown's Budget statement on Tuesday, Michael Howard compared the chancellor's figures to the prime minister's claims about Iraq's weapons of mass destruction...The Lib Dems are also keen to highlight the trust issue, with Charles Kennedy has claiming voters had a "fundamental lack of trust in the prime minister". And the Green Party unveiled a billboard opposite the Palace of Westminster accusing the government of lying over the Iraq war...Former education secretary Estelle Morris told BBC News 24 that there was a "real problem of trust" between the public and the politicians. She said she did not feel her own colleagues could be trusted, but suggested the "three-cornered relationship" between the press, politicians and the public had a hand in the issue. The public was often turned off by sitting on the sidelines in "the battle of words" between the politician and the journalist, she added. Lib Dem foreign affairs spokesman Menzies Campbell said the Iraq war had hit trust in politicians hard. "Issues of war and peace, life and death do have a very damaging effect on the credibility of politicians". Martin Bell, who won the Tatton seat from Tory Neil Hamilton on anti-corruption platform, said politicians often failed to see themselves as others did. "We need public figures we trust to tell the truth and who can see themselves as others see them."

'I don't trust politicians' is a sentiment shared by many across the UK, as new polling for the BBC reveals. Eight out of 10 voters say they don't trust politicians, according to new research conducted for the BBC. Indeed, 87% of the 1,000 people quizzed by BBC News 24 did not express confidence in politicians. The survey's findings, released shortly after the polling was completed, predicted that public trust would be "key" to the outcome of the next general election.

Tories have been quick to highlight the perceived erosion of public trust in Prime Minister Tony Blair, following his claims about Iraq's weapons of mass destruction, which have since come under intense scrutiny. But, despite these concerns, a significant 61% of respondents stated that the issue of trust would have no bearing on whether or not they would vote in the next election, which is widely anticipated to be held on 5 May. When asked what they did find trustworthy, a striking 87% said they had little faith in promises made by politicians, and a staggering 92% believed politicians never "kept their word" after gaining office.

Three-quarters (73%) of the electorate said they would not commit themselves to supporting any particular party before the election campaign was fully underway. Foreign Secretary Jack Straw addressed Labour activists in his constituency of Blackburn on Wednesday, asserting that voters would decide who they believed represented the "best" option in terms of "trust" and integrity. This assessment, he argued, would be paramount in the run-up to the general election. He further suggested that the government's strong track record on the economy would help to persuade people to "reinvest" their trust in the Labour party, despite ongoing Tory cynicism. The Conservatives, however, are relentlessly pressing their attack on the government's credibility. Following the Chancellor's Budget, Conservative leader Michael Howard declared that the election was not about finding imaginary 'weapons of mass destruction' but about the government's honesty and trustworthiness. The Liberal Democrats have also positioned public trust as a key electoral issue, with party leader Charles Kennedy claiming voters had been handed a "raw deal" by the two main parties. And the Green Party unveiled a new campaign billboard this week, starkly criticising the government's involvement in the war in Iraq.

Shadow Education Secretary Theresa Morris, in an interview with BBC News 24, was emphatic that the Conservatives aimed to rebuild "trust between the public and the political establishment." She did acknowledge that her own party was not universally trusted, "but insisted that they were genuinely willing to listen to the public, and that the incumbent government had a hand in the current crisis of public confidence. The public feels often disappointed and misled by the promises of politicians," she elaborated. Liberal Democrat leader Charles Kennedy said the war in Iraq had severely eroded public trust in politicians, "and had caused a damaging effect on their overall credibility". He went on to say that those who had won popular support on a clear and principled platform, demonstrated that politicians should be judged by the same standards as others. "They need to re-earn the trust of the electorate by being open and honest."
