reconstruction:
The BBC understands that the UK's opposition Conservatives are set to announce plans for mandatory health screening for all immigrants seeking to settle in the country if they win the next General Election. The party's plan:

Under the proposals, people who wish to live in the UK and are from outside the European Union for more than six months, would be required to undergo a full medical examination, including chest x-ray tests if appropriate. Those coming from outside the European Union who wish to stay in the UK for longer periods would specifically have to prove they do not carry certain serious infectious diseases, including Tuberculosis (TB), Hepatitis B, and HIV. A positive test for any of these conditions would automatically mean that their visa application would be refused. This would be decided by medical professionals.

Applicants would therefore have to prove they would be acceptable on public health grounds. If they were considered unlikely to be acceptable, for example if they posed a significant public health risk, then their application would be denied. The Conservatives intend to impose strict new conditions on those seeking to enter the UK or to remain here for extended periods. They state that if an applicant were to be found to be a carrier of a serious infectious disease, they would not be allowed to enter the country to work or to come here permanently. Those entering for less than six months would generally not be subject to the same health checks, unless they intended to work in sensitive sectors such as health, childcare or education, where they would require a more thorough screening.

Children who are born and resident in Britain permanently would not have to pay for healthcare. Furthermore, those under 16 years of age would be exempt from these checks if they were applying with their parents, and their parents had already undergone and passed the required health screening. Anyone denied entry to Britain because of a potential threat to public health would be immediately sent back to their home country. However, in certain cases, they might be offered the opportunity to undergo further medical tests to ensure they do not pose a direct and imminent risk of spreading infectious diseases within the UK.

Official statistics show that TB has increased by 25% in the 10-year period ending in 2008, a statistic the Conservatives frequently highlight. The Tories argue there should be much more rigorous screening into the health of all migrants entering the country. They will also require migrants to provide explicit evidence of where they intend to live in their home country and show precisely how they will support themselves financially if they were to return. This measure aims to reduce the burden on the NHS. The system, once established and fully operational, would allow immigration officials to more effectively detect people with serious conditions like TB, particularly if they come from high-risk countries where such diseases are more prevalent.

Recent pilot checks were carried out on 175,000 passengers at Heathrow Airport and 10,000 at Gatwick. From these checks alone, over 100 infectious TB cases were found. A further 47 individuals were found to pose some kind of health risk or require further investigation. The party believes this new and comprehensive system, which they describe as both robust and fair, and "modelled" on successful schemes in Australia and New Zealand, would have very little impact on legitimate migrants.

The document, controversially titled "desperate measures to control Britain's broken immigration and asylum system", was published last week. It outlines plans for mandatory health screening for high-risk migrants before they are given clearance to enter the UK. Anyone diagnosed with an infectious disease would be asked to defer their travel plans and then to receive appropriate medical treatment in their home country before reapplying. The Liberal Democrats warned the Conservatives that they "are indulging in thinly veiled racist rhetoric in an attempt to appeal to prejudice rather than reason and evidence".

Broadband use in the US is expanding rapidly. More than half of businesses now use it, with their business broadband subscriptions having jumped 38% in the past year, said the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC). The commission reported that there were 32 million connections as of June 2004. However, the US ranked a disappointing 13th by a telecoms industry survey in 2004 - a position that prompted a federal pledge to ensure affordable broadband access for all Americans by 2007.

According to the report, broadband is being increasingly utilised for a variety of entertainment and information services, with a strong focus on streaming video, music and online games. The number of broadband lines on US networks rose to 32.5 million for the year to June 2004, up from 23.5 million in 2003.

The majority of these connections hook up via Asymmetric Digital Subscriber Line (ADSL) technology over existing phone lines. This method accounts for 18.6 million lines. In contrast, cable modem connections comprise 11.4 million, according to the FCC report.

Foxx was named best actor for his acclaimed portrayal of legendary musician Ray Charles, a role for which he had already won a Golden Globe. Swank took best actress for her powerful performance as a determined female boxer in Clint Eastwood's gritty drama Million Dollar Baby.

The modest independent comedy Sideways, one of the season's breakout favourites, saw its ensemble cast take home the award for outstanding performance by a cast in a motion picture. The Screen Actors Guild (SAG) Awards are often considered a strong indicator for the Oscars, with many past winners going on to triumph at the Academy Awards. In the supporting categories, Cate Blanchett triumphed for her meticulously crafted role as Hollywood icon Katharine Hepburn in Martin Scorsese's epic The Aviator. Veteran Morgan Freeman was named best supporting actor for his poignant role as the wise boxing gym manager in Million Dollar Baby.

"Thank you for allowing me to be a part of this, thank you for putting us all together for this incredible journey," Swank said as she accepted her trophy in Los Angeles. Foxx dedicated his award to the late Ray Charles, emotionally stating, "He taught us so much, he opened up so many doors... and a young African-American kid from Terrell, Texas, can stand up here tonight and accept this award." He also warmly thanked director Clint Eastwood for the opportunity to work on 'Ray'.

"I bow," said Freeman, who is 74, humorously comparing his age to his fellow nominees. "I'm the person you get when you want talent, and I'm 74, so that I've still got something to offer the world."

original: Camera phones are 'must-haves'..Four times more mobiles with cameras in them will be sold in Europe by the end of 2004 than last year, says a report from analysts Gartner...Globally, the number sold will reach 159 million, an increase of 104%. The report predicts that nearly 70% of all mobile phones sold will have a built-in camera by 2008. Improving imaging technology in mobiles is making them an increasingly "must-have" buy. In Europe, cameras on mobiles can take 1.3 megapixel images. A significant row has erupted over the use of the colour orange, focusing on a new mobile phone service launched by EasyJet's founder, Sir Stelios Haji-Ioannou. The dispute pits Sir Stelios's EasyGroup against established mobile operators concerning the prominent use of the colour in his new "EasyMobile" brand. EasyGroup has launched a legal offensive, challenging claims over its right to use the distinctive orange hue.

The EasyMobile service, a low-cost alternative, heavily features orange in its branding. This has led to accusations of "trademark passing off" from other entities in the telecommunications sector. Sir Stelios remains defiant, asserting his group's long-established association with the colour.

"EasyGroup has made it clear that its low-cost mobile network, EasyMobile, while embracing orange as a key visual identifier, cannot and should not be confused with any other 'Orange' brand currently operating in the market," a spokesperson for EasyGroup said in a statement. "We firmly believe we have strong rights associated with the use of this colour for our expanding range of 'Easy' brands."

"I am not afraid of this fight. The colour orange is intrinsically linked to our identity; it is our right and our own colour, which has become synonymous with the 'Easy' brand during the last 10 years, starting with EasyJet."

The EasyGroup, known for its budget-friendly ventures, has consistently used orange across its portfolio, from EasyJet airlines to EasyCar rentals and EasyHotel. The move into mobile telecommunications with EasyMobile is a natural extension of this strategy, aiming to replicate the success of its other low-cost services.

The EasyMobile service is a joint venture, designed to offer straightforward, budget-friendly mobile phone options. It leverages existing network infrastructure and includes innovative features, such as the ability to purchase top-up cards and airtime, which will be powered by T-Mobile, indicating a partnership with the established network operator. This collaboration aims to provide reliable service while maintaining the 'easy' ethos of affordability and simplicity. The legal battle highlights the intensity of competition in the telecommunications sector and the significant value attached to brand identity. Both sides are gearing up for what could be months of complex legal proceedings over the proprietary use of a single colour.

reconstruction:
Over the past two decades, of the most profound technological shifts, this 10th anniversary of Yahoo's founding sees The web has undergone remarkable change. A key architect in making the World Wide Web accessible was Yahoo, a pioneering company founded in the mid-1990s. It shaped how early internet users discovered and navigated online content. Its origins trace back to a project set up by University students David Filo and Jerry Yang, whose vision helped lay the groundwork for the modern web.

Their journey began in 1994, while both were doctoral candidates at Stanford. What started as a personal project, born out of keeping a curated directory of their web-browsing discoveries, quickly grew in popularity. They were organising their own lists of favourite websites, but soon realised others could benefit. This hobby swiftly became popular among fellow students and early internet adopters. Recognising the potential for a broader service, the two business partners decided to formalise their venture. It was initially dubbed 'Jerry's Guide to the World Wide Web', reflecting its informal origins.

The rebranding to 'Yahoo!' was pivotal. The firm founders liked the dictionary definition of 'Yahoo' as a rude, unsophisticated, or uncouth person. This irreverent choice referenced coarse, brutish creatures in Jonathan Swift's classic, 'Gulliver's Travels'. The name reflected the raw, untamed nature of the internet at the time, and their anti-establishment spirit.

As Jerry Yang famously quipped, "We were not civilised," encapsulating the brand's early identity and the dot-com era's rebellious spirit. This unique approach, combined with a rapidly expanding user base, quickly attracted investor attention. It was a model which recognised the immense commercial potential of structuring online information. They have since gone through many iterations, but initial success was propelled by early financial backing. And in 1995 they successfully persuaded Capital venture firms, notably Sequoia Capital, which had a strong track record in Computer and technology investments, to fund Yahoo with a crucial initial investment of $2m (£1.04m). This seed funding allowed Yahoo to expand operations, hire staff, and develop its platform, positioning it for rapid growth.

The company's meteoric rise continued, and an Initial Public Offering (IPO) followed in 1996. The stock market reacted with enthusiasm, and the company quickly soared in valuation, becoming one of the darlings of the dot-com boom. At its peak, Yahoo's market capitalisation reached staggering figures, with its stock price hitting over $50.7, making its co-founders billionaires. This euphoric growth was followed by the abrupt burst of the dot-com bubble in the early 2000s, which saw many internet companies collapse. Despite widespread devastation, Yahoo, though significantly impacted, proved to be a "hard" survivor. It was among a still select handful of companies to navigate the dot-com crash relatively intact, a testament to its strong brand and diversified services.

However, the internet landscape evolved rapidly. The intense competition, particularly with new players like Google, proved a significant challenge. Google's innovative search algorithms quickly overshadowed Yahoo's directory-based approach, redefining how users found information. The firm's struggle to adapt led to strategic re-evaluation and various attempts at reinvention. Despite difficulties, the company remained a prominent force, continuously adapting as the internet changed the lives of consumers. Its journey reflects the dynamic nature of the digital world.

Through its various services, the internet wanted to do more than just provide information; it sought to foster connection. But it's more than just a tool for retrieving data – it's a platform where much more can be done, where people can share experiences and interact with each other in unprecedented ways. The rise of social media and user-generated content further underscored this shift, moving the web from a static repository to a dynamic, interactive space. It's been a truly transformative journey.

reconstruction:
**Gaming Takes Off in India's Rapidly Expanding Mobile Market**

India's burgeoning mobile gaming sector is experiencing an unprecedented surge, positioning the nation as a significant player in the global digital entertainment landscape. A new report highlights explosive growth, driven by a youthful, tech-savvy population and increasingly accessible technology.

The Indian mobile gaming market, still in its nascent stages, was expected to generate $26m (£13.8m) by the end of 2004, according to projections from industry analysts at MDR's Wireless Intelligence. This initial figure, while modest compared to established Western markets, represents a foundational stepping stone for what is anticipated to be a colossal expansion over the next few years.

Several key factors are fueling this rapid uptake. As of October, the number of mobile phone subscribers in India had soared to 44.9 million. This figure starkly contrasts with the mere 1.4 million landline connections across the country, underscoring the dominance of mobile technology in bridging communication gaps. The widespread availability of cheap handsets, coupled with India's vast demographic of under-25s – a highly receptive and enthusiastic consumer base – means that mobile phones are no longer just communication tools but have become 'must-have' gadgets, essential for social connection and entertainment.

Projections indicate a truly transformational period ahead. The market is forecast to bring in a staggering $336m (£178m) by 2009. This exponential growth is expected to place India firmly among the top global mobile gaming markets, contributing significantly to the worldwide industry's revenue. Furthermore, subscriber numbers are set to skyrocket, with estimates suggesting that 220 million people will be using mobile phones by 2009.

This dynamic expansion has not gone unnoticed by the industry. "This market has attracted substantial investment and creativity from a diverse range of players, including content developers, telecom operators, musicians, and has fostered the emergence of highly innovative business models," stated the MDR's Wireless Intelligence report. The core appeal, according to analysts, remains simple: "Mobile gaming is about fun; it offers a key element of accessible entertainment, and represents a truly lucrative opportunity for all involved, from game developers to network providers and, ultimately, the players themselves." Big developers and mobile operators are increasingly keen to offer an extensive array of games and interactive content to capture this burgeoning audience.

Despite the rapid growth, India's mobile penetration still lags behind more developed economies. In 2003, only about 10% of Indian households owned a mobile phone. While current estimates suggest roughly 20% of India's total population now own a mobile, this pales in comparison to well over 50% penetration rates seen in many European countries. Penetration in rural areas, while increasing, remains significantly lower than in urban centers.

However, this disparity presents a unique opportunity. India is perfectly positioned to make the most of this growth, following a trend common in many developing nations. These countries are often able to 'leapfrog' slower, traditional fixed-line infrastructure, jumping straight to mobile technology which is quicker to deploy and more cost-effective for consumers in dispersed populations. This ability to bypass older technologies allows for accelerated adoption and innovation.

As India's infrastructure continues to develop and mobile data services become even more widespread and affordable, the mobile gaming sector is set to become an even more powerful force, solidifying India's role as a mobile-first entertainment powerhouse.

Hitachi, the Japanese electronics giant, has unveiled its new 'Emiew' (Excellent Mobility and Interactive Existence as Workmate) robot. This humanoid is designed to rival Sony's Qrio robots.

Emiew stands 1.3m (4.2ft) tall and, unlike legged humanoids, is wheel-based, allowing quick and smooth movement. It was demonstrated to reporters from the press in Japan on Tuesday and will be shown publicly later this month. The robot has sophisticated sensors and advanced navigation capabilities to avoid obstacles. Explaining Hitachi's choice of 'wheel feet' for Emiew, a spokesman for Hitachi's Mechanical Laboratory, said: "We want to bring robot-people into everyday life, and for that, robots must be safe and easy to coexist with."

"We make robots designed to live alongside people. This means making them slower and safer than industrial robots, yet capable of useful tasks," he added. Emiew can move at speeds of up to 3.7m/s (approximately 8.3mph). Its 'wheel feet' are like those of a scooter, allowing for agile movement. With the ability to understand human speech, identify faces, and react to gestures and emotions, Emiew is designed to interact naturally and intuitively with people. It reacts "like a person walking through crowded shopping districts in a future city without bumping into anyone", a Hitachi spokesman said, highlighting its advanced collision avoidance.

Hitachi said Emiew can understand and respond to around 100 spoken words, making it suitable for "practical use as a guide or receptionist in offices or public spaces". The dream of a personal robot companion has long been a staple of science fiction and popular culture, but widespread practical application has long been hampered by the limitations of current technology. At the recent AAAI (American Association for Artificial Intelligence) conference for researchers, a different group of roboticists highlighted other approaches to humanoid design. Some researchers use a human-like body for their robots and aim to have both sophisticated locomotion and manipulation capabilities, which requires significant computing power and complex programming. Honda's Asimo was "born" five years ago, making its debut in 2000. Since then, developers of humanoid robots have tried to outdo each other with what their creations can do, pushing the boundaries of what is possible. Asimo, for instance, has visited the US, Asia, and Europe as part of a high-profile world tour. It has demonstrated abilities such as jogging too, and can even carry a tray of drinks, showing off its remarkable dexterity. It is capable of moving at speeds of 3km/h (1.8mph), which Honda claims is almost as fast as Sony's popular Qrio robot.

Last year, Toyota, another Japanese car giant, stepped into the robot development ring, unveiling a trumpet-playing humanoid robot that could also conduct an orchestra. By 2007, the global market for "leisure" robots is estimated to reach $2.5 billion, and for industrial robots, a massive $137 billion (according to Eurostats figures). By 2010, an estimated 4.1 million robots will be doing housework in Japan alone, according to projections by the Economic Commission for Europe. Hitachi hopes Emiew will find a home in many offices and public spaces across the world, and perhaps even one day, in your home, assisting with daily tasks.

original: Lifestyle 'governs mobile choice'..Faster, better or funkier hardware alone is not going to help phone firms sell more handsets, research suggests...Instead, phone firms keen to get more out of their customers should not just be pushing the technology for its own sake. Consumers are far more interested in how handsets fit in with their lifestyle than they are in screen size, onboard memory or the chip inside, shows an in-depth study by telecommunications company Ericsson. "Historically in the industry there has been too much focus on using technology," said Dr Michael Bjorn, senior advisor on mobile media at Ericsson's consumer and enterprise lab. "We have to stop saying that these technologies will change their lives," he said. "We should try to speak to consumers in their own language and help them see how it fits in with what they are doing," he told the BBC News website...For the study, Ericsson interviewed 14,000 mobile phone owners on the ways they use their phone. "People's habits remain the same," said Dr Bjorn. "They just move the activity into the mobile phone as it's a much more convenient way to do it."..One good example of this was diary-writing among younger people, he said. While diaries have always been popular, a mobile phone -- especially one equipped with a camera -- helps them keep it in a different form. Youngsters' use of text messages also reflects their desire to chat and keep in contact with friends and again just lets them do it in a slightly changed way. Dr Bjorn said that although consumers do what they always did but use a phone to do it, the sheer variety of what the new handset technologies make possible does gradually drive new habits and lifestyles. Ericsson's research has shown that consumers divide into different "tribes" that use phones in different ways. Dr Bjorn said groups dubbed "pioneers" and "materialists" were most interested in trying new things and were behind the start of many trends in phone use. "For instance," he said, "older people are using SMS much more than they did five years ago." This was because younger users, often the children of ageing mobile owners, encouraged older people to try it so they could keep in touch...Another factor governing the speed of change in mobile phone use was the simple speed with which new devices are bought by pioneers and materialists. Only when about 25% of people have handsets with new innovations on them, such as cameras, can consumers stop worrying that if they send a picture message the person at the other end will be able to see it...Once this significant number of users is passed, use of new innovations tends to take off. Dr Bjorn said that early reports of camera phone usage in Japan seemed to imply that the innovation was going to be a flop. However, he said, now 45% of the Japanese people Ericsson questioned use their camera phone at least once a month. In 2003 the figure was 29%. Similarly, across Europe the numbers of people taking snaps with cameras is starting to rise. In 2003 only 4% of the people in the UK took a phonecam snap at least once a month. Now the figure is 14%. Similar rises have been seen in many other European nations. Dr Bjorn said that people also used their camera phones in very different ways to film and even digital cameras. "Usage patterns for digital cameras are almost exactly replacing usage patterns for analogue cameras," he said. Digital cameras tend to be used on significant events such as weddings, holidays and birthdays. By contrast, he said, camera phones were being used much more to capture a moment and were being woven into everyday life.

He decreed after the 2003 World Cup that players should have a decent conditioning period during the year. That became a reality at the end of last summer with a 10-week period at the start of the this season. It may have annoyed his Scottish, and in particularly Welsh, cousins who huffed and puffed at the disrespect apparently shown to the Celtic League. We will say nothing of Mike Ruddock ''poaching'' eight of the Dragons side that faced Leinster on Sunday. But, like O'Sullivan, he was well within his rights, particularly when you are talking about the national side and pride that goes along with it. The IRFU has thrown their weight behind O'Sullivan, who must be glad that in the main, there is centrally-controlled contracts. Brian O'Driscoll, the talismanic captain, stands on the precipice of destiny, his eyes fixed on the horizon of what could be Ireland's greatest rugby era. There is a palpable sense that he is primed for glory, the collective aspirations of a nation converging upon his shoulders. The gunpowder is loaded, ready for ignition, as Ireland look to O'Driscoll to lead their resurgence this season, a campaign laden with expectation and historical significance.

It was Eddie O'Sullivan, the meticulous coach, who decreed that the 2003 World Cup campaign should be nothing short of decent – a baseline expectation that, for a nation starved of consistent global success, was itself ambitious. He has worked tirelessly to forge a squad capable of making that ambition a reality at the conclusion of the summer's intensive 10-week preparation period. The meticulous planning, the gruelling training camps, and the tactical blueprints have all been meticulously crafted with one goal in mind: to compete at the very highest level.

Such audacious claims, however, are not without their critics and observers. It may well have been his Scottish counterparts, in particular, who huffed and puffed, apparently to the Celtic League management, over perceived advantages or perceived slights. Yet, Eddie O'Sullivan's men, eight of whom have faced the intense pressure of international challenges multiple times, much like O'Driscoll himself, are well within their rights to believe in their potential. They understand that when the pressure mounts and things go awry, they must stand united. They have thrown their full weight and unwavering support behind O'Driscoll, believing implicitly in his leadership and vision, knowing that their collective fate hinges on their ability to execute under pressure. There is no turning back from this commitment.

However, the path to glory is rarely smooth. There are whispers of discontent, particularly regarding coaching decisions. Bar Keith Wood, who, by this stage of his illustrious career, was just a shadow of the powerhouse he once was, a casualty of O'Sullivan's sometimes ruthless selection policy at the heart of this evolving Irish squad. There is undoubtedly some doubt surrounding O'Sullivan's handling of certain player relationships and, at times, his public pronouncements. The media, ever watchful, has not shied away from questioning the wisdom behind some of his choices and his communication strategy, particularly when dealing with the removal of veteran players from the team dynamic.

Nevertheless, O'Sullivan's grand plan is also informed by observing the tribulations of others. That same attrition may yet hit England, whose seasoned players have been visibly overworked through an arduous club and international calendar, leading to concerns about fatigue and burnout. O'Sullivan, one would hope, possesses the foresight to learn from their potential mistakes, avoiding the pitfall of excessively burdening his key players. The wisdom of transferring that lesson into Ireland's player management strategy, ensuring freshness and peak performance when it matters most, will be critical.

As in many rugby quarters across the emerald isle, this season brings with it renewed Grand Slam hopes, the highest they have been since Karl Mullen's legendary side achieved the clean sweep back in 1948. That historical precedent hangs heavy in the air, a potent reminder of what is possible but also how rare such an achievement is. With Lansdowne Road, the spiritual home and darling of Irish rugby, positioned once again as a fortress, the dream feels more tangible than it has in decades. You see, the point is, they can go contrary to all expectations, both positive and negative. It is a matter of belief, yes, but also of seizing the moment and learning from the past.

Despite the historical anxieties and the weight of expectation, Ireland's current side are making a very salient point with their performances. After 19 years without a major championship trophy, they are demonstrating a potent blend of resilience and flair that can further that collective belief. The sheer skill displayed by these players, from the explosive backline to the powerful forward pack, they truly have it in spades. There is no denying the quality or commitment within this squad. He, Brian O'Driscoll, embodies this spirit, a leader who understands that this season's championship is fundamentally different; it is not merely about competing, but about proving their capability. original: Web radio takes Spanish rap global..Spin the radio dial in the US and you are likely to find plenty of Spanish-language music. But what you will not find is much Spanish-language hip-hop...Hip-hop and rap are actually quite popular in the Spanish-speaking world, but local artists are having trouble marketing their work abroad. But now, a US company is bringing rap and hip-hop en espanol to computer users everywhere. Los Caballeros de Plan G are one of Mexico's hottest hip-hop acts. They have a devoted fan base in their native Monterrey. But most Mexican hip-hop fans, not to mention fans in most of the Spanish-speaking world, rarely get a chance to hear the group's tracks on the radio..."You can't really just go on the radio and listen to hip-hop in Spanish... it's just not accessible," says Manuel Millan, a native of San Diego, California. "It's really hard for the Spanish hip-hop scene to get into mainstream radio. You usually have a very commercialised sound and the groups are not really known around the country or around the world." Millan and two friends set out to change that - they wanted to make groups like Los Caballeros de Plan G accessible to fans globally...Mainstream radio stations were not going to play this kind of music, and starting their own broadcast station was economically impossible. So, Millan and his friends launched a website called latinohiphopradio.com. The name says it all: it is web-based radio, devoted to the hottest Spanish language rap and hip-hop tracks. The site, which is in both in English and Spanish, is meant to be easy to navigate. All the user has to do is download a media player. There are no DJs. It is just music streamed over the net for free. Suddenly, with the help of the website, Los Caballeros de Plan G are producing "export quality" rap...The web might be just the right medium for Spanish language hip-hop right now. The genre is in what Millan calls its "infant stage". But the production values are improving, and artists such as Argentina's Mustafa Yoda are pushing to make it better and better. Mustafa Yoda is currently one of the hottest tracks on latinohiphopradio.com. "He's considered the Eminem of Argentina, and the Latin American hip-hop scene," Millan says. "He really hasn't had that much exposure as far as anywhere in the world, but he's definitely the one to look out for as far as becoming the next big thing in the Spanish-speaking world." Currently, the Chilean group Makisa is also in latinohiphopradio.com's top 10, as is Cuban artist Papo Record. "Every country's got it's own cultural differences and they try to put those into their own songs," Millan says. Latinohiphopradio.com has been up and running for a couple of months now. The site has listeners from across the Spanish speaking world. Right now, Mexico leads the way, accounting for about 50% of listeners. But web surfers in Spain are logging in as well - about 25% of the web station's traffic comes from there. That is not surprising as many consider Spain to be the leader in Spanish-language rap and hip-hop. Millan says that Spain is actually just behind the United States and France in terms of overall rap and hip-hop production. That might be changing, though, as more and more Latin American artists are finding audiences...But one Spaniard is still firmly in latinohiphopradio.com's top 10. His name is Tote King and Manuel Millan says that he is the hip-hop leader in Spain. On his track Uno Contra Veinte Emcees, or One Against 20 Emcees, Tote King shows he is well aware of that fact. "It's basically him bragging that he's one of the best emcees in Spain right now," Millan says. "And it's pretty much true. He has the tightest productions, and his rap flow is impeccable, it's amazing." Latinohiphopradio.com is hoping to expand in the coming year. Millan says they want to include more music and more news from the world of Spanish language hip-hop and rap...Clark Boyd is technology correspondent for The World, a BBC World Service and WGBH-Boston co-production.

reconstruction:
Rap music has long transcended geographical and linguistic barriers, evolving into a truly global phenomenon that speaks to youth culture across continents. From the bustling streets of New York to the vibrant rhythms of Tokyo and the pulsating energy of Buenos Aires, its influence is undeniable. However, for a significant segment of this vast musical landscape—specifically, Spanish-language hip-hop—the journey to mainstream recognition remains fraught with challenges. While its beats and powerful lyrical narratives resonate deeply with a massive and devoted audience throughout the Spanish-speaking world, artists consistently find themselves having trouble securing the kind of widespread exposure that could catapult their careers to the next level, particularly on traditional radio platforms. This disparity highlights a crucial void in the global music industry, where immense talent struggles against systemic barriers to reach its full potential.

The struggle is multi-faceted. When listeners, eager to discover the latest sounds from their favourite Spanish-speaking MCs, spin the radio dial, they are often met with silence. Mainstream radio, predominantly driven by commercial interests and a focus on English-language content, has largely overlooked the rich tapestry of Spanish-language hip-hop. "If you try to find Spanish-language hip-hop on commercial radio, you'll discover it's almost non-existent," explains Millan, the visionary behind LatinHipHopRadio.com. "Major broadcasting networks often see it as a niche market, or they demand prohibitive fees for airplay, making it economically impossible for independent artists and smaller labels to compete. Many talented groups or solo artists, like Caballeros de Plan, who are among the hottest acts right now with a truly devoted following across Latin America and the United States, still can't get their music on mainstream radio to make their unique brand of hip-hop accessible to a wider audience." This lack of mainstream support leaves a vast fan base underserved and a burgeoning genre without a vital platform for growth and discovery. The economic realities mean that without significant financial backing, a broadcast presence for these artists becomes an insurmountable hurdle.

It was this glaring gap that spurred Millan to create LatinHipHopRadio.com. The website, launched recently, is designed to be a sanctuary for Spanish-language hip-hop. "We wanted to make Spanish-language hip-hop truly accessible to its fans, bridging the divide between artists and their audience," Millan says. The site, available both in Spanish and English, is incredibly easy to navigate. Its clean interface and intuitive design ensure that users can quickly find what they're looking for, whether it's the latest tracks, artist interviews, or genre news. All the media, from high-quality audio streams to exclusive video content, is just streamed directly, offering a seamless and free listening experience. There are no complicated downloads or subscription barriers, simply pure, unadulterated hip-hop delivered straight to listeners' devices. This direct-to-fan model circumvents the traditional gatekeepers of radio, empowering artists and giving listeners unprecedented access to a diverse range of music they wouldn't otherwise hear.

Suddenly, a vibrant digital community is emerging, giving voice to hundreds of artists and connecting millions of fans. "We are still in the infant stage, no doubt," Millan admits with a tone of humble optimism, "but the response has been overwhelmingly positive. The quality of production we're seeing from artists is astounding; they are pushing the genre forward, constantly making better and better music." He highlights figures like Mustafa Yoda, a veteran artist whose influence continues to shape the scene. "Mustafa is currently one of the most respected and prolific voices in the underground and Latin hip-hop scene," Millan states emphatically. "He's had incredible collaborations with some of the biggest names in the world, transcending language barriers with his raw talent and lyrical prowess. He's definitely one of the big Spanish-language MCs whose artistry and impact are felt across the globe. original: Yukos sues four firms for $20bn..Russian oil firm Yukos has sued four companies for their role in last year's forced state auction of its key oil production unit Yuganskneftegas...Yukos is claiming more than $20bn (£11bn) in damages after Yugansk was sold in December to settle back taxes. The four companies named in the law suit are gas giant Gazprom, its unit Gazpromneft, investment company Baikal, and state oil firm Rosneft. Yukos submitted the suit in Houston, where it filed for bankruptcy. As well as suing for damages, Yukos has asked the US court to send its tax dispute with the Russian government to an international arbitrator. It also has submitted a reorganisation plan as part of its Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing...The clash between Yukos and the Kremlin came to a head last year when Yukos was hit with a bill of more than $27bn in back taxes and unpaid fines. To settle the bill, Russia forced Yukos to sell off Yuganskneftegas...Yukos called the sale illegal and has turned to courts in the US in an effort to regain control of the oil production business. It also has vowed to use all legal means at its disposal to go after any firm that tries to buy or take control of its assets. Earlier this month it sued the Russian government for $28.3bn. Analysts have questioned whether a US court has any jurisdiction over Russian companies, while Moscow officials have dismissed Yukos' legal wrangling as meaningless. In Houston, bankruptcy Judge Letitia Clark will start a two-day hearing on 16 February to hear arguments on whether a US court is the proper forum for the case...The threat of legal action from Yukos and its bankruptcy filing in Houston did have an effect on last year's auction, however. Concerned that it would be caught up in a court battle, Gazprom and Gazpromneft withdrew from the auction, and Yuganskneftegas was sold to little-known investment firm Baikal Finance Group. A few days later, Baikal gave control of the company to state-run oil group Rosneft for $9.3bn. Rosneft, meanwhile, has agreed to merge with Gazprom, bringing a large chunk of Russia's very profitable oil business back under state control. Yukos claims that the rights of its shareholders have been ignored and that is has been punished for the political ambitions of its founder Mikhail Khodorkovsky. Mr Khodorkovsky, once Russia's richest man, is in prison, having been charged with fraud and tax evasion and repeatedly denied bail.

The **firm** confirmed it had **sued four** companies involved **in** what was widely described as **the year's key oil** asset sale. The claim **is for $20bn (£11bn)**, an amount Yukos is seeking in connection with the controversial sale of its main production subsidiary, Yuganskneftegas, which occurred **in December**. The **four companies** specifically targeted in the legal action include state-controlled **gas** giant Gazprom, its oil exploration and production **unit Gazpromneft**, the obscure **investment company Baikal** Finance (which initially acquired Yuganskneftegas), and state-owned oil **firm Rosneft**. Yukos **submitted the** legal challenge to a Moscow court, while simultaneously grappling **for bankruptcy** protection in other jurisdictions. The company is **suing for damages**, asserting that its **tax** liabilities, currently under dispute **with** a **Russian arbitrator**, are politically motivated and have led to an illegal asset strip. **It also plans** to continue its robust defence **as** its own forced **11** bankruptcy proceedings progress globally, aiming to reclaim its stolen assets and reputation.

**The company** and **its** main subsidiaries were **a year** ago **hit with a** colossal **bill of more** than **$27bn** for alleged back taxes, a move widely seen as precipitating its downfall. This crippling **bill**, which Yukos vehemently contested, directly led to the auction and eventual sale of its most valuable production unit, **Yuganskneftegas**. The asset was subsequently acquired by Baikal Finance, a little-known entity, before swiftly being transferred **to the** ownership of **an** existing state-controlled oil **business**, Rosneft. Yukos had **vowed all its** efforts **to** prevent any **firm** from being able to **buy** Yuganskneftegas in what it called a "sham" auction. reconstruction:
My memories of Bob Marley's 60th birthday celebrations bring back a flood of recollections from his active years. Chris Partridge, then a keen observer of the music press, and later working closely with Marley's team, shared some vivid stories. He worked tirelessly promoting Marley's music and message from 1977, a pivotal year, right up until his untimely death in 1981.

One of Partridge’s most enduring memories dates back to 1977. Bob Marley's groundbreaking album, *Exodus*, released on Island Records, was showcased with a legendary series of concerts. The standout performance was his electrifying show at the Rainbow Theatre in London. What he did on that stage, and the profound impact of the music, truly marked him as a global phenomenon.

It was in 1977 that Marley's music transcended its reggae roots, gaining mainstream international acclaim. For five intense years, he toured relentlessly, spreading his message of peace, love, and unity, achieving truly global superstar status.

By 1979, Bob Marley and The Wailers were unequivocally the biggest touring act in the world. I distinctly remember the sheer scale and intensity of seeing him perform in those unforgettable concerts. His stage presence was something truly unique, almost spiritual.

He possessed a mesmeric charisma, an energy that few performers have ever managed to emulate, let alone surpass. He was one of the most captivating live artists ever to grace the stage, and his performances were legendary.

I have often reflected on Bob's unique blend of vulnerability and immense power. There was a raw, undeniable force within him that manifested itself not just in his music, but in his very being. He didn't hesitate to use his platform to speak out against injustice. I recall a leading music writer of the era stating, without reservation, that he was perhaps 'the greatest performer I'd ever seen.' He was truly a visionary, a man ahead of his times, whose influence resonated across cultures and generations.

Partridge vividly recalls a specific incident from 1978. They were at the BBC Television Centre in London for an appearance on the iconic music show *Top of the Pops*. A photographer from the *Daily Mirror* newspaper was present to capture some backstage moments. Bob was scheduled to head directly to a rehearsal session, but his love for football momentarily took precedence. He came into the room, seemingly oblivious to the schedule, and immediately wanted to resume a vigorous game of football in the corridor. It was a classic Marley moment.

Yet, despite his playful diversion, his professionalism quickly took over. He settled down, and within 10 minutes, he was entirely focused, demonstrating his remarkable ability to switch gears. It was clear that he was fully committed to the task at hand, dedicated to the very end of every performance and every project. That very anecdote encapsulates the dual nature of his spirit: the spontaneous, joyful individual and the intensely disciplined artist.

The last time Chris Partridge saw Bob Marley perform live was during his European tour in 1980. Marley was scheduled to play four days of major indoor concerts at the Crystal Palace National Sports Centre in London. It was a monumental undertaking, showcasing his immense popularity even as his health was beginning to decline.

Beyond music, Bob Marley was profoundly passionate about football. He was an incredibly talented player himself, often engaging in fierce matches wherever he went. He often spoke about his lifelong dream of seeing his beloved Jamaica team qualify for and play in the World Cup – a dream that, sadly, remained unfulfilled during his lifetime.

Marley's music, initially emerging from Jamaica, found a global audience alongside the burgeoning disco scene of the 1970s. But it was in the decades after his death, particularly the 1980s and 1990s, that his legacy truly solidified. He became an undisputed global icon, the voice of the oppressed and a powerful symbol for the developing world, especially the African continent.

By 1991, exactly ten years after his death, Marley's posthumous influence had grown exponentially. His songs of struggle and liberation had found their way into the hearts of millions across Africa for the first time, igniting a cultural and political awakening.

Many argue that Bob Marley is, in his own right, perhaps the greatest cultural figure of the 20th century. His profound significance to Africa, in particular, would be comparable to the impact of figures like Mahatma Gandhi, Martin Luther King Jr., or even John Lennon in the Western world.

No disrespect is intended to those other revered artists, but in Marley's case, his influence and stature as the ultimate symbol of hope and freedom across the African continent was unique, perhaps even unparalleled in its depth and reach.

It's a poignant historical note that in 1981, the very year of his passing, Bob Marley had planned an extensive tour of Africa. Dates were provisionally scheduled for various nations, including Gabon, Zimbabwe, and Guinea, marking a return to the continent he so deeply revered.

He died, of course, in May 1981, at the young age of 36, but his message and music were immediately embraced globally, continuing to spread far and wide. We simply cannot make the assertion that he was at the height of his creative powers at 36, because his potential was still expanding. It makes no sense whatsoever to suggest his career was on a downhill trajectory; if anything, he was entering a new phase of artistic and spiritual maturity.

Bob Marley was always profoundly optimistic about Africa's future, firmly believing in its eventual liberation and prosperity, that its people would ultimately sort themselves out and rise to their full potential. He had a perfect, unwavering belief in the fundamental goodness of mankind and its capacity for positive change.

I'm sure today he would have continued to speak out passionately on global issues. Firstly, about the devastating Aids epidemic that disproportionately affected so much of the continent and its people, and then about the ongoing struggles for economic justice and environmental protection worldwide.

His final studio album, 'Uprising,' released just before his death, featured the profound and enduring track 'Redemption Song' – one of the classics of his entire oeuvre, a powerful acoustic ballad that served as a final, resonant testament to his indomitable spirit and his timeless message of emancipation.

original: EU-US seeking deal on air dispute..The EU and US have agreed to begin talks on ending subsidies given to aircraft makers, EU Trade Commissioner Peter Mandelson has announced...Both sides hope to reach a negotiated deal over state aid received by European aircraft maker Airbus and its US rival Boeing, Mr Mandelson said. Airbus and Boeing accuse each other of benefiting from illegal subsidies. Mr Mandelson said the EU and US hoped to avoid having to resolve the dispute at the World Trade Organisation (WTO)..."With this agreement the EU and US have confirmed their willingness to resolve the dispute which has arisen between them," Mr Mandelson said. "I hope our negotiations in the next three months will lead to an agreement ending subsidies to development and production of large civil aircraft." Last year, the US terminated an agreement with the EU, reached in 1992, which limits the subsidies countries can hand over to civil aircraft makers. The US filed a complaint against Brussels with the WTO over state aid to Airbus, prompting a retaliatory EU complaint over US support for Boeing. However, both sides agreed to suspend their requests for WTO arbitration at the beginning of December, to allow bilateral talks to continue. EADS and BAE Systems, the European defence and aerospace firms which own Airbus, welcomed Mr Mandelson's announcement. "It has always been preferable that any differences between the US and Europe on this matter be overcome through constructive discussion rather than through legal recourse," the companies said in a joint statement...Separately, the world's largest package delivery company, UPS, said it had placed an order for 10 Airbus A380 superjumbo freight-carrying jets, with an option to buy 10 more of the triple-decker aircraft. The US company said it needed to expand its air freight capacity following strong international growth, and would begin receiving deliveries of the A380s from 2009. However, UPS said it was cutting a previous order for smaller Airbus A300s from 90 planes to 53. So far, Airbus has delivered 40 A300s to UPS. Airbus overtook Boeing as the world's largest manufacturer of commercial airliners in 2003.

The European Union and the US have agreed to begin ending their subsidies to airliner manufacturers, Trade Commissioner Mandelson announced today. The agreement is designed to reach a state where European aerospace maker Airbus and its US rival Boeing, Mr. Mandelson said, would no longer be benefiting from such state subsidies, with other aerospace manufacturers around the world also benefiting from a more level playing field. For some time, the EU had hoped to resolve the long-standing dispute at the World Trade Organisation (WTO), but bilateral talks eventually led to this breakthrough.

"This serious disagreement, and the fundamental differences between them, has arisen," Mr. Mandelson stated in a press conference. "I hope this agreement will pave the way for the more rational and sustainable development of civil aviation in the long term."

Last year, the United States unilaterally terminated a bilateral agreement, which was originally made in 1992, concerning aircraft subsidies between the two major trading blocs. The US then formally filed a complaint at the WTO, alleging illegal state aid for Airbus, while the EU promptly counter-filed, alleging illegal US support for Boeing in return. Both sides had been threatening to take further retaliatory action at the beginning of this year, escalating the dispute, but this new agreement will allow the vital discussions to continue in a more constructive spirit.

EADS, Airbus's parent company, and BAE Systems, the firms which jointly own the European aircraft manufacturer, warmly welcomed the news of the breakthrough. "It is hoped that future differences will now be settled through constructive discussion rather than costly and time-consuming legal action," the companies said in a joint statement issued today.

Separately, the US cargo giant UPS announced it had placed a significant order for 10 A380 superjumbo freighters, with an additional option for 10 more of the huge aircraft. The company stated that these new planes would substantially expand its capacity on key international routes, and it expected to begin receiving the first A380s from 2009 onwards. However, UPS also said it was retiring a significant number of its older A300-600 freighters – 90 aircraft in total, starting with 53 of them initially – and replacing some with 40 new A300-600 freighters, a decision that has implications for the older model's future. Boeing famously lost its position as the world's largest maker of commercial aircraft to Airbus in 2003.

The United States has launched a significant legal offensive against two individuals it identifies as among the world's most prolific and damaging spammers, in a concerted bid to stop their pervasive operations. A federal lawsuit was filed this week, aiming to permanently halt their activities and recover substantial penalties for their alleged violations of anti-spam legislation. The action underscores an escalating effort by US authorities to combat the pervasive problem of unsolicited commercial electronic mail.

The civil complaint targets Ryan P. Pitylak and Mark Stephen Trotter, accusing them of orchestrating a vast and sophisticated spamming enterprise. Their associated companies, including Optin Leads LLC and Leadplex Inc, are named as central to the operation. Authorities allege that these entities have been responsible for the transmission of many millions of unsolicited bulk e-mails, inundating inboxes across the nation and globally. This widespread distribution network is cited as a primary reason for their designation as "world's top spammers."

"This relentless assault on our digital lives must be stopped," declared the US Attorney General, commenting on the lawsuit. He emphasised that "the aggravating and pervasive flood of spam is one of the most significant problems facing consumers and businesses today." The legal action aims to dismantle an operation that has not only annoyed countless recipients but also posed significant security risks and economic burdens through its deceptive practices.

The lawsuit specifically alleges that the defendants' extensive wrongdoing failed to comply with the relevant provisions of the Controlling the Assault of Non-Solicited Pornography and Marketing (CAN-SPAM) Act of 2003. This landmark federal legislation was enacted to establish requirements for commercial messages, give consumers the right to have companies stop e-mailing them, and spell out tough penalties for violators. The complaint details how Mr. Trotter's company, in particular, repeatedly breached the core tenets of this act, undermining its effectiveness.

Beyond federal anti-spam legislation, the suit also cites violations of state-level Deceptive Trade Practices Acts. Prosecutors contend that the messages sent by the pair routinely employed deceptive tactics. These included the use of misleading or false subject lines designed to trick recipients into opening emails, and a systematic failure to clearly identify the messages as advertising. Furthermore, the defendants are accused of offering products for which they had no legitimate license to sell, adding another layer of fraudulent activity to their operations.

The lawsuit highlighted two other serious accusations, asserting that many of the claims made within the unsolicited messages were entirely groundless and misleading. This often involved exaggerated promises or non-existent offers, further duping unsuspecting individuals. Compounding these issues, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), which has been conducting its own investigations into the defendants, has also specifically noted that a significant portion of the emails distributed by the operation were of a sexually explicit or pornographic nature, often targeting vulnerable users.

The FTC's findings underscore distinct violations of the CAN-SPAM Act's technical requirements. The Commission stated that the spam messages frequently did not contain valid physical addresses for the sender, a mandatory element under the law. Moreover, they often failed to clearly mention that they were advertisements, bypassing another critical consumer protection. Crucially, the senders frequently obscured their true identities, not giving the sender's real name or identifiable business, making it nearly impossible for recipients to opt out or trace the source of the unwanted communication.

For their alleged extensive and systematic violations, all three companies named in the suit—Optin Leads LLC, Leadplex Inc, and potentially others—along with the two individual defendants, Ryan P. Pitylak and Mark Stephen Trotter, could face substantial cash penalties. The CAN-SPAM Act allows for fines of up to $16,000 per email, meaning the total penalties could run into many millions of dollars given the alleged volume of messages sent. Beyond financial repercussions, the FTC is also vigorously seeking a court order to impose a permanent injunction against the defendants, which would effectively bar them from engaging in any future spamming activities and compel them to comply with federal law.

This legal action is part of a broader, intensified effort by US authorities to curb the global phenomenon of spam, which continues to clog internet infrastructure and defraud users worldwide. The collaboration between the Justice Department and agencies like the FTC reflects a comprehensive approach to tackling operators who exploit digital communication for illicit gain. Authorities hope that such high-profile cases will serve as a strong deterrent to other spammers and help reclaim the integrity of online communication channels for legitimate use.

The Liberal Democrats today launched their general election campaign, unveiling their core policy platform. Party leader Charles Kennedy told activists that this would be an 'honest' election, sharply contrasting their approach with what he characterised as the negative campaigning tactics of Labour and the Conservatives. He positioned his party as offering a straightforward choice to voters.

Two significant political battlegrounds are set to dominate the debate: the economy and taxation, alongside public service funding. The election campaign will certainly feature an increasing array of spending pledges. This ensures intense scrutiny of the Labour government's financial record and other parties' previous pledges on how the public pound is spent. Voters are looking for tangible improvements.

Central to their strategy, Mr. Kennedy is promising a new top rate of income tax for individuals earning over £100,000 annually. This revenue will fund a comprehensive package of new public policies including the complete abolition of university tuition fees, universal free personal care for the elderly, and substantial cuts to council tax bills. Additionally, the Liberal Democrats will propose a 3p increase in the basic rate of income tax, specifically earmarked to fund significant improvements in core public services, directing funds towards the National Health Service and improving educational standards.

The Conservative Party leadership immediately attacked these Liberal Democrat policies, dismissing them as both fiscally irresponsible and economically unworkable. Shadow Treasury spokespersons insisted that such ambitious pledges could not be funded sustainably without straining the national economy, potentially leading to increased government borrowing or broader tax rises. They labelled the plans a 'recipe for economic chaos'.

The Tories further contended that the Liberal Democrats' overall package of public service proposals would, by their calculations, ultimately cost an estimated £35bn – a figure they argued was wildly unrealistic. In contrast, the Liberal Democrats asserted they had meticulously mapped out how to fund £22bn of their new spending commitments with clear proposals. However, commentators noted there is still little detailed information about the specific funding mechanisms or proposed spending cuts that the other main parties will propose in their own forthcoming manifestos.

For many political observers, the core argument advanced by the Liberal Democrats regarding higher taxation on wealthier individuals and increased public spending resembles the intense ideological debate that raged between Labour and the Tories throughout the 1980s and early 1990s, concerning wealth redistribution and the state's role in welfare provision.

Indeed, the Liberal Democrats are increasingly seen as explicitly championing a 'wealth tax' on the well-off and high earners as a principal mechanism to fund public service expansion and improvement. This strategic emphasis comes amid recent opinion polls consistently suggesting that a substantial proportion of the public harbours deep concerns about the current state and overall level of public services, particularly the NHS and education.

Similarly, the general election campaign is anticipated to be heavily dominated by discussions around the state of the economy, the contentious issue of immigration, and law and order. This thematic focus Mr. Kennedy has repeatedly described as 'artificial' or manufactured. He argues this focus is a distraction compared to what he views as Mr. Howard's more narrow and divisive approach, often accusing the Conservative leader of scaremongering tactics.

Once again, with Labour and the Conservatives emphasizing immigration controls and national security, Mr. Kennedy has adopted a different strategic approach. He notably made headlines by effectively declaring the general election 'over' before it formally began, wryly suggesting the outcome was a foregone conclusion. He has also firmly stressed his party's commitment not to enter into any post-election coalition agreement with either Labour or the Conservatives, aiming to dispel voter uncertainty.

Mr. Kennedy articulated his deeply held belief that for the country to be governed by a single dominant political party with an overwhelming parliamentary majority would, in effect, amount to a 'one-party state'. Such a scenario, he views as fundamentally unhealthy and detrimental to a vibrant and functioning democracy, leading to a lack of accountability. He passionately advocates for a more pluralistic political landscape.

This general election campaign is therefore shaping up to be one of the most unpredictable and potentially transformative in a generation. The Liberal Democrats are fervently hoping to finally break the entrenched two-party mould of British politics. It is a long-held dream that has been dreamed many times before by their party, but one they genuinely believe is now closer to becoming a reality, offering a real and credible alternative to the electorate.

He added that "by pledging the £150,000 threshold, the Liberal Democrats are making it genuinely possible for thousands more first-time buyers to get on the property ladder and achieve their dreams."

Paul Schrader's original version of The Exorcist prequel, officially titled Dominion: Prequel to the Exorcist, is finally set to be screened publicly for the first time on 18 March at the Brussels International Fantastic Film Festival. The film delves into the early experiences of Father Merrin, the iconic character from the original 1973 horror classic, The Exorcist. This particular cut represents the first vision for the prequel, which was originally filmed before director Renny Harlin was brought in to make his own significantly altered version, released to cinemas in 2004.

Back in 2001, acclaimed actor Liam Neeson was originally cast in the pivotal role of Father Merrin. However, in an unexpected turn of events in 2002, just a month before principal photography was due to commence, Stellan Skarsgard was brought in to replace Neeson. Father Merrin was, of course, famously portrayed by the legendary Max Von Sydow in the 1973 original.

Principal photography for Schrader's ambitious version of the prequel took place entirely in Morocco, costing an estimated $32m. However, in 2003, executives at the production studio Morgan Creek decided to controversially shelve Schrader's completed cut, openly complaining that 'it was not scary enough' for their liking.

As Schrader's more psychological and less gore-focused vision was deemed unsuitable by the studio, Renny Harlin - the director behind high-octane action films like Die Hard 2 and Cliffhanger - was subsequently brought in to completely reshoot the film. He drastically changed much of the original film's content and style, though Skarsgard's central performance in the lead role was thankfully retained. Harlin's overhauled version, ultimately retitled Exorcist: The Beginning, was released in the UK in 2004 and, despite its troubled production, went on to gross a respectable $76m (£40.7m) worldwide. Schrader's original cut, by contrast, has not yet been seen in cinemas in the UK and, disappointingly for fans, is not yet available on DVD.

Other notable films scheduled to feature prominently at the festival in the Belgium capital, which runs its course from 11-26 March, include the highly anticipated horror sequel The Ring 2 and an adapted version of a popular cult classic from the independent circuit.

Stars pay tribute to actor Ossie Davis. Spike Lee and Alan Alda led tributes at a New York service for the veteran actor.

Davis, a prolific actor and civil rights activist, died aged 87 on 4 February 2005. His wife, actress Ruby Dee, his co-star for 56 years, was present at the Saturday service. Former US president Bill Clinton delivered a eulogy.

"I have never known a president of the United States," said Clinton, "who in his own time, in his own way, gave more of himself, who gave more to me than Ossie Davis."

Davis, 87, was found dead on Saturday morning in his Miami Beach hotel room, where he was making a film. He made his acting debut on Broadway in 1950 in No Time for Sergeants. He frequently appeared in films directed by Spike Lee, including Do the Right Thing, Jungle Fever, Malcolm X, and Get on the Bus.

Attallah Shabazz, daughter of Malcolm X, delivered a moving tribute to Davis at the service. "America has lost one of its finest citizens," she said of the man she knew as Ossie.

"Ossie was a gentle giant, and he is still with us," said actor Danny Glover, his friend for many years. "He was a truly remarkable individual."

"I hope that someday we'll have dignity in the way we're portrayed anyway," added Ruby Dee, Davis's co-star and wife for over 50 years, referring to the goals Ossie pursued throughout his life.

Earlier in the day, thousands had gathered at a Harlem church to pay respects to Davis.

"He made a difference through his art and activism. It was his vision, his choices that made him the man he was, and for those ideals he made and for which he fought, we are forever in his debt," said Spike Lee, himself an activist for 60 years. His contributions were as significant as they were heartfelt.

original: BT offers equal access to rivals..BT has moved to pre-empt a possible break-up of its business by offering to cut wholesale broadband prices and open its network to rivals...The move comes after telecom regulator Ofcom said in November that the firm must offer competitors "real equality of access to its phone lines". At the time, Ofcom offered BT the choice of change or splitting into two. Ofcom is carrying out a strategic review aimed at promoting greater competition in the UK telecom sector. BT's competitors have frequently accused it of misusing its status as the former telecoms monopoly and controller of access to many customers to favour its own retail arm...This latest submission was delivered to the watchdog ahead of a deadline for the second phase of its review..."Central to the proposals are plans by BT to offer operators lower wholesale prices, faster broadband services and transparent, highly-regulated access to BT's local network," the former monopoly said in a statement. "The United Kingdom has the opportunity to create the most exciting and innovative telecoms market in the world," BT chief executive Ben Verwaayen said. "BT has a critical role to play, and today we are making a set of far-reaching proposals towards that framework," he said. BT wants lighter regulation in exchange for the changes, as well as the removal of the break-up threat...The group is to set up a new Access Services division - with a separate board which would include independent members - to ensure equal access for rivals to the "local loop", the copper wires that run between telephone exchanges and households. The company also unveiled plans to cut the wholesale prices of its most popular broadband product by about 8% from April in areas of high customer demand...It added that it plans to invest £10bn in the next five years to create a "21st Century network". To meet the growing demand for greater bandwidth, BT said it would begin trials in April with a view to launching higher-speed services nationally from the autumn...Telecom analysts Ovum welcomed the move, saying BT had "given a lot of ground"..."The big question now is whether the industry, and particularly Ofcom feels BT's proposals go far enough ...Now the real negotiation begins," director of telecoms research Tony Lavender said. Internet service provider (ISP) Plus.net also backed the proposals saying "we will be entirely happy if Ofcom accepts them". "BT has been challenged to play fair and its plans will introduce a level playing field. The scenario now is how well people execute their business plans as a service provider," chief executive Lee Strafford said. Chris Panayis, managing director of ISP Freedom2surf said that it would make the situation clearer for business. "I think it's the first productive thing we've had from BT," he said...AOL backed the price cuts but said regulation was still needed to ensure a level playing field. "This is a reminder to Ofcom that as long as BT can change the dynamics of the whole broadband market at will, the process of opening up the UK's local telephone network to infrastructure investment and competition remains fragile," a spokesman said. "Ofcom needs to return to regulation of the wholesale broadband service [IPStream] and provide more robust rules for local loop unbundling if consumers are to see the benefits of increased competition and infrastructure investment." More than 100 telecom firms, consumer groups and other interested parties are expected to make submissions to the regulator during this consultation phase. Ofcom is expected to spend the next few weeks examining the proposals before making an announcement within the next few months.

reconstruction:
BT offers a compromise to pre-empt a break-up of its operations by opening up its network to competitors. The November deadline had been set for BT to make a firm offer to its competitors for access to its local lines. At the time, the telecoms watchdog, Ofcom, had given BT a choice: either make an acceptable offer or face a forced split of its operations. This move was aimed at promoting greater competition and innovation across the telecom sector. Competitors frequently complain that BT still leverages its former telecoms monopoly and its ownership of key infrastructure, like the local network and its wholesale arm, Openreach, to the detriment of fair competition.

This decision by the telecoms watchdog, Ofcom, marks a crucial moment in the second phase of its review into the UK broadband market. BT's new plans, if implemented, would offer lower wholesale prices, faster connection speeds, and pave the way for more exciting and innovative telecoms services across the United Kingdom.

"BT has a critical role in the UK's digital economy, but we need to see a set of far-reaching changes to its operational practices," said Ed Richards, Ofcom's chief executive. "These lighter-touch changes, if properly implemented and monitored, are designed to avert the more drastic threat of a full structural separation. Our aim is to open up unbundled access to BT's copper wires and local exchanges to all competitors on a fair and equal basis."

The company also announced it would cut its wholesale broadband prices by about 8% from July, a move it said was driven by high demand and efficiency gains. BT plans to invest more than £10bn over the next five years to create a "21st Century Network" designed to meet growing demand for high-speed internet. It said it had developed its plans in close consultation with the wider industry and had "given a lot of thought" to addressing concerns raised by rivals.

The rest of the industry, however, remains largely unconvinced that BT's proposals go far enough to truly level the playing field. "Now," said Paul Barford, director of business development at Carphone Warehouse's TalkTalk Group, "we'll have to see if Ofcom's final proposals will be robust enough, and crucially, if BT genuinely accepts and implements them fully."

"BT has been repeatedly challenged to improve its service quality and its overall relationship with their customers," said Costas Panayis, managing director of Freedom2surf. He stressed that the "first thing" BT needs to do is completely open up its local loop network to allow true competition, he said, adding that mere gestures would not suffice.

While some competitors cautiously backed the proposed price cuts, many reiterated that the new regulation must create a truly level playing field, not just symbolic changes. "Ofcom believes that as BT implements these changes, the market dynamics will shift significantly, allowing the UK's consumers and businesses to benefit from greater choice, lower prices, and more innovative services," an Ofcom spokesperson said.

"Ofcom needs to tighten its regulation of wholesale broadband services, particularly BT's dominant IPStream product, and provide a robust framework for all market players to see tangible benefits from increased competition and new infrastructure investment."

More than 100 telecom operators, consumer groups, and other interested parties are expected to make detailed submissions to Ofcom regarding these proposals. Ofcom expects to spend the next few weeks carefully considering all feedback before making a final decision in the next few months.

France's Economy Ends 2004 on a Strong Note, Driven by Consumer Spending Boost

France's economy maintained its robust performance during the final months of 2004, driven, according to a new report, by a significant surge in consumer spending. The national statistical office INSEE announced on Tuesday that Gross Domestic Product (GDP) expanded by a healthy 0.8% in the fourth quarter, compared with the previous three months, exceeding many analysts' forecasts.

This strong acceleration in the fourth quarter propelled France's overall economic growth for 2004 to a robust 2.3%, marking the strongest annual expansion in two years. This performance highlighted the resilience of domestic demand and positioned France as a leading performer within the eurozone, offering a positive contrast to some of its neighbours.

Consumer spending proved the primary engine, recording a substantial 1.2% increase in the fourth quarter. This surge in household expenditure was a pivotal factor, significantly accelerating the overall pace of economic expansion. Analysts attributed this robust showing to renewed consumer confidence and a steady, albeit cautious, improvement in the labour market, fostering a willingness to spend despite lingering economic uncertainties.

"France is experiencing strong economic growth," said Marc Touati, an economist at Natexis Banques Populaires. "Even if inflation is a concern, consumer spending is high. But households have also increased their savings." This creates a gap where "they can't get a rate in the market that truly closes the perceived gap between financial security and economic uncertainty," he added.

Despite the largely positive news, challenges persist. Unemployment figures are still around 10%, remaining a key socio-economic issue that the government continues to grapple with. Nevertheless, France's economic situation is proving remarkably robust compared to many European partners, a point the French government was quick to highlight with satisfaction, reiterating its commitment to fostering continued growth.

Adding to the positive picture, business investment also climbed 1.3% in the fourth quarter, marking the biggest increase in over a year. This indicates growing confidence among businesses to expand and invest in future capacity, suggesting the current growth spurt is becoming more broadly based, not solely reliant on consumption.

Nicolas Claquin, an economist at CCF, commented, "It's a strong economic performance." He noted, "Growth in 2004 was mainly by consumer spending. Here, though, consumption remains strong, and investment is also picking up, which is a very encouraging sign."

Looking ahead, while strong momentum from 2004 is expected to carry into the new year, overall growth is predicted to slow slightly to around 2.0% for 2005. This anticipated moderation is attributed to potential global economic headwinds and ongoing structural reforms. However, the underlying strength of consumer demand and increasing business confidence provide a solid foundation for continued expansion in the coming year.

However, AOL's traditional access business lost 464,000 dial-up subscribers in the quarter. The company's overall profit was boosted by 8% thanks to stronger online advertising and efforts to encourage existing customers to upgrade their broadband speed.

The company had previously restated its 2000 and 2003 financial results with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), which helped contribute to TimeWarner's stronger reported fourth-quarter profits. TimeWarner is still in negotiations with market regulators concerning its AOL unit. It hopes to settle charges of accounting fraud for approximately $300m, an amount that is currently under review by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The SEC had previously been unable to agree on a settlement figure, having originally sought $500m. TimeWarner also continues to negotiate for a settlement with music publisher Bertelsmann over allegations of a disputed advertising pact, which had drawn significant regulatory scrutiny.
