original: TV calls after Carroll error..Spurs boss Martin Jol said his team were "robbed" at Manchester United after Pedro Mendes' shot clearly crossed the line but was not given..."The referee is already wearing an earpiece so why can't we just stop the game and get the decision right," said Jol after the 0-0 draw. "But at the end of the day it's so obvious that Pedro's shot was over the line it's incredible. "We feel robbed but it's difficult for the linesman and referee to see it." Mendes shot from 50 yards and United goalkeeper Roy Carroll spilled the ball into his own net before hooking it clear. Jol added: "We are not talking about the ball being a couple of centimetres or an inch or two over the line, it was a metre inside the goal. "What really annoys me is that we are here in 2005, watching something on a TV monitor within two seconds of the incident occurring and the referee isn't told about it..."We didn't play particularly well but I am pleased - even now - with a point, although we should have had three." Mendes could not believe the 'goal' was not given after seeing a replay. He said: "My reaction on the pitch was to celebrate. "It was a very nice goal, it was clearly over the line - I've never seen one so over the line and not given in my career. "It's really, really over. What can you do but laugh about it? It's a nice goal and one to keep in my memory even though it didn't count. "It's not every game you score from the halfway line." Manchester United manager Sir Alex Ferguson sympathised with Tottenham and said the incident highlighted the need for video technology. "I think it hammers home what a lot of people have been asking for and that's that technology should play a part in the game," Ferguson told MUTV. "What I was against originally was the time factor in video replays. "But I read an article the other day which suggested that if a referee can't make up his mind after 30 seconds of watching a video replay then the game should carry on..."Thirty seconds is about the same amount of time it takes to organise a free-kick or take a corner or a goal-kick. So you wouldn't be wasting a lot of time. "I think you could start off by using it for goal-line decisions. I think that would be an opening into a new area of football." Arsenal boss Arsene Wenger also used the incident to highlight the need for video technology. "When the whole world apart from the referee has seen there should be a goal at Old Trafford, that just reinforces what I feel - there should be video evidence," said Wenger. "It's a great example of where the referee could have asked to see a replay and would have seen in five seconds that it was a goal."

Tottenham Hotspur manager Martin Jol expressed disbelief and anger after his side were denied a clear goal against Manchester United in a 0-0 Premier League draw at Old Trafford. The controversial incident, which occurred in the 50th minute, saw a Spurs midfielder's long-range shot clearly cross the line before being scooped out by United goalkeeper Roy Carroll, but neither the referee nor his linesman allowed the goal. The decision immediately ignited a furious debate about the use of technology in football, with both managers and rival clubs weighing in on the incident.

Jol was visibly incensed after the final whistle, lamenting the missed opportunity for his team. "It was a clear goal," Jol stated emphatically. "The ball was definitely over the line. The linesman was in a perfect position to see it, and with the referee wearing a microphone, you wonder why there wasn't better communication to ensure the correct decision was made. After a 0-0 draw, this feels like we were truly robbed. In the end, it wasn't given, so the game finishes 0-0, which is just incredible. We feel utterly robbed, though I understand it's a difficult job for the linesman, it was so clear for everyone to see."

The contentious moment came just five minutes into the second half when a Tottenham midfielder unleashed a speculative shot from nearly the halfway line. The ball sailed over Roy Carroll's head, bounced clearly over the goal-line, and then spun back out before the United goalkeeper belatedly hooked it away.
A Tottenham player, central to the incident, spoke of his immediate reaction and frustration. "It was in by an inch or two, it was absolutely a goal," he insisted. "My immediate reaction was to celebrate, because I saw it go in. It really saddens me that we are in 2005, and on a television monitor within moments, you can clearly see that the ball crossed the line, yet the referee isn't told about it and the decision stands. They should stop play at that point; technology should be used to confirm such clear decisions. I believe it was a goal, and it was clearly over the line - I've never had a goal like that go against me in my career. What can you do about it? It's a nice memory to keep, the thought of having scored such a spectacular goal, but it doesn't count if it's not given. It was a clear score, even if it came from the halfway line."

Manchester United manager Sir Alex Ferguson, while benefiting from the decision, expressed sympathy for Tottenham and used the incident to reiterate his support for goal-line technology. "I sympathised with Tottenham," Ferguson admitted. "It was a clear decision that went against them. I think for them, it's a great shame that such technology isn't being used in the game, because it was a major factor in the outcome of this match. But the rules are such that the referee cannot change his mind after 30 seconds of play, or once the game has restarted with a throw-in, a goal-kick or a corner, prevent him from reconsidering. So that's how it has to be based on current regulations. I think you could solve this problem by implementing goal-line technology. I think it would be a simple and effective addition to the game, ensuring such injustices are avoided in the future."

The controversy at Old Trafford quickly reignited calls from across the football world for the introduction of goal-line technology. Arsenal, long-time advocates for technological aids in decision-making, were quick to use the controversy to renew their pleas for change.
An Arsenal spokesman stated: "The whole world has seen what happened at Old Trafford, what more evidence should we need? Video technology should absolutely be used in situations like this. It would have been a great service to the game and to Tottenham if they had asked to see the replay. It would have unequivocally shown that the ball was five inches over the line, a clear goal, and the outcome of the match could have been entirely different. This incident simply underlines the urgent need for FIFA and football's lawmakers to embrace modern solutions to prevent such blatant errors." The incident has added further weight to the ongoing debate about football's resistance to technology, with proponents arguing it would enhance fairness and accuracy without significantly disrupting the flow of the game.

Among the highly anticipated inclusions are early demo versions of iconic tracks, B-sides that rarely saw the light of day, and seminal live recordings. Fans are particularly keen to hear a powerful performance of their anthem 'Smells Like Teen Spirit' captured during a pivotal Nirvana stage show in 1991.

"There are a whole lot of options like this springing up on the web and one has to think carefully about what the market is going to be," she said. "Blind people have specialised screen readers available to them which will do the job these technologies do in a more sophisticated way," she added...The site uses a technology dubbed PanaVox, which takes web text and converts it into synthesised speech. In the past speech technology has only been compatible with broadband because of the huge files it downloads but CEC says its compression technology means it will also work on slower dial-up connections. Visitors to Speegle may notice that the look and feel of the site bears more than a passing resemblance to the better known, if silent, search engine Google. Google has no connection with Speegle and the use of bright colours is simply to make the site more visible for those with visual impairments, said Mr Renton. "It is not a rip-off. We are doing something that Google does not do and is not planning to do and there is truth in the saying that imitation is the sincerest form of flattery," he said. Speegle is proving popular with those learning English in countries such as Japan and China. "The site is bombarded by people just listening to the words. reconstruction:
Manchester United strolled into FA Cup quarter-finals

Manchester United secured their place in the FA Cup quarter-finals with a comfortable 2-0 victory over Everton at a typically hostile Goodison Park. Goals from Quinton Fortune and Cristiano Ronaldo sealed United's progress in a match where they largely dominated possession and chances. The win sends Sir Alex Ferguson's side into the last eight of the competition, keeping their hopes of silverware alive against a spirited but ultimately outclassed Everton side.

United started brightly, overcoming the initial jeers from the home crowd. Paul Scholes was at the heart of much of United's early attacking play, pulling the strings in midfield with his customary precision. The breakthrough arrived on 23 minutes when Quinton Fortune, following up on a scramble inside the penalty area, powerfully headed home from close range after Everton's defence failed to clear a corner. It was a well-taken goal that settled United's nerves and asserted their control over the game. Wayne Rooney, returning to his former club, had the best chance prior to the goal, firing wide from six feet after good work down the left flank. The match was always going to be a flashpoint, a derby-like atmosphere even if not officially a derby, with tackles flying in and plenty of passion on display. United, however, remained disciplined and focused, asserting their authority from the 19th minute onwards.

United continued to dictate play, displaying a supreme level of passing and movement that Everton struggled to match. They took a deserved lead into the half-time interval, having comfortably dominated without creating too many clear-cut opportunities beyond the opening goal. Everton's attacking efforts were largely nullified by United's solid defensive pairing of Rio Ferdinand and Mikaël Silvestre, with Roy Carroll rarely troubled in the United goal during the first 45 minutes, despite the best efforts of Kevin Kilbane and James McFadden.

The second half began with United still on the front foot, pressing for a second goal to solidify their advantage. They almost doubled their lead in the 48th minute when a low shot from Cristiano Ronaldo from about 25 yards out forced Nigel Martyn, Everton's veteran goalkeeper, into a fine diving save, parrying the ball clear with a full-stretch effort. Martyn was in inspired form, keeping his side in the game with several crucial interventions. And Everton's big moment almost arrived on the hour mark, when a rare foray forward saw a goal-bound shot unleashed, but the United defence was alert and bravely cleared the danger at the last moment.

However, United eventually doubled their lead on 57 minutes, securing their advantage beyond doubt. Cristiano Ronaldo, who had been a persistent threat throughout the game, picked up the ball on the right wing, cut inside past an Everton defender and unleashed a powerful, dipping shot that flew past Martyn into the bottom corner. The Everton keeper could only watch as Ronaldo celebrated a brilliant individual goal, demonstrating his growing influence. United's two-goal cushion provided them with supreme confidence for the remainder of the match, allowing them to control the tempo and manage the game effectively.

Everton pushed for a way back, bringing on substitutes to try and spark their attack. James McFadden and Lee Carsley worked tirelessly in midfield, but United's midfield, anchored by Roy Keane and Paul Scholes, maintained a stranglehold on the game. Alan Stubbs and David Weir battled hard in the Everton defence, but were often outpaced by the pace and trickery of Ronaldo and Rooney. Despite a spirited effort in the closing stages, and some hopeful shots from distance, Everton were ultimately denied any clear route back into the game, with United closing out a comfortable victory. Their search for an equaliser saw United's defence hold firm, as one attack saw Stubbs outpaced, and their efforts were denied by a resilient United backline, denying them any solace.

Manchester United manager Sir Alex Ferguson commented: "It was a very professional performance by us. Everton battled hard, and Goodison is always a difficult place to come. But we were disciplined and played some excellent football. That boy Ronaldo is a special player. He's persistent and always wants to be involved. I don't know how many fouls he can take and still wants to play; he's truly an amazing player with such resilience and drive."

U2 were officially inducted into the prestigious Rock and Roll Hall of Fame this week, a momentous occasion for the Irish rock giants. Bruce Springsteen, a fellow rock legend and long-time admirer, inducted U2 into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, in a lavish ceremony held in New York City. The event, which marked the 50th anniversary of rock and roll, saw the induction of several iconic artists, including The Pretenders, The O'Jays and the legendary soul singer Percy Sledge.
Addressing the star-studded audience, U2 frontman Bono declared: "We have no claim to one another, but we are a family," said Bono, his voice resonating with gratitude. He was joined on stage by bassist Adam Clayton Jr, who recounted the band's humble beginnings, explaining they formed U2 at Mount Temple Comprehensive School in 1977, when he was just 18 years old. Springsteen, in his humorous and heartfelt induction speech, affectionately mocked Bono as the man who "once single-handedly brought back the mullet", before praising U2 as "one of the best and most endearingly in-your-face bands in rock 'n' roll". Springsteen further quipped that Bono was of such stature, that it was 20 years before he knew the other members' names...

The induction ceremony also featured powerful performances and moving tributes. Following their acceptance, members of U2, demonstrating their collaborative spirit, joined the Pretenders' formidable leader Chrissie Hynde to perform 'My City Was Gone', a poignant and electrifying rendition that brought the house down.
"It's a miracle we're here at all," said Hynde, 53, her voice filled with raw emotion as she accepted The Pretenders' honour. "Our dearly departed guitarist James Honeyman-Scott and bassist Pete Farndon, whom we would have loved to share this incredible moment with, both tragically died from drug overdoses," the singer said, reflecting on the band's turbulent past and the friends they had lost too soon. Later in the evening, soul legend Percy Sledge, whose iconic rendition of 'When a Man Loves a Woman' captivated generations, was also posthumously honoured. His long-time manager, Philip Stewart, his eyes welling with pride, simply stated: "Man, Percy is one of the best vocalists this world has ever known".

The celebrations continued with an energetic tribute to rhythm and blues. Pop superstar and actor Justin Timberlake graciously introduced soul group The O'Jays, a gospel-style quartet from Ohio, who thrilled the audience by performing their two best-known songs, 'Love Train' and 'For the Love of Money.' "They performed something soulful, something that truly touches the soul," said Timberlake, clearly impressed by their enduring talent and vibrant stage presence. The O'Jays, known for their harmonious vocals and socially conscious lyrics, reminded everyone of the power of music to inspire and unite.

The evening's diverse roster of performers and inductees spanned the spectrum of rock and roll's history. Highlights included a heartfelt tribute to blues and rock pioneers. The show's climactic moments were powerful performances by rock 'n' roll pioneer Bo Diddley, who still exuded magnetic energy, and a special blues segment featuring guitar virtuosos Eric Clapton and Robbie Robertson of The Band. Legendary bluesman B.B. King, the revered 'King of the Blues' and a cornerstone of American music, guitarist extraordinaire, was also present, his very presence inspiring awe. For many in attendance, it was like seeing a living legend perform, a rare and cherished experience. "My course was my destiny," King famously declared during a previous interview, a sentiment that underscored his lifelong dedication to the blues. In a memorable moment, Eric Clapton joined King on stage for a stirring and emotional duet of 'The Thrill Is Gone'." Adding to the night's legendary feel, rock 'n' roll pioneer and fellow Hall of Fame inductee Jerry Lee musician Lewis continued his wild and uninhibited antics, the 69-year-old 'Killer' pounding over his keyboard with furious abandon and even kicking the piano a couple of times, a signature move that delighted the roaring crowd. The ceremony concluded with a celebratory mood, cementing the legacies of these musical titans for future generations.

"How Do You Live?" Charms Japan Box Office. Oscar-winning Hayao Miyazaki's latest animated feature, "How Do You Live?", has set a new box office record in Japan. The highly anticipated film, produced by Studio Ghibli, took an astounding 1.5bn yen ($14.3m) in its opening weekend alone. This impressive debut marks the biggest three-day opening for any film released by the acclaimed studio.

The film is Hayao Miyazaki's first full-length work since "The Wind Rises" (2013), which won an Academy Award for Best Animated Feature. While "The Wind Rises" was a more grounded, biographical drama, "How Do You Live?" returns to the fantastical elements Miyazaki is renowned for. The new movie is loosely based on a 1937 children's novel of the same name by Genzaburo Yoshino, a philosophical tale exploring themes of life, death, and identity. Its deep narrative and stunning animation have garnered significant attention from both critics and audiences.

The film has continued to attract massive takings from Japanese cinema-goers, according to distributor Toho. Early reports indicate it has already surpassed several of Miyazaki's previous blockbusters in terms of initial gross. The intricate plot follows Mahito Maki, an 18-year-old boy, who, after his mother's death, is trapped in a mysterious, otherworldly tower and guided by a talking heron. Here, he encounters a strange old woman and embarks on a journey of self-discovery within a fantastical realm. Its two-hour running time has not deterred audiences, with many cinemas reporting sold-out screenings. reconstruction:
Sun Microsystems has unveiled a new "pay-as-you-go" service, allowing businesses and researchers to acquire computing power by the hour, rather than investing in expensive hardware. This initiative marks a significant step into the burgeoning market for on-demand computing resources, promising flexibility and cost-efficiency.

Customers can access powerful systems from Sun for as little as $1 (53p) per hour, making high-performance computing more accessible. The service, dubbed 'Sun Grid', aims to democratise access to processing capabilities. So-called grid computing, which pools disparate resources to act as a single, powerful virtual supercomputer, is becoming increasingly important as organisations seek to manage complex data analysis, simulations, and other intensive tasks without incurring massive capital expenditures. Sun’s new offering aims to facilitate this, creating a vast, accessible grid of shared resources.

The technology underpinning the Sun Grid service has been rigorously tested. "The pilot project was put in the water, allowing us to refine and further develop the service in real-world conditions," explained a senior company officer. The company believes this on-demand model will fundamentally alter how businesses approach their computing infrastructure. "Why build your own costly grid when you can simply rent it for a buck an hour, scaling up or down as your needs change?" questioned a Sun Microsystems Computing executive based in California, highlighting the economic appeal of the new platform.

Sun is primarily targeting IT managers and chief technology officers in businesses seeking flexible computing solutions. However, the company has already seen considerable interest beyond traditional corporate clients. Early indications suggest strong uptake from academic institutions and researchers in various scientific and engineering sectors, as well as smaller start-ups and other industries looking to leverage powerful computing without the overheads.

A unique aspect of the Sun Grid service is its innovative leveraging of distributed computing power. The service taps into the massive collective processing strength generated by as many as 5,000,000 individual computers currently participating in the distributed Folding@home experiment, a global initiative run by Stanford University for biomedical research. By harnessing this vast network, Sun Grid can offer unparalleled scalability and processing muscle. Users can access these powerful servers simultaneously, distributing their workloads efficiently across the grid for each individual task, effectively turning millions of personal computers into a collective supercomputer.

While the base hourly rate starts at $1, a benchmark 12 hours of computing on the new platform is offered at $12 (£6.30). Sun Microsystems will be operating its new Sun Grid service from its own robust infrastructure. Initially, the company will house the core infrastructure and intelligently utilise its extensive idle server capacity within its global data centres to deliver the service, ensuring efficiency and reliability from day one.

Sun's entry into this space puts it in direct competition with established players. It has to compete with similar cloud computing services that already exist in the market. Cloud-based computing services are now widely offered by industry giants such as Amazon Web Services (AWS) with its EC2 offering, and IBM, which has been expanding its on-demand services for enterprises. Gordon Brown shrugged off concerns about the economy as he delivered his Pre-Budget Report. The Chancellor announced a freeze on fuel duty, a £1bn package for local councils and an extension of paternity leave – measures the Treasury said he had slightly increased the cost of. The Chancellor described his plans as striking a balance between "prudence and investment" but Oliver Letwin, the Shadow Chancellor, immediately attacked the rising government debt, dubbing Mr Brown's forecasts "fanciful and reckless". The Chancellor insisted Mr Brown's "golden rule" on public borrowing would be met, but revealed public sector net borrowing was set to rise sharply in the coming years, reaching a total of £170bn. Mr Letwin argued the report 'takes out the heart of the government's economic credibility'. He criticised the rising public spending, stating it was 'not the government's money, but the taxpayer's money'. He then called for 'tough choices to be made'. He added: "This week gave the impression of a chancellor who offered a message of complacency and missed a crucial opportunity." He warned of serious challenges, from the falling dollar to rapid interest rate rises in the UK, but noted: "There was not a word about it"." He also called on the Treasury to 'open up the books to the National Audit Office', asserting that decisions on tax should be based on some public thinking and proper scrutiny. BBC economics editor Evan Davis said the chancellor was taking "a gamble...". Mr Brown's insistence that there was no "gloating" was widely interpreted as a defensive stance. In his speech, Mr Brown set out a 10-year strategy for the economy if Labour wins the next general election.

The package includes a £285m investment for paternity leave, which will increase from six to two weeks, with fathers able to transfer up to six months of unused maternity leave from the mother. He pledged to introduce flexible working for parents of 15-year-olds by 2007, extending the right from those with children aged six and under. He also announced funding for 24-hour childcare provision, aiming to ensure facilities are available from 0800-1800GMT to look after children while parents were working or studying. Taken together, these measures, Mr Brown said, would help to create "a welfare state fit for its time and for the future". He also announced a direct hand-out for pensioners, in the form of a one-off payment of £50 for those aged over 70, to be paid as part of their winter fuel allowance. In a widely anticipated move designed to keep council tax rises below 5%, the Chancellor announced an extra £1bn for local councils. This is in addition to the government's long-standing commitment to its two fiscal rules - to borrow only for public investment over the economic cycle and to keep national debt "low and prudent" as a proportion of the economy. Borrowing for the current financial year, 2003/04, is now forecast to be £35bn - £2.5bn lower than the £37.5bn forecast in March's Budget, the Chancellor confirmed. However, this is then forecast to fall to £31bn in 2005/06 - £2bn higher than the Budget forecast for that year. Inflation is forecast to remain stable at 1.75% this year and 2% in the coming years, Mr Brown stated. He pledged an extra £105m for innovation, research and development, and for enhanced counter-terrorism measures. Business groups, including the CBI, had called for further government action to improve competitiveness and skills and reduce bureaucracy on businesses. The Liberal Democrats, however, said the report was 'a wasted opportunity on family issues, on housing, and on childcare'. A spokesman added: "This is effectively a pre-general election report with little to offer the country's pressing needs."

original: Big war games battle it out..The arrival of new titles in the popular Medal Of Honor and Call of Duty franchises leaves fans of wartime battle titles spoilt for choice...The acclaimed PC title Call of Duty has been updated for console formats, building on many of the original's elements. For its part, the long-running Medal of Honor series has added Pacific Assault to its PC catalogue, adapting the console game Rising Sun. Call of Duty: Finest Hour casts you as a succession of allied soldiers fighting on World War 2 battlefronts including Russia and North Africa. It is a traditional first-person-viewed game that lets you control just one character, in the midst of a unit where cohorts constantly bark orders at you. On a near-identical note, Medal of Honor: Pacific Assault does all it can to make you feel part of a tight-knit team and plum in the middle of all-out action. Its arenas are the war's Pacific battles, including Guadalcanal and Pearl Harbour. You play one character throughout, a raw and rather talkative US soldier...Both games rely on a carefully stage-managed structure that keeps things ticking along. When this works, it is a brilliant device to make you feel part of a story. When it does not, it is tedious...A winning moment is an early scene in Pacific Assault, where you come under attack at the famous US base in Hawaii. You are first ushered into a gunboat attacking the incoming waves of Japanese planes, then made to descend into a sinking battleship to rescue crewman, before seizing the anti-aircraft guns. It is one of the finest set-pieces ever seen in a video game. This notion of shuffling the player along a studiously pre-determined path, forcibly witnessing a series of pre-set moments of action, is a perilous business which can make the whole affair feel stilted rather than organic. The genius of something like Half Life 2 is that it skilfully disguises its linear plotting by various means of misdirection. This pair of games do not really accomplish that, being more concerned with imparting a full-on atmospheric experience...Call of Duty comes with a suitably bombastic score and overblown presentation. Finest Hour has a similar determination, framing everything in moody wartime music, archive footage and lots of reflective voice-overs...Letting you play a number of different roles is an interesting ploy that adds new dimensions to the Call of Duty endeavour, even if it sacrifices the narrative flow somewhat. The game's drawback could be said to be its format; tastes differ, but these wartime shooters often do seem to work better on PC. The mouse control is a big reason why, along with the sharper graphics a top-end computer can muster and the apparent notion that PC games are allowed to get away with a bit more subtlety. Call of Duty on PC was more detailed, plot-wise and graphically, and this new adaptation feels a little rough and ready. Targeting with the PS2 controller proved tricky, not helped by unconvincing collision-detection. You can shoot an enemy repeatedly with zero question as to your aim, yet the bullets will just refuse to hit him. Checkpoints are so few and far between that when you get shot, which happens regularly, you are set harshly far back, and will find yourself covering vast tracts of scorched earth again and again. The game wants to be a challenge, and is, and many players will like it for that. It is as dynamic a battlefield simulator as you will experience and even if it is not as refined as its PC parent, the sense of being part of the action is thoroughly impressive...Both of these games feature military colleagues who are disturbingly bad shots and prone to odd behaviour. And in Pacific Assault in particular, their commands and comments are irritatingly meaningless...But the teamwork element in titles like this is superficial, designed to add atmosphere and camaraderie rather than affect the gameplay mechanics at all. Of the two games, Pacific Assault gets more things right, including little points like auto-saving intelligently and having tidier presentation. It engages you very well and also looks wonderful, making the most of the lush tropical settings that are reminiscent of the glorious Far Cry, although we had to ramp up the settings on a high-spec machine to get the most out of them. Finest Hour is by no means bad, and it is only because the PC original was so dazzling that this version sometimes feels underwhelming. Those looking for a wartime game with plenty of atmosphere and a hearty abundance of enemies to shoot will be contented. But they will also have a niggling puzzlement as to why it does not break a little more ground rather then just being competent.

reconstruction:
The autumn gaming season brings with it a fresh barrage of high-profile releases, and among the biggest games out are two new entries into the fiercely contested World War II first-person shooter genre. Gamers are presented with a difficult choice between the latest Call of Duty offering and another instalment from the long-running Medal of Honor series, both vying for attention in a crowded market.

Call of Duty: Finest Hour, the franchise's first foray specifically designed for console platforms, arrives updated for console players, building on many of the successful gameplay mechanics and narrative approaches established by its acclaimed PC predecessors. It aims to translate the intensity and cinematic feel of the series to a different audience, with adapted controls and mission structures tailored for consoles.

For those seeking a different front, the long-established Medal of Honor series has returned with Pacific Assault, taking players to the brutal battlegrounds of the Pacific theatre. This release stands alongside Call of Duty: Finest Hour as a major contender in the World War 2 game arena, following a succession of titles that have previously focused on the European and North African fronts. Both titles promise to immerse players in the gritty realities of wartime combat, albeit through different narrative lenses and gameplay philosophies.

Both games are quintessential first-person shooters. Call of Duty: Finest Hour lets the player control not just a single character throughout the entire campaign, but rather several distinct characters across different Allied forces – a design choice that offers varied perspectives on the conflict, from American infantry to British commandos and Russian partisans. Medal of Honor: Pacific Assault, by contrast, keeps you tethered to a single protagonist, Private Thomas Conlin, throughout its narrative arc. However, it still incorporates a strong sense of squad-based combat, with AI unit members barking orders and offering crucial support, fostering a feeling of genuine teamwork and reliance. Noteworthy is how Pacific Assault manages to knit together its various missions and set-pieces into a remarkably cohesive and all-action experience, making the player feel like an integral part of a larger historical struggle.

There's a particular brutal beauty in Pacific Assault's portrayal of the war in the Pacific. Throughout the campaign, rather than feeling like disconnected skirmishes, the game's missions build upon each other, creating a sense of escalating stakes and a tangible journey. Both games generally rely on a stage-structure, moving players from one objective to the next within defined levels, aiming for a cinematic progression. When this structure works, it serves as an effective narrative device, pushing you forward through dramatic sequences. An early mission in Pacific Assault, for instance, has you fighting as part of the US Marine Corps, struggling to secure a beachhead amidst heavy fire, with the feeling of winning being a hard-fought, fleeting moment under overwhelming odds. Finest Hour, too, has its share of memorable, if isolated, set-pieces. One particularly intense sequence in Finest Hour sees you initially engage Japanese planes as an anti-aircraft gunner, defending your ship from aerial bombardment. Later, the game shifts perspective, and you are made to experience the terrifying chaos of being a crewman on a rapidly sinking aircraft carrier, a truly harrowing and immersive moment for the player. These moments are among the most impactful in the game, demonstrating the developers' ambition to create an immersive, if often linear, experience that aims to stand out from other World War II titles of the era.

While Finest Hour aims for a determined, cinematic feel with its heavily series-set moments, the overall narrative often feels like a stilted affair rather than an organic, flowing story. Its plotting, especially when compared to some of its contemporaries, particularly Medal of Honor: Pacific Assault, struggles to maintain a consistent emotional connection with the player characters or their plight. This is not to say that the game does not excel in other areas; it is clearly concerned with a high level of presentation, including detailed graphics, evocative music, and strong voice-overs, all of which contribute significantly to the atmosphere but can't entirely compensate for a disjointed plot or lack of character development.

The decision in Call of Duty: Finest Hour to let players assume multiple roles across different Allied perspectives, while an interesting ploy that certainly adds dimensions to the Call of Duty endeavour by showcasing various fronts, ultimately sacrifices the somewhat more personal and continuous narrative thread that a single protagonist provides. While it offers undeniable variety, it can prevent players from forming a deep, sustained attachment to any one specific character or squad, thereby diluting the emotional impact of the conflict and making the player feel less invested in the outcome of individual stories.

Call of Duty: Finest Hour could be said to have its own unique console identity, but too often, its mechanics and overall feel seem like a direct port from its PC brethren, rather than a game meticulously built from the ground up for its target console platforms. For this reason, along with a certain lack of innovation when compared to other high-end computer games with similar themes available on PC, it sometimes struggles to carve out its own distinct niche in the console market, feeling somewhat less refined than it could have been.

Medal of Honor: Pacific Assault, by comparison, often feels more detailed, plot-wise, offering a coherent character arc for Private Conlin and his immediate squad that feels more engaging and personal. This commitment to narrative depth, allowing players to witness the bond between soldiers forged in combat, is one of its stronger suits. The game takes the time to build relationships between the squad members, making their fates feel far more significant to the player as they progress through the brutal Pacific campaign.

Unfortunately, Call of Duty: Finest Hour on the PS2, in particular, proves tricky in execution due to several technical shortcomings. Players frequently encounter frustrating issues with enemy detection, where adversaries will repeatedly spot you with zero question as to how they could possibly have seen you through cover or from afar, yet will sometimes inexplicably ignore obvious threats right in front of them. This inconsistent and often illogical AI can lead to infuriating and immersion-breaking moments, undermining the realism the game strives for.

Adding significantly to the frustration is a checkpoint system that is often far too sparse and unforgiving. Checkpoints are so few and far between that when you inevitably die, which often happens harshly and unexpectedly, it forces you to re-do significant and lengthy tracts of gameplay again and again. This design choice, rather than adding to the challenge or tension, merely serves to artificially inflate play time through monotonous repetition and can quickly wear thin on even the most patient players, leading to exasperation rather than enjoyment.

To a frustrating degree, this sparse checkpointing and inconsistent AI will test your patience. This is the often difficult core experience if it is not its technical prowess that defines the game, despite the graphics otherwise being impressive, especially for a console title of its generation. The visual fidelity and the sheer scale of the battles are certainly strong points that capture the chaotic intensity of war, but they cannot entirely overcome the fundamental gameplay frustrations that plague the experience. The AI of your squadmates, while attempting to be helpful and provide tactical support, is another feature prone to erratic and unhelpful behaviour. In particular, they often seem to get in the way, fail to provide cover effectively, or get themselves killed in baffling, easily avoidable ways, irritatingly contributing little to the tactical execution of missions and making them feel more like liabilities than assets.

Ultimately, the promised teamwork in Finest Hour feels largely superficial, designed more to evoke a sense of camaraderie that the player rarely truly experiences or benefits from in a meaningful gameplay sense. It's more about window dressing and cinematic moments than a core, functional mechanic that enhances strategic play or deepens player investment in the squad.

Of the two major World War II shooters released this season, Medal of Honor: Pacific Assault is generally the more polished and satisfying experience. Its mission design is often more thoughtful and varied, and its system for saving progress, intelligently placed and more frequent, makes the overall progression feel tidier and less aggravating, allowing players to focus on the action rather than fearing repeated retries.

Pacific Assault offers you wonderful, cinematic moments that are truly reminiscent of the very best in the genre, creating a powerful and immersive sense of being in the thick of a historical conflict, from the chaos of Pearl Harbor to the brutal jungle fighting. While its high-spec PC requirements might deter most casual players, those who can run it will undoubtedly find a rewarding and engaging experience that delivers on its promises. Call of Duty: Finest Hour, by stark contrast, only too often was so underwhelming in its execution and lacked the consistent polish and narrative cohesion of its rival.

Overall, Finest Hour often ends up looking a bit dated in its design and suffers from a lack of a distinct identity that sets it apart from its acclaimed PC counterparts or its direct competitor. It also does little to break new ground or innovate within the genre, rather proving merely competent in most aspects, and sometimes even frustrating, rather than truly innovative or outstanding. While it has its occasional moments of intense action and impressive visual spectacle, it ultimately falls short of the high standards set by other entries in the Call of Duty series, leaving players with a sense of missed opportunity.

The popular musical Mamma Mia! is finally making its Swedish premiere in Stockholm, a truly special event given that it brought together for the first time in over 20 years, the four iconic members of Abba – Bjorn Ulvaeus, Benny Andersson, Agnetha Fältskog and Anni-Frid Lyngstad. This new production of the musical will become the first to be entirely performed in Swedish, a significant moment for the country that gave birth to the pop phenomenon. They questioned if opening the way for the entertainment industry to sue file-sharers could deter innovation. They also said that file-trading firms had some responsibility for inducing people to piracy...The lawsuit, brought by 28 of the world's largest entertainment firms, has raged for several years. Legal experts agree that if the Supreme Court finds in favour of the music and movie industry they would be able to sue file-trading firms into bankruptcy. But if the judge rules that Grokster and Morpheus - the file-sharers at the centre of the case - are merely providers of technology that can have legitimate as well as illegitimate uses, then the music and movie industry would be forced to abandon its pursuit of file-sharing providers. Instead, they would have to pursue individuals who use peer-to-peer networks to get their hands on free music and movies. The hi-tech and entertainment industries have been divided on the issue. Intel filed a document with the Supreme Court earlier this month in defence of Grokster and others, despite misgivings about some aspects of the file-sharing community. It summed up the attitude of many tech firms in its submission which states that its products "are essentially tools, that like any other tools, capable of being used by consumers and businesses for unlawful purposes"...Asking firms to second-guess the uses that its technologies would be put to, and to build in ways of preventing illegitimate use, would stifle innovation, it said. The Electronic Frontier Foundation, a civil rights watchdog, is also defending StreamCast Networks, the company behind the Morpheus file-sharing software. The case raises a question of critical importance at the border between copyright and innovation, it said. It cites, as do many, the landmark ruling in 1984 which found that Sony should not be held responsible for the fact that its Betamax video recorder could be used for piracy. Defenders remain optimistic that the judges will rule in favour of the peer-to-peer networks, upholding the precedent set by the Sony Betamax case. A small band of supporters were outside the court as the lawyers entered, wearing "Save Betamax" t-shirts. He said that while file-trading software can be used to illegally trade movies and music, conceptually the technology had "some really excellent uses"...Based on Tuesday's hearing it seems unlikely that the Betamax ruling will be overturned but file-sharing firms might still be held responsible for encouraging or inducing piracy. Grokster's lawyer argued that the company should be judged by its current behaviour rather than what it did when it first set up. But this argument was dismissed as "ridiculous" by Justice David Souter. CEA boss Mr Shapiro thinks the case is the most important that the Supreme Court will hear this year. "It's about preserving America's proud history of technological innovation and protecting the ability of consumers to access and utilise technology," he said. The case has already been heard by two lower courts and both found in favour of the peer-to-peer networks. They ruled that despite being used to distribute millions of illegal songs, file-sharing could also be used to cheaply distribute software, government documents and promotional copies of music.

reconstruction:
The United States Supreme Court is currently mulling the future of online file-sharing, a decision that could have profound implications for both the entertainment industry and technology companies across the globe. Judges at the nation's highest court have spent days hearing extensive evidence and legal arguments in a landmark file-sharing case that pits Hollywood studios and record labels against technology firms offering peer-to-peer software.

The powerful entertainment industry, representing a vast array of artists, content creators, and producers of copyrighted material, argues vehemently that the widespread use of file-sharing software ultimately facilitates and encourages massive copyright infringement, costing them billions in lost revenue. They contend that the current way file-sharing networks operate could severely stifle innovation in the creative arts, making it difficult for artists to earn a living from their work. The entertainment firms insist that the companies behind these peer-to-peer technologies bear a direct responsibility for the rampant piracy occurring on their platforms. This heated battle, which has raged in the US for over 28 months, has deeply divided the entertainment and technology sectors.

Many legal experts and industry analysts fear that should the Court rule in favour of the file-sharing companies, it would effectively cripple the music and movie industry's ability to protect its intellectual property and compel technology firms into taking action against infringing users. This could lead to a dramatic shift in how content is created and distributed. Specifically, if Morpheus – the popular peer-to-peer network at the very centre of this contentious case – and other similar software providers are deemed to be operating legally, then the music industry, along with film studios, would effectively have to abandon its current pursuit of legal action and damages against them, leaving them with few avenues for recourse.

Instead, it has been suggested that they might be forced to consider unconventional strategies, such as embracing and using the very same file-sharing networks to distribute their own music and movies, potentially changing the entire business model. The legal and ethical arguments surrounding this case have profoundly divided opinion within both the technology community and the entertainment world. Even tech giants like Intel, the world's largest chip maker, earlier this week weighed in by filing an amicus brief in defence of file-sharing technology, though also expressing some misgivings about aspects of the file-sharing community and its practices. This highlights the complex nature of the debate.

Intel's brief seemed to sum up the prevalent attitude among many in the broader tech sector, arguing: "These innovative tools, which empower consumers and businesses alike, should not be condemned as unlawful simply because a minority might choose to misuse them for illicit purposes." A second significant argument put to the court by the file-sharing defendants is that their software has many legitimate and beneficial uses beyond mere copyright infringement.

The prominent Electronic Frontier Foundation, a leading digital civil rights group, has taken on the crucial role of representing Grokster, one of the key companies behind the widely used Morpheus file-sharing software, fighting vigorously on its behalf. The core of the case in question lies in the legal battle between the powerful music and movie industries and Grokster, along with other similar file-sharing providers. Its ultimate outcome is widely seen as crucial because it hinges directly on a landmark Supreme Court ruling from 1984, which famously held that Sony could not be held liable for copyright infringement simply because its Betamax video recorder could be used to tape television shows for later viewing. The key principle established was that a technology with 'substantial non-infringing uses' could not be banned.

Consequently, the file-sharing companies remain highly optimistic that this established rule of substantial non-infringing use, previously applied to technologies like the Betamax VCR, will also extend to their peer-to-peer software, thereby protecting them from liability. Outside the court building, a small band of dedicated supporters, proudly wearing 'Free Grokster' t-shirts and holding protest placards, gathered to voice their support. They fervently argue that the Betamax ruling essentially stands as a Magna Carta for responsible technological innovation, a foundational principle that has successfully upheld innovation for the past 20 years, according to a statement from the Consumer Electronics Association.

These supporters argue passionately that attempting to prevent file-sharing is fundamentally akin to trying to prevent the printing press from being used to illegally copy books. They believe that while some misuse exists, on the whole, the technology has been overwhelmingly beneficial for communication and information sharing. A spokesperson for Grokster vehemently stated that its software can be legitimately used for sharing non-copyrighted music, independent films, and academic papers, highlighting that the technology has "excellent uses" that are entirely legal.

Even if Tuesday's Supreme Court ruling, based on the Betamax precedent, is overturned, file-sharing companies could still be held liable for 'inducing' copyright infringement under a separate legal theory, adding another layer of complexity to the case. Grokster's legal team, led by its lawyer, argued persuasively that the company merely provides a neutral technological tool to its users, rather than actively controlling or directing what those users choose to do or share when they set up and operate their file-sharing connections. However, that argument was fiercely challenged and described as 'woefully inadequate' by lawyers representing the entertainment industry. They asserted that the Court's ultimate decision is fundamentally about preserving its 'proud history of protecting the rights of consumers' and creators from rampant theft, a principle crucial for the future of creative industries, he said. Similar and equally complex arguments have been heard in numerous lower courts across the country, where file-sharing networks have consistently argued that they are merely providing a neutral platform for individuals to share legitimate, non-copyrighted songs, and that the file-sharing technology can also be effectively used to distribute promotional material for new artists and independent works.

London's iconic black cabs, known for their reliability and distinctive presence, unfortunately, also serve as an unwitting repository for an astonishing array of forgotten items. A recent survey has highlighted the sheer scale of the problem, revealing that more than 63,000 mobile phones alone have been left behind in these vehicles over the past year. This staggering figure translates to several phones being misplaced in each cab annually across the capital, underscoring a pervasive issue of absent-mindedness among passengers. While modern devices are increasingly smaller and more compact, making them easier to slip out of pockets or bags unnoticed, the volume of lost property continues to climb.

Beyond the ubiquitous mobile phone, the survey also catalogued a significant number of other valuable electronic gadgets. Between 5,000 and 5,800 Personal Digital Assistants (PDAs), including once-popular devices like BlackBerrys and various Pocket PCs, were reported lost. Many of these, despite being identifiable by serial numbers or registered licences, were regrettably not reunited with their original owners, indicating the challenges inherent in the lost property recovery process. The emotional and financial cost of such losses can be substantial, as these devices often hold not just personal data but also critical business information.

The human element behind these statistics often provides a touch of warmth amid the frustrating reality of lost property. In one particularly heartwarming instance, a passenger identified only as Ms. Khan reportedly left her purse in a cab. It was later returned to her by a kind-hearted individual who, much to her surprise and delight, turned out to be the well-known actor Hugh Grant. While stories of celebrity good Samaritan acts are rare, they highlight the honesty that often prevails in the system, even when it’s under strain. However, such positive outcomes are not always the norm. For example, the recovery rate for lost laptops remains stubbornly low, with only about 71% of these crucial devices successfully making their way back to their owners. This is particularly concerning for Londoners, who, despite their reliance on these portable computers for work and personal use, are often not the best at consistently backing up their data, meaning the loss of the physical device can also mean the irrecoverable loss of vital information.

A broader, comparative study conducted across several major European cities – including Helsinki, Oslo, Munich, and Stockholm – sheds further light on international trends in lost property. The research found that residents of Copenhagen, Denmark, were losing mobile phones at a significantly higher rate than their more vigilant neighbours in Germany and Sweden. This cross-European analysis suggested that cultural habits and differing levels of caution might play a role in how frequently items are misplaced. The study implicitly advocated for greater personal responsibility and awareness regarding personal belongings.

A key piece of advice emerging from these findings is the importance of ensuring devices are clearly marked with contact details. It is a wise bet, experts suggest, to always carry some form of identification on your person, and equally important, to have recovery information prominently displayed or digitally stored on your devices. Without such precautions, you stand to lose not just the expensive gadget itself, but a wealth of personal information: photographs, crucial contacts, banking details, and access to social media accounts. The growing trend of consumers investing in the latest, shiny, expensive smartphones and tablets means the financial impact of such losses is continually escalating, making proactive measures even more critical.

To help mitigate the problem, proposals are being considered for the creation of a centralised database where owners can register the unique IMEI (International Mobile Equipment Identity) or serial numbers of their devices. This system would greatly facilitate the return of lost or stolen items, connecting them directly back to their rightful owners. This proactive approach is becoming increasingly vital given the alarming crime statistics: up to 50% of all street-level theft and "snatch-and-grab" incidents now specifically target mobile phones. Law enforcement agencies and transport operators are now exploring and implementing such initiatives to provide users with more robust tools for recovery and to act as a stronger deterrent to thieves.

Beyond electronics, the forgotten items left in cabs can be astonishingly diverse. London’s cab drivers, who serve as unwitting custodians of this lost property, often recount the most unusual discoveries. Over the years, many drivers have found truly peculiar items among the else left behind. Stories abound of a pet dog being found asleep on the back seat, a valuable antique violin carefully placed on the parcel shelf, or even, bizarrely, a set of false teeth or an uncashed lottery ticket worth a significant sum. These anecdotes, while often amusing, underscore the chaotic nature of urban life and the moments of distraction that can lead to unexpected losses. The public is reminded to always double-check their surroundings before exiting a vehicle, ensuring that nothing important, however big or small, is inadvertently left behind.

But Indonesian, Indian and Hong Kong stock markets reached record highs on Wednesday, suggesting that investors do not fear a major economic impact...The highs showed the gap in outlook between investors in large firms and individuals who have lost their livelihoods...Investors seemed to feel that some of the worst-affected areas - such as Aceh in Indonesia - were so under-developed that the tragedy would little impact on Asia's listed companies, according to analysts. "Obviously with a lot of loss of life, a lot of time is needed to clean up the mess, bury the people and find the missing. But it's not necessarily a really big thing in the economic sense," said ABN Amro chief Asian strategist Eddie Wong. Expectations of strong corporate earnings in 2005 drove the Indonesian stock exchange in Jakarta to a record high on Wednesday. In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng index may be benefiting in part from the potential for its listed property companies to gain from rebuilding contracts in the tsunami-affected regions of South East Asia. In Sri Lanka, some economists have said that as much as 1% of annual growth may be lost. Jean-Pierre Jeunet's World War I epic, *A Very Long Engagement*, starring Audrey Tautou, has topped the nominations for France's prestigious Cesar Awards, receiving an impressive 12 nods. This achievement comes despite a recent court ruling that had initially deemed the film, distributed by Warner Bros., as "not eligible enough" for some categories. The controversy arose after the film was shown at a festival and received an earlier commercial release in Belgium.

The Academie des Arts et Techniques du Cinema, which organises the awards, subsequently modified its rules to ensure the inclusion of *A Very Long Engagement*, allowing its director, Jean-Pierre Jeunet, to receive nominations for Best Film and Best Director.

Last November, a court had ruled that the film was ineligible for prizes because it had been screened at a film festival to government officials and also released commercially in certain territories months prior to the official French theatrical release. The Academy's previous guidelines stated that films must have been released in French cinemas between March 1, 2004, and February 28, 2005, to qualify for the 2005 awards.

Other highly-nominated French films include Olivier Marchal's police thriller *36 Quai des Orfèvres*, Arnaud Desplechin's family drama *Kings and Queen*, and Abdellatif Kechiche's coming-of-age story *Games of Love and Chance*, which have also garnered significant attention.

Nominations for Best Actor feature Mathieu Kassovitz for *36 Quai des Orfèvres*, Gérard Jugnot for the popular musical drama *Les Choristes*, Philippe Torreton for *L'Équipier*, and Benoît Poelvoorde for his role in *Podium*. In the Best Actress category, Maggie Cheung received a nod for her performance in *Clean*, and Yolande Moreau for *When the Sea Rises*.

The nominations for Best Foreign Film include Michael Moore's controversial documentary *Fahrenheit 9/11*, Sofia Coppola's critically acclaimed *Lost in Translation*, Michel Gondry's imaginative *Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind*, and Alejandro González Iñárritu's intense drama *21 Grams*.

The glittering awards ceremony is scheduled to take place on 26 February in Paris. This year, popular French comedian and actor Gad Elmaleh is set to host the event, along with revered actress and former Bond girl Carole Bouquet, who will preside over the ceremony.

This current inpatient target was set when the assembly government extended its second offer guarantee scheme, which gives patients the option of having their treatment outside Wales...Details about funding to resource the new targets are expected in the New Year. In England, the current target for inpatients - seeing a consultant to having an operation - is six months. Dr Richard Lewis, Welsh secretary of the British Medical Association (BMA), welcomed the new targets "to make further and faster progress on waiting lists". "However, much remains to be done on waiting lists and waiting times because Wales still lags a long way behind England," he said. "But let us not forget two thirds of those waiting for treatment now are waiting less than six months, and these targets affect the small minority of patients in Wales that are waiting far too long." reconstruction:
NHS cuts waiting lists to the lowest levels seen in Wales, bringing them closer to those in England. The Health Minister announced that no patient would be waiting more than 18 months for outpatient treatment by March 2006. She highlighted that the last patient waiting more than 12 months for an outpatient appointment was seen in January 2006. The new waiting list figures showed a significant and encouraging drop, reflecting concerted efforts across the health service.

This positive development was supported by the Welsh government's patient offer scheme, which gives patients the option of having treatment outside Wales if their local waiting times are deemed too long. This initiative, designed to empower patients and reduce backlogs, required a substantial resource injection at the start of the New Year to facilitate its implementation. While significant progress has been made in certain areas, the current target for inpatients - those needing a hospital bed for elective procedures - is still set at six months, indicating ongoing challenges in this domain.

The Welsh branch of the British Medical Association (BMA), reacting to the new "progress on waiting times" statistics, acknowledged the improvements but cautioned that "much remains to be done because there is still a long way to go," according to a spokesman. He further elaborated: "The health system must be reformed with the fundamental principle that patients receive a consistent and equitable level of care all over Wales, regardless of their postcode." Health Minister Sue Hutt, a Welsh Labour representative, further elaborated on the government's plans for continued improvement in this critical area.

On Wednesday, the Welsh Assembly Government announced a new investment of £264m for a range of health services. This significant funding package is specifically targeting further waiting times reductions, improvements in key priority clinical areas, and modernising pay structures within the National Health Service.

Ms Hutt stated that considerable progress had been made in cutting "long waits" over the past year, demonstrating the effectiveness of the government's strategies. She expressed confidence that the administration was "turning the tide on waiting list reductions," emphasizing that the specified targets - for example, for an urgent operation or to see a specialist - were consistently being met across the country.

However, she acknowledged that while two-thirds of those currently waiting for treatment are now waiting less than six months, other, more ambitious targets affecting the whole of Wales are still "far from being universally achieved," suggesting continued challenges in certain sectors or geographical areas.

Jocelyn Thomas, Plaid Cymru's health spokesman, was highly critical of the announcement, stating: "It's exactly the same targets they set in 1999, and they are still not meeting them. That's the second time Labour has demonstrably failed on this fundamental policy, leaving patients in limbo."

For the Welsh Conservatives, Jonathan Williams called the target "utterly unambitious and lacking in foresight, failing to address the root causes of the problem." He added, unequivocally: "They simply aren't doing enough to tackle the endemic problem of NHS waiting lists, and patients deserve better."

First Minister Rhodri Morgan, defending the government's record, conceded during a press briefing: "We are putting money in but waiting lists are still coming through the system at a rate that concerns us." He went on to say: "The problem has been that the money has not always gone down effectively to the frontline services, which is a common criticism that we hear repeatedly."

The latest official figures, released by the Welsh Assembly Government, reveal that the number of people waiting more than 18 months for treatment has fallen by a significant 9.8%. Statistics illustrate a decline from 785 people in the previous quarter to 708 currently awaiting treatment.

Furthermore, those waiting more than 12 months also saw a substantial drop, decreasing from 7,613 patients to 6,630, representing a commendable fall of 12.9%. These figures collectively signify a noticeable improvement in overall waiting times across the health board areas.

In total, there are currently 305,775 people waiting for some form of treatment within the Welsh NHS, a welcome reduction from the previous total of 311,764.

original: Peer-to-peer nets 'here to stay'..Peer-to-peer (P2P) networks are here to stay, and are on the verge of being exploited by commercial media firms, says a panel of industry experts...Once several high-profile legal cases against file-sharers are resolved this year, firms will be very keen to try and make money from P2P technology. The expert panel probed the future of P2P at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas earlier in January. The first convictions for P2P piracy were handed out in the US in January. William Trowbridge and Michael Chicoine pleaded guilty to charges that they infringed copyright by illegally sharing music, movies and software. Since the first successful file-sharing network Napster was forced to close down, the entertainment industry has been nervous and critical of P2P technology, blaming it for falling sales and piracy. But that is going to change very soon, according to the panel...The music and film industries have started some big legal cases against owners of legitimate P2P networks - which are not illegal in themselves - and of individuals accused of distributing pirated content over networks. But they have slowly realised that P2P is a good way to distribute content, said Travis Kalanick, founder and chairman of P2P network Red Swoosh, and soon they are all going to want a slice of it. They are just waiting to come up with "business models" that work for them, which includes digital rights management and copy-protection standards...But, until the legal actions are resolved, experimentation with P2P cannot not happen, said Michael Weiss, president of StreamCast Networks. Remembering the furore around VCRs when they first came out, Mr Weiss said: "Old media always tries to stop new media. "When they can't stop it, they try to control it. Then they figure out how to make money and they always make a lot of money." Once the courts decided that the VCR in itself was not an illegal technology, the film studios turned it into an extremely lucrative business. In August 2004, the San Francisco-based US Court of Appeals ruled in favour of Grokster and StreamCast, two file-sharing networks. The court said they were essentially in the same position that Sony was in the 1980s VCR battle, and said that the networks themselves could not be deemed as illegal...P2P networks usually do not rely on dedicated servers for the transfer of files. Instead it uses direct connections between computers - or clients. There are now many different types of P2P systems than work in different ways. P2P nets can be used to share any kind of file, like photos, free software, licensed music and any other digital content. The BBC has already decided to embrace the technology. It aims to offer most of its own programmes for download this year and it will use P2P technology to distribute them. The files would be locked seven days after a programme aired making rights management easier to control. But the technology is still demonised and misunderstood by many. The global entertainment industry says more than 2.6 billion copyrighted music files are downloaded every month, and about half a million films are downloaded a day. Legal music download services, like Apple iTunes, Napster, have rushed into the music marketplace to try and lure file-sharers away from free content. Sales of legally-downloaded songs grew tenfold in 2004, with 200 million tracks bought online in the US and Europe in 12 months, the IFPI reported this week. But such download services are very different from P2P networks, not least because of the financial aspect...There are several money-spinning models that could turn P2P into a golden egg for commercial entertainment companies. Paid-for-pass-along, in which firms receive money each time a file is shared, along with various DRM solutions and advertiser-based options are all being considered. "We see there are going to be different models for commoditising P2P," said Marc Morgenstern, vice president of anti-piracy firm Overpeer..."Consumers are hungry for it and we will discover new models together," agreed Mr Morgenstern. But many net users will continue to ignore the entertainment industry's potential controlling grip on content and P2P technology by continuing to use it for their own creations. Unsigned bands, for example, use P2P networks to distribute their music effectively, which also draws the attention of record companies looking for new artists to sign. "Increasingly, what you are seeing on P2P is consumer-created content," said Derek Broes, from Microsoft. "They will probably pay an increasing role in helping P2P spread," he said. Looking into P2P's future, file sharing is just the beginning for P2P networks, as far as Mr Broes is concerned. "Once some of these issues are resolved, you are going to see aggressive movement to protect content, but also in ways that are unimaginable now," he said. "File-sharing is the tip of the iceberg."

A recent legal action against P2P piracy handed down a significant ruling, signaling a toughening stance.

They argue that P2P technology itself is not inherently illegal, and the focus should be on legitimate business models rather than punitive lawsuits. The legal position of P2P users – whether they are violating copyright by merely making files available, not just downloading – is often a point of contention. Many believe that the industry "tries" to scare people into compliance through high-profile legal battles, but that this approach is ultimately unsustainable. P2P, or peer-to-peer, technology fundamentally allows users to transfer files directly from one computer to another, without the need for a central server to store or distribute the content. The fundamental principle of P2P systems is decentralization. The majority of P2P systems work by connecting users directly, forming a vast network of shared resources. P2P users share music, films, software, images, and documents directly with each other, and P2P software manages the connections, searches, and file transfers across this distributed network. This architecture makes it resilient to shutdowns and difficult to police, as there is no single point of control or failure.

Some industry observers suggest that P2P technology could actually provide a powerful, legitimate distribution channel for artists and content creators, bypassing traditional intermediaries and reaching audiences directly. However, significant hurdles remain in developing viable business models that can ensure artists are fairly compensated. Some believe that with the right framework, P2P could be a revolutionary force for good.

Despite the legal battles, many industry figures concede that P2P is here to stay. The future of P2P, therefore, lies in its legitimate application. original: Souped-up wi-fi is on the horizon..Super high-speed wireless data networks could soon be in use in the UK...The government's wireless watchdog is seeking help on the best way to regulate the technology behind such networks called Ultra Wideband (UWB). Ofcom wants to ensure that the arrival of UWB-using devices does not cause problems for those that already use the same part of the radio spectrum. UWB makes it possible to stream huge amounts of data through the air over short distances. One of the more likely uses of UWB is to make it possible to send DVD quality video images wirelessly to TV screens or to let people beam music to media players around their home. The technology has the potential to transmit hundreds of megabits of data per second. UWB could also be used to create so-called Personal Area Networks that let a person's gadgets quickly and easily swap data amongst themselves. The technology works over a range up to 10 metres and uses billions of short radio pulses every second to carry data. At the recent Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas products with UWB chips built-in got their first public airing...Currently, use of UWB is only allowed in the UK under a strict licencing scheme. "We're seeking opinion from industry to find out whether or not we should allow UWB on a licence-exempt basis," said a spokesman for Ofcom...Companies have until 24 March to respond. In April the EC is due to start its own consultation on Europe-wide adoption of UWB. The cross-Europe body for radio regulators, known as the European Conference of Postal and Telecommunications Administrations (CEPT), is carrying out research for this harmonisation programme. Early sight of the CEPT work has caused controversy as some think it over-emphasises UWB's potential to interfere with existing users. By contrast a preliminary Ofcom report found that it would be quite straight-forward to deploy UWB without causing problems for those that already use it. The Ofcom spokesman said it was considering imposing a "mask" or set of technical restrictions on UWB-using devices. "We would want these devices to have very strict controls on power levels so they can not transmit a long way or over a wide area," he said. Despite the current restrictions the technology is already being used. Cambridge-based Ubisense has about 40 customers around the world using the short-range radio technology, said David Theriault, standards and regulatory liaison for Ubisense. He said that UWB was driving novel ways to interact with computers. "It's like having a 3D mouse all the time," he said. He said that European decisions on what to do with UWB allied with IEEE decisions on the exact specifications for it would help drive adoption. Prior to its adoption as a way for gadgets and computers to communicate, UWB was used as a sensing technology. It is used to spot such things as cracks under the surface of runways or to help firemen detect people through walls.

"Bollywood has truly gone global," says Taran Adarsh, editor of Indian film journal Trade Guide. "Directors are now attempting to woo non-Asian audience to increase their share in the overseas film market." "Hollywood or Bollywood, it's the box office that determines whether something is a passing phase or a trend," says Adarsh...Kisna - the Warrior Poet opens in the UK on 21 January.
